A chronological reference

Every person of whom Scripture records something substantive — what they did right, what they did wrong, and the passages that support it.

Primeval Period

0010

Adam

The first man, formed directly by God from the dust of the ground, and the head of the human race.

Family

No human parents; formed by God (Genesis 2:7). Husband of Eve (Genesis 2:22-25). Father of Cain, Abel, and Seth by name (Genesis 4:1, 4:2, 4:25), and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:4). Luke's genealogy calls him the son of God (Luke 3:38), meaning direct origin rather than descent.

Chronology

Lived 930 years (Genesis 5:5) - a figure explicitly stated in Scripture. Anno Mundi 0 to 930 by calculation from Genesis 5; the traditional Ussher equivalent is 4004-3074 BC, which is a seventeenth-century calculation and not a biblical date.

Life Synopsis

Adam was formed of the dust and became a living soul when God breathed into him (Genesis 2:7). He was placed in the garden of Eden to dress it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), and given one prohibition: not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death (Genesis 2:16-17). He named all the cattle, the fowl, and every beast of the field, and among them no help meet was found for him (Genesis 2:19-20). God then made the woman from his side, and Adam received her with the words "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23).

The serpent approached the woman, not Adam. She took of the fruit and ate, "and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat" (Genesis 3:6). Their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they hid themselves from God among the trees (Genesis 3:7-8). Questioned directly, Adam blamed the woman and, by implication, God who gave her: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Genesis 3:12).

God's sentence on Adam names the specific ground: he hearkened to his wife's voice above God's command. The earth was cursed for his sake, and he would eat of it in sorrow and sweat until he returned to the dust (Genesis 3:17-19). After the sentence - and this order matters - Adam named his wife Eve, "because she was the mother of all living" (Genesis 3:20). God clothed them both with coats of skins (Genesis 3:21), then drove the man from the garden and barred the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:22-24).

Outside Eden, Adam fathered Cain and Abel, lived to see one murder the other, and afterward fathered Seth in his own likeness (Genesis 4:25, 5:3). He lived 930 years and died (Genesis 5:5).

What They Did Right

  • Exercised the authority God gave him in naming every creature. Scripture records the act without qualification: Genesis 2:19-20.
  • Received his wife with recognition and welcome rather than indifference: Genesis 2:23.
  • Named his wife Eve, "the mother of all living," after the curse had been pronounced. This appears to indicate some expectation of continued life rather than only death, though Scripture does not state his motive: Genesis 3:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ate the forbidden fruit in direct violation of an explicit command. Scripture explicitly condemns this: Genesis 2:16-17; Genesis 3:6; Romans 5:12-14.
  • Hid from God rather than confessing: Genesis 3:8-10.
  • Shifted blame to his wife and implicitly to God: Genesis 3:12.
  • Paul states that Adam was not deceived, distinguishing his transgression from Eve's: 1 Timothy 2:14. His was open-eyed disobedience.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats Adam less as a moral example than as a representative head. No New Testament passage commends his faith; none pronounces his condemnation either. His three recorded good acts are all from before the Fall or immediately after it, and Scripture records no repentance. God's clothing of him in Genesis 3:21 is presented as divine initiative, not as a response to contrition. The text does not specify his eternal state, and this reference does not either.

Significance

Adam is the federal head of the human race. "By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men" (Romans 5:12). "In Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22). He is "the first man Adam," set deliberately against Christ, "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). The whole doctrine of imputed sin and imputed righteousness is argued from the parallel between the two. He also stands at the head of the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:38) and of the Chronicler's record (1 Chronicles 1:1).

Death / Outcome

Died at 930 years (Genesis 5:5). Last mention in Scripture: Jude 1:14, where Enoch is called "the seventh from Adam."

Scripture

Genesis 1:26-28; Genesis 2:7-25; Genesis 3:1-24; Genesis 4:1, 4:25; Genesis 5:1-5; 1 Chronicles 1:1; Luke 3:38; Romans 5:12-14; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 15:45; 1 Timothy 2:13-14; Jude 1:14
0020

Eve

The first woman, made by God from Adam's side; "the mother of all living."

Also called the woman

Family

Made from Adam (Genesis 2:21-22); wife of Adam; mother of Cain, Abel, and Seth (Genesis 4:1, 4:2, 4:25).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her creation falls within the Eden narrative, so she is placed at Anno Mundi 0 by context, but Scripture gives no age for her at any point and does not record her death.

Life Synopsis

God declared that it was not good for the man to be alone and made a help meet for him (Genesis 2:18). She was formed from Adam's side while he slept (Genesis 2:21-22). She is called "the woman" throughout the Eden narrative and is not named Eve until after the judgment (Genesis 3:20).

The serpent approached her with a question about God's command. She answered by citing it, but added a clause - "neither shall ye touch it" - which does not appear in the prohibition as God gave it in Genesis 2:16-17 (Genesis 3:2-3). The serpent flatly denied the penalty and impugned God's motive (Genesis 3:4-5). Seeing the tree was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise, she took and ate, and gave to her husband (Genesis 3:6).

Questioned by God, she told the truth without evasion beyond the actual facts: "The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat" (Genesis 3:13). Her judgment was multiplied sorrow in conception and childbearing, and a changed relation to her husband (Genesis 3:16). But the promise of Genesis 3:15 - that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head - is spoken over her, and the whole line of redemption runs from it.

Her two recorded speeches after Eden both credit God. At Cain's birth: "I have gotten a man from the Lord" (Genesis 4:1). After Abel's murder, at Seth's birth: "God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew" (Genesis 4:25). Scripture does not record her death.

What They Did Right

  • Answered the serpent by citing God's command rather than ignoring it, though she altered it in the citing: Genesis 3:2-3.
  • Told the truth when God questioned her, without shifting blame beyond the facts: Genesis 3:13.
  • Credited the Lord at the birth of Cain: Genesis 4:1.
  • Credited God's appointment at the birth of Seth, after losing two sons in one day: Genesis 4:25.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ate the forbidden fruit and gave it to her husband. Scripture explicitly treats this as transgression: Genesis 3:6; 1 Timothy 2:14.
  • Added to God's command the words "neither shall ye touch it" (Genesis 3:3), which are absent from Genesis 2:16-17. Scripture records the discrepancy without calling it sin; it is noted here as a difference in the text, not as an accusation.
  • Was deceived. Paul states this explicitly and distinguishes it from Adam's transgression: 1 Timothy 2:14; 2 Corinthians 11:3.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents Eve as both the deceived party in the first transgression and the woman through whom the promise runs. She is never condemned by name in the New Testament, though her deception is twice held up as a warning to churches. Both of her recorded utterances after the Fall acknowledge God, which is more than is recorded of Adam.

Significance

The promise of Genesis 3:15 is given with reference to her seed, and it is the first statement of redemption in Scripture. She is the mother of all living (Genesis 3:20) and therefore stands behind every genealogy in the Bible. Paul twice appeals to her experience: to establish an order of creation (1 Timothy 2:13-14) and to warn the Corinthians against subtle corruption of mind (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record her death. Last mention: 2 Corinthians 11:3.

Scripture

Genesis 2:18-25; Genesis 3:1-24; Genesis 4:1-2, 4:25; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:13-14
003130

Cain

Firstborn son of Adam and Eve; a tiller of the ground; the first murderer.

Family

Son of Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:1); brother of Abel and Seth. Married; his wife is unnamed and her origin is not stated (Genesis 4:17). Father of Enoch (Genesis 4:17).

Chronology

Primeval; born after the expulsion from Eden, before AM 130. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

Brought an offering of the fruit of the ground, which the Lord did not respect (Genesis 4:3–5). Warned directly by God that sin lay at the door and could be mastered (Genesis 4:7). Killed his brother Abel in the field, then denied it: "I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?" (Genesis 4:8–9). Sentenced to be a fugitive; given a protective mark (Genesis 4:11–15). Departed from the Lord's presence, built a city, named it after his son (Genesis 4:16–17).

What They Did Right

  • Brought an offering to the Lord of the fruit of the ground: Genesis 4:3. Scripture records the act but states that the Lord did not respect it, and 1 John 3:12 says his works were evil. It is recorded conduct, not a commendation.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was wroth and his countenance fell when his offering was not respected, after God had reasoned with him directly: Genesis 4:5-7.
  • Murdered his brother Abel. The text notes he first talked with him, indicating premeditation: Genesis 4:8.
  • Lied to God and answered with contempt: "I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?": Genesis 4:9.
  • Explicitly condemned in the New Testament: he was "of that wicked one," and woe is pronounced on those who go in his way: 1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11.

Character Assessment

Condemned. His works were evil (1 John 3:12); woe is pronounced on those who go "in the way of Cain" (Jude 1:11). No repentance is recorded — his reply in Genesis 4:13 laments the sentence, not the sin.

Significance

Cain is the first person born of a woman, the first murderer, and the head of a line that Genesis 4 traces to Lamech's boast of vengeance. He is Scripture's first case of a warning given directly by God and refused (Genesis 4:6-7), and the New Testament uses him three times as a negative pattern.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last mention: Jude 1:11.

Scripture

Genesis 4:1–17, 4:25; Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11.
004130

Abel

Second son of Adam and Eve; a keeper of sheep; the first person murdered and the first declared righteous.

Family

Son of Adam and Eve; younger brother of Cain (Genesis 4:2). No wife or children are mentioned.

Chronology

Primeval; died before AM 130. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

Brought the firstlings of his flock and their fat, and the Lord respected his offering (Genesis 4:4). Murdered by Cain (Genesis 4:8); his blood is said to cry from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

What They Did Right

  • Brought the firstlings of his flock and the fat - both the first and the best: Genesis 4:4.
  • Offered by faith a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, and obtained witness that he was righteous: Hebrews 11:4.
  • Called "righteous Abel" by Christ: Matthew 23:35.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This is an absence of record, not a claim of sinlessness.

Character Assessment

Commended without qualification. He offered "by faith... a more excellent sacrifice" and obtained witness that he was righteous (Hebrews 11:4); Jesus calls him "righteous Abel" (Matthew 23:35). Nothing negative is recorded.

Significance

Abel is the first person in Scripture declared righteous, the first martyr, and the first entry in the roll of faith after creation. Christ measures the whole span of shed innocent blood from Abel onward (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). Hebrews sets his blood against the blood of Christ, which "speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:24).

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Cain in the field (Genesis 4:8); his blood is said to cry from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Last mention: Hebrews 12:24.

Scripture

Genesis 4:2–11, 4:25; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 3:12.
005

Lamech (of the line of Cain)

Fifth from Cain; the first polygamist recorded in Scripture. Distinct from Lamech the father of Noah.

Family

Son of Methusael, fifth in descent from Cain through Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, and Methusael (Genesis 4:17-18). Husband of Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). Father of Jabal, Jubal, Tubal-cain, and Naamah (Genesis 4:20-22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable — the Cainite line carries no ages and no synchronism with Genesis 5.

Life Synopsis

Took two wives, Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). Boasted to them of killing a man who had wounded him, and claimed a vengeance seventy-sevenfold — escalating the sevenfold protection God had given Cain into a personal warrant (Genesis 4:23–24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took two wives - the first polygamy recorded in Scripture. Genesis records it without explicit condemnation, but it stands against the pattern of Genesis 2:24, which Christ affirms in Matthew 19:4-6.
  • Boasted to his wives of killing a man for wounding him: Genesis 4:23.
  • Claimed a vengeance seventy-sevenfold for himself, escalating the sevenfold protection God had granted Cain into a personal warrant: Genesis 4:24 compared with Genesis 4:15.

Character Assessment

Nothing commendable is recorded. Genesis reports the polygamy and the boast without explicit condemnation, but the boast is self-evidently a celebration of vengeance, and it stands against the pattern of Genesis 2:24.

Significance

Lamech's boast is the only extended speech recorded from the line of Cain, and Genesis places it as the culmination of that line immediately before returning to Seth and the note that men began to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26). The structure sets self-exalting vengeance against the beginning of worship.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last mention: Genesis 4:24.

Scripture

Genesis 4:18–24.
006

Adah (wife of Lamech)

One of the two wives of Lamech the Cainite; mother of Jabal and Jubal. Not to be confused with Adah the Hittite wife of Esau (Genesis 36:2), a different woman in a later period.

Family

Wife of Lamech, descendant of Cain (Genesis 4:19); mother of Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:20-21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The Cainite line carries no ages and no synchronism with the line of Seth, so no chronological placement is possible beyond the pre-Flood period.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records that Lamech took her as one of two wives, that she bore Jabal and Jubal, and that Lamech addressed her by name in his boast about killing a man (Genesis 4:19-23). No words or actions of her own are recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of her. She is included because the text records her name, her marriage, her two named sons, and her being addressed directly by name - substantially more than a bare genealogical listing.

Significance

Named as one of the two wives in the first polygamous marriage recorded in Scripture, and mother of the man Genesis credits with originating tent-dwelling and cattle-keeping.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:23.

Scripture

Genesis 4:19-23
007

Zillah

The second wife of Lamech the Cainite; mother of Tubal-cain and Naamah.

Family

Wife of Lamech, descendant of Cain (Genesis 4:19); mother of Tubal-cain and of Naamah (Genesis 4:22).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. As with the whole Cainite line, no ages or synchronisms are given.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records that Lamech took her as his second wife, that she bore Tubal-cain and Naamah, and that Lamech addressed her by name in his boast (Genesis 4:19-23). No words or actions of her own are recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of her. She is included on the same basis as Adah: named, married, mother of two named children, and addressed directly by name.

Significance

Mother of Tubal-cain, whom Genesis credits with instructing every artificer in brass and iron, and of Naamah, the only daughter named in the Cainite genealogy.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:23.

Scripture

Genesis 4:19-23
008

Jabal

Son of Lamech by Adah; originator of pastoral nomadism — "the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle."

Family

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jubal; half-brother of Tubal-cain and Naamah (Genesis 4:20-22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:20, in a single clause.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records his cultural achievement without moral evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the achievement and attaches no moral verdict, favourable or otherwise.

Significance

Named as the originator of a whole way of life - tent-dwelling and cattle-keeping - which becomes the manner of life of the patriarchs themselves.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:20.

Scripture

Genesis 4:20.
009

Jubal

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jabal; originator of music — "the father of all such as handle the harp and organ."

Family

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jabal (Genesis 4:21).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:21, in a single clause.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His achievement is recorded without evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered.

Significance

Named as the originator of music, an art that later fills the worship of Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:21.

Scripture

Genesis 4:21.
010

Tubal-cain

Son of Lamech by Zillah; the first metalworker — "an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron."

Family

Son of Lamech by Zillah; brother of Naamah; half-brother of Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:22. Note that he is recorded as a teacher of the craft, not merely a practitioner.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered.

Significance

Named as the first metalworker and, notably, as a teacher of the craft rather than merely a practitioner.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:22.

Scripture

Genesis 4:22.
011130

Seth

Third named son of Adam and Eve; head of the line through which the genealogy runs to Noah and ultimately to Christ.

Also called Sheth

Family

Son of Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:25); father of Enos (Genesis 5:6) and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:7).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 130, when Adam was 130 (Genesis 5:3); died Anno Mundi 1042. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 912 years (Genesis 5:8).

Life Synopsis

Seth was born after Abel's murder, and Eve named him with the words, "For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew" (Genesis 4:25). Adam begat him "in his own likeness, after his image" (Genesis 5:3) - a statement about human transmission after the Fall rather than a comment on Seth. He fathered Enos, and the note follows immediately: "then began men to call upon the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26). He lived 912 years and died.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. What Scripture records is his position rather than his conduct. The clause about men beginning to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26) has "men" as its subject, not Seth, and this reference does not credit him with an act the text does not attribute to him.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture assesses Seth by his place in the line rather than by anything he did. He is included in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:38) and heads the Chronicler's list after Adam (1 Chronicles 1:1).

Significance

The line of promise runs through Seth rather than Cain, and the genealogy of Genesis 5, of 1 Chronicles 1, and of Luke 3 all pass through him.

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years: and he died" (Genesis 5:8).

Scripture

Genesis 4:25-26; Genesis 5:3-8; 1 Chronicles 1:1; Luke 3:38
012235

Enos

A man of the line of Seth; fourth from Adam.

Also called Enosh

Family

Son of Seth; father of Cainan and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 235, died Anno Mundi 1140 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 90 years before fathering Cainan, and 905 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Cainan, the further years he lived, and his death. Genesis 4:26 attaches to his birth the note that "then began men to call upon the name of the Lord," but the subject of that clause is men generally, and the text does not specify what part, if any, Enos took in it.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life - his age at fatherhood and his total lifespan - which is more than a bare name, and which forms part of the chronological framework of the primeval period.

Significance

A link in the line from Adam through Seth to Noah, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:36-38).

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Enos were 905 years: and he died" (Genesis 5).

Scripture

Genesis 5; 1 Chronicles 1:1-3; Luke 3:36-38

015460

Jared

A man of the line of Seth; seventh from Adam.

Family

Son of Mahalaleel; father of Enoch and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 460, died Anno Mundi 1422 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 162 years before fathering Enoch, and 962 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Enoch, the further years he lived, and his death. He is the father of Enoch, but Scripture does not credit him with Enoch's walk with God, and neither does this reference. His 962 years are the second-longest lifespan recorded in Scripture.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life - his age at fatherhood and his total lifespan - which is more than a bare name, and which forms part of the chronological framework of the primeval period.

Significance

A link in the line from Adam through Seth to Noah, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:36-38).

Death / Outcome

016622

Enoch (son of Jared)

Seventh from Adam; prophet; the man who did not die. Distinct from Enoch the son of Cain.

Family

Son of Jared (Genesis 5:18); father of Methuselah (Genesis 5:21) and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:22); great-grandfather of Noah.

Chronology

Primeval. Born AM 622, translated AM 987 [traditional: 3382–3017 BC]. 365 years on earth — the shortest span in Genesis 5, and the only one not ending "and he died."

Life Synopsis

Walked with God three hundred years, the phrase repeated for emphasis (Genesis 5:22, 5:24). Taken by God without dying (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5). Prophesied of coming judgment on the ungodly (Jude 1:14–15).

What They Did Right

  • Walked with God three hundred years - the phrase is stated twice: Genesis 5:22, 5:24.
  • Pleased God, and had that testimony before his translation: Hebrews 11:5.
  • Was translated by faith so that he did not see death: Hebrews 11:5.
  • Prophesied of the Lord's coming in judgment on the ungodly: Jude 1:14-15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Commended without qualification. He "pleased God" before his translation (Hebrews 11:5). One of only two men in Scripture recorded as not having died.

Significance

One of only two men in Scripture who did not die (with Elijah, 2 Kings 2:11). His translation stands in the middle of a genealogy whose refrain is "and he died," and it is the first indication in Scripture that death is not necessarily the end of a man's walk with God. Jude preserves his prophecy, the earliest recorded prophecy in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

He did not die: "and he was not; for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Last mention: Jude 1:14-15.

Scripture

Genesis 5:18–24; 1 Chronicles 1:3; Luke 3:37; Hebrews 11:5; Jude 1:14–15.
017687

Methuselah

A man of the line of Seth; ninth from Adam.

Also called Mathusala

Family

Son of Enoch; father of Lamech and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 687, died Anno Mundi 1656 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 187 years before fathering Lamech, and 969 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Lamech, the further years he lived, and his death. His 969 years are the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible. By the arithmetic of Genesis 5 his death falls in the year of the Flood, but Scripture does not state whether he died before it or in it, and popular expositions that attach meaning to his name or to this coincidence go beyond the text.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

0191056

Noah

Tenth from Adam; the man through whom the human race and the land animals were preserved through the Flood; the second head of humanity.

Also called Noe

Family

Son of Lamech (Genesis 5:28-29); grandson of Methuselah. His wife is unnamed (Genesis 6:18). Father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Genesis 5:32). Eight persons in all were preserved (1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:5).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 1056; 600 years old when the flood came (Genesis 7:6, 7:11); lived 350 years after it; died at 950 (Genesis 9:28-29). Those ages are explicitly stated in Scripture; the Anno Mundi figures are calculated from Genesis 5. Traditional Ussher equivalent 2948-1998 BC.

Life Synopsis

Noah was named by his father Lamech with a hope attached: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the Lord hath cursed" (Genesis 5:29). He appears in a generation the text describes as filled with violence and corruption, and against that background Scripture says simply, "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 6:8). He is called "a just man and perfect in his generations," and one who "walked with God" (Genesis 6:9).

God revealed his purpose to destroy the earth and commanded Noah to build an ark to precise specifications (Genesis 6:13-21). Twice the record states his obedience in almost identical words: "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he" (Genesis 6:22), and "Noah did according unto all that the Lord commanded him" (Genesis 7:5). Peter adds that he was "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5), and Hebrews that he acted "moved with fear," and by doing so "condemned the world" (Hebrews 11:7).

In his six hundredth year the fountains of the great deep were broken up (Genesis 7:11). He entered the ark with his household and the animals, and the Lord shut him in (Genesis 7:16). After the waters abated he sent out a raven and then a dove three times, reading the state of the earth by what returned (Genesis 8:6-12). On leaving the ark his first recorded act was to build an altar and offer burnt offerings (Genesis 8:20). God responded with the covenant never again to destroy the earth by water, and set the rainbow as its token (Genesis 9:8-17).

Afterward Noah became a husbandman and planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine, was drunken, and lay uncovered in his tent (Genesis 9:20-21). Ham saw and told; Shem and Japheth covered him walking backward (Genesis 9:22-23). On waking he pronounced a curse on Canaan and blessings involving Shem and Japheth (Genesis 9:24-27). He lived 350 years after the flood and died at 950 (Genesis 9:28-29).

What They Did Right

  • Found grace in the eyes of the Lord: Genesis 6:8.
  • Described by God's own record as just, perfect in his generations, and a man who walked with God: Genesis 6:9.
  • Obeyed God's instructions completely, a point the text makes twice: Genesis 6:22; Genesis 7:5.
  • Built an altar and offered burnt offerings immediately on leaving the ark, before any other recorded act: Genesis 8:20.
  • Acted by faith, moved with fear, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith: Hebrews 11:7.
  • Named by God through Ezekiel, with Daniel and Job, as a byword for personal righteousness: Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20.
  • Called a preacher of righteousness: 2 Peter 2:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • Became drunk on wine from his own vineyard and lay uncovered within his tent: Genesis 9:20-21. Scripture records this plainly but does not explicitly condemn him for it, and does not state whether he understood the effect of the wine. It is a recorded failure whose moral weight the text leaves unstated, and it should not be pressed further than that.

Character Assessment

One of the strongest character commendations in the Old Testament. Every reference to Noah outside Genesis is positive - two in Ezekiel, four in the New Testament - and the drunkenness is never mentioned again in Scripture. Yet Genesis records that failure without softening it, immediately after his greatest deliverance. The honesty of that juxtaposition is characteristic of the biblical record.

Significance

Noah is the second head of humanity; every person alive descends from him and his three sons (Genesis 9:19). The Noahic covenant, with the rainbow as its sign, is the first covenant in Scripture given with an outward token, and it underwrites the stability of the natural order (Genesis 8:22, 9:8-17). Christ uses the days of Noah as the pattern of the world's condition at his coming (Matthew 24:37-38; Luke 17:26-27), and Peter draws from the ark a figure of salvation (1 Peter 3:20-21).

Death / Outcome

Died at 950 years (Genesis 9:29). Last mention: 2 Peter 2:5.

Scripture

Terah

Family

Son of Nahor (Genesis 11:24). Father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran (Genesis 11:26-27); grandfather of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. His wife is not named in Genesis.

Chronology

Born AM 1878, died in Haran aged 205 [traditional: 2126–1921 BC].

Took Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur of the Chaldees intending Canaan, but settled in Haran (Genesis 11:31). Died there (Genesis 11:32).

What They Did Right

  • Took Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur of the Chaldees with Canaan as the stated destination: Genesis 11:31. The text records the action without commending it, and Acts 7:2-4 indicates the call came to Abram before Haran, so the relative agency is not spelled out.

What They Did Wrong

  • Served other gods. This is Scripture's one explicit evaluation of him, and it is negative: Joshua 24:2.
  • Settled in Haran rather than continuing to Canaan, though Canaan was the stated destination: Genesis 11:31. Scripture does not explicitly call this a failure, and does not state whether it was disobedience, prudence, or circumstance. The moral status is uncertain and is left so here.

Character Assessment

Scripture's one direct verdict is negative: he "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). Whether stopping short of Canaan was disobedience, prudence, or circumstance, the text does not specify. Acts 7:2–4 indicates God's call came to Abram before Haran, which bears on whose migration it was. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:34).

Significance

Terah stands at the hinge between the postdiluvian genealogy and the call of Abraham, and in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:34). His migration begins the movement toward Canaan that his son completes.
