062

Judith and Bashemath (wives of Esau)

Hittite wives whom Esau married at forty. Two distinct women, recorded only jointly.

Family

Two distinct women, recorded only jointly. Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, both married by Esau at forty (Genesis 26:34).

Chronology

Patriarchal; Esau's fortieth year.

Life Synopsis

"And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:34–35).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The evaluation Scripture gives concerns their effect, not their conduct: they "were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35). Nothing either woman did or said is recorded.

Character Assessment

The evaluation is of their effect, not their conduct — Scripture records nothing either woman did. The grief is attributed to the marriages, and Rebekah cites the daughters of Heth as her reason for sending Jacob away (Genesis 27:46).

Significance

Their marriages are the stated cause of Rebekah's weariness of life and of her stated reason for sending Jacob to Padan-aram (Genesis 27:46), and so contribute to the separation of the brothers. Note that the list of Esau's wives in Genesis 36:2-3 gives different names and parentage - an unresolved discrepancy in the text, recorded here rather than harmonized.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 26:35.

Scripture

Genesis 26:34–35; Genesis 27:46. Note: Esau's wives are listed with different names and parentage in Genesis 36:2–3, an unresolved discrepancy.
063

Laban

Son of Bethuel; brother of Rebekah; father of Leah and Rachel; Jacob's father-in-law and employer for twenty years.

Family

Son of Bethuel (Genesis 28:5); brother of Rebekah (Genesis 24:29); father of Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:16) and of sons (Genesis 31:1). Called the Syrian (Genesis 25:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. His dealings with Jacob span twenty years (Genesis 31:38, 31:41).

Life Synopsis

Laban first appears when Abraham's servant comes for Rebekah. He ran out to the man at the well - and the text notes what he had just seen: "when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister's hands" (Genesis 24:29-31). He welcomed the servant and, with Bethuel, answered, "The thing proceedeth from the Lord: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good" (Genesis 24:50).

A generation later Jacob arrived fleeing Esau. Laban received him, and after a month proposed wages. Jacob offered seven years for Rachel; Laban agreed, then on the wedding night gave Leah, justifying it afterward by local custom, and required another seven years (Genesis 29:18-28). Over the following years he changed Jacob's wages ten times (Genesis 31:7, 31:41), while his own house prospered - he acknowledged that he had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake (Genesis 30:27).

When Jacob left secretly, Laban pursued him seven days and overtook him in Gilead, having been warned by God in a dream not to speak either good or bad to Jacob (Genesis 31:22-24). He confronted Jacob over the departure and over his stolen images, searched the tents, and found nothing (Genesis 31:26-35). Jacob's answer is the fullest indictment in the passage: twenty years of service, torn beasts borne by himself, frost by night and drought by day, and wages changed ten times (Genesis 31:38-42).

They made a covenant at a heap of stones, called Galeed and Mizpah, agreeing that neither would pass it to harm the other. Laban kissed his sons and daughters, blessed them, and returned to his place (Genesis 31:43-55).

What They Did Right

  • Received Abraham's servant hospitably and acknowledged the Lord's hand in the matter: Genesis 24:31, 24:50.
  • Received Jacob into his house as kin: Genesis 29:13-14.
  • Acknowledged that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake: Genesis 30:27.
  • Obeyed God's warning in the dream and did not harm Jacob: Genesis 31:24, 31:29.
  • Entered a covenant of peace and parted with a blessing on his daughters and grandchildren: Genesis 31:43-55.

What They Did Wrong

  • Substituted Leah for Rachel on the wedding night, a deliberate deception, and used it to extract seven further years of labour: Genesis 29:23-27.
  • Changed Jacob's wages ten times: Genesis 31:7, 31:41. Jacob states this to his face and Laban does not deny it.
  • Kept household images, which his daughter stole and which he pursued Jacob to recover, calling them "my gods": Genesis 31:19, 31:30.
  • Claimed at the parting that everything Jacob had was his own - "all that thou seest is mine" - after twenty years of Jacob's labour: Genesis 31:43.

Character Assessment

Scripture never pronounces a formal verdict on Laban, but the narrative is not neutral. His first recorded action follows the sight of gold; his central act is a deception that cost his son-in-law seven years; and his own daughters say of him, "Are we not counted of him strangers? for he hath sold us, and hath quite devoured also our money" (Genesis 31:14-15). Against this stands genuine hospitality, obedience to God's warning, and a covenant kept. He is not a villain in the text so much as a grasping man whom God restrained.

Significance

Laban is the human instrument by which Jacob the deceiver is himself deceived - the elder daughter substituted for the younger, answering Jacob's own substitution of himself for the elder son. Through his daughters Leah and Rachel, and their handmaids, the twelve tribes of Israel are born. The Mizpah covenant (Genesis 31:49) has passed into common religious usage, often detached from its original setting as a boundary agreement between two men who did not trust each other.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance: Genesis 31:55, returning to his own place.

Scripture

Genesis 24:29-60; Genesis 25:20; Genesis 27:43; Genesis 28:2-5; Genesis 29:5-30; Genesis 30:25-43; Genesis 31:1-55
064

Leah

Elder daughter of Laban; Jacob's first wife by Laban's substitution; mother of six of the twelve tribal patriarchs and of Dinah.

Family

Daughter of Laban (Genesis 29:16); elder sister of Rachel. Wife of Jacob (Genesis 29:23-25). Mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah (Genesis 29:32-35; Genesis 30:17-21). Mistress of Zilpah (Genesis 30:9).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her death is not narrated; Jacob states she was buried in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:31).

Life Synopsis

Leah is introduced with a comparison that sets the terms of her life: "Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured" (Genesis 29:17). Laban gave her to Jacob in place of Rachel on the wedding night, and Jacob discovered it only in the morning (Genesis 29:23-25). The text then states plainly that Leah was hated, and that "when the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren" (Genesis 29:31).

The names she gave her sons trace her hope and its disappointment. Reuben: "Surely the Lord hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." Simeon: "the Lord hath heard that I was hated." Levi: "now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons." Then Judah, where the pattern breaks: "Now will I praise the Lord" (Genesis 29:32-35). She stops asking for her husband's love and praises God.

When she left off bearing she gave Zilpah to Jacob, and two more sons were counted to her (Genesis 30:9-13). She bought a night with Jacob from Rachel for her son's mandrakes and bore Issachar, then Zebulun, and afterward Dinah (Genesis 30:14-21). When Jacob told his wives that God had commanded him to return, she answered with Rachel that they would go (Genesis 31:14-16).

When Esau approached, Jacob arranged his family in order of preference, placing the handmaids first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last (Genesis 33:1-2) - a public ranking she would have understood. Scripture does not narrate her death, but Jacob, dying in Egypt, names Machpelah as the place "where I buried Leah" (Genesis 49:31).

What They Did Right

  • Praised the Lord at the birth of Judah, moving beyond her plea for her husband's affection: Genesis 29:35.
  • Acknowledged God in the naming of each of her sons: Genesis 29:32-35; Genesis 30:18, 30:20.
  • Agreed with Rachel to leave Laban's house at Jacob's word: Genesis 31:14-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • Participated in the wedding-night deception of Jacob: Genesis 29:23-25. Scripture assigns the initiative to Laban and records nothing that Leah said or chose; her degree of responsibility is not stated, and this reference does not assign one.
  • Bargained for a night with her husband using her son's mandrakes, and met him with "thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee": Genesis 30:15-16. The text records it without comment.

Character Assessment

Leah is the unloved wife, and Scripture says so without euphemism. But the record consistently shows God's regard for her precisely in that condition: he saw that she was hated and opened her womb (Genesis 29:31). Six of the twelve tribes come from her, including both the priestly tribe and the royal one. The elders of Bethlehem later bless Ruth by invoking "Rachel and Leah, which two did build the house of Israel" - and they name Rachel first but bless in the line of Leah (Ruth 4:11-12).

Significance

Leah is the mother of Levi, from whom the priesthood came, and of Judah, from whom came David and Christ (Genesis 29:34-35; Matthew 1:2-3). The covenant line runs through the wife Jacob did not choose. She lies in Machpelah with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Jacob (Genesis 49:31), while Rachel is buried by the roadside.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not narrate her death. Jacob states that he buried her in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:31).

Scripture

Genesis 29:16-35; Genesis 30:9-21; Genesis 31:4-16; Genesis 33:1-7; Genesis 34:1; Genesis 49:31; Ruth 4:11
065

Rachel

Younger daughter of Laban; the wife Jacob loved; mother of Joseph and Benjamin.

Family

Daughter of Laban (Genesis 29:16); younger sister of Leah; niece of Rebekah. Wife of Jacob (Genesis 29:28). Mother of Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 30:22-24; Genesis 35:16-18). Mistress of Bilhah (Genesis 30:3-4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She died on the way to Ephrath while Jacob was returning from Padan-aram (Genesis 35:16-19). Her age is not recorded.

Life Synopsis

Jacob met Rachel at the well, watered her father's flock, kissed her and wept aloud (Genesis 29:9-11). She was "beautiful and well favoured," and Jacob served seven years for her, "and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her" (Genesis 29:17-20). Laban substituted Leah on the wedding night, and Jacob served another seven years (Genesis 29:23-28).

She was loved but barren while her sister bore sons, and the rivalry between them shapes the whole account. "Give me children, or else I die," she said to Jacob, and his anger was kindled (Genesis 30:1-2). She gave Bilhah her handmaid to him and counted the two sons born as her own victory: "With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed" (Genesis 30:3-8). She bargained with Leah for her son's mandrakes in exchange for a night with Jacob (Genesis 30:14-16).

At length "God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb," and she bore Joseph, saying, "The Lord shall add to me another son" (Genesis 30:22-24). When Jacob left Padan-aram she stole her father's images and hid them in the camel's furniture, sitting on them while Laban searched - and Jacob, not knowing, had pronounced death on whoever had taken them (Genesis 31:19, 31:32-35).

The second son came at the cost of her life. In hard labour near Ephrath the midwife told her she would have a son; as her soul departed she named him Ben-oni, and his father called him Benjamin. She was buried on the way to Ephrath, and Jacob set a pillar on her grave (Genesis 35:16-20).

What They Did Right

  • Consented to the marriage arrangement and waited through Jacob's years of service: Genesis 29:18-28.
  • Agreed with Leah to leave Laban's house when Jacob told them what God had shown him: Genesis 31:14-16.
  • Named her firstborn Joseph in acknowledgment that God had taken away her reproach: Genesis 30:23-24.

What They Did Wrong

  • Envied her sister: "Rachel envied her sister," the text states directly: Genesis 30:1.
  • Demanded children of Jacob as though he could give them, provoking his anger: Genesis 30:1-2.
  • Stole her father's household images and lied to conceal them: Genesis 31:19, 31:34-35. The theft is stated as fact; the deception of Laban is recorded without comment, but it placed her under Jacob's unwitting curse.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents Rachel as deeply loved and deeply unhappy, and does not hide the envy that ran alongside. Her recorded speech is dominated by rivalry with her sister. Yet the record also shows God remembering her and hearkening to her (Genesis 30:22), and Israel's elders later invoke her and Leah together as the two who built the house of Israel (Ruth 4:11).

Significance

Mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so of the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin. Her tomb near Bethlehem became a landmark (Genesis 35:19-20; 1 Samuel 10:2). Jeremiah pictures her weeping for her children and refusing comfort (Jeremiah 31:15), which Matthew applies to the slaughter of the infants at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

Death / Outcome

Died in hard labour bearing Benjamin, on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem; buried there under a pillar Jacob set up (Genesis 35:16-20; Genesis 48:7).

Scripture

Genesis 29:6-30; Genesis 30:1-24; Genesis 31:4-35; Genesis 33:1-7; Genesis 35:16-20; Genesis 48:7; Ruth 4:11; 1 Samuel 10:2; Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18

Bilhah

Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife; mother of Dan and Naphtali.

Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife (Genesis 29:29; Genesis 30:4). Mother of Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:5-8).

Given by Rachel to Jacob so that Rachel might "have children by her" (Genesis 30:3–4). Bore Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:5–8). Later, Reuben lay with her, and "Israel heard it" (Genesis 35:22).

No verdict is offered on Bilhah. In both episodes she is acted upon rather than acting, and Scripture records no words of hers.

Significance

Mother of two tribal patriarchs, Dan and Naphtali. Reuben's act with her (Genesis 35:22) is the stated ground of his forfeited birthright (Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).

Death / Outcome

Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife; mother of Gad and Asher.

Family

Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife (Genesis 29:24; Genesis 30:9). Mother of Gad and Asher (Genesis 30:10-13).

Chronology

Patriarchal; Jacob's years in Padan-aram.

Given by Leah to Jacob when Leah left off bearing (Genesis 30:9). Bore Gad and Asher (Genesis 30:10–13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. She acts nowhere in the narrative and speaks nowhere; the naming of both her sons is Leah's.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. As with Bilhah, she acts nowhere in the narrative and speaks nowhere — the naming of both sons is Leah's.

Significance

Mother of two tribal patriarchs, Gad and Asher.

068

Reuben

Firstborn son of Jacob by Leah.

Family

Firstborn son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:32). Father of four sons (Genesis 46:9).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Brought mandrakes to his mother (Genesis 30:14). Lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22). Alone among the brothers, moved to save Joseph — "Let us not kill him... Shed no blood" — intending to return him to his father, and rent his clothes on finding the pit empty (Genesis 37:21–22, 37:29–30). Offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 42:37).

What They Did Right

  • Alone among the brothers, moved to save Joseph: "Let us not kill him... Shed no blood," intending to return him to his father: Genesis 37:21-22.
  • Rent his clothes on finding the pit empty: Genesis 37:29-30.
  • Offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin's safe return: Genesis 42:37.
  • Reminded his brothers of their guilt over Joseph rather than concealing it: Genesis 42:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine: Genesis 35:22. Jacob names this explicitly as the reason for his forfeited pre-eminence: Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1.
  • Jacob's verdict is "Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel": Genesis 49:4.

Character Assessment

Mixed, and Scripture is explicit about both sides. Jacob's deathbed verdict names the dignity and the disqualification together: "Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed" (Genesis 49:3–4). His attempts to protect Joseph and Benjamin are recorded without comment but stand in the narrative to his credit.

Significance

The firstborn who lost the birthright, which passed to Joseph's sons (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). His repeated attempts to protect Joseph and Benjamin are recorded without comment but stand to his credit in the narrative, making his record genuinely mixed rather than simply negative.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:3-4.

Scripture

Genesis 29:32; Genesis 30:14; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 37:21–30; Genesis 42:22, 42:37; Genesis 49:3–4.
069

Simeon

Second son of Jacob by Leah; head of the tribe of Simeon.

Family

Second son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:33); brother of Levi and Dinah. Father of six sons (Genesis 46:10).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

With Levi, killed all the males of Shechem's city by deceit while they were sore from circumcision, and answered Jacob's rebuke: "Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?" (Genesis 34:25–31). Bound and held hostage in Egypt by Joseph (Genesis 42:24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His answer to Jacob - "Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?" (Genesis 34:31) - states a genuine grievance, but Scripture does not commend the act it defends.

What They Did Wrong

  • With Levi, deceived the men of Shechem with a proposal of circumcision and killed all the males while they were sore: Genesis 34:13-26.
  • Explicitly condemned by Jacob: "instruments of cruelty are in their habitations... Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel": Genesis 49:5-7. The stated ground is the anger and the cruelty.

Character Assessment

Condemned by Jacob, explicitly and at his deathbed: "instruments of cruelty are in their habitations... Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce" (Genesis 49:5–7). The stated ground is the anger and the cruelty, not the defence of Dinah as such.

Significance

Head of the tribe of Simeon. Jacob's sentence - "I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel" (Genesis 49:7) - is fulfilled in Simeon's inheritance being absorbed within Judah's territory (Joshua 19:1-9). He was the brother Joseph bound and held in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:5-7.

Scripture

Genesis 29:33; Genesis 34:25–31; Genesis 42:24, 42:36; Genesis 43:23; Genesis 49:5–7.

Levi

Third son of Jacob by Leah; head of the tribe from which Israel's priesthood came.

Family

Third son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:34); brother of Simeon and Dinah. Father of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari (Genesis 46:11).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Acted with Simeon at Shechem (Genesis 34:25–31). Lived 137 years (Exodus 6:16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • With Simeon, deceived and slaughtered the men of Shechem: Genesis 34:13-26.
  • Explicitly condemned with Simeon at Jacob's deathbed: Genesis 49:5-7.

Character Assessment

Condemned with Simeon in Genesis 49:5–7, and the sentence — "I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel" — is worth noting as a judgment later turned to a different end in the Levites' dispersed priestly settlement. Nothing commendable is recorded of Levi personally.

Significance

Head of the tribe from which Israel's priesthood came. The scattering pronounced as judgment in Genesis 49:7 is turned to a different purpose in the Levites' dispersed priestly settlement throughout Israel (Joshua 21:1-42) - a striking instance of a sentence becoming a service, though Genesis itself does not draw the connection. He lived 137 years (Exodus 6:16).

Death / Outcome

Scripture records his age at death, 137 years (Exodus 6:16), but does not narrate his death.

Scripture

Genesis 29:34; Genesis 34:25–31; Genesis 49:5–7; Exodus 6:16.
071

Judah

Fourth son of Jacob by Leah; head of the royal tribe; ancestor of David and of Christ.

Family

Son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:35). Married the daughter of Shuah, a Canaanite (Genesis 38:2). Father of Er, Onan, and Shelah by her, and of the twins Pharez and Zarah by Tamar (Genesis 38:3-5, 38:29-30).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Born in Padan-aram during Jacob's twenty years with Laban; alive at the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:12, 46:28).

Life Synopsis

Judah was Leah's fourth son, born when she said, "Now will I praise the Lord" (Genesis 29:35). His first significant act is a bad one. When the brothers had cast Joseph into the pit and sat down to eat, it was Judah who proposed selling him: "What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites" (Genesis 37:26-27). The proposal spared Joseph's life and profited the brothers, and it is presented as neither mercy nor justice.

Genesis 38 then interrupts the Joseph narrative for Judah's own story. He went down from his brethren, married a Canaanite woman, and had three sons. Er was wicked and the Lord slew him; Onan refused the levirate duty and was slain also (Genesis 38:6-10). Judah sent his daughter-in-law Tamar home as a widow, promising Shelah when he was grown, and did not give him. Tamar veiled herself and sat by the way; Judah, taking her for a harlot, went in to her and left his signet, bracelets, and staff as pledge (Genesis 38:14-18). When told three months later that she was pregnant by whoredom, he ordered her burnt - until she produced his pledges. His response is the turning point of his life: "She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son" (Genesis 38:26). He acknowledged the wrong publicly, at his own cost.

The change holds. When famine required Benjamin to go to Egypt, Judah gave himself as surety: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him" (Genesis 43:8-9). When the cup was found in Benjamin's sack, it was Judah who stepped forward with the longest speech in Genesis, recounting the whole matter and offering himself as a slave in his brother's place: "let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord" (Genesis 44:18-34). The man who sold one brother offered himself for another. Jacob sent him ahead to Goshen to prepare the way (Genesis 46:28), and gave him the ruling oracle: the sceptre would not depart from Judah until Shiloh came (Genesis 49:8-12).

What They Did Right

  • Acknowledged his own fault publicly when he could have destroyed the evidence: "She hath been more righteous than I": Genesis 38:26.
  • Became surety for Benjamin with his own life: Genesis 43:8-9.
  • Offered himself as a bondman in Benjamin's place, and made the plea that broke Joseph: Genesis 44:18-34.
  • Was sent ahead by Jacob to prepare the way into Goshen - a mark of trust: Genesis 46:28.

What They Did Wrong

  • Proposed selling Joseph into slavery for profit: Genesis 37:26-27.
  • Married a Canaanite woman: Genesis 38:2. Genesis records this without explicit condemnation, though it stands against the pattern Abraham and Isaac insisted on for their sons (Genesis 24:3; Genesis 28:1).
  • Withheld Shelah from Tamar, leaving her a widow indefinitely, and later admitted it as the wrong it was: Genesis 38:11, 38:26.
  • Went in to a woman he believed to be a harlot: Genesis 38:15-18.
  • Ordered Tamar burnt for the very sin he had himself committed with her: Genesis 38:24.

Character Assessment

One of the clearest arcs of moral change in Genesis. Judah begins by selling a brother for twenty pieces of silver and ends by offering his own freedom to spare another. Between the two stands Genesis 38, where he is confronted with his hypocrisy and does not evade it. Scripture records his failures in unusual detail - the sale, the Canaanite marriage, the harlot, the double standard - and then gives him the royal oracle anyway. The record neither excuses him nor disqualifies him.

Significance

Judah is the royal tribe. Jacob's oracle - "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come" (Genesis 49:10) - is one of the central messianic prophecies of the Old Testament. David descends from him through Pharez and Tamar (Ruth 4:18-22), and so does Christ, who is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Matthew 1:2-3; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance in Genesis: Genesis 49:8-12, receiving Jacob's blessing.

Scripture

Genesis 29:35; Genesis 37:26-27; Genesis 38:1-30; Genesis 43:3-10; Genesis 44:14-34; Genesis 46:12, 46:28; Genesis 49:8-12; Ruth 4:12, 4:18-22; Matthew 1:2-3; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5

Scripture offers no assessment of him as an individual. He is included because his birth, naming, and the oracle over him are recorded, which is more than a bare name in a list.

078

Joseph

Eleventh son of Jacob and firstborn of Rachel; sold into Egypt as a slave and raised to be ruler over all the land under Pharaoh.

Also called Zaphnath-paaneah

Family

Son of Jacob and Rachel (Genesis 30:22-24); full brother of Benjamin. Husband of Asenath, daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On (Genesis 41:45). Father of Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50-52).

Chronology

Seventeen when sold (Genesis 37:2); thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46); died at 110 (Genesis 50:26). These ages are explicitly stated in Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Joseph was seventeen, feeding the flock with his brothers, and brought their father their evil report. Israel loved him more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours, "and when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him" (Genesis 37:2-4). Two dreams of sheaves and stars, which he told, deepened the hatred (Genesis 37:5-11). Sent to check on them at Dothan, he was stripped, cast into a pit, and sold to Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver; his coat was dipped in goat's blood and carried to his father (Genesis 37:23-33).

In Egypt he served Potiphar, and the Lord was with him so that he was made overseer of the whole house (Genesis 39:1-6). Potiphar's wife solicited him daily; he refused, naming the reason: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" When she caught his garment he fled and left it in her hand, and was imprisoned on her false accusation (Genesis 39:7-20). In prison the keeper committed all the prisoners to him (Genesis 39:21-23). He interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's butler and baker exactly as they fell out, and asked the butler to remember him - who forgot him two full years (Genesis 40:1-23).

When Pharaoh dreamed, the butler remembered. Joseph, brought from the dungeon, disclaimed the ability - "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace" (Genesis 41:16) - interpreted seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and proposed a plan. Pharaoh set him over all Egypt at thirty (Genesis 41:38-46). He gathered grain, and the famine came.

His brothers came to buy corn and bowed before him without knowing him. Over two visits he tested them - the demand for Benjamin, Simeon held hostage, the money returned, the cup in Benjamin's sack - until Judah offered himself in Benjamin's place. Then Joseph wept aloud and made himself known: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt" (Genesis 45:1-4). His interpretation of it all is the theological centre of the story: "be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves... for God did send me before you to preserve life" (Genesis 45:5-8). He brought his father and household into Goshen, sustained Egypt through the famine, and after Jacob's death reassured his frightened brothers: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20). He died at 110, having charged them to carry up his bones (Genesis 50:24-26).

What They Did Right

  • Refused Potiphar's wife day after day, naming the sin as against God: Genesis 39:8-10.
  • Fled rather than argue when physically seized, at the cost of his position and his freedom: Genesis 39:12.
  • Served faithfully in every position - Potiphar's house, the prison, and all Egypt - so that each master trusted him completely: Genesis 39:4, 39:22-23; Genesis 41:40-44.
  • Gave God the credit for interpretation rather than claiming it: Genesis 40:8; Genesis 41:16.
  • Wept over his brothers and forgave them, though he had absolute power to destroy them: Genesis 45:1-15; Genesis 50:19-21.
  • Provided for his family and for Egypt through seven years of famine: Genesis 45:9-11; Genesis 47:11-12.
  • Charged his brethren concerning his bones, in faith that God would bring Israel out: Genesis 50:24-25; Hebrews 11:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Brought his brothers' evil report to their father: Genesis 37:2. Scripture records this without moral comment - whether it was faithfulness or tale-bearing is not stated.
  • Told his dreams to brothers who already hated him, and to his father, who rebuked him for it: Genesis 37:5-11. Again the text records the rebuke without endorsing or condemning Joseph.
  • Scripture records no sin of Joseph. This is an absence of record, not a claim of sinlessness, which Scripture makes of no one but Christ.

Character Assessment

Joseph is one of a very small number of substantial biblical figures of whom no wrongdoing is recorded. His two questionable acts as a boy - the report and the dreams - are set down without moral judgment, and interpreters differ over them. What Scripture does record at length is integrity under injustice: he was sold by his brothers, lied about by his master's wife, and forgotten by a man he had helped, and in none of those does he retaliate. Hebrews commends the last act of his life, his charge concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22).

Significance

Through Joseph the family of Jacob was preserved alive through famine, and the descent into Egypt took place that set up the Exodus (Genesis 45:5-8; Genesis 50:20). His two sons became two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, receiving a double portion in place of the birthright forfeited by Reuben (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). His statement in Genesis 50:20 - "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" - is one of Scripture's clearest expressions of God's providence working through human wrongdoing without excusing it. Stephen recounts his history in his defence before the council (Acts 7:9-18).

Death / Outcome

Died in Egypt at 110 years, was embalmed and put in a coffin, having made Israel swear to carry his bones up (Genesis 50:24-26). His bones were carried out at the Exodus and buried at Shechem (Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32).

Scripture

Genesis 30:22-24; Genesis 37:1-36; Genesis 39:1-23; Genesis 40:1-23; Genesis 41:1-57; Genesis 42:1-45:28; Genesis 46:28-47:31; Genesis 48:1-22; Genesis 50:1-26; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32; Acts 7:9-18; Hebrews 11:22
079

Benjamin

Youngest son of Jacob, and the only one born in Canaan; Rachel's second son.

Family

Youngest son of Jacob, by Rachel (Genesis 35:18); full brother of Joseph; the only one of Jacob's sons born in Canaan. Father of ten sons (Genesis 46:21).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Born near Ephrath; his dying mother named him Ben-oni and his father renamed him Benjamin (Genesis 35:16–18). Kept back from Egypt by Jacob, who feared losing him (Genesis 42:4, 42:38). Brought at last under Judah's surety (Genesis 43:8–14). Given five times the portion at Joseph's table (Genesis 43:34), and three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of raiment at the reunion (Genesis 45:22). The cup was planted in his sack, precipitating Judah's plea (Genesis 44:2–34).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records not one word spoken by Benjamin in the whole of Genesis, though he is central to two chapters. He is the occasion of the test rather than an actor in it.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Scripture records not one word spoken by Benjamin in the whole of Genesis, though he is central to two chapters — he is the occasion of the test rather than an actor in it. Jacob's deathbed word is of the tribe: "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (Genesis 49:27).

Significance

Head of the tribe of Benjamin, from which came Saul, Israel's first king (1 Samuel 9:1-2), and Saul of Tarsus, who calls himself of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5). His dying mother named him Ben-oni and his father renamed him Benjamin (Genesis 35:18). Jacob's word over him is of the tribe: "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (Genesis 49:27).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:27.

Scripture

Deborah (Rebekah's nurse)

Nurse to Rebekah, who travelled with her from Padan-aram and remained with the family into Jacob's generation. Distinct from Deborah the judge and prophetess.

Nurse to Rebekah, who travelled with her from Padan-aram (Genesis 24:59) and remained with the household into Jacob's generation. Not to be confused with Deborah the judge and prophetess (Judges 4:4).

What They Did Wrong

No verdict is offered. A servant whose death is marked by a named place and public mourning, which is more honour than Genesis records for most of the free-born.

A servant whose death is marked by a named place and public mourning - the oak was called Allon-bachuth, and the place-name is generally understood to mean oak of weeping, though Genesis does not translate it. That is more honour than Genesis records for many of the free-born, and it indicates the regard in which she was held.

081

Dinah

Daughter of Jacob by Leah.

Family

Daughter of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 30:21); sister of Simeon and Levi.

Chronology

Patriarchal; after Jacob's return to Canaan.

Life Synopsis

Went out to see the daughters of the land; Shechem "took her, and lay with her, and defiled her" (Genesis 34:1–2). Her brothers' revenge followed; she was taken out of Shechem's house (Genesis 34:26). Listed among those who went into Egypt (Genesis 46:15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This must be stated carefully. Scripture records nothing that Dinah said and no wrongdoing on her part. The text is explicit that she was defiled - the language of Genesis 34:2 places the act on Shechem. Readings that assign her blame for going out to see the daughters of the land read into Genesis 34:1 something the verse does not say.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing that Dinah said and no wrongdoing on her part. The text is explicit that she was defiled — the language places the act on Shechem. Readings that assign her blame for going out read something into Genesis 34:1 that is not there.

Significance

The violation of Dinah and her brothers' revenge is the occasion of Jacob's rebuke of Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:30) and of the curse on their anger at his deathbed (Genesis 49:5-7), which in turn determines the scattering of those two tribes in Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 46:15, among those who went into Egypt.

Scripture

Genesis 30:21; Genesis 34:1–31; Genesis 46:15.
