Pharaoh's daughter

Unnamed. The daughter of the king of Egypt who drew the infant Moses out of the river and raised him as her own son. Scripture gives no name, and this reference assigns none.

Family

Daughter of a king of Egypt (Exodus 2:5). Adoptive mother of Moses (Exodus 2:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She came down to wash at the river with her maidens and saw the ark among the flags. Opening it, she saw the child weeping, "and she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children" (Exodus 2:5-6). She knew what he was and saved him anyway, under her own father's decree. When the child's sister offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse, she agreed and paid wages for it (Exodus 2:7-9). When the boy was grown she took him as her son and named him Moses, "Because I drew him out of the water" (Exodus 2:10).

What They Did Right

  • Had compassion on a condemned Hebrew infant and preserved him, knowing what he was: Exodus 2:6.
  • Provided for his nursing and paid for it: Exodus 2:9.
  • Raised him as her own son: Exodus 2:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and one sustained act of mercy, taken against her own father's edict. Hebrews credits the hiding of Moses to his parents' faith and says nothing of her motive; Exodus attributes it simply to compassion.

Significance

Her compassion placed the deliverer of Israel inside the household of the oppressor, where he received the Egyptian learning Stephen notes (Acts 7:22). Hebrews marks the moment Moses renounced the standing she gave him as the act of faith that defined his life (Hebrews 11:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Exodus 2:10; referred to in Acts 7:21 and Hebrews 11:24.

Scripture

Exodus 2:5-10; Acts 7:21; Hebrews 11:24

The Hebrew who challenged Moses

Unnamed. One of two Hebrews found striving on the day after Moses killed the Egyptian; the man who rejected Moses' authority.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In Moses' fortieth year (Acts 7:23).

Life Synopsis

Moses went out a second day and found two Hebrews striving together. He said to the one who did the wrong, "Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow?" The man answered, "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian?" Moses feared, and said, "Surely this thing is known" (Exodus 2:13-14). It was this exchange that sent him into forty years of exile.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • He was the one doing the wrong in the quarrel, which is how Exodus identifies him: Exodus 2:13.
  • Rejected Moses' intervention with contempt and a threat of exposure: Exodus 2:14. Scripture does not explicitly condemn him, but Stephen uses the refusal as the pattern of Israel's treatment of its deliverers: Acts 7:27, 7:35.

Character Assessment

A man of one recorded sentence, and Scripture gives that sentence lasting weight. Stephen quotes it twice in his defence before the council, making it the type of Israel's rejection of the one God sent (Acts 7:27, 7:35), which is the whole argument of his speech.

Significance

His words drove Moses into Midian, where the forty years of preparation and the burning bush followed. Stephen makes his rejection of Moses the prefiguring of the rejection of Christ.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 7:27-28.

Exodus 2:13-14; Acts 7:26-28, 7:35
122

Reuel

Priest of Midian; father-in-law of Moses; the counsellor who reorganised Israel's system of judgment.

Also called Jethro, Raguel

Family

Priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16; Exodus 18:1). Father of seven daughters, of whom Zipporah married Moses (Exodus 2:16-21). Called Reuel in Exodus 2:18 and Jethro from Exodus 3:1 onward; Scripture uses both names without explanation, and interpreters differ over whether these are two names for one man or a personal name and a title. This reference notes the question rather than deciding it.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

When Moses fled to Midian he sat down by a well. Reuel's seven daughters came to water their father's flock and were driven off by shepherds; Moses stood up, helped them, and watered the flock. They came home early, and their father asked why. On hearing of the Egyptian who had helped them, he said, "Where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread." Moses was content to dwell with him, and he gave him Zipporah his daughter (Exodus 2:16-21).

After the Exodus he came to Moses in the wilderness with Zipporah and her two sons. Hearing all that the Lord had done, he rejoiced, and said, "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods," and offered a burnt offering and sacrifices to God (Exodus 18:9-12).

The next day he watched Moses judging the people from morning to evening and told him plainly, "The thing that thou doest is not good. Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee." He counselled him to teach the ordinances, appoint able men who fear God and hate covetousness as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and to judge only the great matters himself. "So Moses hearkened to the voice of his father in law, and did all that he had said" (Exodus 18:13-24).

What They Did Right

  • Showed hospitality to a fugitive and gave him a home and a wife: Exodus 2:20-21.
  • Confessed the Lord's greatness and offered sacrifice to him: Exodus 18:10-12.
  • Told Moses the truth about an unsustainable practice, at the risk of the relationship: Exodus 18:17-18.
  • Gave counsel that named the qualifications for judges - able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness: Exodus 18:21.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is a Midianite priest who confesses the God of Israel, and the only man in the Pentateuch whose advice Moses is recorded as taking. The passage is notable for where the wisdom comes from: not from Sinai, but from a father-in-law outside the covenant people, and Moses adopts it without hesitation.

Significance

His counsel established Israel's judicial structure, which Moses recounts in Deuteronomy 1:9-18 as the origin of the system of rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. The qualifications he named for judges are quoted and applied far beyond their setting.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He returned to his own land (Exodus 18:27).

Scripture

Exodus 2:16-22; Exodus 3:1; Exodus 4:18; Exodus 18:1-27; Numbers 10:29; Deuteronomy 1:9-18

Zipporah

Daughter of Reuel the priest of Midian; wife of Moses; the woman who circumcised her son at the inn.

Family

Daughter of Reuel, also called Jethro (Exodus 2:16-21); one of seven sisters. Wife of Moses; mother of Gershom and Eliezer (Exodus 18:3-4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Zipporah was one of the seven daughters of the priest of Midian whom Moses defended at the well; her father gave her to Moses to wife, and she bore Gershom (Exodus 2:16-22).

Her one recorded act is sudden and difficult. As Moses returned to Egypt, "it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the Lord met him, and sought to kill him. Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me. So he let him go" (Exodus 4:24-26). Exodus does not explain who was under threat, why, or what her words meant. The passage is among the most obscure in the Pentateuch, and this reference does not supply an explanation the text withholds.

She and her two sons were later sent back to her father, and Jethro brought them to Moses in the wilderness (Exodus 18:2-6).

What They Did Right

  • Acted immediately at the inn, and the threat was lifted: Exodus 4:25-26. Scripture records the act and its effect without stating her motive or commending her explicitly.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Her words, "Surely a bloody husband art thou to me," are recorded without evaluation. They have been read as reproach and as confession; Scripture does not say.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her one scene and no interpretation of it. What can be said with confidence is that she acted, that the circumcision was performed, and that the Lord let Moses go. Everything beyond that is inference, and the passage has resisted agreement for as long as it has been read.

Significance

Her act at the inn brought Moses' household into compliance with the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 17:10-14) at the moment he was being sent to demand that Pharaoh release the covenant people. Numbers 12:1 records that Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses over an Ethiopian woman he had married; whether that is Zipporah or another wife is disputed and Scripture does not resolve it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Exodus 18:2-6.

Scripture

Exodus 2:21-22; Exodus 4:20, 4:24-26; Exodus 18:2-6

Gershom (son of Moses)

Firstborn son of Moses and Zipporah, born in Midian.

Family

Son of Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 2:22); brother of Eliezer.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Born during Moses' forty years in Midian.

Life Synopsis

"And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land" (Exodus 2:22). He was sent back to Midian with his mother and brought again to Moses in the wilderness by Jethro (Exodus 18:2-5). His descendants are named among the Levites (1 Chronicles 23:15-16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his birth, his name and its stated meaning, his return with his mother, and his descendants. Nothing he said or did is recorded.

Significance

His name preserves Moses' own account of his years in Midian: a stranger in a strange land. Note that Moses' sons receive no inheritance of office - the priesthood went to Aaron's line and the leadership to Joshua, and Scripture nowhere presents this as a grievance.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 26:24.

Scripture

Exodus 2:22; Exodus 18:3; 1 Chronicles 23:15-16; 1 Chronicles 26:24
125

Eliezer (son of Moses)

Second son of Moses and Zipporah. Not to be confused with Eliezer of Damascus, Abram's steward, or with Eleazar the son of Aaron.

Family

Son of Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 18:4); brother of Gershom.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Named in the account of Jethro bringing Moses' family to him in the wilderness: "And the name of the other was Eliezer; for the God of my father, said he, was mine help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh" (Exodus 18:4). His descendants are named among the Levites (1 Chronicles 23:15-17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his birth, the meaning Moses attached to his name, and his descendants. Nothing he said or did is recorded.

Significance

His name is Moses' testimony that God delivered him from Pharaoh's sword, recorded in the naming of a child rather than in a speech.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 26:25.

Scripture

Exodus 18:4; 1 Chronicles 23:15-17; 1 Chronicles 26:25
126

Pharaoh (of the Exodus)

Unnamed. The king of Egypt who refused Moses' demand through ten plagues and pursued Israel to the Red Sea. Scripture gives no personal name and this reference assigns none. He is a different man from the Pharaoh of the oppression, who died while Moses was in Midian (Exodus 2:23).

Family

Not recorded, except that his firstborn died in the tenth plague (Exodus 12:29).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Traditional chronologies place the Exodus in the fifteenth century BC; the identification of the king is a matter of external reconstruction, not of Scripture, and remains disputed.

Life Synopsis

Moses and Aaron came before him with the demand to let Israel go, and his first recorded words set the terms of the whole confrontation: "Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go" (Exodus 5:2). He responded by increasing the people's burdens, requiring them to gather their own straw (Exodus 5:6-9).

Through the plagues a pattern repeats: pressure, a promise to release them, and a reversal once the plague lifted. After the frogs he called for Moses and promised to let them go, then hardened his heart when there was respite (Exodus 8:8-15). He offered partial concessions - sacrifice in the land, only the men, leave the flocks - and Moses refused each (Exodus 8:25-28; Exodus 10:8-11, 10:24-26). His own servants said to him, "Knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?" (Exodus 10:7). He finally told Moses, "Get thee from me... for in that day thou seest my face thou shalt die" (Exodus 10:28).

After the death of the firstborn, including his own, he called Moses and Aaron by night and drove Israel out (Exodus 12:29-32). He then changed his mind again, took six hundred chosen chariots, and pursued them to the sea, where the waters returned upon the host and "there remained not so much as one of them" (Exodus 14:5-9, 14:28).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Refused to acknowledge the Lord and refused to release Israel: Exodus 5:2.
  • Increased the people's burdens in retaliation for the request: Exodus 5:6-19.
  • Repeatedly promised release and then reneged once each plague was lifted: Exodus 8:15, 8:32; Exodus 9:34-35.
  • Threatened Moses with death: Exodus 10:28.
  • Pursued Israel after releasing them: Exodus 14:5-9.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. Scripture describes both that he hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 8:32; Exodus 9:34) and that the Lord hardened it (Exodus 9:12; Exodus 10:1, 10:20), and it does not reconcile the two for the reader. Paul takes up the case directly in Romans 9:17-18, quoting God's word to Pharaoh that he was raised up so that God's name might be declared in all the earth. This is one of the most contested passages in Scripture on divine sovereignty and human responsibility, and this reference records the tension rather than resolving it.

Significance

His resistance is the occasion of the plagues, the Passover, and the crossing of the sea - the founding acts of Israel's national existence, rehearsed throughout the Old Testament and in the New. Paul makes him the standing example of a ruler raised up to display God's power (Romans 9:17).

Death / Outcome

Scripture states that the waters covered the chariots, the horsemen, and all the host of Pharaoh that came into the sea, and that not one of them remained (Exodus 14:28). Whether Pharaoh himself entered the sea is not stated in Exodus; Psalms 136:15 says God overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea.

Scripture

Exodus 5:1-23; Exodus 7:1-12:36; Exodus 14:1-31; Psalms 136:15; Romans 9:17-18
127

Elisheba

Wife of Aaron; mother of the first priestly generation of Israel.

Family

Daughter of Amminadab and sister of Naashon, prince of Judah (Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7). Wife of Aaron; mother of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar (Exodus 6:23).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Named once: "And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar" (Exodus 6:23). Nothing she said or did is recorded. She lived to see two of her sons consumed by fire before the Lord and two of them serve as priests.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her a single verse. It is included because that verse establishes her name, her father, her brother, her husband, and her four sons - substantially more than a bare name in a list, and it links the priestly line to the royal tribe.

Significance

Her marriage joins the house of Levi to the house of Judah at the founding of the priesthood: her brother Naashon is the prince of Judah and an ancestor of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:20; Matthew 1:4). All four of Israel's first priests were her sons.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is named once, in Exodus 6:23.

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; Ruth 4:19-20; Matthew 1:4
128

Nahshon

Prince of the children of Judah in the wilderness; ancestor of David and of Christ.

Also called Naashon, Naasson

Family

Son of Amminadab (Numbers 1:7); brother of Elisheba, Aaron's wife (Exodus 6:23). Father of Salmon (Ruth 4:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Active during the wilderness period.

Life Synopsis

Nahshon was appointed prince of the tribe of Judah at the numbering in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; Numbers 2:3). He offered first among the twelve princes at the dedication of the altar, on the first day (Numbers 7:12-17). Judah under his command set out first whenever the camp moved (Numbers 10:14). Nothing he said is recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His offices and his offering are recorded without moral evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his position, his precedence among the princes, and his place in the genealogy, but nothing of his character. He is included because the recorded offices and actions are substantive.

Significance

He stands in the direct line from Judah to David and to Christ: Nahshon begat Salmon, Salmon begat Boaz (Ruth 4:20-22; Matthew 1:4-5; Luke 3:32). Through his sister Elisheba the royal tribe is joined to the priestly line at its founding.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in the genealogies: Luke 3:32.

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; Numbers 2:3; Numbers 7:12-17; Numbers 10:14; Ruth 4:20-22; 1 Chronicles 2:10-11; Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:32
129

Amminadab

Father of Nahshon the prince of Judah, and of Elisheba the wife of Aaron; a link in the line to David and to Christ.

Also called Aminadab

Family

Son of Ram (Ruth 4:19). Father of Nahshon, prince of the children of Judah (Numbers 1:7; Numbers 2:3), and of Elisheba, whom Aaron took to wife (Exodus 6:23).

Chronology

At the time of the Exodus, by his children (Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7).

Life Synopsis

He is named as the father of Elisheba: "And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar" (Exodus 6:23), and as the father of Nahshon, who was appointed prince of Judah and offered first at the dedication of the altar (Numbers 1:7; Numbers 7:12).

He stands in the genealogy at the close of Ruth - "Ram begat Amminadab, and Amminadab begat Nahshon" (Ruth 4:19-20) - and in both New Testament genealogies of Christ (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:33). Nothing he said or did is recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his son, his daughter, and his place in a list. He is entered because both of his named children stand at the head of something: his son led Judah in the wilderness, and his daughter married the first high priest.

Significance

Through his daughter Elisheba he is grandfather of the whole Aaronic priesthood, and through his son Nahshon he stands in the line from Judah to David and to Christ.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; Numbers 2:3; Numbers 7:12-17; Numbers 10:14; Ruth 4:19-20; 1 Chronicles 2:10; Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:33
130

Salmon

Son of Nahshon; husband of Rahab and father of Boaz; a link in the line to David and to Christ.

Also called Sala, Salma

Family

Son of Nahshon (Ruth 4:20). Matthew records that he begat Boaz of Rachab, that is Rahab (Matthew 1:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. His marriage places him in the generation after the conquest.

Life Synopsis

The genealogy at the close of Ruth gives the bare line: "And Nahshon begat Salmon, and Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed" (Ruth 4:20-21).

Matthew adds the detail that is not in the Old Testament record: "And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth" (Matthew 1:5), which identifies his wife as Rahab. Nothing he said or did is recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his father, his son, and - only in Matthew - his wife. Nothing else. The one substantive fact is the marriage, and it is remarkable: a man of the tribe of Judah married the harlot of Jericho who had hidden the spies.

Significance

Through him Rahab enters the line of David and of Christ. Two of the four women named in Matthew's genealogy, Rahab and Ruth, belong to his household in successive generations - his wife and his daughter in law.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Ruth 4:20-21; 1 Chronicles 2:11; Matthew 1:4-5; Luke 3:32
131

Hur

A leader in Israel who, with Aaron, held up Moses' hands at Rephidim and was left in charge of the people during Moses' ascent of Sinai.

Family

Not stated in Exodus. He is the grandfather of Bezaleel (Exodus 31:2), and 1 Chronicles 2:19-20 names a Hur of the tribe of Judah, son of Caleb and Ephrath, as Bezaleel's grandfather; the identification is likely but Exodus does not make it explicitly.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

At Rephidim, while Joshua fought Amalek, Moses went to the top of the hill with Aaron and Hur. When Moses' hands were heavy they put a stone under him, and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, one on one side and one on the other, "and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun," and Amalek was discomfited (Exodus 17:10-13).

When Moses went up into the mount he left instruction with the elders: "Behold, Aaron and Hur are with you: if any man have any matters to do, let him come unto them" (Exodus 24:14). Scripture records nothing further of him, and he is notably absent from the account of the golden calf, where Aaron acts alone.

What They Did Right

  • With Aaron, held up Moses' hands until sunset so that Israel prevailed over Amalek: Exodus 17:12.
  • Was trusted with joint charge of the people in Moses' absence: Exodus 24:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records only two things about him, and both are marks of trust. He is one of a small number of men in the Pentateuch given authority alongside Aaron. His disappearance from the narrative after Exodus 24:14 is unexplained; the text simply does not mention him again, and speculation about what became of him has no basis in Scripture.

Significance

The scene at Rephidim, in which victory depends on two men supporting the arms of a third, has been drawn on constantly in teaching on shared burden and intercession. His grandson Bezaleel was the chief craftsman of the tabernacle.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Exodus 17:10-13; Exodus 24:14; Exodus 31:2; Exodus 35:30; 1 Chronicles 2:19-20
132

Joshua

Son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim; Moses' minister, Israel's military commander, one of the two faithful spies, and the man who led Israel into Canaan.

Also called Oshea, Jehoshua, Jesus (Acts 7:45)

Family

Son of Nun (Exodus 33:11); of the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 13:8). Originally named Oshea; Moses called him Jehoshua (Numbers 13:16).

Chronology

Date not established precisely by Scripture. He died at 110 (Joshua 24:29). He was of an age to command in battle at Rephidim, early in the wilderness period, and lived through the forty years and the conquest.

Life Synopsis

Joshua first appears without introduction, chosen by Moses to lead the fighting at Rephidim: "Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek" (Exodus 17:9). He did so, and discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword while Moses' hands were held up.

He is next called Moses' minister. He went up with Moses into the mount of God (Exodus 24:13), and when Moses returned to the camp, Joshua "departed not out of the tabernacle" (Exodus 33:11). Coming down from the mount he heard the noise of the camp and took it for the noise of war (Exodus 32:17).

He was one of the twelve sent to search Canaan. Ten brought back an evil report; Joshua and Caleb rent their clothes and pleaded with the congregation: "The land, which we passed through to search it, is an exceeding good land... Only rebel not ye against the Lord" (Numbers 14:6-9). The congregation spoke of stoning them. Of that entire generation, only those two entered the land (Numbers 14:30, 14:38).

God named him as Moses' successor, "a man in whom is the spirit," and Moses laid his hands on him before Eleazar and the congregation (Numbers 27:18-23). After Moses' death he was charged to be strong and of a good courage and to meditate in the law day and night (Joshua 1:6-9). He led Israel over Jordan, took Jericho, and conducted the campaigns of the conquest, then divided the land by lot among the tribes.

At the end of his life he gathered Israel to Shechem, rehearsed God's dealings with them, and set the choice before them: "Choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord" (Joshua 24:15). He died at 110, and Israel served the Lord all his days and all the days of the elders that outlived him (Joshua 24:29-31).

What They Did Right

  • Fought Amalek at Moses' command and prevailed: Exodus 17:9-13.
  • Remained at the tabernacle when others departed: Exodus 33:11.
  • With Caleb, brought a faithful report of the land and urged the people not to rebel, at the risk of being stoned: Numbers 14:6-10.
  • Was named by God as a man in whom is the spirit, and commissioned before the whole congregation: Numbers 27:18-23.
  • Led Israel into the land and divided the inheritance: Joshua 11:23; Joshua 14:1.
  • Set his own house before the nation as an example of covenant loyalty: Joshua 24:15.
  • Scripture's summary is that Israel served the Lord all his days: Joshua 24:31.

What They Did Wrong

  • Urged Moses to forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying in the camp, and was rebuked: "Enviest thou for my sake?": Numbers 11:28-29. Scripture records the rebuke without further condemnation.
  • Made a league with the Gibeonites without asking counsel of the Lord, deceived by their pretence of coming from a far country: Joshua 9:14-15. The text names the failure explicitly: "and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord."

Character Assessment

One of the most consistently commended figures in the Old Testament, and one of only two men of his generation permitted to enter the land. Scripture nevertheless records two failures plainly, one of them - the Gibeonite league - with an explicit statement of what went wrong. His record is of a faithful man who twice acted without asking, not of a flawless one.

Significance

Joshua completed what Moses could not: the entry into the land promised to Abraham. His name is the Hebrew form of the name given to Christ, and Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8 both use it in arguing that the rest he gave was not the final rest. The charge given to him in Joshua 1:8-9 concerning meditation in the law and courage is among the most frequently cited passages in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Died at 110 years and was buried in the border of his inheritance in Timnathserah in mount Ephraim (Joshua 24:29-30).

Scripture

Exodus 17:9-14; Exodus 24:13; Exodus 32:17; Exodus 33:11; Numbers 11:28-29; Numbers 13:8, 13:16; Numbers 14:6-10, 14:30-38; Numbers 27:18-23; Deuteronomy 31:7-8; Joshua 1:1-9; Joshua 6:1-27; Joshua 9:14-15; Joshua 24:1-31; Acts 7:45; Hebrews 4:8
133

Bezaleel

Son of Uri, of the tribe of Judah; the chief craftsman of the tabernacle; the first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God.

Family

Son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah (Exodus 31:2). 1 Chronicles 2:19-20 traces the line through Caleb and Ephrath.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He worked at Sinai in the second year after the Exodus.

Life Synopsis

"See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah: and I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exodus 31:2-3). The gifts named are practical: to devise cunning works, to work in gold, silver, and brass, to cut and set stones, and to carve timber (Exodus 31:4-5).

He was given Aholiab as his associate, and with him the ability to teach was included in the gift (Exodus 35:34). He made the ark, the mercy seat, the table, the candlestick, the altars, and the court, and "made all that the Lord commanded Moses" (Exodus 37:1-38:22). The people brought so much material that the workmen had to tell Moses to restrain them (Exodus 36:5-7).

What They Did Right

  • Made all that the Lord commanded Moses, which is the text's own summary of his work: Exodus 38:22.
  • Taught others the craft alongside doing it himself: Exodus 35:34.
  • God's own commendation is the strongest statement: he was called by name and filled with the spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all manner of workmanship: Exodus 31:2-3; Exodus 35:30-31.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives him a commendation of an unusual kind. He is the first person in the Bible described as filled with the Spirit of God, and the gifting is for craftsmanship rather than prophecy or leadership - a fact the text states without any hint that it is a lesser thing.

Significance

Bezaleel built the tabernacle, its furniture, and the ark of the covenant. His calling establishes that skilled work is a matter of divine gifting, and it is the first and clearest biblical statement that the Spirit equips people for making things. He is remembered by name generations later, when Solomon's temple was being planned (2 Chronicles 1:5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 1:5.

Scripture

Exodus 31:1-11; Exodus 35:30-35; Exodus 36:1-2; Exodus 37:1-29; Exodus 38:22; 1 Chronicles 2:20; 2 Chronicles 1:5
134

Aholiab

Son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan; associate to Bezaleel in the building of the tabernacle; an engraver, cunning workman, and embroiderer.

Family

Son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan (Exodus 31:6).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He worked at Sinai in the second year after the Exodus.

Life Synopsis

God appointed him with Bezaleel: "And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the hearts of all that are wise hearted I have put wisdom" (Exodus 31:6). He is described as "an engraver, and a cunning workman, and an embroiderer in blue, and in purple, and in scarlet, and fine linen" (Exodus 38:23). Both he and Bezaleel were given the ability to teach others (Exodus 35:34).

What They Did Right

  • Worked with Bezaleel on all that the Lord commanded for the tabernacle: Exodus 36:1-2; Exodus 38:23.
  • Was given, with Bezaleel, the ability to teach the craft to others: Exodus 35:34.
  • Named by God as one endowed with wisdom of heart for the work: Exodus 31:6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His inclusion alongside Bezaleel is worth noting on its own terms: Bezaleel was of Judah, the royal tribe, and Aholiab of Dan, the tribe later most associated with idolatry in Israel (Judges 18:30-31). The two were set to the same work by name.

Significance

With Bezaleel he built the tabernacle and taught the craft to others, so that the work outlived the two of them. The pairing of a man of Judah with a man of Dan at the making of the sanctuary is recorded without comment, but it stands against any reading of tribal worth in Israel's founding work.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Exodus 38:23.

Scripture

Exodus 31:6; Exodus 35:34-35; Exodus 36:1-2; Exodus 38:23
135

Nadab (son of Aaron)

Eldest son of Aaron; one of the first priests of Israel; consumed by fire for offering strange fire before the Lord.

Family

Son of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23); brother of Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He had no children (Numbers 3:4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died at the tabernacle in the wilderness of Sinai (Numbers 3:4).

Life Synopsis

Nadab was among those called up the mount with Moses, Aaron, Abihu, and seventy elders, where "they saw the God of Israel" and did eat and drink (Exodus 24:9-11) - an extraordinary privilege given to very few. He was consecrated with his father and brothers as a priest (Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 8).

"And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord" (Leviticus 10:1-2). Moses' explanation to Aaron was, "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me" - and Aaron held his peace. Their bodies were carried out of the camp in their coats (Leviticus 10:3-5).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He was among those who went up the mount and saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-11), and was consecrated a priest, but Scripture records these as things granted to him rather than as commendations of him.

What They Did Wrong

  • Offered strange fire before the Lord, "which he commanded them not": Leviticus 10:1. Scripture states the offence in terms of what God had not commanded rather than describing what the fire was. Numbers 26:61 repeats the charge. The immediately following prohibition on wine and strong drink for priests (Leviticus 10:8-9) has led many to connect the two, but the text does not state that connection, and this reference does not assert it.

Character Assessment

A severe and compressed record: privileged above almost anyone in Israel, consecrated to the highest office, and destroyed within days of his consecration for an act of unauthorised worship. Scripture offers no mitigation and no commendation, and gives the reason in a single clause - the Lord had not commanded it.

Significance

The deaths of Nadab and Abihu establish at the very founding of the priesthood that access to God is on God's terms alone. The principle Moses states, "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me" (Leviticus 10:3), governs the whole sacrificial system that follows.

Death / Outcome

Consumed by fire from the Lord before the tabernacle, with his brother Abihu; he had no children (Leviticus 10:1-2; Numbers 3:4).

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:1, 24:9-11; Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 10:1-7; Numbers 3:2-4; Numbers 26:61; 1 Chronicles 24:1-2
136

Abihu

Second son of Aaron; one of the first priests of Israel; consumed with his brother Nadab for offering strange fire.

Family

Son of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23); brother of Nadab, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He had no children (Numbers 3:4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Abihu went up the mount with Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and seventy elders of Israel, and saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9-11). He was consecrated as a priest with his father and brothers (Exodus 28:1). With Nadab he took a censer, put fire and incense in it, and offered strange fire before the Lord which he had not commanded; fire went out from the Lord and devoured them both (Leviticus 10:1-2).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not: Leviticus 10:1; Numbers 26:61.

Character Assessment

Identical in the record to his brother Nadab, and assessed the same way. Scripture treats the two as acting together and records no distinction between them.

Significance

With Nadab, his death establishes the seriousness of unauthorised approach to God at the founding of the priesthood, and it is why the succession passed to Eleazar.

Death / Outcome

Consumed by fire from the Lord with Nadab; he had no children (Leviticus 10:1-2; Numbers 3:4).

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:1, 24:9-11; Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 10:1-7; Numbers 3:2-4; Numbers 26:61
137

Eleazar (son of Aaron)

Third son of Aaron; successor to his father as high priest; oversaw the division of the land with Joshua. Not to be confused with Eliezer of Damascus or Eliezer the son of Moses.

Family

Son of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23). Married one of the daughters of Putiel; father of Phinehas (Exodus 6:25).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He succeeded Aaron in the fortieth year after the Exodus (Numbers 20:25-28) and outlived Joshua (Joshua 24:33).

Life Synopsis

Eleazar was consecrated a priest with his father and brothers (Exodus 28:1). After the deaths of Nadab and Abihu he became chief over the Levites, with oversight of the sanctuary (Numbers 3:32; Numbers 4:16).

When Aaron was to die, Moses brought them up mount Hor, stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them on Eleazar, who came down as high priest (Numbers 20:25-28). He was named with Joshua and the princes to divide the inheritance among the tribes (Numbers 34:17; Joshua 14:1), and it was through him that Joshua was to enquire of the Lord by the judgment of Urim (Numbers 27:21). He stood with Joshua at the assignment of the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities (Joshua 21:1). The daughters of Zelophehad brought their case before him and Moses (Numbers 27:2).

What They Did Right

  • Took up the high priesthood at his father's death and continued the office through the conquest: Numbers 20:26-28.
  • Served with Joshua in dividing the inheritance among the tribes: Numbers 34:17; Joshua 14:1.
  • Was the appointed means by which Joshua was to enquire of the Lord: Numbers 27:21.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a long and uninterrupted service and nothing against him. He is one of the very few figures in the Pentateuch of whom no failure is recorded, and his career spans from the consecration at Sinai to the settlement of the land.

Significance

The high priestly line ran through him. His son Phinehas succeeded him, and the office remained in his house (1 Chronicles 6:4-15). His joint role with Joshua established the pattern of priestly and civil authority operating together in the division of the inheritance.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried in a hill that pertained to Phinehas his son, in mount Ephraim (Joshua 24:33).

Scripture

Exodus 6:23, 6:25; Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 10:6-16; Numbers 3:32; Numbers 4:16; Numbers 20:25-28; Numbers 27:2, 27:21-22; Numbers 34:17; Joshua 14:1; Joshua 21:1; Joshua 24:33
138

Ithamar

Fourth and youngest son of Aaron; a priest with charge over the service of the tabernacle.

Family

Son of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23); brother of Nadab, Abihu, and Eleazar.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Ithamar was consecrated a priest with his father and brothers (Exodus 28:1). He was given oversight of the accounting of the tabernacle materials (Exodus 38:21), and charge over the service of the sons of Gershon and of Merari in carrying the tabernacle (Numbers 4:28, 4:33). He is named with Eleazar in the rebuke over the sin offering after the death of Nadab and Abihu, when Moses was angry that it had not been eaten in the holy place, and accepted Aaron's answer (Leviticus 10:12-20).

What They Did Right

  • Served faithfully in the offices given him, including the accounting of the tabernacle and charge over the Gershonites and Merarites: Exodus 38:21; Numbers 4:28, 4:33.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He is included in Moses' rebuke of Leviticus 10:16-18 over the sin offering, but Aaron's answer satisfied Moses and the matter is not pursued: Leviticus 10:19-20.

Character Assessment

Scripture records steady administrative service and no failure. His portion of the record is unglamorous - inventories and transport duties - which is itself a fair picture of much of the priestly work.

Significance

A second priestly line descended from him alongside Eleazar's. Eli, the priest at Shiloh in the days of Samuel, was of the house of Ithamar, and the courses of the priests in David's time were divided between the two houses (1 Chronicles 24:3-6).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Exodus 6:23; Exodus 28:1; Exodus 38:21; Leviticus 10:6, 10:12-20; Numbers 4:28, 4:33; 1 Chronicles 24:1-6
139

Mishael

A Levite, son of Uzziel; one of the two men who carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp. Not to be confused with Mishael the companion of Daniel, also called Meshach.

Family

Son of Uzziel, who was the uncle of Aaron (Leviticus 10:4); brother of Elzaphan; cousin of Aaron.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He acted at the tabernacle in the wilderness of Sinai.

Life Synopsis

After fire from the Lord consumed Nadab and Abihu for offering strange fire, Aaron and his surviving sons were forbidden to leave the sanctuary or to mourn. Moses therefore called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, and said, "Come near, carry your brethren from before the sanctuary out of the camp." "So they went near, and carried them in their coats out of the camp; as Moses had said" (Leviticus 10:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed a difficult and defiling instruction without recorded hesitation, at a moment when fire had just fallen: Leviticus 10:4-5.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act and no words. He was given a task nobody would want, at the most frightening moment in the history of the young priesthood, and he did it exactly as told. The text notes the obedience plainly: "as Moses had said."

Significance

His service allowed the priesthood to continue without interruption, since Aaron and his surviving sons were forbidden to touch the dead or to leave the sanctuary (Leviticus 10:6-7).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Leviticus 10:5.

Scripture

Exodus 6:22; Leviticus 10:4-5
140

Elzaphan

A Levite, son of Uzziel; carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu from the sanctuary; chief of the house of the Kohathites.

Also called Elizaphan

Family

Son of Uzziel, uncle of Aaron (Leviticus 10:4); brother of Mishael.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

With his brother Mishael he was called by Moses to carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp, and did so (Leviticus 10:4-5). He was appointed chief of the house of the father of the families of the Kohathites (Numbers 3:30), the Levitical division charged with the most holy things of the sanctuary.

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed Moses in removing the bodies from before the sanctuary: Leviticus 10:4-5.
  • Was entrusted with the chief place over the Kohathites: Numbers 3:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records obedience in a hard task and a position of responsibility, and nothing against him.

Significance

Chief of the Kohathites, the family responsible for the ark and the vessels of the sanctuary (Numbers 4:4-15). His house is named again among the Levites in David's day (1 Chronicles 15:8).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 29:13, where his sons are named among the Levites who cleansed the house of the Lord.

Scripture

Exodus 6:22; Leviticus 10:4-5; Numbers 3:30; 1 Chronicles 15:8; 2 Chronicles 29:13
141

Shelomith (daughter of Dibri)

An Israelite woman of the tribe of Dan; mother of the man stoned for blaspheming the name of the Lord.

Family

Daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan (Leviticus 24:11). Her son's father was an Egyptian (Leviticus 24:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The incident occurred in the wilderness of Sinai.

Life Synopsis

Scripture names her in a parenthesis while recounting her son's offence: "and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan" (Leviticus 24:11). Her son, whose father was an Egyptian, quarrelled with a man of Israel in the camp and blasphemed the name of the Lord. He was put in ward until the mind of the Lord should be shown, and was then brought out of the camp and stoned (Leviticus 24:10-14, 24:23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Nothing she said or did is recorded. Scripture names her without attaching blame to her for her son's act.

Character Assessment

She is named and nothing more is said of her. It is worth noting that Scripture takes the trouble to record her name, her father, and her tribe while leaving her son unnamed - the reverse of its usual practice, and a detail the text does not explain.

Significance

The incident involving her son produced the statute on blasphemy and the law of equal justice for the stranger and the homeborn: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country" (Leviticus 24:22).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is named once, in Leviticus 24:11.

Scripture

Leviticus 24:10-23
142

The son of Shelomith

Unnamed. The son of an Israelitish woman and an Egyptian father, put to death for blaspheming the name of the Lord.

Family

Son of Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan; his father was an Egyptian (Leviticus 24:10-11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He went out among the children of Israel, and he and a man of Israel strove together in the camp. In the course of the quarrel "the Israelitish woman's son blasphemed the name of the Lord, and cursed" (Leviticus 24:10-11). He was brought to Moses and put in ward until the mind of the Lord should be shown. The Lord commanded that he be brought outside the camp, that all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and that the congregation stone him. It was done (Leviticus 24:12-14, 24:23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Blasphemed the name of the Lord and cursed: Leviticus 24:11. The judgment that followed came by direct word from the Lord (Leviticus 24:13-16).

Character Assessment

Scripture records the offence, the process, and the sentence, and nothing else about the man. It is careful to note that the matter was not decided by Moses on his own authority: he was held until the mind of the Lord was made known.

Significance

His case is the occasion of the law on blasphemy, and of the accompanying statement that the same law binds the stranger and the homeborn alike (Leviticus 24:16, 24:22).

Death / Outcome

Stoned outside the camp by the congregation, at the commandment of the Lord (Leviticus 24:23).

Scripture

Leviticus 24:10-23
143

Hobab

Son of Raguel the Midianite; brother-in-law or father-in-law of Moses; invited to guide Israel through the wilderness.

Family

Son of Raguel the Midianite (Numbers 10:29). The King James Version of Numbers 10:29 can be read as making either Hobab or Raguel the father-in-law of Moses, and Judges 4:11 calls Hobab the father in law of Moses. The relationship is genuinely ambiguous in the text and this reference does not resolve it.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He appears as Israel departed from Sinai.

Life Synopsis

As Israel prepared to leave Sinai, Moses said to him, "We are journeying unto the place of which the Lord said, I will give it you: come thou with us, and we will do thee good: for the Lord hath spoken good concerning Israel." Hobab answered, "I will not go; but I will depart to mine own land, and to my kindred." Moses pressed him: "Leave us not, I pray thee; forasmuch as thou knowest how we are to encamp in the wilderness, and thou mayest be to us instead of eyes" (Numbers 10:29-31). Scripture does not record his final answer. Judges 1:16 and Judges 4:11 indicate that his descendants did settle among Israel, which suggests he went, but Numbers leaves the reply unrecorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records his refusal and Moses' second appeal, but not his decision.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

An unfinished account. Moses valued his knowledge of the wilderness enough to plead with him twice and to offer him a share in the promise. The text simply stops without telling us what he chose, though the later presence of his descendants in Israel points one way.

Significance

The children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah (Judges 1:16), and Heber the Kenite, of the children of Hobab, is named in the account of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:11). Jael, who killed Sisera, was of that household.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention of his descendants: Judges 4:11.

Scripture

Numbers 10:29-32; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11
144

Eldad

One of two men on whom the Spirit rested in the camp, and who prophesied there rather than at the tabernacle.

Family

Not recorded. He was of the seventy elders written down by Moses (Numbers 11:26).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

When the burden of the people became too heavy for Moses, God took of the spirit that was upon him and put it on seventy elders, who prophesied. "But there remained two of the men in the camp, the name of the one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them; and they were of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp" (Numbers 11:26). A young man ran and told Moses, and Joshua said, "My lord Moses, forbid them." Moses answered, "Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord's people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them!" (Numbers 11:27-29).

What They Did Right

  • The Spirit rested upon him and he prophesied: Numbers 11:26. Moses explicitly refused to have him silenced and wished the same gift on the whole nation: Numbers 11:29.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Joshua urged Moses to forbid them, but Moses rebuked the objection rather than the men.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and the incident functions to commend rather than to censure. He was among those written down, and the Spirit came on him where he was.

Significance

Moses' answer - "would God that all the Lord's people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them" - anticipates the promise of Joel 2:28-29 that God would pour out his spirit upon all flesh, which Peter cites at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-18).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Numbers 11:27.

Scripture

Numbers 11:16-29
145

Medad

One of two men on whom the Spirit rested in the camp, and who prophesied there rather than at the tabernacle.

Family

Not recorded. One of the seventy elders written down by Moses (Numbers 11:26).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Named with Eldad as one of the two men who remained in the camp when the seventy went out to the tabernacle. The Spirit rested on him and he prophesied in the camp. Joshua asked Moses to forbid them, and Moses refused, wishing that all the Lord's people were prophets (Numbers 11:26-29).

What They Did Right

  • The Spirit rested upon him and he prophesied, and Moses defended him: Numbers 11:26, 11:29.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Identical in the record to Eldad, and assessed the same way. Scripture treats the two as a pair.

Significance

With Eldad, the occasion of Moses' wish that the Spirit would rest on all God's people.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Numbers 11:27.

Scripture

Numbers 11:16-29
146

Caleb

Son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, of the tribe of Judah; one of the twelve spies, and one of only two men of his generation to enter the land.

Family

Son of Jephunneh the Kenezite (Numbers 13:6; Joshua 14:6). Father of Achsah, whom he gave to Othniel (Joshua 15:16-17).

Chronology

Forty years old when Moses sent him to spy out the land, and eighty-five when he claimed his inheritance (Joshua 14:7, 14:10). Both figures are explicitly stated.

Life Synopsis

Caleb was sent with eleven others to search out Canaan. Ten returned saying the land ate up its inhabitants and the people were giants. "And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it" (Numbers 13:30). When the congregation still refused, he and Joshua rent their clothes and pleaded with them not to rebel, and the congregation spoke of stoning them (Numbers 14:6-10).

God's verdict on him is unusually personal: "But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it" (Numbers 14:24). The phrase "wholly followed the Lord" is applied to him repeatedly (Numbers 32:12; Deuteronomy 1:36; Joshua 14:8-9, 14:14).

Forty-five years later he came to Joshua at Gilgal and asked for the hill country: "Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the Lord spake in that day... if so be the Lord will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out." He was eighty-five, and said his strength was as it had been at forty (Joshua 14:10-12). Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron, and he drove out the three sons of Anak (Joshua 14:13-14; Judges 1:20). He offered his daughter Achsah to whoever took Kirjathsepher, and Othniel took it (Joshua 15:16-17).

What They Did Right

  • Brought back a faithful report of the land and urged the people to go up at once: Numbers 13:30.
  • With Joshua, pleaded with the congregation not to rebel, at the risk of being stoned: Numbers 14:6-10.
  • God's own testimony: he had another spirit with him and followed the Lord fully: Numbers 14:24.
  • Described four separate times as having wholly followed the Lord: Numbers 32:12; Deuteronomy 1:36; Joshua 14:8-9, 14:14.
  • At eighty-five asked for the hardest territory in the land, where the giants were, rather than an easy portion: Joshua 14:10-12.
  • Drove out the three sons of Anak from Hebron: Joshua 15:14; Judges 1:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One of the most consistently commended men in the Old Testament, and one of very few of whom Scripture records no failure at all. The formula used of him - that he wholly followed the Lord - is repeated by Moses, by God, and by Joshua. His request for the mountain at eighty-five is the clearest picture in Scripture of faith that has not softened with age.

Significance

With Joshua, the only man of the Exodus generation to enter the land, and living proof that the forty years of wandering were a judgment on unbelief rather than on the generation as such. His inheritance at Hebron placed the burial place of the patriarchs in the hands of a man who had believed God when the nation would not. His son-in-law Othniel became the first of the judges (Judges 3:9-11).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 1:20.

Scripture

Numbers 13:6, 13:30; Numbers 14:6-10, 14:24, 14:30, 14:38; Numbers 26:65; Numbers 32:12; Deuteronomy 1:36; Joshua 14:6-15; Joshua 15:13-19; Judges 1:12-20; 1 Chronicles 4:15
147

The ten spies

Unnamed as a body but named individually: the ten men sent to search Canaan who brought back an evil report, and died of the plague before the Lord.

Family

One ruler from each of ten tribes. Shammua of Reuben, Shaphat of Simeon, Igal of Issachar, Palti of Benjamin, Gaddiel of Zebulun, Gaddi of Manasseh, Ammiel of Dan, Sethur of Asher, Nahbi of Naphtali, and Geuel of Gad (Numbers 13:4-15). Caleb of Judah and Oshea, that is Joshua, of Ephraim went with them and are entered separately.

Chronology

In the second year after the Exodus, at the time of the firstripe grapes (Numbers 13:20).

Life Synopsis

They were sent from Paran to search the land - to see whether it was good or bad, the people strong or weak, few or many, and to bring of the fruit. They went up, searched forty days, and returned with a branch with one cluster of grapes borne between two on a staff (Numbers 13:17-25).

Their report began truthfully: "We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it. Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great" (Numbers 13:27-28).

Caleb stilled the people and said, "Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it. But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we."

"And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature... and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight" (Numbers 13:30-33).

The congregation wept all night, spoke of returning to Egypt, and of stoning Joshua and Caleb. The sentence followed: none of that generation over twenty would see the land, and they would wander forty years, a year for each day of the search.

"And the men, which Moses sent to search the land, who returned, and made all the congregation to murmur against him, by bringing up a slander upon the land, even those men that did bring up the evil report upon the land, died by the plague before the Lord. But Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, which were of the men that went to search the land, lived still" (Numbers 14:36-38).

What They Did Right

  • They went up and searched the land as they were sent, forty days, and brought back its fruit: Numbers 13:21-26.
  • Their report opened truthfully: the land did flow with milk and honey: Numbers 13:27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Concluded that Israel was not able to go up: Numbers 13:31.
  • Brought up an evil report and a slander upon the land, calling it a land that ate up its inhabitants: Numbers 13:32; Numbers 14:36.
  • Measured themselves and the enemy without reference to God: "we were in our own sight as grasshoppers": Numbers 13:33.
  • Made all the congregation to murmur against Moses: Numbers 14:36.

Character Assessment

Scripture is careful about what their fault was and was not. They were not wrong about the walls or the giants - Caleb did not dispute either. The charge is that they went from what they had seen to what Israel could not do, leaving God out of the reckoning, and then spread it. The phrase Scripture uses is not error but slander.

Significance

Their report cost a generation the land and cost Israel forty years in the wilderness, a year for each day they searched (Numbers 14:34). Hebrews and Psalms both return to it as the pattern of unbelief that keeps people out of God's rest (Psalms 95:8-11; Hebrews 3:16-19).

Death / Outcome

All ten died by the plague before the Lord (Numbers 14:37).

Scripture

Numbers 13:1-14:38; Deuteronomy 1:22-36; Psalms 95:8-11; Psalms 106:24-26; Hebrews 3:16-19
148

Korah

A Levite of the family of Kohath; leader of the rebellion against the authority of Moses and Aaron.

Also called Core

Family

Son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi (Numbers 16:1); cousin of Moses and Aaron. His children did not die with him (Numbers 26:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The rebellion occurred during the wilderness period, after the refusal of the land.

Life Synopsis

Korah, with Dathan, Abiram, and On, took two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown, and rose up before Moses. Their charge was that leadership had been usurped: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the Lord is among them: wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the Lord?" (Numbers 16:1-3).

Moses fell on his face, and put the matter to a test: each man was to take a censer and offer incense before the Lord, and the Lord would show whom he had chosen. He also charged Korah specifically with despising the Levitical service already given him and seeking the priesthood as well: "seek ye the priesthood also?" (Numbers 16:8-11).

The congregation was told to depart from the tents of the rebels. The ground clave asunder, and the earth swallowed them, their houses, and all that belonged to Korah, and they went down alive into the pit (Numbers 16:31-33). Fire came out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who offered incense (Numbers 16:35). Their censers were beaten into plates for a covering of the altar, as a memorial that no stranger should come near to offer incense (Numbers 16:39-40).

Numbers records one further detail: "Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not" (Numbers 26:11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Gathered a company against Moses and Aaron and challenged their leadership: Numbers 16:1-3.
  • Despised the Levitical service he had been given and sought the priesthood as well: Numbers 16:9-10.
  • The Psalms name the sin as envy: "They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord": Psalms 106:16.
  • Jude makes his rebellion a standing warning: men perish "in the gainsaying of Core": Jude 1:11.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. The charge Moses brought is precise, and it is not that Korah wanted responsibility but that he already had it and wanted more: he was a Levite with a place at the sanctuary, and he wanted the priesthood too. Scripture treats this as contempt for a gift rather than mere ambition. The judgment was immediate and public, and the New Testament cites it as a type of rebellion against God-given authority.

Significance

The rebellion produced the memorial covering of the altar (Numbers 16:38-40) and the budding of Aaron's rod (Numbers 17:1-10), both intended to settle the question of who might approach God. Notably, his line survived: the sons of Korah are named in the titles of eleven Psalms and served as singers in the temple (1 Chronicles 6:31-38; Psalms 42, 44-49, 84-85, 87-88). Judgment fell on the man and not on his house.

Death / Outcome

Swallowed alive by the earth with his household and all that belonged to him (Numbers 16:31-33).

Scripture

Exodus 6:21; Numbers 16:1-40; Numbers 26:9-11; Numbers 27:3; Psalms 106:16-18; Jude 1:11
149

Dathan

A Reubenite; one of the leaders of the rebellion against Moses.

Family

Son of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben (Numbers 16:1); brother of Abiram and Nemuel (Numbers 26:8-9).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Dathan joined Korah in rising against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1-3). When Moses sent to call him and his brother Abiram, they refused to come, and their answer is one of the sharpest speeches in the Pentateuch: "We will not come up: Is it a small thing that thou hast brought us up out of a land that floweth with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, except thou make thyself altogether a prince over us?" They called Egypt the land flowing with milk and honey - inverting the description of Canaan - and accused Moses of failing to deliver what he promised (Numbers 16:12-14).

He stood in the door of his tent with his wife, sons, and little children. The ground clave asunder and the earth swallowed him, his household, and all that belonged to him (Numbers 16:27, 16:31-33).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Rose up against Moses and Aaron with Korah: Numbers 16:1-3.
  • Refused Moses' summons and accused him of self-appointment and of bringing them out to die: Numbers 16:12-14.
  • Called Egypt the land flowing with milk and honey, reversing God's description of the promised land: Numbers 16:13.
  • Numbers 26:9 names him again with the explicit note that he "strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the Lord."

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Numbers goes out of its way to record his words, and the words are the case against him: contempt for the deliverance, nostalgia for Egypt, and the charge that Moses had made himself a prince. Numbers 26:9 makes explicit what the rebellion actually was - striving against the Lord.

Significance

With Abiram he is remembered in Israel's later confession of national sin (Psalms 106:17) and cited by Moses in Deuteronomy as an example the next generation should remember (Deuteronomy 11:6).

Death / Outcome

Swallowed alive by the earth with his household (Numbers 16:31-33).

Scripture

Numbers 16:1-35; Numbers 26:8-11; Deuteronomy 11:6; Psalms 106:17
150

Abiram

A Reubenite; brother of Dathan; one of the leaders of the rebellion against Moses.

Family

Son of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben (Numbers 16:1); brother of Dathan and Nemuel.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Abiram acted throughout with his brother Dathan. He joined Korah's company, refused Moses' summons, and made the same accusation - that Moses had brought them out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness, and had made himself a prince over them (Numbers 16:1-3, 16:12-14). He stood in his tent door with his family and was swallowed alive when the ground opened (Numbers 16:27, 16:31-33).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Rose up against Moses and Aaron: Numbers 16:1-3.
  • Refused Moses' summons and joined in the accusation against him: Numbers 16:12-14.
  • Numbers 26:9 records that he strove against Moses and Aaron in the company of Korah, "when they strove against the Lord."

Character Assessment

Identical in the record to his brother Dathan, and assessed the same way. Scripture consistently names the two together and records no distinction between them.

Significance

Named with Dathan in Israel's later confession (Psalms 106:17) and in Moses' charge to the next generation (Deuteronomy 11:6).

Death / Outcome

Swallowed alive by the earth with his household (Numbers 16:31-33).

Scripture

Numbers 16:1-35; Numbers 26:8-11; Deuteronomy 11:6; Psalms 106:17
151

On (son of Peleth)

A Reubenite named as one of the four who initiated the rebellion against Moses, and who then disappears from the account.

Family

Son of Peleth, of the sons of Reuben (Numbers 16:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He is named once: "Now Korah, the son of Izhar... and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men" (Numbers 16:1). He is never mentioned again. He is absent from the confrontation, from the judgment, and from the later summaries in Numbers 26:9-11, Deuteronomy 11:6, and Psalms 106:17, all of which name Dathan, Abiram, and Korah but not On.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • He is named among those who took men and rose against Moses: Numbers 16:1.

Character Assessment

A genuinely open case. He is named as one of the four instigators and then vanishes from a narrative that follows the other three to their deaths. Scripture gives no explanation - whether he withdrew, was spared, or was simply not mentioned again is not stated. Traditional Jewish commentary supplies an account of his wife persuading him to withdraw; that is extra-biblical and is not adopted here. The honest position is that the text names him once and is silent thereafter.

Significance

His disappearance from the record is itself notable, given how carefully Numbers, Deuteronomy, and the Psalms track the fate of the other three.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named once, in Numbers 16:1.

Scripture

Numbers 16:1
152

The man who gathered sticks on the sabbath

Unnamed. A man found gathering sticks on the sabbath day in the wilderness, and put to death for it by the direct command of the Lord.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day." Those who found him brought him to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation. "And they put him in ward, because it was not declared what should be done to him." The Lord said he should surely be put to death, and the congregation stoned him outside the camp, as the Lord commanded Moses (Numbers 15:32-36).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Gathered sticks on the sabbath day, in violation of the fourth commandment and of the specific prohibition on kindling a fire (Exodus 20:8-11; Exodus 35:3): Numbers 15:32. The sentence came by direct word from the Lord: Numbers 15:35.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the act, the uncertainty about the penalty, the direct enquiry, the divine answer, and the execution. It records nothing else about him - not his name, his tribe, his motive, or whether he knew what he was doing. The narrative's own emphasis falls on the fact that Israel did not presume to judge: they held him until the mind of the Lord was made known.

Significance

The incident, placed immediately after the law distinguishing sins of ignorance from presumptuous sin (Numbers 15:27-31), establishes the seriousness of the sabbath in Israel. It is one of only two occasions in the Pentateuch where a case is held over pending direct enquiry of God; the other is the blasphemer of Leviticus 24.

Death / Outcome

Stoned outside the camp by the congregation, at the commandment of the Lord (Numbers 15:36).

Scripture

Numbers 15:32-36; Exodus 20:8-11; Exodus 31:14-15; Exodus 35:3
153

Sihon

King of the Amorites at Heshbon; refused Israel passage and was destroyed.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned east of Jordan in the fortieth year of the wilderness period.

Life Synopsis

Israel sent messengers asking to pass through his land by the king's highway, promising to turn aside into no field or vineyard and to drink no well water. "And Sihon would not suffer Israel to pass through his border: but Sihon gathered all his people together, and went out against Israel into the wilderness" (Numbers 21:21-23). Israel smote him with the edge of the sword and possessed his land from Arnon to Jabbok. Deuteronomy adds that the Lord hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, in order to deliver him into Israel's hand (Deuteronomy 2:30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Refused Israel peaceful passage and attacked them: Numbers 21:23. Scripture records the refusal and the attack; Deuteronomy 2:30 states that the Lord hardened his spirit for this purpose, a statement the text makes without qualifying Sihon's own responsibility.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as an obstacle removed rather than as a man assessed. Deuteronomy 2:30 introduces the same tension found in the account of Pharaoh - divine hardening alongside human refusal - and, as there, the text does not reconcile the two.

Significance

The defeat of Sihon and Og gave Israel its first territory, east of Jordan, allotted to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Numbers 32:33). The victory is rehearsed repeatedly as evidence of God's power: in Moses' addresses (Deuteronomy 3:2-6), in Joshua's charge (Joshua 24:8), in Nehemiah's prayer (Nehemiah 9:22), and in two Psalms (Psalms 135:11; Psalms 136:19).

Death / Outcome

Slain with his sons and all his people; Israel possessed his land (Numbers 21:24-25; Deuteronomy 2:33).

Scripture

Numbers 21:21-31; Deuteronomy 2:24-37; Deuteronomy 3:2-6; Joshua 24:8; Nehemiah 9:22; Psalms 135:11; Psalms 136:19
154

Og

King of Bashan; the last of the remnant of giants; destroyed with all his people at Edrei.

Family

Not recorded, except that he had sons who died with him (Numbers 21:35).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Og went out against Israel with all his people to battle at Edrei. "And the Lord said unto Moses, Fear him not: for I have delivered him into thy hand, and all his people, and his land; and thou shalt do to him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites." Israel smote him, his sons, and all his people until none was left alive, and possessed his land (Numbers 21:33-35).

Deuteronomy adds a detail Israel evidently found remarkable: he remained of the remnant of giants, and his bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits broad (Deuteronomy 3:11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Went out to battle against Israel: Numbers 21:33. Scripture records no negotiation, and records the attack without further evaluation.

Character Assessment

As with Sihon, Scripture presents him as an enemy overthrown rather than a character assessed. The detail of his stature and his iron bedstead is recorded to convey the scale of what God delivered into Israel's hand, and the Lord's word to Moses - "Fear him not" - indicates that fear was the natural response.

Significance

With Sihon, his defeat secured the territory east of Jordan and became a standing example of God's power in Israel's memory. His kingdom of Bashan went to the half tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32:33; Deuteronomy 3:13). He is named in the recitals of Joshua 24, Nehemiah 9, and two Psalms.

Death / Outcome

Slain with his sons and all his people at Edrei; none was left alive (Numbers 21:35).

Scripture

Numbers 21:33-35; Numbers 32:33; Deuteronomy 3:1-13; Joshua 12:4-5; Joshua 13:12; Nehemiah 9:22; Psalms 135:11; Psalms 136:20
155

Balak

King of Moab, son of Zippor; hired Balaam to curse Israel.

Family

Son of Zippor (Numbers 22:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned in Moab in the fortieth year of the wilderness period.

Life Synopsis

Balak saw what Israel had done to the Amorites and was sore afraid. Rather than fight, he sent to Pethor for Balaam, saying, "Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people; for they are too mighty for me" (Numbers 22:2-6). His messengers came with the rewards of divination in their hand. When Balaam refused, Balak sent more princes, more honourable, with the promise of great honour and whatever Balaam asked (Numbers 22:15-17).

When Balaam came, Balak took him to three different high places to curse Israel, and three times a blessing came instead. His anger was kindled and he smote his hands together: "I called thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast altogether blessed them these three times. Therefore now flee thou to thy place" (Numbers 24:10-11). Balaam then delivered a fourth oracle, unbidden, prophesying a Star out of Jacob and a Sceptre out of Israel that would smite the corners of Moab (Numbers 24:17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Sought to have Israel cursed by hired divination: Numbers 22:5-6.
  • Attempted repeatedly to purchase a different answer, moving Balaam from place to place and raising his offer: Numbers 22:15-17; Numbers 23:13, 23:27.
  • Micah names his counsel as something Israel must remember against him: "O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted": Micah 6:5.
  • Revelation records that Balaam taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel: Revelation 2:14.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as a man trying to buy a supernatural outcome and failing at every attempt. His fear was reasonable and his method was not. The account is largely comic at his expense: he pays a great deal to hear his enemies blessed three times and then prophesied over a fourth.

Significance

His attempt to curse Israel produced instead four oracles of blessing, including the Star out of Jacob prophecy (Numbers 24:17), read as messianic. God's overruling of the curse is cited later as a mercy Israel should remember (Deuteronomy 23:4-5; Joshua 24:9-10; Nehemiah 13:2; Micah 6:5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Numbers 24:25, where he went his way.

Scripture

Numbers 22:1-24:25; Joshua 24:9-10; Judges 11:25; Micah 6:5; Revelation 2:14
156

Balaam

Son of Beor, of Pethor; a diviner hired by Balak to curse Israel, who blessed them instead, and who afterward counselled the seduction that brought a plague on Israel.

Family

Son of Beor (Numbers 22:5); called the son of Bosor in 2 Peter 2:15.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Balak sent for Balaam with the rewards of divination. God came to him at night and said plainly, "Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed" (Numbers 22:12). He sent the messengers away. Balak sent more honourable princes with a greater offer, and Balaam answered that he could not go beyond the word of the Lord for a house full of silver and gold - and then asked God again. He was told that if the men came to call him he might go, but must speak only what God said (Numbers 22:18-20).

He went, "and God's anger was kindled because he went" (Numbers 22:22). The angel of the Lord stood in the way with a drawn sword, visible to the ass but not to the prophet, until the ass was given speech and Balaam's eyes were opened (Numbers 22:23-31).

Three times Balak set him on a high place, and three times he blessed Israel: "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the Lord hath not defied?" (Numbers 23:8). His fourth oracle, given unasked, foretold a Star out of Jacob and a Sceptre out of Israel (Numbers 24:17).

He could not curse Israel, so he found another way. Numbers 31:16 records the outcome plainly: "Behold, these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the Lord in the matter of Peor." Israel joined itself to Baalpeor through the daughters of Moab and Midian, and twenty-four thousand died in the plague (Numbers 25:1-9). Balaam was killed with the sword among the Midianites (Numbers 31:8).

What They Did Right

  • Refused the first embassy and would not go when God forbade it: Numbers 22:13.
  • Declared that he could not go beyond the word of the Lord to do less or more: Numbers 22:18; Numbers 24:13.
  • Spoke only what God gave him to speak, and blessed Israel three times against the wishes of the man paying him: Numbers 23:8, 23:11-12, 23:20.
  • Prophesied the Star out of Jacob and the Sceptre out of Israel: Numbers 24:17.

What They Did Wrong

  • Asked God a second time about a matter God had already settled: Numbers 22:19. God's anger was kindled at his going (Numbers 22:22).
