A wife or concubine of a dead king carried a claim on his throne, which is why Solomon read Adonijah's request as he did (compare 2 Samuel 3:7; 2 Samuel 16:21-22). Her name is the hinge of the last act of David's succession.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 2:22.

Scripture

1 Kings 1:1-4, 1:15; 1 Kings 2:17-25
282

Benaiah

Son of Jehoiada; a mighty man of David's; captain of the guard, and made captain of the host by Solomon; executor of Solomon's judgments.

Family

Son of Jehoiada, a valiant man of Kabzeel (2 Samuel 23:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served under David and Solomon.

Life Synopsis

"He slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow." He also killed an Egyptian of great stature, plucking the spear out of his hand and killing him with it. He was honourable among the thirty and was set over David's guard (2 Samuel 23:20-23).

He refused to join Adonijah (1 Kings 1:8), and when David gave the order for Solomon's anointing he answered, "Amen: the Lord God of my lord the king say so too" (1 Kings 1:36). He went down with Zadok and Nathan and set Solomon on the mule.

Under Solomon he executed Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei, and was set over the host in Joab's place (1 Kings 2:25, 2:34-35, 2:46).

What They Did Right

  • Performed exceptional acts of courage recorded in detail: 2 Samuel 23:20-21.
  • Stayed loyal to David's declared succession when Joab and Abiathar did not: 1 Kings 1:8, 1:36.
  • Was set over the host and over the guard by two kings: 2 Samuel 23:23; 1 Kings 2:35.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He carried out three executions at Solomon's command, including Joab at the altar (1 Kings 2:29-34). Scripture presents these as the king's judgments and records no fault in the executioner.

Character Assessment

Scripture records courage and unbroken loyalty and nothing against him. He is one of the few men to serve at the top of both David's and Solomon's administrations.

Significance

His loyalty at the moment of Adonijah's attempt was decisive for Solomon's accession, and his appointment over the host ended the house of Zeruiah's grip on the army.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 27:5-6.

Scripture

2 Samuel 8:18; 2 Samuel 23:20-23; 1 Kings 1:8-44; 1 Kings 2:25-46; 1 Kings 4:4; 1 Chronicles 11:22-25; 1 Chronicles 27:5-6
283

Hadadezer

Son of Rehob, king of Zobah; defeated repeatedly by David, and the occasion of the Ammonite and Syrian war.

Also called Hadarezer

Family

Son of Rehob (2 Samuel 8:3). His servants included the kings who were tributary to him (2 Samuel 10:19).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. During David's reign.

Life Synopsis

"David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates. And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen." When the Syrians of Damascus came to help him, David slew twenty and two thousand of them (2 Samuel 8:3-6).

David took the shields of gold that were on his servants and brought them to Jerusalem, and from two of his cities exceeding much brass, which Solomon afterward used for the sea, the pillars, and the vessels of the temple (2 Samuel 8:7-8; 1 Chronicles 18:8).

After the Ammonites had humiliated David's ambassadors and hired Syrian help, the Syrians were beaten by Joab, "and when the Syrians saw that they were smitten before Israel, they gathered themselves together. And Hadarezer sent, and brought out the Syrians that were beyond the river." David gathered all Israel, crossed Jordan, and killed the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen; Shobach the captain of the host died there. "And when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them. So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more" (2 Samuel 10:15-19).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his campaigns and his defeats and passes no moral verdict on him.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats him as a military opponent rather than a moral subject. He is the most formidable of David's enemies by the numbers given, and the note that ends the account - the Syrians feared to help the Ammonites any more - marks the end of organised resistance north of Israel in David's reign.

Significance

The brass taken from his cities was used by Solomon for the brasen sea, the pillars, and the vessels of the house of the Lord (1 Chronicles 18:8). His defeats extended Israel's border to the Euphrates, the furthest extent recorded.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His servants made peace with Israel and served them (2 Samuel 10:19).

Scripture

2 Samuel 8:3-12; 2 Samuel 10:15-19; 1 Kings 11:23; 1 Chronicles 18:3-10; 1 Chronicles 19:16-19
284

Hanun

Son of Nahash, king of Ammon; humiliated David's ambassadors and brought on the Syrian war.

Family

Son of Nahash (2 Samuel 10:1-2).

Chronology

During David's reign, after Nahash's death.

Life Synopsis

"Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants for his father."

"And the princes of the children of Ammon said unto Hanun their lord, Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? hath not David rather sent his servants unto thee, to search the city, and to spy it out, and to overthrow it?"

"Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away. When they told it unto David, he sent to meet them, because the men were greatly ashamed: and the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return" (2 Samuel 10:1-5).

"And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David," they hired the Syrians of Bethrehob and Zoba, and of Maacah and Ishtob - thirty-three thousand men. Joab and Abishai divided the army between them, Joab saying, "Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the Lord do that which seemeth him good." The Syrians fled, and the Ammonites fled after them (2 Samuel 10:6-14).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Believed his princes' suspicion and treated an embassy of comfort as espionage: 2 Samuel 10:3-4.
  • Shaved half the beards of David's servants and cut away their garments, and sent them away so shamed that they could not enter the city: 2 Samuel 10:4-5.
  • Hired thirty-three thousand Syrians against Israel: 2 Samuel 10:6.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a young king who took bad counsel and turned an act of kindness into a war. The narrative is careful to show David's intention first, so that the insult is unprovoked, and equally careful to record David's response to his humiliated men - not vengeance first, but shelter at Jericho until their beards were grown.

Significance

His insult began the Ammonite and Syrian war, in the course of which David remained at Jerusalem and saw Bathsheba, and Uriah was killed at the siege of Rabbah (2 Samuel 11:1-27; 2 Samuel 12:26-31).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 19:6.

Scripture

2 Samuel 10:1-14; 1 Chronicles 19:1-9
285

Adoniram

Officer over the tribute and the levy under David, Solomon, and Rehoboam; stoned to death by Israel at the division of the kingdom.

Also called Adoram, Hadoram

Family

Son of Abda (1 Kings 4:6).

Chronology

He served from David's reign into Rehoboam's (2 Samuel 20:24; 1 Kings 12:18).

Life Synopsis

He is named over the tribute under David (2 Samuel 20:24), and "Adoniram the son of Abda was over the levy" under Solomon (1 Kings 4:6). He had charge of the thirty thousand men raised out of all Israel who went to Lebanon by courses, ten thousand a month (1 Kings 5:13-14).

When Israel rejected Rehoboam's answer and departed to their tents, "then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute; and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. Therefore king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem" (1 Kings 12:18).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his office under three kings and no act of his own. He administered the forced labour that Israel complained of, and the text charges the burden to Solomon and Rehoboam rather than to him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a long career in one office and a death that says more about his master than about him. Sending the man in charge of the levy to a people who had just demanded the levy be lightened is the last recorded decision of Rehoboam's before he fled, and it made the division permanent.

Significance

His killing was the point at which the breach became irreparable. He served longer in a single post than almost any official named in the historical books.

Death / Outcome

Stoned to death by all Israel (1 Kings 12:18; 2 Chronicles 10:18).

Scripture

2 Samuel 20:24; 1 Kings 4:6; 1 Kings 5:13-14; 1 Kings 12:18; 2 Chronicles 10:18
286

Zabud

Son of Nathan; a principal officer of Solomon, and the king's friend.

Family

Son of Nathan (1 Kings 4:5).

Chronology

During Solomon's reign.

Life Synopsis

Named once, in the list of Solomon's princes: "And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend" (1 Kings 4:5).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One clause, and nothing recorded of him but an office and a description. The description is the reason for the entry: the king's friend is a title Scripture gives to only one other man, Hushai the Archite, who was David's friend (2 Samuel 15:37; 1 Chronicles 27:33).

Significance

With Hushai he is one of two men in Scripture holding the office of the king's friend, which appears to have been a formal position at court rather than a description of affection.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

1 Kings 4:5; compare 2 Samuel 15:37; 1 Chronicles 27:33
287

Genubath

Son of Hadad the Edomite by the sister of Pharaoh's queen; brought up in Pharaoh's household among his sons.

Family

Son of Hadad the Edomite and the sister of Tahpenes the queen (1 Kings 11:19-20).

Chronology

During Solomon's reign, in the account of the adversaries God raised up (1 Kings 11:14).

Life Synopsis

Hadad the Edomite had fled to Egypt as a little child when Joab destroyed the males in Edom. "And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen."

"And the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh" (1 Kings 11:19-20).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Two verses, and nothing of his own is recorded. He is included because the detail is unusual and deliberate: an Edomite child, weaned by the queen of Egypt, raised in Pharaoh's house among Pharaoh's own sons.

Significance

His father Hadad was one of the adversaries God stirred up against Solomon after his idolatry (1 Kings 11:14-25).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

1 Kings 11:19-20
288

Solomon

Son of David and Bathsheba; third king of Israel; builder of the temple; granted wisdom beyond any before or after, and turned away in his old age.

Also called Jedidiah

Family

Son of David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:24); named Jedidiah by Nathan (2 Samuel 12:25). Married Pharaoh's daughter and many strange women; "he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines" (1 Kings 11:1-3). Father of Rehoboam by Naamah an Ammonitess (1 Kings 14:21).

Chronology

Reigned forty years in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:42). The temple was begun in the fourth year of his reign, four hundred and eighty years after the Exodus (1 Kings 6:1).

Life Synopsis

Solomon was anointed while David lived, after Adonijah's attempt, and secured the kingdom by executing Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei and removing Abiathar (1 Kings 1:32-2:46).

At Gibeon God appeared to him in a dream and offered him whatever he asked. He asked for "an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad," and God gave him wisdom and also the riches and honour he had not asked (1 Kings 3:5-13). The judgment of the two harlots and the living child followed, "and they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment" (1 Kings 3:16-28). He spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and people came from all kings of the earth to hear him (1 Kings 4:29-34).

He built the temple in seven years with Hiram's timber and craftsmen, and his own house in thirteen. At the dedication he stood before the altar, spread out his hands to heaven, and prayed one of the longest prayers in Scripture - and it is largely about foreigners, sin, exile, and the plea that God would hear from heaven and forgive (1 Kings 8:22-53). The glory filled the house.

The queen of Sheba came and found the half had not been told her. Silver was as stones in Jerusalem. He had ships, horses out of Egypt, and forty thousand stalls (1 Kings 10:1-29).

"But king Solomon loved many strange women... his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father." He went after Ashtoreth and Milcom and built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:1-8). God was angry, having appeared to him twice, and told him the kingdom would be rent from his son, with one tribe left for David's sake (1 Kings 11:9-13). Adversaries were raised up: Hadad, Rezon, and Jeroboam. He sought to kill Jeroboam, who fled to Egypt (1 Kings 11:14-40). He reigned forty years and died.

What They Did Right

  • Loved the Lord and walked in David's statutes at the beginning of his reign: 1 Kings 3:3.
  • Asked for an understanding heart to judge the people rather than long life, riches, or the lives of his enemies: 1 Kings 3:5-12.
  • Judged the case of the two harlots with the discernment that made his wisdom famous: 1 Kings 3:16-28.
  • Built the temple according to the charge given to David: 1 Kings 6:1-38.
  • Prayed at the dedication for God to hear the stranger who came from a far country for God's name's sake: 1 Kings 8:41-43.
  • Blessed the congregation and acknowledged that not one word of God's promise had failed: 1 Kings 8:56.
  • Christ cites his wisdom and his glory as real, while declaring both surpassed: Matthew 6:29; Matthew 12:42.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made affinity with Pharaoh and married his daughter: 1 Kings 3:1.
  • Sacrificed and burnt incense in high places: 1 Kings 3:3.
  • Multiplied horses out of Egypt, and silver and gold, against the law given for kings: 1 Kings 10:26-29; compare Deuteronomy 17:16-17.
  • Loved many strange women of the nations God had forbidden, taking seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines: 1 Kings 11:1-3.
  • His wives turned away his heart, and he went after Ashtoreth and Milcom: 1 Kings 11:4-6. Scripture's verdict is explicit: "Solomon did evil in the sight of the Lord."
  • Built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem: 1 Kings 11:7-8.
  • Sought to kill Jeroboam after God had told him the kingdom would be divided: 1 Kings 11:40.
  • Laid a heavy yoke and grievous service on Israel, which his son's refusal to lighten split the kingdom: 1 Kings 12:4.
  • Nehemiah names him as the standing warning: "did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?... nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin": Nehemiah 13:26.

Character Assessment

No life in Scripture has a steeper descent from a higher point. He asked for wisdom rather than wealth and was given both; he built the house of God and prayed a prayer of extraordinary depth at its dedication; and he ended building shrines to Chemolch and Molech on a hill overlooking that same temple. Scripture attributes the fall to a specific and mundane cause repeated three times - his wives turned away his heart - and notes with particular weight that God had appeared to him twice (1 Kings 11:9). His wisdom did not preserve him, which is a point the narrative makes without needing to state it.

Significance

Builder of the first temple, and the king under whom Israel reached its greatest extent and wealth. Traditionally the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon, and of Psalms 72 and 127 by their titles; each of those books ascribes itself to him in its opening verse (Proverbs 1:1; Ecclesiastes 1:1; Song of Solomon 1:1). The Song of Solomon names no one else of whom Scripture records a history, and so contributes no other entry to this work. His reign is the high point of the united kingdom, and his idolatry is the stated cause of its division (1 Kings 11:11-13). Christ invokes both his glory and his wisdom, and declares a greater than Solomon present (Matthew 12:42).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers after reigning forty years, and was buried in the city of David (1 Kings 11:42-43).

Scripture

2 Samuel 12:24-25; 1 Kings 1:1-11:43; 1 Chronicles 22:1-29:25; 2 Chronicles 1:1-9:31; Nehemiah 13:26; Psalms 72 title; Proverbs 1:1; Ecclesiastes 1:1; Song of Solomon 1:1, 3:7-11, 8:11-12; Matthew 6:29; Matthew 12:42
289

Hiram (king of Tyre)

King of Tyre; supplied cedar, fir, and craftsmen for the temple and for Solomon's house; a lifelong ally of David and Solomon.

Also called Huram

Family

King of Tyre (1 Kings 5:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was contemporary with both David and Solomon.

Life Synopsis

"Hiram was ever a lover of David" (1 Kings 5:1). He had sent cedar trees, carpenters, and masons to build David a house (2 Samuel 5:11). When Solomon succeeded, Hiram sent his servants to him, and Solomon proposed a contract for cedar and fir from Lebanon in exchange for food for his household. "And Hiram rejoiced greatly, and said, Blessed be the Lord this day, which hath given unto David a wise son over this great people" (1 Kings 5:2-9).

He supplied timber, gold, and workmen throughout the building. Solomon gave him twenty cities in Galilee, which displeased him - he called them Cabul - but he still sent six score talents of gold (1 Kings 9:11-14). His navy served with Solomon's, bringing gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:26-28).

What They Did Right

  • Was ever a lover of David, and dealt honourably with both kings: 1 Kings 5:1.
  • Blessed the Lord for giving David a wise son - a confession from a Gentile king: 1 Kings 5:7.
  • Supplied all the timber and craftsmen Solomon desired: 1 Kings 5:8-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He was displeased with the cities Solomon gave him and named them Cabul (1 Kings 9:12-13). Scripture records the displeasure without evaluating it, and notes that he sent gold nonetheless.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is one of a series of foreign figures in the historical books who deal generously with Israel and speak well of Israel's God, and his contribution to the temple was indispensable.

Significance

The temple was built with Tyrian timber, gold, and skill. The alliance he began with David lasted a generation and was the foundation of Solomon's maritime trade.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 9:21.

Scripture

2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Kings 5:1-18; 1 Kings 9:10-28; 1 Kings 10:11, 10:22; 1 Chronicles 14:1; 2 Chronicles 2:3-16
290

The queen of Sheba

Unnamed. A queen who came from a far country to prove Solomon with hard questions and confessed that the half had not been told her.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Hearing of Solomon's fame concerning the name of the Lord, she came to prove him with hard questions, with a very great train, camels bearing spices, gold, and precious stones. "And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not" (1 Kings 10:1-3).

Seeing his wisdom, his house, his table, his servants, his ministers and their apparel, his cupbearers and his ascent to the house of the Lord, "there was no more spirit in her." She said, "It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me... Blessed be the Lord thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the Lord loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice" (1 Kings 10:4-9). She gave a hundred and twenty talents of gold, spices, and precious stones, and returned to her own country.

What They Did Right

  • Travelled from a far country to seek wisdom, and came with hard questions rather than flattery: 1 Kings 10:1-2.
  • Acknowledged the truth of what she found, admitting she had not believed the report: 1 Kings 10:6-7.
  • Blessed the Lord God of Israel and attributed Solomon's throne to God's love for Israel and to judgment and justice: 1 Kings 10:9.
  • Christ commends her: "The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon": Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her, and Christ's use of her is the strongest commendation given to any Gentile in the Old Testament narrative: she is set up as the judge of a generation that would not come to hear one greater than Solomon.

Significance

Her visit is the high-water mark of Solomon's fame, and her confession that God set him on the throne "to do judgment and justice" states the purpose of the monarchy from an outsider's mouth. Christ's citation of her makes her a permanent witness against unbelief.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She returned to her own country (1 Kings 10:13).

Scripture

1 Kings 10:1-13; 2 Chronicles 9:1-12; Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31
291

Jeroboam (son of Nebat)

A servant of Solomon made king over the ten tribes; set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan; the man by whose sin every later king of Israel is measured.

Family

Son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda; his mother was Zeruah, a widow (1 Kings 11:26). Father of Abijah and Nadab (1 Kings 14:1, 14:20).

Chronology

Reigned twenty-two years over Israel (1 Kings 14:20).

Life Synopsis

Solomon saw that he was industrious and made him ruler over the burden of the house of Joseph. Ahijah the Shilonite met him with a new garment, rent it in twelve pieces, and gave him ten, with the promise that if he would keep God's statutes God would build him a sure house as he had built for David. Solomon sought to kill him and he fled to Egypt (1 Kings 11:26-40).

On Solomon's death he returned and led the appeal to Rehoboam to lighten the yoke. When Rehoboam refused, Israel made Jeroboam king over the ten tribes (1 Kings 12:1-20).

He then reasoned that if the people went up to sacrifice at Jerusalem their hearts would turn back to Rehoboam and they would kill him. "Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt." He set one in Bethel and one in Dan, made priests of the lowest of the people who were not of Levi, and ordained a feast in the eighth month "which he had devised of his own heart" (1 Kings 12:26-33).

A man of God from Judah cried against the altar at Bethel; Jeroboam put out his hand to have him seized and his hand dried up, and the altar was rent. He asked the man of God to entreat for him and his hand was restored - and "after this thing Jeroboam returned not from his evil way" (1 Kings 13:1-34).

When his son Abijah fell sick he sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah, now blind. The prophet knew her and sent back a sentence: God had rent the kingdom from David's house and given it to him, and he had done evil above all before him, casting God behind his back; his house would be swept away, and the child would die when she entered the city (1 Kings 14:1-18).

What They Did Right

  • He was a mighty man of valour and industrious, which is why Solomon promoted him: 1 Kings 11:28.
  • He asked the man of God to entreat the Lord for the restoring of his hand: 1 Kings 13:6. Scripture records the request without commending him, and immediately records that he did not turn from his evil way.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made two calves of gold and told Israel these were the gods that brought them out of Egypt: 1 Kings 12:28.
  • Made priests of the lowest of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi: 1 Kings 12:31.
  • Devised a feast of his own heart in the eighth month, in imitation of the feast in Judah: 1 Kings 12:32-33.
  • Did not return from his evil way even after his hand was withered and restored: 1 Kings 13:33.
  • Ahijah's charge is the fullest statement of it: he had done evil above all that were before him, made other gods and molten images, and cast God behind his back: 1 Kings 14:9.
  • The phrase "the sin of Jeroboam, who made Israel to sin" becomes the standing formula by which the northern kings are condemned for the next two centuries: 1 Kings 15:34; 1 Kings 16:26; 2 Kings 17:21-23.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and given a significance in Scripture beyond almost any other bad king. He received a genuine promise of a sure house on the same terms David had, and destroyed it within a chapter by an act of political calculation - the calves were not a lapse of faith but a policy, adopted because he reasoned about what would keep him on the throne. Scripture records his reasoning in his own words, which is what makes the condemnation so total.

Significance

His calves became the permanent religion of the northern kingdom, and 2 Kings 17:21-23 names his sin as the reason Israel was finally carried away to Assyria. Nineteen kings of Israel follow him and all but one are condemned in terms of him.

Death / Outcome

"The Lord struck him, and he died" (2 Chronicles 13:20); 1 Kings 14:20 records he slept with his fathers after twenty-two years, and Nadab his son reigned.

Scripture

1 Kings 11:26-40; 1 Kings 12:1-14:20; 1 Kings 15:29-30; 2 Kings 17:21-23; 2 Chronicles 13:1-20
292

Ahijah the Shilonite

A prophet of Shiloh who told Jeroboam he would receive ten tribes, and afterward pronounced the destruction of his house.

Family

Of Shiloh (1 Kings 11:29).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was old and blind by the time of Jeroboam's later years (1 Kings 14:4).

Life Synopsis

He found Jeroboam in the way, clad in a new garment, and the two were alone in the field. He caught the garment and rent it in twelve pieces, giving ten to Jeroboam with the word that God would rend the kingdom out of Solomon's hand - and with a conditional promise of a sure house if he would walk in God's ways (1 Kings 11:29-39).

Years later Jeroboam's wife came in disguise to enquire about their sick son. Ahijah's eyes were set by reason of age and he could not see, but the Lord had told him she was coming. He called out as she entered the door, "Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings," and delivered the sentence on the house of Jeroboam and on Israel (1 Kings 14:1-16).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's word to Jeroboam plainly, both the promise and the condition: 1 Kings 11:31-38.
  • Delivered the judgment on Jeroboam's house to the king's own wife, unflinchingly and to her face: 1 Kings 14:6-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. Both his messages are recorded in full, and the second is one of the harshest in the historical books, delivered by a blind old man to a queen who had come in disguise.

Significance

His two prophecies frame the whole of Jeroboam's career, and the second was fulfilled in the extinction of his house by Baasha (1 Kings 15:29). His words also contain the first prediction of Israel's uprooting beyond the river (1 Kings 14:15). He is named as a recorder of Solomon's acts (2 Chronicles 9:29).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 10:15.

Scripture

1 Kings 11:29-39; 1 Kings 12:15; 1 Kings 14:1-18; 1 Kings 15:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29; 2 Chronicles 10:15
293

Rehoboam

Son of Solomon; first king of Judah after the division; lost ten tribes by refusing to lighten his father's yoke.

Family

Son of Solomon by Naamah an Ammonitess (1 Kings 14:21). He had eighteen wives and threescore concubines, twenty-eight sons and threescore daughters (2 Chronicles 11:21).

Chronology

"Rehoboam was forty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem" (1 Kings 14:21).

Life Synopsis

All Israel came to Shechem to make him king and asked him to lighten the grievous service his father had put on them. He asked three days. The old men who had stood before Solomon advised him to speak good words and be their servant for ever; the young men who had grown up with him advised the opposite. He forsook the old men's counsel and answered roughly: "My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions" (1 Kings 12:1-14).

Israel answered, "What portion have we in David?" and departed. He sent Adoram over the tribute and Israel stoned him to death, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem in his chariot. He gathered Judah and Benjamin to fight, but Shemaiah the man of God forbade it, "for this thing is from me," and they obeyed (1 Kings 12:16-24).

Judah did evil in his reign, building high places, images, and groves, "and there were also sodomites in the land" (1 Kings 14:22-24). In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and Solomon's shields of gold, and Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place (1 Kings 14:25-27). Chronicles adds that when the princes and the king humbled themselves at Shemaiah's word, God said he would not destroy them but they would be Shishak's servants (2 Chronicles 12:6-8), and gives the final assessment: "he did evil, because he prepared not his heart to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 12:14).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed the word of Shemaiah and did not go up to fight against Israel: 1 Kings 12:22-24.
  • Humbled himself with the princes when Shemaiah brought the word about Shishak, and the wrath of the Lord turned from him: 2 Chronicles 12:6-7.
  • Strengthened Judah and sheltered the priests and Levites who came to him out of Israel, and walked in the way of David and Solomon for three years: 2 Chronicles 11:13-17.

What They Did Wrong

  • Forsook the counsel of the old men and answered the people roughly: 1 Kings 12:8, 12:13-14.
  • Allowed high places, images, groves, and sodomites in Judah: 1 Kings 14:22-24.
  • Forsook the law of the Lord when he was established and strong: 2 Chronicles 12:1.
  • Chronicles gives the summary charge: "he did evil, because he prepared not his heart to seek the Lord": 2 Chronicles 12:14.

Character Assessment

A mixed but largely poor record. His one great failure was a single conversation, and Scripture notes that the outcome was nonetheless from God, to fulfil the word by Ahijah (1 Kings 12:15). He obeyed a prophet twice and humbled himself once, and Chronicles credits three good years. The final verdict names the root: he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord.

Significance

Under him the kingdom divided permanently, and Judah's separate history begins. His loss of the temple treasures to Shishak within five years marks how quickly Solomon's wealth was stripped. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:7).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David (1 Kings 14:31).

Scripture

1 Kings 11:43-14:31; 2 Chronicles 9:31-13:7; Matthew 1:7
294

The man of God from Judah

Unnamed. A prophet sent to cry against the altar at Bethel, who obeyed in the great thing and disobeyed in the small, and was killed by a lion.

Family

Not recorded. Of Judah (1 Kings 13:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In the reign of Jeroboam.

Life Synopsis

He came by the word of the Lord to Bethel and cried against the altar while Jeroboam stood by it: a child named Josiah would be born to David's house and would burn men's bones on it. He gave a sign, and the altar was rent and the ashes poured out. Jeroboam put out his hand to have him seized and his hand dried up; at the prophet's entreaty it was restored (1 Kings 13:1-6).

Jeroboam invited him home for refreshment and a reward. He refused: "If thou wilt give me half thine house, I will not go in with thee... for so was it charged me by the word of the Lord, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest" (1 Kings 13:7-10).

An old prophet of Bethel overtook him and invited him home. He refused again with the same words, until the old prophet said, "I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him." He went back and ate. As they sat at table the word of the Lord came to the old prophet, who cried out that because he had disobeyed, his carcase would not come to the sepulchre of his fathers (1 Kings 13:11-22). A lion met him on the way and killed him, and stood by the carcase with the ass, killing neither (1 Kings 13:23-28).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered the word against the altar in the king's presence and gave the sign: 1 Kings 13:1-5.
  • Entreated the Lord for the king whose hand was withered against him: 1 Kings 13:6.
  • Refused the king's hospitality and reward outright, citing the charge given him: 1 Kings 13:8-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Turned back and ate and drank in Bethel on the word of another man, contrary to the direct charge God had given him: 1 Kings 13:19. The judgment names the fault exactly: "thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the Lord" (1 Kings 13:21).

Character Assessment

One of the most sobering accounts in the historical books. He withstood a king and refused a bribe, and was undone by a fellow prophet claiming a later revelation. Scripture explicitly states that the old prophet lied to him, and equally explicitly holds him responsible for believing it against a word he had received directly. The narrative offers no softening.

Significance

His prophecy named Josiah by name generations before his birth, and 2 Kings 23:15-18 records its fulfilment and Josiah's sparing of his sepulchre. The episode is the Old Testament's clearest warning that a new message contradicting a known command is to be refused however impressive its source.

Death / Outcome

Killed by a lion on the road, and buried by the old prophet in his own grave at Bethel (1 Kings 13:24-30).

Scripture

1 Kings 13:1-32; 2 Kings 23:15-18
295

The old prophet of Bethel

Unnamed. An old prophet dwelling in Bethel who lied to the man of God from Judah, brought him back, and afterward buried him and mourned him.

Family

He had sons (1 Kings 13:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

His sons told him what the man of God had done at the altar. He saddled his ass, overtook him under an oak, and invited him home. When refused, he said, "I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house... But he lied unto him" (1 Kings 13:11-18).

As they sat at table, the word of the Lord came to the old prophet - genuinely, this time - and he cried out the sentence against his guest (1 Kings 13:20-22). Hearing afterward that a lion had killed him, he went and fetched the body, mourned over him saying "Alas, my brother!", laid him in his own grave, and charged his sons: "When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones: for the saying which he cried by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel... shall surely come to pass" (1 Kings 13:29-32).

What They Did Right

  • Mourned the man he had destroyed, buried him in his own grave, and affirmed that his prophecy against Bethel would certainly come to pass: 1 Kings 13:29-32.

What They Did Wrong

  • Lied, claiming an angel had spoken to him by the word of the Lord, and so brought the man of God to his death: 1 Kings 13:18. Scripture states the lie flatly and gives no motive for it.

Character Assessment

Scripture never explains why he did it, and never states a judgment on him. What it records is that he lied, that the true word then came through him against his own guest, and that he afterward honoured the dead man and staked his own burial on the truth of his prophecy. He is one of the strangest figures in the historical books.

Significance

His request to be buried beside the man of God preserved both graves, and Josiah spared them when he burned the bones at Bethel three centuries later (2 Kings 23:17-18).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 13:31-32.

Scripture

1 Kings 13:11-32; 2 Kings 23:17-18
296

The wife of Jeroboam

Unnamed. Sent in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah to ask about her sick son, and told the child would die as she entered the city.

Family

Wife of Jeroboam; mother of Abijah (1 Kings 14:1-2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Jeroboam told her to disguise herself so she would not be known as his wife and to go to Ahijah at Shiloh with ten loaves, cracknels, and a cruse of honey (1 Kings 14:1-3).

Ahijah could not see, but the Lord had warned him. He called out as she came in at the door, "Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings." He gave her the sentence on the house of Jeroboam, and told her that when her feet entered the city the child would die, "and all Israel shall mourn for him, and bury him: for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel in the house of Jeroboam" (1 Kings 14:5-13). She arose, departed, and came to Tirzah, "and when she came to the threshold of the door, the child died" (1 Kings 14:17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. She carried out her husband's instruction and returned with the message. Scripture records no words of hers at all.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The disguise was Jeroboam's plan (1 Kings 14:2). Scripture records that she went and that the pretence was useless, and passes no verdict on her.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her nothing to say and no assessment. Her walk home carrying a sentence she could not avert, arriving at the threshold as the child died, is one of the bleakest journeys in the historical books.

Significance

The message she carried announced the end of Jeroboam's house and the eventual uprooting of Israel beyond the river (1 Kings 14:15-16). Her son Abijah is the only member of Jeroboam's house of whom Scripture records any good thing.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 14:17.

Scripture

1 Kings 14:1-18
297

Abijah (son of Jeroboam)

A son of Jeroboam who died as a child; the only one of Jeroboam's house in whom God found some good thing.

Family

Son of Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:1). Not to be confused with Abijam king of Judah.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He fell sick, and his father sent his mother in disguise to the prophet Ahijah. The answer included a word about the child: he alone of Jeroboam's house would come to the grave and be mourned by all Israel, "because in him there is found some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel in the house of Jeroboam" (1 Kings 14:1-13). He died as his mother crossed the threshold, and all Israel mourned and buried him (1 Kings 14:17-18).

What They Did Right

  • God's own testimony is the whole of it: in him there was found some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel: 1 Kings 14:13. Scripture does not say what it was.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing that he said or did, only God's assessment of him and his early death. The verdict is unique in the account of Jeroboam's house and is stated without explanation. His death is presented as mercy - he alone came to a grave and was mourned, while the rest of the house was to be swept away.

Significance

He is the one recorded exception in a house condemned entirely, and the passage is Scripture's clearest instance of God noting good in a single member of a family under judgment.

Death / Outcome

Died at Tirzah as his mother crossed the threshold; all Israel mourned him (1 Kings 14:17-18).

Scripture

1 Kings 14:1-18
298

Abijam

Son of Rehoboam; second king of Judah after the division; walked in his father's sins but was preserved for David's sake.

Also called Abijah (king of Judah)

Family

Son of Rehoboam; his mother was Maachah the daughter of Abishalom (1 Kings 15:2). Called Abijah in Chronicles.

Chronology

Reigned three years in Jerusalem (1 Kings 15:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father. Nevertheless for David's sake did the Lord his God give him a lamp in Jerusalem, to set up his son after him, and to establish Jerusalem" (1 Kings 15:3-4). There was war between him and Jeroboam all his days (1 Kings 15:6-7).

Chronicles records more: standing on mount Zemaraim he addressed Jeroboam's army, appealing to the covenant of salt given to David, denouncing the golden calves and the priests made of the lowest of the people, and declaring "God himself is with us for our captain." Judah cried to the Lord, and God smote Jeroboam; five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell, and Abijah took Bethel and other cities (2 Chronicles 13:4-20).

What They Did Right

  • Appealed publicly to the covenant with David and to the lawful priesthood and worship, and declared that God was with Judah: 2 Chronicles 13:4-12.
  • Judah cried to the Lord and prevailed "because they relied upon the Lord God of their fathers": 2 Chronicles 13:14-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked in all the sins of his father: 1 Kings 15:3.
  • His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as David's had been: 1 Kings 15:3.

Character Assessment

A genuinely divided record between the two accounts. Kings condemns him without qualification; Chronicles preserves a speech of considerable theological force and a victory attributed to reliance on the Lord. Both are Scripture and both stand. What Kings adds is the explanation of why he survived at all: not his own merit but David's, and God's purpose to keep a lamp in Jerusalem.

Significance

His reign preserved the Davidic line through a period when Judah's own kings did not deserve it - which is the point 1 Kings 15:4 makes explicitly. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:7).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David (1 Kings 15:8).

Scripture

1 Kings 14:31-15:8; 2 Chronicles 13:1-22; Matthew 1:7
299

Asa

Son of Abijam; third king of Judah; a reformer who removed idols and deposed his own grandmother, but relied on Syria rather than God at the end.

Family

Son of Abijam (1 Kings 15:8); Maachah the daughter of Abishalom is called his mother, meaning grandmother (1 Kings 15:10, 15:13). Father of Jehoshaphat (1 Kings 15:24).

Chronology

Reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem (1 Kings 15:10).

Life Synopsis

"And Asa did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, as did David his father." He put away the sodomites and all the idols his fathers had made, "And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt it by the brook Kidron." The high places were not removed, but his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days (1 Kings 15:11-14).

Chronicles adds that when Zerah the Ethiopian came with a host of a thousand thousand, Asa cried to the Lord: "Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee" - and the Ethiopians were overthrown (2 Chronicles 14:9-12). Azariah the prophet met him with a word, and he took courage and renewed the covenant (2 Chronicles 15:1-15).

Later, threatened by Baasha, he took silver and gold out of the treasures of the house of the Lord and hired Benhadad of Syria to break his league with Israel (1 Kings 15:16-20). Hanani the seer rebuked him for relying on Syria rather than on the Lord, "for the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him." Asa was wroth and put him in a prison house, and oppressed some of the people (2 Chronicles 16:7-10). "And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians" (2 Chronicles 16:12).

What They Did Right

  • Did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, as David: 1 Kings 15:11.
  • Removed the sodomites and the idols his fathers had made: 1 Kings 15:12.
  • Deposed his own grandmother from being queen and burned her idol: 1 Kings 15:13.
  • His heart was perfect with the Lord all his days: 1 Kings 15:14.
  • Cried to the Lord against overwhelming odds, resting on him: 2 Chronicles 14:11.
  • Renewed the covenant and gathered Judah to seek the Lord with all their heart: 2 Chronicles 15:8-15.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did not remove the high places: 1 Kings 15:14.
  • Hired Benhadad of Syria with the treasures of the house of the Lord instead of relying on God: 1 Kings 15:18-19; 2 Chronicles 16:7-9.
  • Imprisoned Hanani the seer for the rebuke and oppressed some of the people: 2 Chronicles 16:10.
  • In his disease sought the physicians and not the Lord: 2 Chronicles 16:12.

Character Assessment

A long and largely faithful reign that soured at the end. The same man who rested wholly on God against a million Ethiopians hired a pagan king with temple silver against a lesser threat, and jailed the prophet who pointed it out. Scripture holds both that his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days (1 Kings 15:14) and that he acted foolishly in relying on Syria (2 Chronicles 16:9), and does not reconcile them for the reader.

Significance

The first of Judah's reforming kings, and the pattern for those who follow: real reform, high places left standing, and a late failure. Hanani's word to him - that God's eyes run to and fro to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him - is among the most quoted verses in Chronicles. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:7-8).

Death / Outcome

Died in the forty-first year of his reign and was buried in his own sepulchre with a very great burning (2 Chronicles 16:13-14).

Scripture

1 Kings 15:8-24; 2 Chronicles 14:1-16:14; Matthew 1:7-8
300

Maachah (mother of Asa)

Daughter of Abishalom; queen mother in Judah, removed from that position by Asa for making an idol in a grove.

Family

Daughter of Abishalom (1 Kings 15:2); mother of Abijam and grandmother of Asa, called his mother in the sense of queen mother (1 Kings 15:10, 15:13).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She was the mother of Abijam and remained queen mother into Asa's reign. "And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt it by the brook Kidron" (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chronicles 15:16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made an idol in a grove: 1 Kings 15:13. Scripture records the act as the stated reason for her removal.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act and its consequence. Nothing she said is preserved.

Significance

Her removal shows the influence the queen mother held in Judah, and that Asa's reform reached into his own household at real personal cost.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 15:16.

Scripture

1 Kings 15:2, 15:10, 15:13; 2 Chronicles 15:16
301

Nadab (king of Israel)

Son of Jeroboam; second king of Israel; reigned two years and was killed by Baasha, ending Jeroboam's house.

Family

Son of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:25).

Chronology

Reigned two years over Israel (1 Kings 15:25).

Life Synopsis

"And he did evil in the sight of the Lord, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kings 15:26). While besieging Gibbethon of the Philistines, Baasha conspired against him and killed him, then destroyed the whole house of Jeroboam, "according unto the saying of the Lord, which he spake by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite" (1 Kings 15:27-30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and walked in his father's sin: 1 Kings 15:26.

Character Assessment

Two years, one verdict, and no recorded act besides a siege. He is the first of the many northern kings summarised in a single condemnatory formula.

Significance

His death fulfilled Ahijah's word against Jeroboam's house, which was cut off entirely (1 Kings 15:29-30).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Baasha at Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27-28).

Scripture

1 Kings 14:20; 1 Kings 15:25-31
302

Baasha

Son of Ahijah of Issachar; killed Nadab and destroyed Jeroboam's house; reigned twenty-four years and received the same sentence he had executed.

Family

Son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar (1 Kings 15:27). Father of Elah (1 Kings 16:6).

Chronology

Reigned twenty-four years over Israel (1 Kings 15:33).

Life Synopsis

He conspired against Nadab at the siege of Gibbethon, killed him, and slew all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed - fulfilling Ahijah's word (1 Kings 15:27-30). He reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah and "did evil in the sight of the Lord, and walked in the way of Jeroboam" (1 Kings 15:33-34).

He warred with Asa and built Ramah to blockade Judah, until Asa hired Benhadad to invade the north and he had to abandon it (1 Kings 15:16-22).

The word of the Lord came by Jehu son of Hanani: "Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel; and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam... behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha, and the posterity of his house." The charge included the killing of Jeroboam's house - for which he was both the instrument of judgment and himself guilty (1 Kings 16:1-7).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and walked in the way of Jeroboam: 1 Kings 15:34.
  • Was charged with provoking God to anger with the work of his hands, and also with killing the house of Jeroboam: 1 Kings 16:7. Scripture holds him accountable for an act that also fulfilled prophecy, without explaining the tension.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. His case raises plainly a difficulty the historical books do not resolve: he destroyed Jeroboam's house in fulfilment of God's word, and God's word against him names that destruction among his sins.

Significance

His dynasty lasted two reigns and was exterminated by Zimri exactly as Jehu had foretold, establishing the pattern of short violent dynasties that runs through the northern kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah (1 Kings 16:6).

Scripture

1 Kings 15:16-16:7; 1 Kings 16:11-13; 2 Chronicles 16:1-6; Jeremiah 41:9
303

Jehu (son of Hanani)

A prophet who pronounced judgment on Baasha and later rebuked Jehoshaphat for helping Ahab. Not to be confused with Jehu king of Israel.

Family

Son of Hanani (1 Kings 16:1); Hanani was the seer who rebuked Asa (2 Chronicles 16:7).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He prophesied under Baasha and was still active under Jehoshaphat.

Life Synopsis

The word of the Lord came to him against Baasha, announcing the destruction of his house (1 Kings 16:1-4, 16:7).

Years later he met Jehoshaphat returning from Ramothgilead: "Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the Lord? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the Lord. Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God" (2 Chronicles 19:2-3). He is named as a recorder of Jehoshaphat's acts (2 Chronicles 20:34).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's judgment on a reigning king of Israel: 1 Kings 16:1-4.
  • Rebuked a good king of Judah for an unequal alliance while acknowledging the good found in him: 2 Chronicles 19:2-3.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His rebuke of Jehoshaphat is a model of balance: the charge is stated first and plainly, and the commendation follows without cancelling it.

Significance

Father and son, Hanani and Jehu, both rebuked kings of Judah for foreign alliances, and both messages are preserved. His record of Jehoshaphat's acts was incorporated into the book of the kings of Israel (2 Chronicles 20:34).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 20:34.

Scripture

1 Kings 16:1-7, 16:12; 2 Chronicles 19:2-3; 2 Chronicles 20:34
304

Elah

Son of Baasha; king of Israel for two years; killed by Zimri while drinking himself drunk.

Family

Son of Baasha (1 Kings 16:6).

Chronology

Reigned two years over Israel (1 Kings 16:8).

Life Synopsis

"And his servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him, as he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza steward of his house in Tirzah. And Zimri went in and smote him, and killed him... and reigned in his stead" (1 Kings 16:9-10). Zimri then destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:11-13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • He was drinking himself drunk in a steward's house while his army was in the field at Gibbethon: 1 Kings 16:9, 16:15. Scripture records the circumstance without a separate charge, and the general condemnation of the house of Baasha covers his sins and his father's (1 Kings 16:13).

Character Assessment

Two years and one recorded scene, and the scene is his death while drunk. Scripture's judgment is delivered against the house rather than the man.

Significance

His death ended the house of Baasha and fulfilled Jehu's prophecy, and touched off the chaos of Zimri, Tibni, and Omri.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Zimri at Tirzah while drunk (1 Kings 16:10).

Scripture

1 Kings 16:6-14
305

Zimri

Captain of half Elah's chariots; killed the king and reigned seven days; burned the palace over himself when Omri besieged him.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

"Did Zimri reign seven days in Tirzah" (1 Kings 16:15).

Life Synopsis

He conspired against Elah, killed him, and destroyed all the house of Baasha, leaving not one that pisseth against a wall, neither of his kinsfolks nor of his friends - fulfilling Jehu's word (1 Kings 16:9-13).

The army at Gibbethon heard of it and made Omri king in the camp that same day. They went up and besieged Tirzah. "And it came to pass, when Zimri saw that the city was taken, that he went into the palace of the king's house, and burnt the king's house over him with fire, and died, for his sins which he sinned in doing evil in the sight of the Lord, in walking in the way of Jeroboam" (1 Kings 16:15-19).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Conspired against and murdered his master: 1 Kings 16:9-10.
  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, walking in the way of Jeroboam - in seven days: 1 Kings 16:19.
  • Jezebel later used his name as a byword for a treacherous servant: "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?": 2 Kings 9:31.

Character Assessment

The shortest reign in Scripture and one of the plainest condemnations. Seven days were enough for the historian to charge him with walking in the way of Jeroboam. His name became proverbial for regicide.

Significance

His coup and immediate destruction cleared the way for Omri, whose dynasty produced Ahab and shaped the next century of the northern kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Burned the king's house over himself and died in the flames when Tirzah was taken (1 Kings 16:18).

Scripture

1 Kings 16:9-20; 2 Kings 9:31
306

Omri

Captain of the host, made king by the army; founded the dynasty of Ahab and built Samaria; did worse than all before him.

Family

Father of Ahab (1 Kings 16:28-29); grandfather or ancestor of Athaliah (2 Kings 8:26).

Chronology

Reigned twelve years over Israel, six of them in Tirzah (1 Kings 16:23).

Life Synopsis

The army at Gibbethon made him king when they heard Zimri had killed Elah. He besieged Tirzah until Zimri burned the palace over himself. Half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath, and the two contended until Tibni died and Omri prevailed (1 Kings 16:16-22).

He bought the hill Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built on it, and named the city after its owner - establishing the capital of the northern kingdom for the rest of its existence (1 Kings 16:24).

"But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord, and did worse than all that were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin, to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities" (1 Kings 16:25-26). Micah later refers to "the statutes of Omri" as a byword for the corruption Israel kept (Micah 6:16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord and did worse than all before him: 1 Kings 16:25.
  • Walked in all the way of Jeroboam: 1 Kings 16:26.
  • His statutes were still being kept generations later and are named by Micah as a ground of judgment: Micah 6:16.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and given the strongest comparative verdict yet - worse than all before him. Scripture allots him six verses and shows no interest in his considerable political achievements beyond the purchase of Samaria.

Significance

Founder of the dynasty that produced Ahab, Ahaziah, Jehoram, and, through Athaliah, nearly destroyed the house of David in Judah. He built Samaria, which became the capital and the name for the northern kingdom in the prophets.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria (1 Kings 16:28).

Scripture

1 Kings 16:16-28; 2 Kings 8:26; 2 Chronicles 22:2; Micah 6:16
307

Tibni

Son of Ginath; followed by half of Israel as a rival to Omri, and died.

Family

Son of Ginath (1 Kings 16:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri. But the people that followed Omri prevailed against the people that followed Tibni the son of Ginath: so Tibni died, and Omri reigned" (1 Kings 16:21-22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his following and his death and passes no judgment on him.

Character Assessment

Two verses. He is included because Scripture records that half the nation followed him and that a civil war was fought over the succession - substantive facts, even though nothing personal is recorded.

Significance

His rivalry with Omri divided Israel for a period and shows how unstable the northern throne had become after three coups in a single generation.

Death / Outcome

"So Tibni died" (1 Kings 16:22). Scripture does not say how.

Scripture

1 Kings 16:21-22
308

Ahab

Son of Omri; king of Israel; married Jezebel and established Baal worship; opposed by Elijah; did more to provoke the Lord than all the kings before him.

Family

Son of Omri (1 Kings 16:29); husband of Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Father of Ahaziah, Jehoram, and Athaliah (1 Kings 22:40; 2 Kings 3:1; 2 Kings 8:18). He had seventy sons in Samaria (2 Kings 10:1).

Chronology

Reigned twenty-two years over Israel in Samaria (1 Kings 16:29).

Life Synopsis

"And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all that were before him... he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him. And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria. And Ahab made a grove; and Ahab did more to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel that were before him" (1 Kings 16:30-33).

Elijah announced a drought of three years, and at its end Ahab met him with, "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" Elijah answered that Ahab and his father's house had troubled Israel by forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). Ahab gathered the prophets to Carmel and watched the contest, then rode to Jezreel before the rain and told Jezebel all that Elijah had done (1 Kings 18:19-46).

When Naboth refused to sell his vineyard, Ahab came home heavy and displeased, lay on his bed, turned away his face, and would eat no bread. Jezebel arranged Naboth's judicial murder and told him to take possession. Elijah met him there: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?... In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood." Ahab said, "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" and heard the sentence on his house (1 Kings 21:1-24). Then he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, lay in sackcloth, and went softly - and God said to Elijah, "Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days" (1 Kings 21:27-29).

He twice defeated Benhadad by the word of unnamed prophets, then let him go with a covenant, and was told his life would go for Benhadad's life (1 Kings 20:1-43). At the last he persuaded Jehoshaphat to go with him to Ramothgilead. Four hundred prophets promised success; Micaiah alone foretold disaster, and Ahab had him imprisoned on bread and water. He disguised himself in the battle, and a man drew a bow at a venture and struck him between the joints of the harness. He was propped up in his chariot until evening and died, and the dogs licked his blood at the pool of Samaria (1 Kings 22:1-38).

What They Did Right

  • Humbled himself when the sentence was pronounced - rending his clothes, fasting, and going softly - and God himself acknowledged it and deferred the judgment: 1 Kings 21:27-29.
  • Obeyed the word of the prophets in the two campaigns against Benhadad: 1 Kings 20:13-21, 20:28-30.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil above all that were before him: 1 Kings 16:30.
  • Married Jezebel, served and worshipped Baal, and built him a house and altar in Samaria: 1 Kings 16:31-32.
  • Made a grove and did more to provoke the Lord than all the kings of Israel before him: 1 Kings 16:33.
  • Called Elijah the troubler of Israel: 1 Kings 18:17.
  • Let Benhadad go against the word of the Lord: 1 Kings 20:42.
  • Coveted Naboth's vineyard and took possession after Jezebel had him murdered: 1 Kings 21:4, 21:16.
  • Imprisoned Micaiah for prophesying truly, saying he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him: 1 Kings 22:8, 22:26-27.
  • Scripture's summary charge: "But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up": 1 Kings 21:25.

Character Assessment

Scripture's harshest verdict on any king of Israel, and it is delivered three separate times in escalating terms. Yet the record is not flat: he obeyed prophets in war, and his humbling after Naboth was genuine enough that God noted it aloud and deferred the judgment a generation. That is one of the most striking moments in the historical books - a real, if temporary, mercy granted to the worst of the northern kings. The account also apportions responsibility carefully: he sold himself to work wickedness, and Jezebel stirred him up.

Significance

Under him Baal worship became the state religion of Israel, which occasioned the ministry of Elijah and the entire prophetic conflict of 1 and 2 Kings. His marriage alliance carried Baal into Judah through his daughter Athaliah. The judgment on his house was executed by Jehu (2 Kings 9:1-10:17).

Death / Outcome

Struck by an arrow shot at a venture at Ramothgilead; he died at evening, the blood ran into the chariot, and dogs licked his blood at the pool of Samaria according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:34-38).

Scripture

1 Kings 16:28-22:40; 2 Kings 9:7-9; 2 Chronicles 18:1-34; Micah 6:16
309

Jezebel

Daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians; wife of Ahab; established Baal worship in Israel, cut off the prophets of the Lord, and engineered Naboth's murder.

Family

Daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians (1 Kings 16:31); wife of Ahab; mother of Ahaziah, Jehoram, and Athaliah.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She survived Ahab and both her sons' accessions and was killed in Jehu's purge.

Life Synopsis

Ahab married her and served Baal (1 Kings 16:31). She cut off the prophets of the Lord, so that Obadiah hid a hundred of them by fifty in a cave (1 Kings 18:4). Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of the groves ate at her table (1 Kings 18:19).

When Ahab told her of Carmel, she sent to Elijah: "So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I make not thy life as the life of one of them by to morrow about this time." Elijah fled for his life (1 Kings 19:1-3).

When Ahab lay sulking over Naboth's vineyard she said, "Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel? arise, and eat bread, and let thine heart be merry: I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth." She wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, proclaimed a fast, set Naboth on high among the people, suborned two sons of Belial to accuse him of blaspheming God and the king, and had him stoned (1 Kings 21:5-15). Elijah's sentence named her: "The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel" (1 Kings 21:23).

When Jehu came to Jezreel she painted her face, tired her head, and looked out at a window, calling, "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" Jehu called up for allies; two or three eunuchs threw her down, and her blood was sprinkled on the wall and on the horses. When they went to bury her they found no more than the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands (2 Kings 9:30-37).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Cut off the prophets of the Lord: 1 Kings 18:4, 18:13.
  • Maintained eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the groves at her own table: 1 Kings 18:19.
  • Swore to kill Elijah: 1 Kings 19:2.
  • Engineered Naboth's judicial murder by forged letters, a proclaimed fast, and suborned false witnesses - using the forms of law and religion to do it: 1 Kings 21:8-14.
  • Scripture states that she stirred up Ahab to work wickedness: 1 Kings 21:25.
  • Jehu names her whoredoms and witchcrafts as being many: 2 Kings 9:22.
  • Her name is used in Revelation for a teacher who seduces God's servants: Revelation 2:20.

Character Assessment

Uniformly and comprehensively condemned. What distinguishes her in the record is not merely idolatry but method: she killed Naboth by writing letters in the king's name, proclaiming a fast, and producing witnesses. Scripture is careful about the apportioning of blame - Ahab sold himself, and she stirred him up - so neither is excused by the other.

Significance

She made Baal the religion of the Israelite court and provoked the ministry of Elijah. Through her daughter Athaliah the same influence nearly extinguished the house of David. Her name is used in Revelation 2:20 as the type of corrupting influence tolerated within the church.

Death / Outcome

Thrown from a window at Jezreel, trampled by horses, and eaten by dogs, so that only her skull, feet, and palms remained - fulfilling Elijah's word (2 Kings 9:30-37; 1 Kings 21:23).

Scripture

1 Kings 16:31; 1 Kings 18:4-19; 1 Kings 19:1-2; 1 Kings 21:1-25; 2 Kings 9:7-10, 9:22, 9:30-37; Revelation 2:20
310

Hiel the Bethelite

The man who rebuilt Jericho in Ahab's days and lost his eldest and youngest sons, fulfilling Joshua's curse.

Family

Of Bethel; father of Abiram and Segub (1 Kings 16:34).

Chronology

In the days of Ahab (1 Kings 16:34).

Life Synopsis

"In his days did Hiel the Bethelite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun" (1 Kings 16:34). Joshua had sworn: "Cursed be the man before the Lord, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it" (Joshua 6:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Rebuilt Jericho under a standing curse pronounced by Joshua some five centuries earlier: 1 Kings 16:34; Joshua 6:26.

Character Assessment

One verse, and Scripture states the outcome as fulfilment rather than coincidence. No further comment is offered on the man, and the text does not say whether he knew of the curse.

Significance

The verse is placed immediately before Elijah's appearance, and it functions as a marker of how far Israel had gone: an ancient word of the Lord was being fulfilled in plain sight in Ahab's reign, and no one is recorded as taking notice.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His two sons died (1 Kings 16:34).

Scripture

Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 16:34
311

Elijah

The Tishbite of Gilead; prophet in the reigns of Ahab and Ahaziah; called down fire on Carmel and was taken up by a whirlwind without dying.

Also called Elias

Family

Not recorded. Called "Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead" (1 Kings 17:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He prophesied under Ahab and Ahaziah of Israel and sent a letter to Jehoram of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:12).

Life Synopsis

He appears without introduction: "As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word" (1 Kings 17:1). He was fed by ravens at the brook Cherith, then sustained by a widow of Zarephath whose barrel of meal did not waste, and raised her son from the dead (1 Kings 17:2-24).

In the third year he met Ahab and proposed the contest at Carmel. Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal called from morning until evening; he mocked them, then repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones, drenched the sacrifice with water three times, and prayed briefly: "Let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel, and that I am thy servant." The fire fell, the people cried "The Lord, he is the God," and the prophets of Baal were killed. He then prayed seven times for rain and outran Ahab's chariot to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:17-46).

Jezebel's threat sent him a day's journey into the wilderness, where he asked to die: "It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers." An angel fed him twice, and he went forty days to Horeb. There God asked him twice what he was doing, and he answered both times that he alone was left. The Lord passed by in wind, earthquake, and fire - and was in none of them - and then came a still small voice. He was given three commissions and told that seven thousand remained who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:1-18).

He met Ahab in Naboth's vineyard with the sentence on his house (1 Kings 21:17-24), and answered Ahaziah's messengers, calling down fire on two companies of fifty and going with the third whose captain begged for his life (2 Kings 1:1-16). He cast his mantle on Elisha, and at the end went over Jordan on dry ground and was taken up by a whirlwind into heaven with a chariot of fire and horses of fire (1 Kings 19:19-21; 2 Kings 2:1-12).

What They Did Right

  • Stood before God and declared the drought at the king's face: 1 Kings 17:1.
  • Obeyed the word to hide at Cherith and then to go to a foreign widow: 1 Kings 17:2-10.
  • Raised the widow's son and gave him to his mother: 1 Kings 17:17-24.
  • Confronted Ahab and four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal alone, and prayed a prayer of eleven words that God answered with fire: 1 Kings 18:36-38.
  • Prayed seven times for rain and did not stop: 1 Kings 18:41-45.
  • Confronted Ahab over Naboth's murder: 1 Kings 21:17-20.
  • James cites him as proof of the power of prayer, insisting he was a man of like passions with us: James 5:17-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • Fled from Jezebel's threat immediately after Carmel, and asked to die: 1 Kings 19:3-4. Scripture records the flight and the despair without condemning them, and records God's response as food, sleep, and a question rather than a rebuke.
  • Claimed twice that he alone was left, which God corrected: seven thousand had not bowed to Baal: 1 Kings 19:10, 19:14, 19:18.

Character Assessment

One of the most commanding figures in the Old Testament, and Scripture is careful not to make him more than a man. The same chapter that records fire falling from heaven at his word records him a day later under a juniper tree asking to die, and God's answer is not a reproof but bread and rest. James makes the point explicitly: he was subject to like passions as we are. His two recorded errors are both errors of despair, and both are met with gentleness.

Significance

He did not die, but was taken up alive (2 Kings 2:11), one of only two men in Scripture of whom this is recorded. Malachi promises that God will send Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5-6), which Christ applies to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12). He appeared with Moses at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

Death / Outcome

He did not die. "There appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire... and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven" (2 Kings 2:11).

Scripture

1 Kings 17:1-19:21; 1 Kings 21:17-29; 2 Kings 1:1-2:12; 2 Chronicles 21:12-15; Malachi 4:5-6; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:3-12; Luke 4:25-26; James 5:17-18
312

The widow of Zarephath

Unnamed. A widow of Zarephath in Zidon who fed Elijah from her last meal and whose son he raised from the dead.

Family

A widow with one son (1 Kings 17:12, 17:17).

Chronology

During the three-year drought in Ahab's reign (1 Kings 17:1, 18:1).

Life Synopsis

Elijah found her gathering sticks at the gate and asked for water and a morsel of bread. She answered, "As the Lord thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die." He told her to make him a little cake first, with the promise that the barrel of meal would not waste nor the cruse of oil fail until the Lord sent rain. "And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah" (1 Kings 17:9-16).

Afterward her son fell sick and died, and she said, "What have I to do with thee, O thou man of God? art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance, and to slay my son?" Elijah carried him up, laid him on his own bed, stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to the Lord; the child revived. She said, "Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in thy mouth is truth" (1 Kings 17:17-24).

What They Did Right

  • Gave her last meal to a stranger on the strength of a prophet's word, with her son starving: 1 Kings 17:12-15.
  • Confessed at the end that the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth: 1 Kings 17:24.
  • Christ cites her as the one widow in all Israel's famine to whom Elijah was sent: Luke 4:25-26.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Her outburst at her son's death is recorded without rebuke (1 Kings 17:18).

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and one act of extraordinary trust. She is a Zidonian - from Jezebel's own country - and she is the person to whom God sent his prophet during a famine in Israel. Christ makes precisely that point in Nazareth, and it nearly cost him his life.

Significance

Her son's raising is the first resurrection recorded in Scripture. Christ's use of her in Luke 4:25-26, alongside Naaman the Syrian, is his statement that God's mercy has always reached beyond Israel - and it is what enraged the synagogue at Nazareth.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 4:26.

Scripture

1 Kings 17:8-24; Luke 4:25-26
313

Obadiah (governor of Ahab's house)

Governor of Ahab's house who feared the Lord greatly and hid a hundred prophets from Jezebel. Not to be confused with the prophet Obadiah.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During the drought in Ahab's reign (1 Kings 18:1-2).

Life Synopsis

"Now Obadiah feared the Lord greatly: for it was so, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, that Obadiah took an hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water" (1 Kings 18:3-4).

Sent out by Ahab to look for grass to save the horses, he met Elijah and fell on his face. Told to go and announce Elijah to the king, he objected at length: the king had searched every nation for him and made them swear he was not found; if the Spirit carried Elijah away after he reported him, Ahab would kill him. He recited what he had done for the prophets and asked, "and now thou sayest, Go, tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah is here: and he shall slay me." Elijah swore he would show himself that day, and Obadiah went (1 Kings 18:7-16).

What They Did Right

  • Feared the Lord greatly, in Ahab's own household: 1 Kings 18:3.
  • Hid a hundred prophets by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water during a famine, at the certain risk of his life: 1 Kings 18:4, 18:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His protest to Elijah is recorded at length and shows fear, but Scripture neither rebukes it nor records Elijah doing so.
