Six months and a single formula. What the passage exists to record is the fulfilment: he was the fourth generation of Jehu, and with his murder the promise made at 2 Kings 10:30 was exactly discharged - no more and no less.

Significance

His death ends the longest dynasty of the northern kingdom and fulfils to the letter the word given to Jehu that his sons would sit on the throne to the fourth generation. After him the northern throne changed hands five times in about twenty years.

Death / Outcome

Struck down before the people by Shallum the son of Jabesh (2 Kings 15:10).

Scripture

2 Kings 10:30; 2 Kings 14:29; 2 Kings 15:8-12
343

Shallum (king of Israel)

Son of Jabesh; killed Zachariah and reigned a full month before being killed by Menahem.

Family

Son of Jabesh (2 Kings 15:10).

Chronology

"And Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the nine and thirtieth year of Uzziah king of Judah; and he reigned a full month in Samaria" (2 Kings 15:13).

Life Synopsis

He conspired against Zachariah, struck him down before the people, and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:10).

"For Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, and came to Samaria, and smote Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria, and slew him, and reigned in his stead. And the rest of the acts of Shallum, and his conspiracy which he made, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel" (2 Kings 15:14-15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Conspired against and murdered the king: 2 Kings 15:10. The record of his reign is summarised as "his conspiracy which he made" (2 Kings 15:15), which is the only act attributed to him.

Character Assessment

A month on the throne, and Scripture records nothing of him but the murder that put him there and the murder that ended it. He is not even given the usual verdict formula - there was no reign to assess.

Significance

His month is the second shortest reign in Scripture after Zimri's seven days, and it begins the rapid collapse of the northern monarchy.

Death / Outcome

Killed at Samaria by Menahem the son of Gadi (2 Kings 15:14).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:10-15
344

Menahem

Son of Gadi; killed Shallum and reigned ten years; smote Tiphsah with great cruelty and bought off the king of Assyria with silver exacted from the wealthy.

Family

Son of Gadi (2 Kings 15:14); father of Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:22).

Chronology

Reigned ten years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 15:17).

Life Synopsis

He came up from Tirzah, killed Shallum at Samaria, and reigned in his stead. "Then Menahem smote Tiphsah, and all that were therein, and the coasts thereof from Tirzah: because they opened not to him, therefore he smote it; and all the women therein that were with child he ripped up" (2 Kings 15:14-16).

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not all his days from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin" (2 Kings 15:18).

"And Pul the king of Assyria came against the land: and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand. And Menahem exacted the money of Israel, even of all the mighty men of wealth, of each man fifty shekels of silver, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back, and stayed not there in the land" (2 Kings 15:19-20).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Smote Tiphsah because it would not open to him, and ripped up all the women in it that were with child: 2 Kings 15:16.
  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not all his days from the sins of Jeroboam: 2 Kings 15:18.
  • Bought the confirmation of his own throne from the king of Assyria with a thousand talents exacted from his people: 2 Kings 15:19-20.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and the cruelty recorded of him at Tiphsah is among the most explicit in the historical books - the same atrocity Elisha had wept over when he foresaw Hazael doing it to Israel (2 Kings 8:12). His purchase of Assyrian support is stated with his motive attached: that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand.

Significance

His tribute is the first recorded payment by Israel to Assyria, and it brought the empire into the land on invitation. Within thirty years Assyria carried the northern kingdom away.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:22).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:14-22
345

Pekahiah

Son of Menahem; king of Israel two years; killed in the palace at Samaria by his own captain Pekah.

Family

Son of Menahem (2 Kings 15:22).

Chronology

Reigned two years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 15:23).

Life Synopsis

"In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Samaria, and reigned two years. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin."

"But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room" (2 Kings 15:23-25).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam: 2 Kings 15:24.

Character Assessment

Two years, one formula, and no recorded act. He is the fourth king of Israel in a row to be murdered by his successor.

Significance

His killing by his own captain continues the sequence of coups that ran from Zachariah to Hoshea and ended in the Assyrian conquest.

Death / Outcome

Killed in the palace of the king's house at Samaria by Pekah with fifty Gileadites (2 Kings 15:25).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:22-26
346

Pekah

Son of Remaliah; a captain who killed Pekahiah and reigned twenty years; joined Rezin against Judah, and lost the northern territories to Assyria.

Family

Son of Remaliah (2 Kings 15:25).

Chronology

Reigned twenty years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 15:27).

Life Synopsis

A captain of Pekahiah, he conspired with fifty Gileadites, killed him in the palace, and reigned in his room. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin" (2 Kings 15:25-28).

With Rezin king of Syria he came up against Jerusalem in the days of Ahaz. Isaiah was sent to tell Ahaz not to fear "for the two tails of these smoking firebrands," and gave the sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:1-16). Chronicles records that he slew in Judah a hundred and twenty thousand in one day, "because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers," and carried away two hundred thousand captives - who were sent home again at the word of the prophet Oded (2 Chronicles 28:5-15).

"In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria. And Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him, and reigned in his stead" (2 Kings 15:29-30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered Pekahiah to take the throne: 2 Kings 15:25.
  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam: 2 Kings 15:28.
  • Made war on Judah with Rezin and besieged Jerusalem: 2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:1.
  • Slew a hundred and twenty thousand in Judah in one day and carried two hundred thousand captive: 2 Chronicles 28:6-8.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Isaiah's dismissal of him and Rezin as two smoking firebrands - stubs of wood already burnt out - is the assessment Scripture gives of the alliance that terrified Ahaz, and it proved accurate: within a few years Assyria had taken half his kingdom and his own captain had killed him.

Significance

His war against Judah drove Ahaz to buy Assyrian help, which made Judah a vassal. His reign saw the first great deportation from the northern kingdom, Galilee and Gilead and Naphtali carried away, a generation before Samaria fell. The Immanuel prophecy was given in response to his invasion.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Hoshea the son of Elah, who reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:30).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:25-31; 2 Kings 16:5; 2 Chronicles 28:5-15; Isaiah 7:1-9
347

Jotham (king of Judah)

Son of Uzziah; king of Judah sixteen years; did right and became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord, though the people still did corruptly. Not to be confused with Jotham the son of Gideon.

Family

Son of Uzziah; his mother was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok (2 Kings 15:33). Father of Ahaz (2 Kings 15:38).

Chronology

"Five and twenty years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 15:33). He judged the people while his father was a leper (2 Kings 15:5).

Life Synopsis

While Uzziah lived in a several house as a leper, "Jotham the king's son was over the house, judging the people of the land" (2 Kings 15:5).

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord: he did according to all that his father Uzziah had done. Howbeit the high places were not removed: the people sacrificed and burned incense still in the high places. He built the higher gate of the house of the Lord" (2 Kings 15:34-35).

Chronicles adds the detail that distinguishes him: "he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord. And the people did yet corruptly." He built cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the forests, and prevailed against the Ammonites, who paid him tribute three years.

"So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God" (2 Chronicles 27:2-6).

What They Did Right

  • Did right in the sight of the Lord, according to all his father had done: 2 Kings 15:34.
  • Entered not into the temple of the Lord - the sin that had made his father a leper: 2 Chronicles 27:2.
  • Built the higher gate of the house of the Lord, and cities, castles, and towers in Judah: 2 Kings 15:35; 2 Chronicles 27:3-4.
  • Became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God: 2 Chronicles 27:6.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did not remove the high places, and the people sacrificed and burned incense there still: 2 Kings 15:35.
  • The people did yet corruptly in his reign: 2 Chronicles 27:2.

Character Assessment

One of Judah's better kings, and Chronicles states the reason for his strength in a single clause: he became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord. The most telling detail is the one Chronicles adds about the temple - he had watched his father struck with leprosy for presuming there, and he did not repeat it. Scripture is careful to separate his conduct from the nation's: he did right, and the people did yet corruptly.

Significance

He held the government during his father's leprosy and then reigned in his own right, and he is the last good king before Ahaz. Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah all date their ministries in part by him (Isaiah 1:1; Hosea 1:1; Micah 1:1). He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:9).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David (2 Kings 15:38; 2 Chronicles 27:9).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:5, 15:7, 15:30-38; 2 Kings 16:1; 1 Chronicles 3:12; 2 Chronicles 26:21-27:9; Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 7:1; Hosea 1:1; Micah 1:1; Matthew 1:9
348

Ahaz

Son of Jotham; king of Judah; sacrificed his son in the fire, stripped the temple to buy Assyrian help, and copied a pagan altar from Damascus.

Family

Son of Jotham (2 Kings 15:38); father of Hezekiah (2 Kings 16:20).

Chronology

"Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 16:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord his God, like David his father. But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yea, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen" (2 Kings 16:2-4).

When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besieged Jerusalem, he sent to Tiglathpileser of Assyria: "I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me." He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and of the palace and sent it as a present (2 Kings 16:5-8). Isaiah met him and offered him a sign, and he refused it with a show of piety - "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord" - and received the sign of Immanuel anyway (Isaiah 7:1-14).

He went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser, saw an altar there, sent the pattern to Urijah the priest, and had one built like it. He offered on it, moved the brasen altar aside, and altered the temple furniture for the king of Assyria's sake (2 Kings 16:10-18). Chronicles adds that in his distress he trespassed yet more, sacrificing to the gods of Damascus "which smote him," saying, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, therefore will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him, and of all Israel" (2 Chronicles 28:22-23). He shut up the doors of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 28:24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked in the way of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim: 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Chronicles 28:2.
  • Made his son to pass through the fire, after the abominations of the heathen: 2 Kings 16:3.
  • Stripped the house of the Lord to hire the king of Assyria rather than trust God: 2 Kings 16:8; 2 Chronicles 28:20-21.
  • Copied a pagan altar from Damascus and rebuilt the temple's arrangement around it: 2 Kings 16:10-16.
  • Sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they had defeated him: 2 Chronicles 28:22-23.
  • Shut up the doors of the house of the Lord and made altars in every corner of Jerusalem: 2 Chronicles 28:24.

Character Assessment

One of the worst kings of Judah, and the record is unusual in giving his reasoning. He sacrificed to the gods of the nation that had beaten him on the explicit theory that their gods were helping them - and Chronicles adds the verdict, "they were the ruin of him." He refused Isaiah's offered sign with language borrowed from piety.

Significance

It was to Ahaz that the sign of Immanuel was given - "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14) - which Matthew applies to the birth of Christ (Matthew 1:22-23). His submission made Judah a vassal of Assyria. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:9).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Jerusalem, but not brought into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel (2 Chronicles 28:27).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:38-16:20; 2 Chronicles 28:1-27; Isaiah 7:1-25; Matthew 1:9
349

Hoshea

Son of Elah; the last king of Israel; conspired with Egypt, was imprisoned by Shalmaneser, and saw Samaria taken and Israel carried away.

Family

Son of Elah (2 Kings 17:1).

Chronology

Reigned nine years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 17:1).

Life Synopsis

He conspired against Pekah and killed him and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:30). "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him" (2 Kings 17:2).

Shalmaneser of Assyria came up and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute. Then the king of Assyria found conspiracy in him, for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present as he had done year by year. He was shut up and bound in prison. The king of Assyria besieged Samaria three years and took it in the ninth year of Hoshea, and carried Israel away to Assyria (2 Kings 17:3-6).

The historian then gives the reason at length: Israel had sinned against the Lord who brought them out of Egypt, feared other gods, walked in the statutes of the heathen, built high places, set up images and groves, served idols, caused their children to pass through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil - and God had testified against them by all the prophets and all the seers, and they would not hear (2 Kings 17:7-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records that he did evil "but not as the kings of Israel that were before him" (2 Kings 17:2), which is a comparative statement rather than a commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord: 2 Kings 17:2.
  • Conspired with Egypt against Assyria and withheld the tribute: 2 Kings 17:4.
  • Murdered Pekah to take the throne: 2 Kings 15:30.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him nine verses and spends the rest of the chapter explaining that the fall of Israel was not really about him. The comparative note that he was not as bad as his predecessors, placed in the account of the kingdom's destruction, makes the point that judgment had been long accumulating.

Significance

The last king of the northern kingdom. Samaria fell in his ninth year and the ten tribes were deported, and 2 Kings 17:7-23 is Scripture's fullest single explanation of why - naming the sin of Jeroboam as the root and the rejection of the prophets as the immediate cause.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was shut up in prison by the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:4).

Scripture

2 Kings 15:30; 2 Kings 17:1-23; 2 Kings 18:9-12
350

Hezekiah

Son of Ahaz; king of Judah; removed the high places and the brasen serpent, trusted God against Sennacherib, and was given fifteen added years.

Also called Ezekias

Family

Son of Ahaz; his mother was Abi the daughter of Zachariah (2 Kings 18:2). Father of Manasseh (2 Kings 20:21).

Chronology

"Twenty and five years old was he when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 18:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father did. He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan." The assessment that follows is one of the strongest in Kings: "He trusted in the Lord God of Israel; so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him" (2 Kings 18:3-5).

He reopened and cleansed the temple his father had shut, restored the Levites and the service, and kept a great passover, inviting even the remnant of the northern tribes; some mocked, but many came, and there was great joy in Jerusalem, the like of which had not been since Solomon (2 Chronicles 29:1-30:27).

Sennacherib came up against all the fenced cities of Judah. Hezekiah first paid tribute, stripping the temple doors (2 Kings 18:13-16). Rabshakeh came to the wall and mocked God to the people in their own language. Hezekiah took the letter into the house of the Lord and spread it before him, praying, "Now therefore, O Lord our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord God, even thou only." Isaiah sent word, and the angel of the Lord smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp (2 Kings 19:1-36).

Sick unto death, he turned his face to the wall and wept, and was given fifteen more years and a sign (2 Kings 20:1-11). Afterward the ambassadors of Babylon came, and he showed them all his treasures. Isaiah asked what they had seen, and told him all would be carried to Babylon and his sons made eunuchs there. Hezekiah answered, "Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken" - and added, "Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?" (2 Kings 20:12-19).

What They Did Right

  • Did right according to all that David did, and removed the high places, which no king before him had done: 2 Kings 18:3-4.
  • Broke the brasen serpent that Moses had made, because Israel had made it an idol: 2 Kings 18:4.
  • Trusted in the Lord God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah before or after: 2 Kings 18:5.
  • Clave to the Lord and departed not from following him, and kept his commandments: 2 Kings 18:6.
  • Reopened and cleansed the house of the Lord which his father had shut: 2 Chronicles 29:3-19.
  • Kept a great passover and invited the remnant of Israel, praying for those who came unprepared: 2 Chronicles 30:1-20.
  • Spread Sennacherib's letter before the Lord and prayed that all the kingdoms of the earth might know God alone: 2 Kings 19:14-19.
  • Accepted Isaiah's word of judgment without protest: 2 Kings 20:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • Stripped the gold from the temple doors and pillars to pay Sennacherib's tribute: 2 Kings 18:15-16.
  • Showed all his treasures to the ambassadors of Babylon: 2 Kings 20:13-18. Chronicles states the cause: "his heart was lifted up," and that God left him to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart: 2 Chronicles 32:25-31.
  • His response to the sentence on his sons - "Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?" - is recorded without comment and reads as relief that judgment would fall after him: 2 Kings 20:19.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him the highest comparative verdict of any king of Judah: none like him before or after in trusting the Lord. It records his failures anyway, and Chronicles names the cause of the last one exactly - his heart was lifted up after the deliverance, and God left him to try him. The reform was genuine and thorough, reaching even to a relic of Moses that had become an idol.

Significance

His reform and passover were the most thorough since Solomon, and his deliverance from Assyria preserved Jerusalem when Samaria had fallen. His added fifteen years produced Manasseh, who undid the reform. His prayer and Isaiah's answer occupy two of the longest narrative passages in the prophets (Isaiah 36-39). He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:9-10).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David; all Judah and Jerusalem did him honour at his death (2 Kings 20:21; 2 Chronicles 32:33).

Scripture

2 Kings 16:20; 2 Kings 18:1-20:21; 2 Chronicles 29:1-32:33; Isaiah 36:1-39:8; Matthew 1:9-10
351

Sennacherib

King of Assyria; took the fenced cities of Judah, besieged Jerusalem and blasphemed the God of Israel, and lost a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in a night.

Family

Father of Adrammelech and Sharezer, who killed him (2 Kings 19:37).

Chronology

He came against Judah in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13).

Life Synopsis

He came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them, and Hezekiah paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (2 Kings 18:13-16). He then sent Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem.

His letter and his messenger's speech both rested on one argument: no god of any nation had delivered its land out of his hand, therefore neither would the Lord (2 Kings 18:33-35; 2 Kings 19:10-13). Isaiah's answer to him is one of the longest prophetic addresses to a foreign king in Scripture, and it turns the argument around: he was the axe in God's hand and had boasted against him who used it, and God would put a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came (2 Kings 19:20-28).

"And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses. So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh." As he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god, two of his sons killed him with the sword (2 Kings 19:35-37).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Reproached and blasphemed the living God, and lifted up his eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel: 2 Kings 19:22.
  • Reckoned the God of Israel among the gods of the nations, which were the work of men's hands: 2 Kings 19:17-18.
  • Boasted of his own conquests as though the axe could boast against him that hewed with it: 2 Kings 19:23-24; Isaiah 10:15.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats him as the type of imperial arrogance. Isaiah's oracle grants that he was genuinely an instrument in God's hand and condemns him precisely for not knowing it. His death, murdered by his own sons in his god's temple, is recorded in one verse without comment.

Significance

The destruction of his army delivered Jerusalem when every other fortified city of Judah had fallen, and it is the single greatest recorded deliverance in the history of the divided kingdom. Isaiah 10:5-19 uses him as the standing illustration of a nation used by God and judged for its pride.

Death / Outcome

Killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer with the sword while worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god (2 Kings 19:37).

Scripture

2 Kings 18:13-19:37; 2 Chronicles 32:1-22; Isaiah 10:5-19; Isaiah 36:1-37:38
352

Rabshakeh

A chief officer of Sennacherib sent to demand Jerusalem's surrender; addressed the people on the wall in Hebrew and mocked their God.

Family

Not recorded. Rabshakeh is an Assyrian office-title rather than a personal name; Scripture uses it as his designation.

Chronology

In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13, 18:17).

Life Synopsis

Sent with Tartan and Rabsaris and a great host, he stood by the conduit of the upper pool and addressed Hezekiah's officers. His argument was systematic: Egypt was a bruised reed that would pierce the hand; if they said they trusted in the Lord, was it not his high places Hezekiah had taken away? He offered two thousand horses if they could set riders on them, and claimed he had come up by the Lord's own word (2 Kings 18:19-25).

Eliakim asked him to speak in Syrian and not in the Jews' language in the ears of the people on the wall. He answered that his master had sent him precisely to the men on the wall, and raised his voice in Hebrew, telling them not to let Hezekiah deceive them, offering them their own vines and fig trees under Assyrian resettlement, and finishing: "Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of mine hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem out of mine hand?" The people held their peace and answered not a word, for the king's commandment was not to answer him (2 Kings 18:26-36).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Deliberately addressed the people over their officers' heads to break their morale: 2 Kings 18:27-28.
  • Ranked the God of Israel with the gods of the nations he had conquered: 2 Kings 18:33-35.
  • Claimed the Lord had sent him, using God's name to serve his own siege: 2 Kings 18:25.
  • Hezekiah and Isaiah both identify his words as reproaching and blaspheming the living God: 2 Kings 19:4, 19:6.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his speech at unusual length, which is itself significant - it is preserved because it is the most articulate case for despair anywhere in the historical books. He knew the political situation, knew about Hezekiah's reform, and turned both against the defenders. The people's silence is recorded as obedience to their king rather than as having no answer.

Significance

His speech is the occasion of Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's greatest oracle. It states the question the whole episode answers: whether the God of Israel is one god among the nations or the Lord of all the kingdoms of the earth.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He returned and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah (2 Kings 19:8).

Scripture

2 Kings 18:17-37; 2 Kings 19:4-8; Isaiah 36:2-37:8
353

Esarhaddon

Son of Sennacherib; succeeded him as king of Assyria after his brothers murdered him.

Family

Son of Sennacherib; brother of Adrammelech and Sharezer (2 Kings 19:37).

Chronology

He reigned after Sennacherib's murder (2 Kings 19:37).

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead" (2 Kings 19:37; repeated in Isaiah 37:38).

He is named once more, by the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin, who told Zerubbabel, "Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither" (Ezra 4:2).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his succession and, in Ezra, that he had resettled peoples in Samaria. It charges him with nothing.

Character Assessment

Scripture names him twice and records no act of his own beyond the resettlement implied in Ezra. He is included because the two mentions together connect the fall of Sennacherib to the mixed population that later opposed the rebuilding of the temple.

Significance

The peoples he brought into the land are the ones who offered to help build the second temple and, on being refused, weakened the hands of the people of Judah and hired counsellors against them (Ezra 4:1-5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38; Ezra 4:2
354

Manasseh (king of Judah)

Son of Hezekiah; king of Judah fifty-five years; the most idolatrous of Judah's kings, who was carried to Babylon in chains and humbled himself there.

Family

Son of Hezekiah; his mother was Hephzibah (2 Kings 21:1). Father of Amon (2 Kings 21:18).

Chronology

"Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and reigned fifty and five years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 21:1) - the longest reign of any king of Judah.

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, after the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel." He rebuilt the high places his father had destroyed, reared altars for Baal, made a grove, worshipped all the host of heaven, built altars in the house of the Lord and in its two courts, made his son pass through the fire, observed times, used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards. He set a graven image of the grove in the house of which God had said, "In Jerusalem will I put my name" (2 Kings 21:2-7).

"So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen." God spoke by his prophets and they would not hearken. "Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another" (2 Kings 21:9-16).

Chronicles alone records the sequel: the king of Assyria's captains took him among the thorns, bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. "And when he was in affliction, he besought the Lord his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord he was God." He took away the strange gods and the idol out of the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord - though the people still sacrificed in the high places (2 Chronicles 33:11-17).

What They Did Right

  • In affliction he besought the Lord, humbled himself greatly, and prayed - and God was intreated of him: 2 Chronicles 33:12-13.
  • Knew after his restoration that the Lord was God: 2 Chronicles 33:13.
  • Removed the strange gods and the idol from the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord: 2 Chronicles 33:15-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • Rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had destroyed and reared altars for Baal: 2 Kings 21:3.
  • Built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 21:5.
  • Made his son pass through the fire, observed times, used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: 2 Kings 21:6.
  • Set a graven image in the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 21:7.
  • Made Judah to do worse than the heathen God had cast out: 2 Kings 21:9.
  • Shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another: 2 Kings 21:16.
  • 2 Kings 24:3-4 names his sins as the reason God would not pardon Judah, and Jeremiah 15:4 says Judah would be removed into all kingdoms of the earth because of him.

Character Assessment

The most striking single case in the Old Testament of both extremes in one life. Kings records only the evil and names it as the cause of Judah's eventual destruction; Chronicles alone preserves the repentance, and records that God heard him. Both are Scripture. What Chronicles does not claim is that the repentance undid the consequences - Judah's course was not reversed, and his own son Amon returned to his father's idols without his father's repentance.

Significance

His reign is named twice as the reason for the exile (2 Kings 24:3-4; Jeremiah 15:4), which raises the hardest question in the historical books: a man personally forgiven whose national damage stood. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza (2 Kings 21:18).

Scripture

2 Kings 20:21-21:18; 2 Kings 23:26; 2 Kings 24:3-4; 2 Chronicles 32:33-33:20; Jeremiah 15:4; Matthew 1:10
355

Amon

Son of Manasseh; king of Judah two years; followed his father's idolatry without his repentance and was murdered by his servants.

Family

Son of Manasseh; his mother was Meshullemeth (2 Kings 21:19). Father of Josiah (2 Kings 21:26).

Chronology

"Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 21:19).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh did. And he walked in all the way that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshipped them: and he forsook the Lord God of his fathers, and walked not in the way of the Lord" (2 Kings 21:20-22). Chronicles adds, "and Amon trespassed more and more," and that unlike his father he did not humble himself before the Lord (2 Chronicles 33:23).

His servants conspired against him and slew him in his own house. The people of the land slew all who had conspired, and made Josiah his son king in his stead (2 Kings 21:23-24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil as his father Manasseh did, and served and worshipped his father's idols: 2 Kings 21:20-21.
  • Forsook the Lord God of his fathers: 2 Kings 21:22.
  • Did not humble himself before the Lord as his father had done, but trespassed more and more: 2 Chronicles 33:23.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and Chronicles draws the comparison that defines him: he inherited his father's sins and not his father's repentance. Two years, and the whole record is a contrast with the man before him.

Significance

His murder brought the eight-year-old Josiah to the throne, under whom Judah's last reform took place. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10).

Death / Outcome

Slain in his own house by his servants (2 Kings 21:23).

Scripture

2 Kings 21:18-26; 2 Chronicles 33:20-25; Matthew 1:10
356

Josiah

Son of Amon; king of Judah from the age of eight; found the book of the law, carried out the most thorough reform in Judah's history, and was killed at Megiddo.

Also called Josias

Family

Son of Amon; his mother was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath (2 Kings 22:1). Father of Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:30-34; 2 Kings 24:17).

Chronology

"Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 22:1). He was named by a prophet some three centuries before his birth (1 Kings 13:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in all the way of David his father, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left" (2 Kings 22:2). Chronicles records that in the eighth year of his reign, while still young, he began to seek after the God of David, and in the twelfth began to purge Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 34:3).

In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan to Hilkiah about the money for repairing the temple, and Hilkiah said, "I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord." When it was read to the king, "he rent his clothes," and sent to enquire of the Lord, "for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book" (2 Kings 22:8-13). Huldah the prophetess answered that the evil would come, but not in his days, because his heart was tender and he had humbled himself.

He gathered all the people, read the book in their ears, and made a covenant to walk after the Lord with all his heart and soul (2 Kings 23:1-3). He then purged the land: the vessels of Baal and the grove burned at Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the houses of the sodomites broken, the high places defiled, Topheth in the valley of the son of Hinnom defiled so that no man could make his son pass through the fire, the horses of the sun taken away, and the altar at Bethel broken down and its bones burned on it - fulfilling the word of the man of God from Judah, whose sepulchre he spared (2 Kings 23:4-20). He kept a passover such as had not been held since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-23).

"And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him" (2 Kings 23:25).

Pharaohnechoh went up against Assyria, and Josiah went out against him. Nechoh sent word that God had sent him and that Josiah should not meddle - and Chronicles states that Josiah "hearkened not unto the words of Nechoh from the mouth of God." He disguised himself and fought in the valley of Megiddo, was shot by the archers, and died (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:20-24). Jeremiah lamented for him, and all Judah mourned.

What They Did Right

  • Did right and walked in all the way of David, turning not aside to the right hand or to the left: 2 Kings 22:2.
  • Began to seek after God while still young: 2 Chronicles 34:3.
  • Rent his clothes at the reading of the law and sent to enquire of the Lord: 2 Kings 22:11-13.
  • Made a covenant before the Lord and had the whole people stand to it: 2 Kings 23:3.
  • Carried out the most thorough purge of idolatry in Judah's history, extending into Israel's territory: 2 Kings 23:4-20.
  • Kept a passover unlike any since the days of the judges: 2 Kings 23:21-23.
  • Scripture's verdict: no king before or after turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might as he did: 2 Kings 23:25.
  • Huldah's word: his heart was tender and he humbled himself before the Lord: 2 Kings 22:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • Went out against Pharaohnechoh and would not hear his warning; Chronicles states that Nechoh's words were from the mouth of God: 2 Chronicles 35:21-22. Kings records the campaign without comment, and Chronicles alone frames it as a failure to hear.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him the highest personal verdict of any king in either kingdom - none like him before or after in turning to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might. The one failure recorded is at the very end and is recorded only by Chronicles. His reform was the most thorough ever carried out, and it did not avert the judgment: 2 Kings 23:26 states that the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his wrath because of Manasseh's provocations.

Significance

Named by a prophet three centuries before his birth (1 Kings 13:2), and the fulfilment recorded in 2 Kings 23:15-18. His reform and his passover were Judah's last, and his death at Megiddo began the twenty-two-year collapse to the exile. Jeremiah lamented him, and the mourning for him became a proverb (2 Chronicles 35:25; Zechariah 12:11). He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10-11).

Death / Outcome

Shot by archers at Megiddo fighting Pharaohnechoh; brought to Jerusalem and buried in his own sepulchre, and lamented by Jeremiah and all Judah (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:23-25).

Scripture

1 Kings 13:2; 2 Kings 21:24-23:30; 2 Chronicles 34:1-35:27; Jeremiah 1:2; Zephaniah 1:1; Matthew 1:10-11
357

Hilkiah

High priest in Josiah's reign; found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.

Family

The high priest (2 Kings 22:4); father of Azariah in the priestly line (1 Chronicles 6:13).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Josiah sent Shaphan the scribe to him about the money gathered for repairing the temple. "And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it" (2 Kings 22:8). He was among those sent to Huldah the prophetess to enquire of the Lord (2 Kings 22:12-14), and afterward carried out the removal of the vessels of Baal and the grove from the temple (2 Kings 23:4).

What They Did Right

  • Reported the finding of the book of the law and handed it over at once rather than concealing it: 2 Kings 22:8.
  • Went with the king's officers to enquire of the Lord by Huldah: 2 Kings 22:14.
  • Carried out the cleansing of the temple at the king's command: 2 Kings 23:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The account does not explain how the book came to be lost in the house of the Lord, nor what he thought of finding it; it records only that he found it and immediately gave it to the king's scribe.

Significance

The book he found produced the reform, the covenant, and the passover of Josiah's reign, and its reading is one of the pivotal moments in Judah's history. His descendant Ezra is traced through the same line (Ezra 7:1).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 35:8.

Scripture

2 Kings 22:4-23:24; 1 Chronicles 6:13; 2 Chronicles 34:9-22; 2 Chronicles 35:8; Ezra 7:1
358

Shaphan

Scribe to Josiah; carried the found book to the king and read it before him; head of a family that repeatedly protected the prophets.

Family

Son of Azaliah the son of Meshullam (2 Kings 22:3). Father of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24), and grandfather of Gedaliah (Jeremiah 39:14).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Sent by Josiah to Hilkiah about the temple repairs, he received the book of the law, read it himself, and reported to the king: "Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king" (2 Kings 22:8-10). When the king rent his clothes, Shaphan was among those sent to Huldah (2 Kings 22:12-14).

What They Did Right

  • Read the book to the king rather than summarising or suppressing it: 2 Kings 22:10.
  • Went with the delegation to enquire of the Lord: 2 Kings 22:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His significance is largely in what his family did afterward: his son Ahikam saved Jeremiah's life, another son Gemariah had a chamber in the temple from which Baruch read the scroll, and his grandson Gedaliah was made governor after the fall of Jerusalem.

Significance

He read the law that started Josiah's reform. Three generations of his household appear in Jeremiah as protectors of the prophet and of the word - one of the clearest instances in Scripture of a family's continuing influence.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 39:14, by reference to his grandson.

Scripture

2 Kings 22:3-14; 2 Chronicles 34:8-20; Jeremiah 26:24; Jeremiah 36:10-12; Jeremiah 39:14
359

Huldah

A prophetess in Jerusalem, consulted by Josiah's officers about the found book of the law; confirmed the judgment and promised Josiah he would be gathered to his grave in peace.

Family

Wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, keeper of the wardrobe; she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college (2 Kings 22:14).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Hilkiah the high priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah went to her. She answered without softening: "Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me, Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read: because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods... therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched."

To the king she sent a separate word: "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the Lord, when thou heardest what I spake against this place... and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord. Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place" (2 Kings 22:15-20).

What They Did Right

  • Gave God's word without softening it, to the high priest and the king's officers: 2 Kings 22:16-17.
  • Distinguished the judgment on the nation from God's answer to the king's own tenderness of heart: 2 Kings 22:18-20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. She is consulted by the high priest and the king's secretary at the most significant moment of Josiah's reign, while Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both prophesying - and the text offers no explanation of why she was chosen, nor any comment on her being a woman. Her answer is the whole of her record and it is entirely direct.

Significance

One of the small number of women called prophetess in Scripture, with Miriam, Deborah, Noadiah, and Anna. Her word authenticated the found book, set the reform in motion, and defined its limits: the reform would be genuine and the judgment would still come.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 34:22-28.

Scripture

2 Kings 22:14-20; 2 Chronicles 34:22-28
360

Jehoahaz (king of Judah)

Son of Josiah; king of Judah three months; deposed by Pharaohnechoh and died in Egypt.

Also called Shallum

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kings 23:31). Called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11.

Chronology

"Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 23:31).

Life Synopsis

The people of the land took him and made him king after his father's death. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done" (2 Kings 23:30-32).

Pharaohnechoh put him in bands at Riblah, put the land to a tribute, made his brother Eliakim king in his place and changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, "and he came to Egypt, and died there" (2 Kings 23:33-34).

Jeremiah's word concerning him: "Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country" (Jeremiah 22:10-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done: 2 Kings 23:32.

Character Assessment

Three months, one verdict. Scripture's fuller comment comes through Jeremiah, who told Judah to mourn not for Josiah who had died but for this son who would never see his country again.

Significance

His deposition by Egypt ended Judah's independence. Every king after him was installed by a foreign power.

Death / Outcome

Died in Egypt (2 Kings 23:34).

Scripture

2 Kings 23:30-34; 2 Chronicles 36:1-4; Jeremiah 22:10-12
361

Jehoiakim

Son of Josiah; installed by Pharaohnechoh; taxed the land for tribute, burned Jeremiah's scroll, and shed innocent blood.

Also called Eliakim

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Zebudah the daughter of Pedaiah (2 Kings 23:36). Originally Eliakim; renamed by Pharaohnechoh. Father of Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:6).

Chronology

"Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 23:36).

Life Synopsis

Made king by Pharaohnechoh, he taxed the land to give the tribute, exacting silver and gold of the people of the land, every man according to his taxation. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done" (2 Kings 23:35-37).

Nebuchadnezzar came up and he became his servant three years, then rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). Bands of Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites were sent against Judah, "according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by his servants the prophets" (2 Kings 24:2).

Jeremiah dictated a scroll to Baruch and it was read in the temple and then before the princes and finally to the king in his winter house. "And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed... Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, neither the king, nor any of his servants, that heard all these words." He ordered Baruch and Jeremiah arrested, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:21-26). Jeremiah also records that he killed the prophet Urijah, having him fetched back from Egypt (Jeremiah 26:20-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done: 2 Kings 23:37.
  • Taxed the people of the land to pay tribute to Egypt: 2 Kings 23:35.
  • Cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it, and neither he nor his servants were afraid nor rent their garments: Jeremiah 36:23-24.
  • Sought to seize Jeremiah and Baruch: Jeremiah 36:26.
  • Had the prophet Urijah brought back from Egypt and killed with the sword: Jeremiah 26:20-23.
  • Jeremiah's charge: his eyes and heart were for covetousness, for shedding innocent blood, for oppression and violence: Jeremiah 22:17.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and given one of the harshest prophetic sentences in Scripture: "He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 22:19). The burning of the scroll is the defining act - deliberate, unhurried, page by page, and without fear.

Significance

His rebellion brought Nebuchadnezzar against Judah and began the deportations. The burning of the scroll and its rewriting with many like words added (Jeremiah 36:32) is Scripture's clearest statement that the word cannot be destroyed by destroying the copy. He stands in the genealogy of Christ under Josiah's line (Matthew 1:11).

Death / Outcome

"So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers" (2 Kings 24:6). Jeremiah 22:18-19 and Jeremiah 36:30 pronounce that he would be buried with the burial of an ass and his body cast out; Scripture does not narrate the manner of his death.

Scripture

2 Kings 23:34-24:7; 2 Chronicles 36:4-8; Jeremiah 22:13-19; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Jeremiah 36:1-32; Daniel 1:1-2; Matthew 1:11
362

Jehoiachin

Son of Jehoiakim; king of Judah three months; carried to Babylon with the treasures and the craftsmen, and released from prison thirty-seven years later.

Also called Jeconiah, Coniah, Jechonias

Family

Son of Jehoiakim; his mother was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan (2 Kings 24:8).

Chronology

"Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months" (2 Kings 24:8). He was released in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity (2 Kings 25:27).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father had done" (2 Kings 24:9). Nebuchadnezzar's servants besieged Jerusalem, and he went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes, and his officers.

Nebuchadnezzar carried out all the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, cut in pieces the vessels of gold that Solomon had made, and carried away all Jerusalem - the princes, the mighty men of valour, the craftsmen and smiths, ten thousand captives - leaving none save the poorest sort of the people of the land (2 Kings 24:10-16).

Jeremiah's word against him was severe: "Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah" (Jeremiah 22:30).

In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Evilmerodach king of Babylon lifted up his head out of prison, spoke kindly to him, set his throne above the throne of the kings with him, changed his prison garments, and gave him a daily allowance all the days of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30). These are the closing verses of 2 Kings.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father had done: 2 Kings 24:9.

Character Assessment

Three months as king and thirty-seven years in prison, and Scripture's verdict on him is a single formula. What the account gives him instead is the last word of the book: a king of Judah alive, released, honoured at a foreign table. The historian ends there without comment, and the placement is not accidental.

Significance

His deportation is the exile Ezekiel dates by (Ezekiel 1:2). Jeremiah's sentence that none of his seed should prosper on David's throne stands alongside his appearance in Matthew's genealogy of Christ as Jechonias (Matthew 1:11-12) - a tension long noted and variously explained, and recorded here without resolution. His release in the closing verses of Kings leaves the Davidic line alive at the end of a book that has just recorded its destruction.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He ate bread before the king of Babylon continually all the days of his life (2 Kings 25:29-30).

Scripture

2 Kings 24:6-16; 2 Kings 25:27-30; 2 Chronicles 36:8-10; Jeremiah 22:24-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34; Ezekiel 1:2; Matthew 1:11-12
363

Zedekiah (king of Judah)

Son of Josiah; last king of Judah; installed by Nebuchadnezzar, rebelled, and saw his sons killed before his eyes were put out.

Also called Mattaniah

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kings 24:18); uncle of Jehoiachin. Originally Mattaniah; renamed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:17).

Chronology

"Zedekiah was twenty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 24:18).

Life Synopsis

Nebuchadnezzar made him king in Jehoiachin's place and changed his name. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done" (2 Kings 24:17-19). Chronicles adds that he humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the Lord, and rebelled against the king who had made him swear by God (2 Chronicles 36:12-13).

He consulted Jeremiah repeatedly and in secret, asking, "Is there any word from the Lord?" and was told plainly to surrender and live. He answered that he was afraid of the Jews that had fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they mock him, and would not do it (Jeremiah 37:17; Jeremiah 38:14-23). He allowed the princes to put Jeremiah into the dungeon and then allowed Ebedmelech to draw him out (Jeremiah 38:4-13).

In the ninth year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem. In the eleventh year the famine was severe and the city was broken up. He fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls and was overtaken in the plains of Jericho, his army scattered. "And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon" (2 Kings 25:1-7).

What They Did Right

  • Sent repeatedly to Jeremiah to enquire of the Lord: Jeremiah 37:3, 37:17; Jeremiah 38:14.
  • Permitted Ebedmelech to draw Jeremiah out of the dungeon: Jeremiah 38:10.
  • Protected Jeremiah from the princes who wanted him dead, though weakly: Jeremiah 38:5, 38:24-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done: 2 Kings 24:19.
  • Rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, breaking an oath sworn by God: 2 Chronicles 36:13; Ezekiel 17:15-19.
  • Humbled not himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord: 2 Chronicles 36:12.
  • Knew what God required and would not do it, for fear of being mocked: Jeremiah 38:19.
  • Told Jeremiah to conceal their conversation from the princes: Jeremiah 38:24-27.

Character Assessment

A weak man rather than a defiant one, and Scripture records the weakness precisely. He enquired of the prophet again and again, in secret, and received the same plain answer each time, and could not act on it because he feared what people would say. The princes overruled him at will - "the king is not he that can do any thing against you" (Jeremiah 38:5). His last recorded sight was the death of his sons.

Significance

The last king of Judah. With him the throne of David ended until Christ, and the temple, the city, and the walls were destroyed in his eleventh year. Ezekiel treats his broken oath to Nebuchadnezzar as an oath despised against God himself (Ezekiel 17:15-19).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was blinded, bound with fetters of brass, and carried to Babylon; Jeremiah 52:11 adds that he was put in prison till the day of his death.

Scripture

2 Kings 24:17-25:7; 2 Chronicles 36:11-21; Jeremiah 21:1-10; Jeremiah 34:1-22; Jeremiah 37:1-38:28; Jeremiah 52:1-11; Ezekiel 17:11-21
364

Nebuchadnezzar

King of Babylon; destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and carried Judah into exile; humbled until he acknowledged that the most High rules in the kingdom of men.

Also called Nebuchadrezzar

Family

Father of Evilmerodach (2 Kings 25:27); Belshazzar is called his son in Daniel 5:2.

Chronology

He reigned over Babylon through the last years of Judah; his first year corresponds to the fourth of Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 25:1).

Life Synopsis

He came against Jehoiakim, who served him three years and rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). He besieged Jerusalem in Jehoiachin's reign, took the treasures and ten thousand captives, and set Zedekiah on the throne (2 Kings 24:10-17). When Zedekiah rebelled he besieged the city, and in the eleventh year it was broken up. Nebuzaradan burned the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:1-10).

Daniel records another side of him: he dreamed of a great image and Daniel interpreted it, and he fell on his face and said, "Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings" (Daniel 2:47). He then set up a golden image and threw three men into a furnace for refusing it, and on seeing them unharmed decreed that no one should speak against their God (Daniel 3:1-30). Warned in a second dream to break off his sins by righteousness, he said twelve months later, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built...by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?" and was driven from men to eat grass as oxen until seven times passed over him (Daniel 4:29-33).

"And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High... Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase" (Daniel 4:34-37).

What They Did Right

  • Acknowledged the God of Daniel as a God of gods and a Lord of kings: Daniel 2:47.
  • Decreed that no one should speak amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: Daniel 3:28-29.
  • After his humbling, blessed, praised, extolled, and honoured the King of heaven, and confessed that those who walk in pride he is able to abase: Daniel 4:34-37.
  • Dealt kindly with Jeremiah, charging Nebuzaradan to look well to him and do him no harm: Jeremiah 39:11-12.

What They Did Wrong

  • Destroyed Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 25:9.
  • Set up a golden image and commanded all to worship it on pain of the burning furnace: Daniel 3:1-6.
  • Said in pride, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?": Daniel 4:30.
  • Slew Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and blinded him: 2 Kings 25:7.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats him in two registers that must be held together. In Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah he is the destroyer of Jerusalem, and also God's own servant used for that purpose (Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6). In Daniel he is a man brought through repeated warnings to a confession of God's sovereignty stated in his own words. The confession in Daniel 4:34-37 is one of the fullest in the Old Testament, and it is spoken by the man who burned the temple.

Significance

He carried Judah into the seventy years of exile that Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 25:11-12), destroyed Solomon's temple, and is the head of gold in the image of Daniel 2. God repeatedly calls him "my servant" in Jeremiah, which is Scripture's plainest statement that God governs through rulers who do not know him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Daniel 4:36 records his restoration to his kingdom with added majesty.

Scripture

2 Kings 24:1-25:22; 2 Chronicles 36:6-21; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6-8; Jeremiah 39:1-14; Jeremiah 52:1-30; Daniel 1:1-4:37; Ezekiel 26:7
365

Nebuzaradan

Captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard; burned the temple and Jerusalem, carried away the captives, and freed Jeremiah with a remarkable speech.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

In the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:8).

Life Synopsis

He came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house, and his army broke down the walls round about. He carried away the rest of the people and the deserters, but left of the poor of the land to be vinedressers and husbandmen (2 Kings 25:8-12). He took the pillars, the sea, and the vessels, and brought the chief priests and officers to Riblah, where they were slain (2 Kings 25:13-21).

Jeremiah records that he took Jeremiah, bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, and released him with these words: "The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place. Now the Lord hath brought it, and done according as he hath said: because ye have sinned against the Lord, and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing is come upon you." He gave him victuals and a reward and let him go where he would, and committed him to Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:1-5).

What They Did Right

  • Left the poor of the land vineyards and fields: 2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 39:10.
  • Released Jeremiah, gave him provisions and a reward, and let him choose where to go: Jeremiah 40:1-5.

What They Did Wrong

  • Burned the house of the Lord and the city, and broke down the walls: 2 Kings 25:9-10. Scripture records these as acts of judgment carried out by Babylon and offers no separate condemnation of the man.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the destruction he executed and, in Jeremiah, a speech in which a Babylonian officer states the theology of the exile more clearly than most of Judah's kings had: God said this would happen because of your sin, and now he has done it. The text passes no verdict on him.

Significance

He carried out the destruction of the temple and the final deportation. His release of Jeremiah preserved the prophet through the fall of the city.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 52:30.

Scripture

2 Kings 25:8-21; Jeremiah 39:9-14; Jeremiah 40:1-5; Jeremiah 52:12-30
366

Gedaliah

Son of Ahikam; made governor over the remnant left in Judah by Nebuchadnezzar; refused to believe a warning of assassination and was murdered.

Family

Son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan (2 Kings 25:22); his father had protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24).

Chronology

After the fall of Jerusalem, in the seventh month (2 Kings 25:25).

Life Synopsis

Nebuchadnezzar made him governor over the people left in the land. He sware to the captains of the forces and their men: "Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you" (2 Kings 25:22-24). Jews returned from Moab, Ammon, and Edom, and gathered wine and summer fruits in abundance (Jeremiah 40:11-12).

Johanan warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to kill him, and offered to kill Ishmael secretly. "But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said unto Johanan the son of Kareah, Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael" (Jeremiah 40:13-16).

In the seventh month Ishmael came with ten men and they ate bread together at Mizpah, and Ishmael rose up and killed him, with the Jews and the Chaldeans that were with him (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1-3). The people fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (2 Kings 25:26).

What They Did Right

  • Reassured the frightened remnant and urged them to settle and serve peaceably: 2 Kings 25:24.
  • Refused to have a man killed on suspicion: Jeremiah 40:16. Scripture records the refusal and its fatal outcome without calling it either virtue or folly.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He disbelieved a true warning, and it cost him his life and scattered the remnant. Scripture states the fact and passes no verdict.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents a decent man in an impossible position, killed at his own table by a guest. His refusal to strike first is recorded plainly, along with the fact that the warning was true. The text does not tell the reader what he should have done.

Significance

His murder ended the last organised Jewish community in the land and drove the remnant into Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them against his counsel (Jeremiah 43:5-7). The fast of the seventh month, mentioned in Zechariah 7:5 and 8:19, is traditionally associated with his death.

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah at Mizpah while eating bread with him (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:2).

Scripture

2 Kings 25:22-26; Jeremiah 39:14; Jeremiah 40:5-41:18
367

Ishmael (son of Nethaniah)

Of the seed royal; murdered Gedaliah at his own table, killed eighty pilgrims, and fled to the Ammonites.

Family

Son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1).

Chronology

In the seventh month after the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:25).

Life Synopsis

He came to Gedaliah at Mizpah with ten men, and they ate bread together. "Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah... and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land." He killed all the Jews and the Chaldean soldiers with him (Jeremiah 41:1-3).

The next day, before anyone knew, eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria with offerings and incense for the house of the Lord, their beards shaven and their clothes rent. He went out weeping to meet them and said, "Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they were in the city he killed them and cast them into a pit, sparing ten who offered him hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey (Jeremiah 41:4-9). He carried away the king's daughters and the remnant captive toward the Ammonites, but Johanan overtook him and recovered them; Ishmael escaped with eight men (Jeremiah 41:10-15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered the governor at his own table after eating bread with him: Jeremiah 41:1-2.
  • Killed the Jews and the Chaldeans at Mizpah: Jeremiah 41:3.
  • Enticed eighty mourning pilgrims into the city with a pretence of weeping and killed them: Jeremiah 41:4-7.
  • Carried the remnant, including the king's daughters, captive toward Ammon: Jeremiah 41:10.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned by the record. His crime is aggravated at every point: the man he killed had sworn to protect the people, the killing followed a shared meal, and the eighty men he murdered were coming to worship. Scripture records that he was acting for Baalis king of the Ammonites (Jeremiah 40:14).

Significance

His murder of Gedaliah destroyed the last Jewish administration in the land and drove the remnant to Egypt in fear of Babylonian reprisal, taking Jeremiah with them.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He escaped with eight men to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:15).

Scripture

2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 40:8, 40:13-16; Jeremiah 41:1-18
368

Evilmerodach

King of Babylon after Nebuchadnezzar; released Jehoiachin from prison and gave him a place at his own table.

Family

Son of Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:27, by succession).

Chronology

In the year that he began to reign, the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity (2 Kings 25:27).

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the year that he began to reign did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison; and spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon; and changed his prison garments: and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life. And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life" (2 Kings 25:27-30).

What They Did Right

  • Lifted a captive king out of prison after thirty-seven years, spoke kindly to him, set his throne above the other kings, changed his garments, and provided for him daily for the rest of his life: 2 Kings 25:27-30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act of kindness and nothing else about him, and places it at the very end of the books of Kings. Nothing is said of his motive.

Significance

His kindness supplies the last four verses of 2 Kings, which end a history of national destruction with a king of David's line alive, out of prison, and eating at a table. The historian offers no comment, and the placement is the comment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34
369

The Shulamite

The woman of the Song of Solomon, addressed once by that name. Whether she is a particular person, or the figure through whom the poem speaks, Scripture does not say, and this entry does not decide it.

Family

She speaks of her mother and of her mother's children, who were angry with her and made her keeper of the vineyards (Song of Solomon 1:6). She speaks of a brother and of the house of her mother (Song of Solomon 8:1-2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The book is ascribed to Solomon in its opening verse (Song of Solomon 1:1).

Life Synopsis

She is named once: "Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee" (Song of Solomon 6:13). Everywhere else she is a voice rather than a named person, and the greater part of the book is hers - she speaks more of it than anyone.

She describes herself at the outset without apology or vanity: "I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon. Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept" (Song of Solomon 1:5-6).

She seeks her beloved through the city by night and is found by the watchmen, who strike her and take away her veil (Song of Solomon 3:1-4; Song of Solomon 5:6-7). She charges the daughters of Jerusalem repeatedly, "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5; 8:4).

The closing words given to her are the book's summary and among the most quoted in Scripture: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned" (Song of Solomon 8:6-7).

What They Did Right

  • Spoke of herself truthfully, neither disparaging nor exalting: Song of Solomon 1:5-6.
  • Sought her beloved persistently and at cost, being struck and stripped of her veil by the watchmen: Song of Solomon 5:6-7.
  • Charged the daughters of Jerusalem three times not to stir up love until it pleased: Song of Solomon 2:7; Song of Solomon 3:5; Song of Solomon 8:4.
  • Spoke the book's central declaration, that love is strong as death and that many waters cannot quench it: Song of Solomon 8:6-7.

What They Did Wrong

  • She says of herself, "mine own vineyard have I not kept" (Song of Solomon 1:6), and in Song of Solomon 5:2-6 she delays in opening to her beloved and finds him withdrawn. Both are her own words about herself; the poem records no charge against her from anyone else, and does not moralise on either.

Character Assessment

A different kind of entry from every other in this work, and the difference should be stated rather than concealed. The Song is a poem, not a narrative: it records no history, no dates, no genealogy, and no events outside the relationship it describes. What can be said is that she is named once, that she speaks more of the book than anyone else in it, and that the words given to her about the strength of love are among the most enduring in Scripture. Whether those are the words of a woman Scripture means us to know as a person, or the voice through which the poem speaks, the text does not settle - and readers have taken the book as a literal love song, as an allegory of God and Israel, and as a figure of Christ and the church, for as long as it has been read.

Significance

Hers is the principal voice of the only book of the Bible given wholly to the love of a man and a woman, and the one book that would otherwise contribute no person to this reference. Her closing declaration in Song of Solomon 8:6-7 is the fullest statement about love in the Old Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Song of Solomon 1:5-6; Song of Solomon 2:7, 2:16; Song of Solomon 3:1-5; Song of Solomon 5:2-8; Song of Solomon 6:13; Song of Solomon 8:1-7
370

Bithiah

A daughter of Pharaoh who became the wife of Mered of the tribe of Judah.

Family

Daughter of Pharaoh; wife of Mered (1 Chronicles 4:18).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She appears in the genealogies of Judah.

Life Synopsis

She is named once, in a genealogy: "And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took" (1 Chronicles 4:18).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, and nothing recorded but her father, her husband, and her sons. She is included because of who she was: a daughter of Pharaoh named in the genealogy of Judah. Her name means daughter of the Lord, which the text does not remark on.

Significance

She is one of a small number of foreign women drawn into Israel and named in its genealogies, with Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 4:18

Further Figures of the Kingdom Period

371

Jabez

A man of Judah, more honourable than his brethren, whose prayer God granted.

Family

Of the tribe of Judah; his mother named him (1 Chronicles 4:9). His brethren are mentioned but not named.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He appears in the genealogies of Judah without chronological anchor.

Life Synopsis

"And Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow."

"And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested" (1 Chronicles 4:9-10). Nothing else is recorded of him. The two verses interrupt a long genealogy and then it resumes.

What They Did Right

  • Was more honourable than his brethren - the Chronicler's own assessment: 1 Chronicles 4:9.
  • Called on the God of Israel, asking for blessing, enlargement, God's hand with him, and to be kept from evil: 1 Chronicles 4:10.
  • God granted him that which he requested: 1 Chronicles 4:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Two verses, and both are favourable. Scripture does not say what made him more honourable than his brethren, does not describe the sorrow of his birth, and does not record what the granted request produced. His prayer includes a petition to be kept from evil that it might not grieve him - a man named for sorrow asking not to cause it.

Significance

His prayer is one of very few in Scripture recorded together with the explicit statement that God granted it. The town of Jabez, where families of scribes dwelt, bears the same name (1 Chronicles 2:55), though Scripture does not connect the two.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 4:9-10; compare 1 Chronicles 2:55
372

Ira the Jairite

A chief ruler about David; named at the close of the list of his officers.

Family

A Jairite (2 Samuel 20:26). Distinct from Ira the Ithrite and Ira the son of Ikkesh, both of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:26, 23:38).

Chronology

During David's reign, after Absalom's rebellion.

Life Synopsis

Named once, as the last item in the list of David's officers: "And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David" (2 Samuel 20:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse and one office. He is entered because the list he closes is the roll of David's administration after the rebellion, and because Scripture distinguishes him carefully from two other men of the same name among the mighty men.

Significance

The parallel list in 2 Samuel 8:18 gives the corresponding place to David's sons, who were chief rulers; the later list names Ira instead, which is the kind of quiet change the historical books record without explaining.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

2 Samuel 20:26; compare 2 Samuel 23:26, 23:38
373

Adino the Eznite
