Chief of David's captains, who lifted his spear against eight hundred at one time.

Also called Josheb-basshebeth, The Tachmonite

Family

Called "the Tachmonite that sat in the seat" (2 Samuel 23:8). 1 Chronicles 11:11 calls him Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, and gives the number as three hundred.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In David's reign.

Life Synopsis

"These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time" (2 Samuel 23:8). The parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:11 reads: "Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time." The difference in name and number between the two passages is a well-known textual question and is noted here rather than resolved.

What They Did Right

  • Chief among David's captains, credited with an exceptional feat of arms: 2 Samuel 23:8; 1 Chronicles 11:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his rank and one feat, with no moral evaluation. He heads the list of David's mighty men.

Significance

First named in the roll of David's mighty men, the record of the soldiers who established the kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Samuel 23:8; 1 Chronicles 11:11
374

Eleazar (son of Dodo)

One of the three mighty men; fought the Philistines until his hand clave to the sword. Not to be confused with Eleazar the son of Aaron.

Family

Son of Dodo the Ahohite (2 Samuel 23:9).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines that were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel were gone away: he arose, and smote the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clave unto the sword: and the Lord wrought a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to spoil" (2 Samuel 23:9-10).

What They Did Right

  • Stood and fought when the men of Israel had gone away, until his hand clave to the sword: 2 Samuel 23:9-10.
  • The text credits the outcome to God: "the Lord wrought a great victory that day": 2 Samuel 23:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one action, and the detail that the army had already retreated is what gives it weight. The victory is attributed to the Lord and the people are recorded as returning only to gather spoil.

Significance

One of the three chief of David's mighty men. He is among the three who broke through the Philistine host to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, which David poured out to the Lord rather than drink (2 Samuel 23:13-17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Samuel 23:9-17; 1 Chronicles 11:12-19
375

Shammah (son of Agee)

One of the three mighty men; stood alone in a field of lentiles and defended it against the Philistines.

Family

Son of Agee the Hararite (2 Samuel 23:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And after him was Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. And the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people fled from the Philistines. But he stood in the midst of the ground, and defended it, and slew the Philistines: and the Lord wrought a great victory" (2 Samuel 23:11-12).

What They Did Right

  • Stood in the midst of a field when the people fled, and defended it: 2 Samuel 23:11-12.
  • The victory is attributed to the Lord: 2 Samuel 23:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one stand over a field of lentiles - a piece of ground of no obvious strategic value - and calls the outcome a great victory wrought by the Lord. The account is included in the roll of the mighty men without further comment.

Significance

One of the three chief mighty men of David.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Samuel 23:11-12; 1 Chronicles 11:12-14
376

Amasai

Chief of the captains; the Spirit came upon him and he declared for David at Ziklag.

Family

Chief of the captains (1 Chronicles 12:18).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. While David was still a fugitive at Ziklag.

Life Synopsis

Men of Benjamin and Judah came to David in the hold, and David went out to meet them and said that if they came peaceably his heart would be knit to them, but if to betray him, God would rebuke it.

"Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee. Then David received them, and made them captains of the band" (1 Chronicles 12:18).

What They Did Right

  • Declared for David under the Spirit's coming upon him, and credited the help to David's God: 1 Chronicles 12:18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, entirely favourable, and unusual for recording that the Spirit came upon a soldier for the purpose of an oath of allegiance.

Significance

His declaration secured a body of men for David during the years of flight, and is one of the clearest statements of loyalty in Chronicles.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 12:16-18
377

Uzzah

A son of Abinadab who put out his hand to steady the ark and was struck dead.

Also called Uzza

Family

Son of Abinadab, in whose house the ark had rested (2 Samuel 6:3); brother of Ahio.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Early in David's reign over all Israel.

Life Synopsis

David brought the ark from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, driven by Uzzah and Ahio, with all Israel playing before the Lord on all manner of instruments.

"And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God" (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Chronicles adds that his hand was on the ark (1 Chronicles 13:9-10).

David was displeased and afraid, called the place Perezuzzah, and would not bring the ark further, leaving it in the house of Obededom for three months (2 Samuel 6:8-11). Three months later he brought it up properly, by the Levites, and said, "For because ye did it not at the first, the Lord our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order" (1 Chronicles 15:13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Put forth his hand and took hold of the ark: 2 Samuel 6:6-7. Scripture calls it his error and records that God's anger was kindled. The law had forbidden touching the holy things on pain of death and required the ark to be carried by the Levites on staves (Numbers 4:15; Exodus 25:14-15). David afterward identified the fault as failing to seek God after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:13), which places responsibility on the whole undertaking and not on Uzzah alone.

Character Assessment

One of the hardest passages in the historical books, and Scripture offers no softening. The act looks instinctive and protective, and the text calls it error and records the death without elaboration. What it does supply is David's later verdict: the fault lay in transporting the ark on a cart at all, contrary to the law, and the whole company bore that.

Significance

His death stopped the procession for three months and caused David to study how the ark was to be moved, so that the second attempt was made by Levites bearing it on their shoulders as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:2, 15:13-15). The place was named Perezuzzah, the breach of Uzzah.

Death / Outcome

Struck dead by God beside the ark at the threshingfloor of Nachon, also called Chidon (2 Samuel 6:7; 1 Chronicles 13:10).

Scripture

2 Samuel 6:1-11; 1 Chronicles 13:1-14; 1 Chronicles 15:11-15; Numbers 4:15
378

Obededom

A Gittite in whose house the ark rested three months, and whose household God blessed; afterward a Levite doorkeeper and singer.

Also called Obed-edom

Family

Called the Gittite (2 Samuel 6:10). 1 Chronicles 26:4-8 names eight sons and records sixty-two of his house as able men for the service.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In David's reign.

Life Synopsis

After Uzzah's death David would not carry the ark into the city of David, "but David carried it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite. And the ark of the Lord continued in the house of Obededom the Gittite three months: and the Lord blessed Obededom, and all his household" (2 Samuel 6:10-11).

David heard of the blessing and went and brought the ark up with gladness (2 Samuel 6:12). Obededom afterward appears among the Levites appointed to minister before the ark and as a porter and singer (1 Chronicles 15:18-24; 1 Chronicles 16:5, 16:38), and his house among the doorkeepers, "for God blessed him" (1 Chronicles 26:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • Received the ark into his house when the king was afraid to take it further: 2 Samuel 6:10.
  • Continued in the service of the ark afterward as porter and singer: 1 Chronicles 15:18-24; 1 Chronicles 16:38.
  • Scripture states twice that the Lord blessed him and his household: 2 Samuel 6:11-12; 1 Chronicles 26:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and states the blessing on his house twice. The contrast with the preceding verses is deliberate: the same ark that had just killed a man blessed a household for three months, and the difference lay in how it was approached rather than in the ark itself.

Significance

The blessing on his house is what moved David to bring the ark to Jerusalem, and his family became a permanent part of the temple service.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 25:24.

Scripture

2 Samuel 6:10-12; 1 Chronicles 13:13-14; 1 Chronicles 15:18-25; 1 Chronicles 16:5, 16:38; 1 Chronicles 26:4-8, 26:15
379

Asaph

A Levite appointed by David as chief of the singers before the ark; a seer, and named in the titles of twelve psalms.

Family

Son of Berachiah, of the sons of Gershom (1 Chronicles 6:39-43). His sons formed a continuing order of temple singers (1 Chronicles 25:1-2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

David appointed Levites to minister before the ark, "Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah," and Asaph was to make a sound with cymbals (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). On the day the ark came up, David delivered a psalm into the hand of Asaph and his brethren (1 Chronicles 16:7).

He and his sons prophesied with harps, psalteries, and cymbals "according to the order of the king" (1 Chronicles 25:1-2). He is called "Asaph the seer" (2 Chronicles 29:30), and his words were used in Hezekiah's restoration of worship. The sons of Asaph continued as temple singers through the monarchy and returned from exile (Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed chief of those who ministered in song before the ark: 1 Chronicles 16:4-5.
  • Prophesied with instruments in the service of the house of God: 1 Chronicles 25:1-2.
  • Called a seer, and his words used in the reformation of worship under Hezekiah: 2 Chronicles 29:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives him an unusual double designation: chief musician and seer. His psalms include some of the most searching in the Psalter.

Significance

Twelve psalms carry his name in their titles - Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 to 83 - including Psalm 73, which sets out the problem of the prosperity of the wicked more directly than any other psalm. His order of singers outlasted the monarchy and the exile.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His descendants are named as late as Nehemiah 11:17.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 6:39; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19; 1 Chronicles 16:4-7, 16:37; 1 Chronicles 25:1-9; 2 Chronicles 29:30; Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44; Psalms 50 title; Psalms 73-83 titles
380

Heman

A Levite singer, grandson of Samuel; the king's seer in the words of God; named in the title of Psalm 88.

Family

Son of Joel, son of Samuel (1 Chronicles 6:33). He had fourteen sons and three daughters (1 Chronicles 25:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

He was appointed with Asaph and Ethan to sound with cymbals of brass (1 Chronicles 15:17-19), and with Jeduthun to give thanks with trumpets and instruments (1 Chronicles 16:41-42).

"All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the Lord, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God" (1 Chronicles 25:5-6). He is named among those whose descendants served under Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:14).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed to the service of song in the house of the Lord and named the king's seer in the words of God: 1 Chronicles 25:5.
  • His whole household - fourteen sons and three daughters - served in the temple music under his direction: 1 Chronicles 25:5-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is a grandson of Samuel serving in David's temple arrangements, which quietly links the last judge to the ordering of worship.

Significance

Psalm 88 carries his name in its title, and it is the darkest psalm in the Psalter, ending without resolution. That the man Scripture calls the king's seer, with seventeen children and a place in the temple choir, is credited with that psalm is worth noting and is not explained by the text.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 6:33; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19; 1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 1 Chronicles 25:1-6; 2 Chronicles 5:12; 2 Chronicles 29:14; Psalms 88 title
381

Jeduthun

A Levite appointed with Asaph and Heman over the service of song; named in the titles of three psalms.

Family

His sons are named among the singers and porters (1 Chronicles 25:3; 1 Chronicles 16:38).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

He was appointed with Heman to give thanks to the Lord, with trumpets and cymbals and instruments of God (1 Chronicles 16:41-42). "Of Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun; Gedaliah, and Zeri, and Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the Lord" (1 Chronicles 25:3). He is called "the king's seer" (2 Chronicles 35:15).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed over the service of song and named as one who prophesied with a harp to give thanks and praise the Lord: 1 Chronicles 25:3.
  • Called the king's seer: 2 Chronicles 35:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. With Asaph and Heman he forms the third of the three orders of temple singers established by David.

Significance

Psalms 39, 62, and 77 name him in their titles. His order of singers continued through the monarchy and appears again after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 1 Chronicles 25:1-6; 2 Chronicles 5:12; 2 Chronicles 35:15; Nehemiah 11:17; Psalms 39 title; Psalms 62 title; Psalms 77 title
382

Shemaiah (the man of God)

A prophet in Rehoboam's reign; forbade the war against Israel and interpreted Shishak's invasion.

Family

Called the man of God (1 Kings 12:22) and the prophet (2 Chronicles 12:5).

Chronology

In the reign of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:22).

Life Synopsis

When Rehoboam assembled a hundred and eighty thousand men to fight Israel, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah: "Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me. They hearkened therefore to the word of the Lord, and returned" (1 Kings 12:22-24).

When Shishak came up, Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the princes and said, "Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak." They humbled themselves and said, "The Lord is righteous." The word of the Lord came again: because they humbled themselves, God would not destroy them but would grant them some deliverance, though they would be Shishak's servants (2 Chronicles 12:5-8). He is named as a recorder of Rehoboam's acts (2 Chronicles 12:15).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's word forbidding a civil war, and was obeyed by a king and an army of a hundred and eighty thousand: 1 Kings 12:22-24.
  • Told Rehoboam and the princes plainly why Shishak had come: 2 Chronicles 12:5.
  • Brought back the word of mercy when they humbled themselves: 2 Chronicles 12:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and records that he was heard on both occasions - an unusual outcome for a prophet in the historical books.

Significance

His first word prevented a war between Judah and Israel at the moment of the division, and his second turned a national judgment into a partial one. He recorded the acts of Rehoboam.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 12:15.

Scripture

1 Kings 12:22-24; 2 Chronicles 11:2-4; 2 Chronicles 12:5-8, 12:15
383

Shishak

King of Egypt; sheltered Jeroboam and later invaded Judah, taking the treasures of the temple and the palace.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

He came up in the fifth year of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25).

Life Synopsis

Jeroboam fled to him from Solomon and stayed in Egypt until Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:40).

"And it came to pass in the fifth year of king Rehoboam, that Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem: and he took away the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the treasures of the king's house; he even took away all: and he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made" (1 Kings 14:25-26). Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place. Chronicles records twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and people without number, and states that Judah became his servants, "that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries" (2 Chronicles 12:2-9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his invasion as God's response to Judah's transgression (2 Chronicles 12:2) and offers no separate verdict on him.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as an instrument of judgment rather than as a man assessed. The detail it dwells on is the loss of Solomon's gold shields and their replacement with brass - the visible measure of how much had been lost in five years.

Significance

His invasion stripped the temple within five years of Solomon's death and made Judah a tributary. God's stated purpose was that they should learn the difference between his service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chronicles 12:8).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He departed from Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:9).

Scripture

1 Kings 11:40; 1 Kings 14:25-28; 2 Chronicles 12:2-9
384

Azariah (son of Oded)

A prophet on whom the Spirit of God came; met Asa returning from battle and called Judah to reform.

Family

Son of Oded (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Chronology

In the reign of Asa (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Life Synopsis

"And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: and he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you." He recited a period when Israel had been without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law, and said, "Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded" (2 Chronicles 15:1-7).

"And when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols out of all the land," renewed the altar, and gathered Judah, Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon to a covenant to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 15:8-15).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered a word that produced the most thorough reform of Asa's reign: 2 Chronicles 15:1-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His message contains one of the clearest conditional statements in the Old Testament - the Lord is with you while you are with him - and it was acted on immediately.

Significance

His word set off Asa's covenant renewal, which drew people from the northern tribes into Judah. The sentence "if ye seek him, he will be found of you" is among the most quoted in Chronicles.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 15:8.

Scripture

2 Chronicles 15:1-8
385

Zerah the Ethiopian

Commander of a host of a thousand thousand who came against Asa and was overthrown.

Family

An Ethiopian (2 Chronicles 14:9).

Chronology

In the reign of Asa (2 Chronicles 14:9).

Life Synopsis

"And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots; and came unto Mareshah." Asa cried to the Lord: "Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude."

"So the Lord smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled" (2 Chronicles 14:9-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his invasion and defeat without moral evaluation of him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the size of his host and its overthrow, and gives its attention entirely to Asa's prayer. He is the occasion of the clearest statement of dependence in Asa's reign.

Significance

His defeat is the victory Hanani later reminded Asa of, when the king had turned to Syria instead of God (2 Chronicles 16:8).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His host fled and was destroyed (2 Chronicles 14:12-13).

Scripture

2 Chronicles 14:9-15; 2 Chronicles 16:8
386

Hanani (the seer)

A seer who rebuked Asa for hiring Syria instead of relying on the Lord, and was imprisoned for it.

Family

Father of Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:1; 2 Chronicles 19:2).

Chronology

In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign (2 Chronicles 16:1, 16:7).

Life Synopsis

"And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the Lord thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand. Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host... yet, because thou didst rely on the Lord, he delivered them into thine hand. For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars" (2 Chronicles 16:7-9).

"Then Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house; for he was in a rage with him because of this thing" (2 Chronicles 16:10).

What They Did Right

  • Rebuked a king who had been faithful for decades, and did so by reminding him of his own earlier faith: 2 Chronicles 16:7-9.
  • Accepted imprisonment rather than soften the message: 2 Chronicles 16:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His rebuke is notable for its method: he did not accuse Asa of a general failure but pointed to the single decision and set it against the king's own past.

Significance

His words in 2 Chronicles 16:9 - that the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him - are among the most quoted in the Old Testament. His son Jehu continued the same ministry to the next generation of kings.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was put in a prison house (2 Chronicles 16:10).

Scripture

2 Chronicles 16:7-10; 1 Kings 16:1, 16:7; 2 Chronicles 19:2; 2 Chronicles 20:34
387

Jahaziel

A Levite of the sons of Asaph on whom the Spirit of the Lord came in the congregation, telling Judah the battle was God's.

Family

Son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph (2 Chronicles 20:14).

Chronology

In the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:14).

Life Synopsis

As all Judah stood before the Lord with their little ones, their wives, and their children, the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jahaziel in the midst of the congregation. He said, "Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's... Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the Lord with you" (2 Chronicles 20:14-17).

Jehoshaphat and all Judah bowed with their faces to the ground, the Levites stood to praise, and in the morning they went out with singers before the army; the enemy destroyed one another (2 Chronicles 20:18-24).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's word to a frightened nation under the Spirit's coming upon him, and it was obeyed: 2 Chronicles 20:14-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He speaks once, in the middle of an assembly, and his words redirect a national crisis.

Significance

His word - the battle is not yours, but God's - is among the most quoted sentences in Chronicles, and it produced the unique spectacle of an army going into battle led by singers.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 20:14.

Scripture

2 Chronicles 20:14-19
388

Eliezer (son of Dodavah)

A prophet of Mareshah who foretold the destruction of Jehoshaphat's ships because of his alliance with Ahaziah of Israel.

Family

Son of Dodavah of Mareshah (2 Chronicles 20:37).

Chronology

Late in the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:35-37).

Life Synopsis

Jehoshaphat joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel to make ships to go to Tarshish. "Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the Lord hath broken thy works. And the ships were broken, that they were not able to go to Tarshish" (2 Chronicles 20:36-37).

What They Did Right

  • Told a good king that his alliance had destroyed his own enterprise, and was proved right immediately: 2 Chronicles 20:37.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse of prophecy and its immediate fulfilment. Scripture records nothing else about him.

Significance

His word is the third recorded rebuke of Jehoshaphat for allying with the house of Ahab, after Micaiah's warning and Jehu son of Hanani's rebuke - a pattern the Chronicler makes unmistakable.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Chronicles 20:35-37
389

Oded

A prophet of the Lord in Samaria who confronted the returning army of Israel and secured the release of two hundred thousand captives of Judah.

Family

Not recorded. Not to be confused with Oded the father of Azariah (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Chronology

In the reign of Ahaz of Judah and Pekah of Israel (2 Chronicles 28:5-9).

Life Synopsis

Israel had taken two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters of Judah captive, with much spoil, and brought them to Samaria.

"But a prophet of the Lord was there, whose name was Oded: and he went out before the host that came to Samaria, and said unto them, Behold, because the Lord God of your fathers was wroth with Judah, he hath delivered them into your hand, and ye have slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven. And now ye purpose to keep under the children of Judah and Jerusalem for bondmen and bondwomen unto you: but are there not with you, even with you, sins against the Lord your God?" (2 Chronicles 28:9-10).

Certain heads of Ephraim stood with him. The armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and the congregation. Men rose up, clothed the naked among them from the spoil, shod them, gave them to eat and drink, anointed them, carried the feeble on asses, and brought them to Jericho to their brethren (2 Chronicles 28:12-15).

What They Did Right

  • Confronted a victorious army alone and told them their victory did not license what they intended: 2 Chronicles 28:9-11.
  • Reminded Israel of their own sins rather than only Judah's: 2 Chronicles 28:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His intervention is one of the most remarkable in Chronicles: a single prophet turned an army back from enslaving two hundred thousand people, and the men who had captured them then clothed, fed, and carried them home. Nothing in the northern kingdom's record resembles it.

Significance

The treatment of the captives - clothed from the spoil, fed, anointed, and the feeble carried on asses to Jericho - is a striking Old Testament parallel to the parable of the good Samaritan, which Christ set on the same road (Luke 10:30-35). Scripture draws no connection, and none is asserted here.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 28:9.

Scripture

2 Chronicles 28:5-15

Exile, Return, and the Persian Court

390

Cyrus

King of Persia; issued the decree permitting the Jews to return and rebuild the house of the Lord; named by Isaiah long before his birth.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

The decree came in the first year of his reign over Babylon (Ezra 1:1).

Life Synopsis

"Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying, Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The Lord God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem" (Ezra 1:1-3).

He brought out the vessels of the house of the Lord which Nebuchadnezzar had taken, and numbered them to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah - five thousand four hundred vessels in all (Ezra 1:7-11). His decree was later found at Achmetha and confirmed by Darius when the work was challenged (Ezra 6:1-5).

Isaiah had named him: "That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid." And: "Thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden... I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me" (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1-5).

What They Did Right

  • Issued the decree for the return and the rebuilding of the house of the Lord: Ezra 1:1-4.
  • Restored the vessels of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, numbered and delivered: Ezra 1:7-11.
  • Acknowledged the Lord God of heaven as the one who had given him his kingdoms and charged him to build: Ezra 1:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. Isaiah's word about him is among the most remarkable in the Old Testament: God calls him his shepherd and his anointed, and says plainly "thou hast not known me" - a man used and named by God without knowing him.

Significance

His decree ended the seventy years of exile that Jeremiah had foretold, and Ezra opens by saying it happened so that Jeremiah's word might be fulfilled. Isaiah named him roughly a century and a half before the event. He is the only foreign ruler in Scripture called God's anointed.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Daniel 10:1.

Scripture

2 Chronicles 36:22-23; Ezra 1:1-11; Ezra 3:7; Ezra 4:3-5; Ezra 5:13-17; Ezra 6:1-14; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1-13; Daniel 1:21; Daniel 6:28; Daniel 10:1
391

Zerubbabel

Son of Shealtiel; governor of Judah at the return; led the first company home and rebuilt the altar and the temple.

Also called Zorobabel, Sheshbazzar

Family

Son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1); of the line of David through Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19, which calls him the son of Pedaiah). Named in both genealogies of Christ (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27).

Chronology

He returned under Cyrus and the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius (Ezra 6:15).

Life Synopsis

He came up with the first company from the captivity (Ezra 2:2). "Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses... for fear was upon them because of the people of those countries" (Ezra 3:2-3). They kept the feast of tabernacles and laid the foundation of the temple, and the old men who had seen the first house wept while others shouted (Ezra 3:8-13).

When the adversaries offered to help build, he answered, "Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the Lord God of Israel" (Ezra 4:1-3). The work was stopped by opposition until the second year of Darius, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and Zerubbabel and Jeshua rose up and began to build again (Ezra 5:1-2).

Zechariah's word to him: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts. Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain... The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it" (Zechariah 4:6-9). Haggai's closing word makes him a signet: "I will take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the Lord, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee" (Haggai 2:23).

What They Did Right

  • Built the altar first, before the foundation of the temple was laid, despite fear of the surrounding peoples: Ezra 3:2-3.
  • Refused the offer of help from those who did not worship the Lord alone: Ezra 4:1-3.
  • Resumed the work at the word of Haggai and Zechariah after years of delay: Ezra 5:1-2.
  • Finished the house, as Zechariah had said his hands would: Zechariah 4:9; Ezra 6:14-15.
  • God's own word: "I will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee": Haggai 2:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Haggai rebuked the people, including the leaders, for dwelling in ceiled houses while the house of God lay waste (Haggai 1:2-4), and Zerubbabel obeyed the word when it came (Haggai 1:12-14).

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He led the first return, restored the altar in a hostile land, and completed a temple that took over twenty years against sustained opposition. Zechariah's word to him - not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit - is spoken to a governor with no army and no independence.

Significance

He rebuilt the temple, and he stands in both genealogies of Christ, carrying the Davidic line through the exile. Haggai's naming of him as a signet reverses the word spoken against his ancestor Jehoiachin, whom God had said he would pluck off as a signet (Jeremiah 22:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Zechariah 4:9-10.

Scripture

1 Chronicles 3:17-19; Ezra 2:2; Ezra 3:2-13; Ezra 4:1-3; Ezra 5:1-2; Nehemiah 7:7; Nehemiah 12:1; Haggai 1:1-2:23; Zechariah 4:6-10; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27
392

Jeshua (the high priest)

Son of Jozadak; high priest at the return; built the altar with Zerubbabel and was shown in Zechariah's vision clothed in filthy garments and given change of raiment.

Also called Joshua the high priest, Jozadak's son

Family

Son of Jozadak, of the high priestly line (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1). Called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah.

Chronology

He returned with the first company under Cyrus and was still serving in the second year of Darius (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1).

Life Synopsis

He came up with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2) and stood up with his brethren the priests to build the altar and offer burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses (Ezra 3:2). He set the priests in their apparel and appointed the Levites to the work (Ezra 3:8-9). With Zerubbabel he refused the adversaries' offer of help (Ezra 4:3), and rose up to build again when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied (Ezra 5:2).

Zechariah saw him "standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. And the Lord said unto Satan, The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan... is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel. And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment" (Zechariah 3:1-4). Crowns were set on his head as a sign concerning the man whose name is The BRANCH (Zechariah 6:11-13).

What They Did Right

  • Built the altar and restored the burnt offerings before the temple was begun: Ezra 3:2-6.
  • Refused the compromised offer of help: Ezra 4:3.
  • Rose up to build again at the prophets' word: Ezra 5:2.
  • Obeyed the voice of the Lord through Haggai and feared before the Lord: Haggai 1:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Zechariah's vision shows him clothed in filthy garments before the angel, which the passage treats as needing removal by God rather than as a specific charge; the iniquity is caused to pass from him and he is clothed with change of raiment: Zechariah 3:3-4.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him directly. The vision of Zechariah 3 is not an accusation but a picture of a priest accused by Satan and cleared by God, and its point is the clothing rather than the filth.

Significance

He restored the priesthood after the exile. Zechariah's vision of his cleansing and crowning points beyond him to "the BRANCH," who would build the temple of the Lord and be a priest upon his throne (Zechariah 6:12-13) - one of the clearest Old Testament statements of a combined priesthood and kingship.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His descendants are traced in Nehemiah 12:10-11.

Scripture

Ezra 2:2; Ezra 3:2-9; Ezra 4:3; Ezra 5:2; Nehemiah 7:7; Nehemiah 12:1, 12:10; Haggai 1:1-14; Haggai 2:2-4; Zechariah 3:1-10; Zechariah 6:11-13
393

Ahasuerus

King of Persia who reigned from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces; deposed Vashti, made Esther queen, and reversed Haman's decree.

Family

Husband of Vashti and afterward of Esther (Esther 1:9; Esther 2:17).

Chronology

The events span from the third year of his reign to the twelfth (Esther 1:3; Esther 3:7).

Life Synopsis

He made a feast of a hundred and eighty days and then seven days more, and on the seventh day, when his heart was merry with wine, sent for Vashti to show her beauty. She refused, and on Memucan's advice she was deposed and a decree sent out that every man should bear rule in his own house (Esther 1:1-22).

Esther was chosen from the gathered virgins and made queen, and he made a great feast (Esther 2:17-18). Mordecai discovered a plot by Bigthan and Teresh and it was written in the book of the chronicles (Esther 2:21-23).

He promoted Haman above all the princes, and when Haman offered ten thousand talents for permission to destroy a certain people, he took his ring off his hand and gave it to him: "The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee." The decree went out and "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed" (Esther 3:1-15).

On a sleepless night he had the chronicles read and learned that Mordecai's service had gone unrewarded, and had Haman lead him through the city in royal apparel (Esther 6:1-11). At Esther's banquet he learned of the plot against her people, went in wrath into the garden, returned to find Haman fallen on the queen's bed, and had him hanged on the gallows he had prepared (Esther 7:1-10). He gave Haman's house to Esther and his ring to Mordecai, and granted a second decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves (Esther 8:1-14).

What They Did Right

  • Rewarded Mordecai for saving his life, once he was reminded of it: Esther 6:1-11.
  • Granted Esther's petition and permitted the Jews to defend themselves: Esther 8:7-11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Sent for his queen to display her beauty before the princes when his heart was merry with wine: Esther 1:10-11.
  • Handed the fate of an entire people to Haman without asking who they were: Esther 3:8-11.
  • Sat down to drink while the city was perplexed by the decree he had just sealed: Esther 3:15.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as impulsive, easily advised, and largely unaware. He deposes a queen on a courtier's counsel, signs away a nation on a favourite's word without asking its name, and reverses himself when the facts reach him. The book never mentions God, and the king's obliviousness is part of how the account works: everything turns on a sleepless night and a book read aloud.

Significance

His decrees frame the whole book. The irrevocability of Persian law - which he could not undo, only counter with a second decree - is the mechanism by which the deliverance had to come, and the feast of Purim commemorates it (Esther 9:20-28).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 10:1-3.

Scripture

Esther 1:1-10:3
394

Vashti

Queen of Ahasuerus; refused to come at the king's command and was deposed.

Family

Queen and wife of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:9).

Chronology

In the third year of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:3).

Life Synopsis

"Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to king Ahasuerus" (Esther 1:9).

On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he commanded the seven chamberlains to bring her before him with the crown royal, "to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on. But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment by his chamberlains: therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him" (Esther 1:10-12).

Memucan advised that she had wronged not the king only but all the princes and people, and that her deed would come abroad to all women so that they would despise their husbands. The decree went out that she should come no more before the king, that her estate be given to another better than she, and that all wives should give honour to their husbands (Esther 1:16-22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records her refusal without stating her reason and without evaluating it. Interpreters have read it as dignity and as insubordination; the text says only that she refused and that the king was wroth.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The charge against her is made by Memucan, a courtier arguing a case, not by the narrator or by God. Scripture reports his speech without endorsing it.

Character Assessment

Scripture is notably silent about her. It records the command, the refusal, the king's anger, and a courtier's political argument, and offers no verdict of its own on any of it. Any assessment of her therefore has to be built on inference, and this reference declines to build one.

Significance

Her removal created the vacancy that Esther filled, and the book's whole deliverance depends on it. The decree that followed is one of the few pieces of domestic legislation recorded in Scripture and it came from a drunken feast.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 2:17.

Scripture

Esther 1:9-2:17
395

Memucan

One of the seven princes of Persia and Media; advised that Vashti be deposed and that a decree go out concerning wives.

Family

Not recorded. One of the seven princes who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom (Esther 1:14).

Chronology

In the third year of Ahasuerus.

Life Synopsis

When the king asked what should be done to Vashti according to law, "Memucan answered before the king and the princes, Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus. For this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes... Thus shall there arise too much contempt and wrath." He advised a royal commandment that she come no more before the king, that her estate be given to another, and that letters go to every province that every man should bear rule in his own house. "And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan" (Esther 1:16-21).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his advice and that the king followed it, without evaluating either. His argument is his own reasoning about political consequences, not a word from God, and the narrative reports it as such.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one speech and its effect, and passes no judgment. What the narrative makes plain is how much followed from a courtier's advice given at a drunken feast: a queen deposed and an empire-wide decree.

Significance

His counsel created the vacancy Esther filled.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named once.

Scripture

Esther 1:13-22
396

Hegai

The king's chamberlain, keeper of the women; showed Esther kindness and advised her what to take before the king.

Family

Not recorded. Chamberlain and keeper of the women (Esther 2:3).

Chronology

In the seventh year of Ahasuerus (Esther 2:16).

Life Synopsis

Esther was brought to the house of the women to his custody. "And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, which were meet to be given her, out of the king's house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women" (Esther 2:8-9).

When her turn came to go in to the king, "she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed" (Esther 2:15).

What They Did Right

  • Showed kindness to Esther and advanced her, without any recorded reason of advantage to himself: Esther 2:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records kindness and nothing else. His judgment about what she should take before the king was sound, and her willingness to accept it rather than choose for herself is recorded as part of why she found favour.

Significance

His favour placed Esther in the best position in the house of the women, and his advice shaped her first appearance before the king.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 2:15.

Scripture

Esther 2:3, 2:8-15
397

Mordecai

A Jew of the tribe of Benjamin in Shushan; brought up Esther, uncovered a plot against the king, refused to bow to Haman, and was advanced to be second in the kingdom.

Family

Son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite carried away with Jeconiah (Esther 2:5-6). Cousin and guardian of Esther, his uncle Abihail's daughter (Esther 2:7, 2:15).

Chronology

From the seventh year of Ahasuerus, when Esther was taken, through the twelfth and after (Esther 2:16; Esther 3:7).

Life Synopsis

He brought up Hadassah, that is Esther, his uncle's daughter, "for she had neither father nor mother... whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter" (Esther 2:7). He charged her not to reveal her people, and walked every day before the court of the women's house to know how she did (Esther 2:10-11).

Sitting in the king's gate he learned of a plot by Bigthan and Teresh and told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai's name; the men were hanged and it was recorded (Esther 2:21-23).

When Haman was promoted, "Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence" (Esther 3:2). Haman, learning he was a Jew, sought to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. Mordecai rent his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried with a loud and bitter cry in the midst of the city (Esther 4:1).

He sent Esther the copy of the decree and charged her to go to the king. When she objected that anyone entering unbidden risked death, he answered: "Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews. For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:13-14).

Haman built a gallows for him; the king, sleepless, read the chronicles and had Haman lead Mordecai through the street in royal apparel proclaiming, "Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour" (Esther 6:1-11). After Haman's fall he received the king's ring, wrote the counter-decree, and became great, "for Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces" (Esther 8:2, 9:4). He wrote to establish the days of Purim (Esther 9:20-22). The book ends: he was "next unto king Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and accepted of the multitude of his brethren, seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed" (Esther 10:3).

What They Did Right

  • Took his orphaned cousin as his own daughter: Esther 2:7.
  • Watched over her daily while she was in the women's house: Esther 2:11.
  • Reported a plot against the king's life and sought no reward: Esther 2:21-23.
  • Refused to bow to Haman, at cost: Esther 3:2-4.
  • Charged Esther to act, without pretending the risk was small, and without claiming to know the outcome - "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?": Esther 4:13-14.
  • Sought the wealth of his people and spoke peace to all his seed: Esther 10:3.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture does not state his reason for refusing to bow to Haman, and does not evaluate the refusal. It notes only that he told them he was a Jew (Esther 3:4).

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His words to Esther in Esther 4:14 are the theological centre of a book that never mentions God: deliverance would arise from another place, so her opportunity was not her leverage but her responsibility, and he does not claim certainty about why she was there.

Significance

With Esther he is the human means of the Jews' preservation, and he established the feast of Purim. His descent from Kish, a Benjamite, and Haman's descent as an Agagite set the conflict against the old enmity between Saul and Agag (1 Samuel 15).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 10:3.

Scripture

Esther 2:5-10:3
398

Esther

A Jewish orphan of Benjamin, brought up by Mordecai; made queen of Persia, and risked her life to petition for her people.

Also called Hadassah

Family

Daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle (Esther 2:15); her Hebrew name was Hadassah (Esther 2:7). Wife of Ahasuerus.

Chronology

Taken to the king in the seventh year of his reign (Esther 2:16).

Life Synopsis

"And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful" (Esther 2:7). Taken into the king's house, she obtained kindness of Hegai and required nothing but what he appointed. "And the king loved Esther above all the women... so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti" (Esther 2:15-17). She had not showed her people, as Mordecai had charged her.

When Mordecai put on sackcloth she sent to know why, and received the decree and his charge. She answered with the risk stated plainly - anyone who came to the king uncalled was put to death unless he held out the golden sceptre, and she had not been called for thirty days. Mordecai's answer came back, and hers followed: "Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:5-16).

On the third day she stood in the inner court and obtained favour. She did not ask at once, but invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second (Esther 5:1-8). At the second she made her petition: "Let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: for we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish." Asked who had dared, she said, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman" (Esther 7:3-6).

Afterward she fell at the king's feet and besought him with tears to reverse Haman's letters, and the counter-decree was written (Esther 8:3-8). She wrote with Mordecai to confirm the days of Purim (Esther 9:29-32).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed Mordecai's charge concerning her people while in the king's house: Esther 2:10, 2:20.
  • Required nothing but what Hegai appointed, when she could have asked for anything: Esther 2:15.
  • Called a three-day fast and went in to the king uncalled at the risk of her life: "if I perish, I perish": Esther 4:16.
  • Waited and prepared rather than making her petition at the first opportunity: Esther 5:4-8.
  • Identified Haman to his face in the king's presence: Esther 7:6.
  • Pleaded with tears for the reversal of the decree after her own life was already safe: Esther 8:3-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • She initially declined Mordecai's charge, citing the law and the thirty days she had not been called: Esther 4:11. Scripture records the hesitation and the change of mind, and does not condemn either.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her beyond an initial hesitation she overcame. Her deliberateness is the most striking thing in the record: she fasted three days first, went in without asking, held two banquets, and named Haman only when the king was ready to hear it. "If I perish, I perish" is not resignation but decision.

Significance

Through her the Jews of the Persian empire were preserved. The book bearing her name is one of two in Scripture named for a woman, and it never mentions God - the deliverance comes through timing, courage, and a sleepless king, which is itself the book's argument about providence. The feast of Purim commemorates the deliverance (Esther 9:26-32).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 9:32.

Scripture

Esther 2:7-9:32
399

Bigthan and Teresh

Two of the king's chamberlains, keepers of the door, who conspired to kill Ahasuerus; discovered by Mordecai and hanged. Two distinct individuals, recorded only together.

Family

Not recorded. Chamberlains and keepers of the door (Esther 2:21).

Chronology

After Esther was made queen (Esther 2:21).

Life Synopsis

"In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king's gate, two of the king's chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name. And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king" (Esther 2:21-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Conspired to assassinate the king: Esther 2:21.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the conspiracy, its discovery, and their execution, with no further detail. Their significance is entirely in what the record of it produced.

Significance

The entry made in the book of the chronicles about Mordecai's part in exposing them was read aloud on the night the king could not sleep, and it is the hinge of the whole deliverance (Esther 6:1-3).

Death / Outcome

Both hanged on a tree (Esther 2:23).

Scripture

Esther 2:21-23; Esther 6:1-3
400

Haman

Son of Hammedatha the Agagite; promoted above all the princes; sought to destroy all the Jews in the empire and was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

Family

Son of Hammedatha the Agagite (Esther 3:1); husband of Zeresh; father of ten sons (Esther 5:10-11; Esther 9:7-10).

Chronology

Promoted after the events of Esther 2; the lot was cast in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus (Esther 3:7).

Life Synopsis

The king promoted him above all the princes, and all the king's servants bowed to him, "but Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence." When told Mordecai was a Jew, "he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone... wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai" (Esther 3:1-6).

He cast Pur, the lot, and then put the case to the king without naming the people: "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people... let it be written that they may be destroyed: and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver" (Esther 3:8-9). The decree went out to kill all Jews, young and old, little children and women, in one day.

He went out joyful from Esther's first banquet, and seeing Mordecai unmoved in the gate, "he was full of indignation." He recounted his glory to his wife and friends and said, "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." Zeresh advised a gallows fifty cubits high, and he had it made (Esther 5:9-14).

Called in by the sleepless king and asked what should be done for the man the king delighted to honour, "Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?" He described royal apparel, the king's horse, and a proclamation - and was made to do it for Mordecai (Esther 6:6-11). At Esther's second banquet he was named, and the king went out in wrath; Haman fell on the queen's bed pleading for his life, and the king returned and took it for assault. Harbonah mentioned the gallows, and he was hanged on it (Esther 7:6-10). His ten sons were hanged also (Esther 9:13-14).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was full of wrath because one man would not bow: Esther 3:5.
  • Sought to destroy an entire people, including little children and women, over a personal slight: Esther 3:6, 3:13.
  • Concealed the identity of the people from the king while obtaining the decree: Esther 3:8.
  • Built a gallows fifty cubits high for a man against whom he had no charge but a refusal to bow: Esther 5:14.
  • Assumed the king could delight to honour no one but himself: Esther 6:6.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture traces the whole plot to a single unbowed head and records his own words about it - all his glory availed him nothing while Mordecai sat in the gate. The account is constructed as a sustained reversal: the gallows, the honour, the banquet, and the ring all pass to the other side.

Significance

He is called an Agagite, which sets the conflict against Saul's failure to destroy Agag king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:8-9), with Mordecai descended from Kish as Saul was. The deliverance from his decree is commemorated in Purim, named from the Pur he cast (Esther 9:24-26).

Death / Outcome

Hanged on the fifty-cubit gallows he had made for Mordecai (Esther 7:10).

Scripture

Esther 3:1-9:25
401

Zeresh

Wife of Haman; advised him to build the gallows for Mordecai, and afterward told him he would surely fall.

Family

Wife of Haman (Esther 5:10); mother of his ten sons.

Chronology

During the events of Esther.

Life Synopsis

Haman called for his friends and Zeresh his wife and recounted the glory of his riches, his sons, and his promotion, and then his frustration over Mordecai. "Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made" (Esther 5:10-14).

After he had led Mordecai through the city, he came home mourning and told her and his friends everything. "Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him" (Esther 6:13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Advised the building of the gallows for Mordecai: Esther 5:14.

Character Assessment

Scripture records two speeches from her and they point in opposite directions: she proposed the gallows and then, one day later, told her husband he would certainly fall. The second is one of the more remarkable statements in the book - a recognition from inside Haman's own house that the outcome was already decided.

Significance

Her second speech, that he would surely fall before a man of the seed of the Jews, is the closest the book of Esther comes to a theological statement, and it is spoken by the wife of the enemy.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Esther 6:13.

Scripture

Esther 5:10-14; Esther 6:13
402

Harbonah

One of the king's chamberlains; mentioned the gallows Haman had built, and Haman was hanged on it.

Family

Not recorded. One of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:10).

Chronology

At Esther's second banquet.

Life Synopsis

When the king returned from the palace garden and found Haman fallen on the queen's bed, "then said Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon" (Esther 7:9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He supplied the information at the decisive moment, including the reminder that Mordecai had spoken good for the king. Scripture records the words without commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, and it settles the matter. Scripture gives no comment on his motive.

Significance

His remark turned the king's wrath into a specific sentence and produced the reversal on which the book turns: the gallows built for Mordecai used for the man who built it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named twice, in Esther 1:10 and Esther 7:9.

Scripture

Esther 1:10; Esther 7:9
403

Ezra

A priest and ready scribe in the law of Moses; led the second return, taught the law, and dealt with the foreign marriages.

Family

Son of Seraiah, traced back to Aaron the chief priest (Ezra 7:1-5).

Chronology

He went up from Babylon in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:7-8).

Life Synopsis

"This Ezra went up from Babylon; and he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the Lord God of Israel had given: and the king granted him all his request, according to the hand of the Lord his God upon him" (Ezra 7:6). The statement that follows defines him: "For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments" (Ezra 7:10).

At the river Ahava he proclaimed a fast, "for I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him." They fasted and God was entreated (Ezra 8:21-23). He weighed out the silver, gold, and vessels to twelve priests and required them to watch and keep them (Ezra 8:24-30).

Told that the people, priests, and Levites had taken foreign wives, "I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied." At the evening sacrifice he fell on his knees, spread out his hands, and prayed one of the great confessions of Scripture: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens" - throughout using "we" and "our" though he had done nothing (Ezra 9:1-15). The people gathered and the matter was dealt with (Ezra 10:1-17).

In Nehemiah's time he brought the book of the law before the congregation, stood on a pulpit of wood, opened the book in the sight of all the people, and read from morning until midday, with the Levites causing the people to understand; "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:1-8).

What They Did Right

  • Prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach it - in that order: Ezra 7:10.
  • Refused a military escort because he had testified to the king that God's hand was on those who sought him: Ezra 8:21-23.
  • Weighed out the treasure publicly and made others accountable for it: Ezra 8:24-34.
  • Confessed the nation's sin as his own, using "we" throughout, though he had no part in it: Ezra 9:5-15.
  • Read the law publicly and had it explained so the people understood: Nehemiah 8:1-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The description in Ezra 7:10 is one of the most quoted summaries of a life in the Old Testament, and the order in it is deliberate: seek, do, then teach. His prayer in Ezra 9 is remarkable for its pronouns - he had not married a foreign wife, and he confesses as though he had.

Significance

He re-established the law as the centre of the returned community's life, and the public reading in Nehemiah 8 is the model of expository teaching in Scripture. Jewish tradition credits him with a large role in collecting the scriptures; that is tradition and not stated in the biblical text.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 12:36.

Scripture

Ezra 7:1-10:44; Nehemiah 8:1-18; Nehemiah 12:26, 12:36
404

Shechaniah (son of Jehiel)

A man of the sons of Elam who proposed the covenant to put away the foreign wives and told Ezra to arise and act.

Family

Son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam (Ezra 10:2).

Chronology

In Ezra's time, after his arrival (Ezra 10:2).

Life Synopsis

While Ezra prayed and wept, casting himself down before the house of God, a very great congregation gathered and wept.

"And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing... Arise; for this matter belongeth unto thee: we also will be with thee: be of good courage, and do it" (Ezra 10:2-4).

What They Did Right

  • Named the sin plainly as "we" while the leader wept, and declared there was yet hope: Ezra 10:2.
  • Told Ezra to arise and act, and pledged the people's support: Ezra 10:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture does not state whether he was himself among those who had taken foreign wives; his father Jehiel is named among the sons of Elam who had (Ezra 10:26), but the text does not say so of him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His speech turns the moment: Ezra was prostrate and weeping, and it was a layman who said there was hope and told the leader to get up and do something.

Significance

His proposal produced the covenant and the process by which the matter was dealt with, and his words "there is hope in Israel concerning this thing" are the turning point of the book of Ezra.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Ezra 10:4.

Scripture

Ezra 10:2-4
405

Nehemiah

Son of Hachaliah; cupbearer to Artaxerxes; rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem in fifty-two days and served as governor of Judah.

Family

Son of Hachaliah (Nehemiah 1:1); his brother Hanani brought him the news from Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:2).

Chronology

He heard the news in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes and returned; he was governor twelve years, and went back to the king in the thirty-second year (Nehemiah 1:1; Nehemiah 5:14; Nehemiah 13:6).

Life Synopsis

His brother Hanani came from Judah and reported that the remnant were in great affliction and reproach, the wall broken down and the gates burned. "And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 1:3-4). His prayer confessed the nation's sin as his own and asked for mercy before the king.

As cupbearer he had never been sad in the king's presence. When the king asked why, "then I was very sore afraid," and he answered honestly, then "prayed to the God of heaven" between the question and his reply, and asked to be sent to rebuild (Nehemiah 2:1-8).

He surveyed the ruins by night, told no one, then called the people: "Ye see the distress that we are in... come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach" (Nehemiah 2:11-18). Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mocked, then conspired to fight. He set a watch, armed the builders so that every one with one hand wrought and with the other held a weapon, and answered, "Our God shall fight for us" (Nehemiah 4:1-23).

When the poor were being mortgaged and enslaved by their own brethren, he was very angry, rebuked the nobles, made them restore lands and usury, and shook his lap. He himself did not take the governor's bread for twelve years "because of the fear of God" (Nehemiah 5:1-19).

He refused four invitations to meet in the plain of Ono - "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" - refused to hide in the temple when told his life was threatened, saying, "Should such a man as I flee?", and finished the wall in fifty-two days, so that the enemies perceived the work was wrought of God (Nehemiah 6:1-16).

Returning after a period at court, he found Tobiah lodged in a temple chamber, the Levites' portions unpaid, the sabbath broken, and mixed marriages again. He cast Tobiah's furniture out, restored the Levites, shut the gates on the sabbath eve, and contended with those who had married foreign wives (Nehemiah 13:4-31).

What They Did Right

  • Wept, fasted, and prayed on hearing of Jerusalem's ruin, confessing his own and his father's house's sin: Nehemiah 1:4-7.
  • Prayed silently in the middle of a conversation with the king before answering: Nehemiah 2:4.
  • Surveyed the damage himself before speaking to anyone: Nehemiah 2:12-16.
  • Armed the builders and set a watch rather than abandoning the work under threat: Nehemiah 4:9, 4:16-18.
  • Rebuked the nobles for exacting usury from their own brethren and made them restore it: Nehemiah 5:6-12.
  • Refused the governor's allowance for twelve years because of the fear of God, and did not buy land: Nehemiah 5:14-16.
  • Refused to leave the work for a negotiation and refused to hide in the temple: Nehemiah 6:3, 6:11.
  • Finished the wall in fifty-two days: Nehemiah 6:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His final reforms include actions he records himself in strong terms - he contended with them, cursed them, smote certain of them, and plucked off their hair (Nehemiah 13:25). Scripture records this without comment and he follows it with a prayer to be remembered for good.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His memoir is unusual for how often it records prayer at ordinary moments - before answering a king, under threat, at the end of a chapter of work. The one place a modern reader may hesitate is Nehemiah 13:25, and the text neither defends nor criticises it.

Significance

He rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, which made the restored community defensible and permanent, and served as governor without taking the allowance due to him. His book is one of only two in the Old Testament written largely in the first person.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His last recorded words are "Remember me, O my God, for good" (Nehemiah 13:31).

Scripture

Nehemiah 1:1-13:31; Ezra 2:2
406

Hanani (brother of Nehemiah)

Brother of Nehemiah; brought word of Jerusalem's ruined state, and was afterward given charge of the city with Hananiah.

Family

Brother of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 1:2; Nehemiah 7:2).

Chronology

In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (Nehemiah 1:1).

Life Synopsis

"That Hanani, one of my brethren, came, he and certain men of Judah; and I asked them concerning the Jews that had escaped, which were left of the captivity, and concerning Jerusalem. And they said unto me, The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire" (Nehemiah 1:2-3).

After the wall was finished, Nehemiah gave charge of Jerusalem to "Hanani my brother, and Hananiah the ruler of the palace: for he was a faithful man, and feared God above many" (Nehemiah 7:2).

What They Did Right

  • Brought a truthful report that set the whole rebuilding in motion: Nehemiah 1:2-3.
  • Was entrusted with charge over Jerusalem: Nehemiah 7:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his report and his appointment and nothing else. The commendation in Nehemiah 7:2 - a faithful man who feared God above many - is grammatically attached to Hananiah rather than to Hanani, and this reference does not claim it for him.

Significance

His report is the occasion of the entire book of Nehemiah.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 12:36.

Scripture

Nehemiah 1:2-3; Nehemiah 7:2; Nehemiah 12:36
407

Sanballat

The Horonite; chief opponent of the rebuilding of Jerusalem; mocked, conspired, and repeatedly tried to draw Nehemiah into a trap.

Family

The Horonite (Nehemiah 2:10). His daughter married a son of Joiada the high priest's son, whom Nehemiah chased away (Nehemiah 13:28).

Chronology

Throughout Nehemiah's governorship (Nehemiah 2:10-13:28).

Life Synopsis

When he heard that a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, "it grieved them exceedingly" (Nehemiah 2:10). He laughed the builders to scorn and asked, "Will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?" (Nehemiah 4:1-2).

When the wall was joined together he conspired with Tobiah, the Arabians, Ammonites, and Ashdodites to fight against Jerusalem (Nehemiah 4:7-8). He then sent four times asking Nehemiah to meet him in a village in the plain of Ono, "but they thought to do me mischief" (Nehemiah 6:1-4). The fifth time he sent an open letter accusing him of planning rebellion and setting up prophets to proclaim him king, adding, "Come now therefore, and let us take counsel together." Nehemiah answered, "There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart" (Nehemiah 6:5-8). He hired Shemaiah and others to make Nehemiah afraid (Nehemiah 6:12-14).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was grieved that someone sought the welfare of Israel: Nehemiah 2:10.
  • Mocked and despised the builders: Nehemiah 4:1-3.
  • Conspired to attack Jerusalem: Nehemiah 4:7-8.
  • Attempted four times to lure Nehemiah into a meeting to do him mischief: Nehemiah 6:2-4.
  • Wrote a false public accusation of rebellion: Nehemiah 6:5-7.
  • Hired prophets to frighten Nehemiah into sin: Nehemiah 6:12-14.

Character Assessment

Uniformly hostile in the record. What is notable is the escalation of method - mockery, then armed conspiracy, then negotiation, then slander, then hired prophecy - and that every stage failed. Nehemiah's answer to the slander is one sentence: you feign them out of your own heart.

Significance

His opposition, and its failure, is the framework of the rebuilding narrative. His marriage alliance with the high priest's family shows how far compromise had reached into the priesthood, and Nehemiah's expulsion of the grandson of the high priest for it is his last recorded act of discipline.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 13:28.

Scripture

Nehemiah 2:10, 2:19; Nehemiah 4:1-8; Nehemiah 6:1-14; Nehemiah 13:28
408

Tobiah

The servant, the Ammonite; joined Sanballat against the rebuilding; connected by marriage to leading families in Judah, and lodged in a temple chamber until Nehemiah threw his goods out.

Family

Called "the servant, the Ammonite" (Nehemiah 2:10). Son in law of Shechaniah the son of Arah; his son Johanan married the daughter of Meshullam (Nehemiah 6:18). Allied to Eliashib the priest (Nehemiah 13:4).

Chronology

Throughout Nehemiah's governorship.

Life Synopsis

He joined Sanballat in grief that someone had come to seek Israel's welfare, and in the mockery: "Now Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, and he said, Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall" (Nehemiah 4:3). He conspired in the plot to attack (Nehemiah 4:7-8) and joined the attempts to lure Nehemiah out (Nehemiah 6:1-14).

Nehemiah records the difficulty he presented: many in Judah were sworn to him, because he was the son in law of Shechaniah and his son had married the daughter of Meshullam; "they reported his good deeds before me, and uttered my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to put me in fear" (Nehemiah 6:17-19).

During Nehemiah's absence, Eliashib the priest, who was allied to him, prepared him a great chamber in the courts of the house of God where the offerings had been stored. Nehemiah returned, "and it grieved me sore: therefore I cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the chamber. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the chambers: and thither brought I again the vessels of the house of God" (Nehemiah 13:4-9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Mocked the builders: Nehemiah 4:3.
  • Conspired to attack Jerusalem: Nehemiah 4:7-8.
  • Sent letters to put Nehemiah in fear: Nehemiah 6:19.
  • Took a chamber in the courts of the house of God, an Ammonite lodged where the offerings belonged: Nehemiah 13:5-8; compare Deuteronomy 23:3.

Character Assessment
