Uniformly hostile, and more dangerous than Sanballat because he was inside the community by marriage. Nehemiah records that nobles of Judah wrote to him and reported his good deeds - the opposition had friends at the highest level, and that is the point of the passage.

Significance

His chamber in the temple is the clearest single image in Nehemiah of what compromise had produced: the room built for the offerings occupied by the man who had tried to stop the wall.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 13:8.

Scripture

Nehemiah 2:10, 2:19; Nehemiah 4:3-8; Nehemiah 6:1-19; Nehemiah 13:4-9
409

Geshem

The Arabian; joined Sanballat and Tobiah in mocking and in the attempts against Nehemiah.

Also called Gashmu

Family

An Arabian (Nehemiah 2:19).

Chronology

During the rebuilding of the wall.

Life Synopsis

"But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?" (Nehemiah 2:19).

He joined in the repeated invitations to the plain of Ono (Nehemiah 6:1-2), and Sanballat's open letter cited him: "It is reported among the heathen, and Gashmu saith it, that thou and the Jews think to rebel" (Nehemiah 6:6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Mocked and despised the builders and raised the charge of rebellion against the king: Nehemiah 2:19.
  • Joined the attempts to draw Nehemiah into a trap: Nehemiah 6:1-2.
  • His name was used to lend weight to a false report of rebellion: Nehemiah 6:6.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his participation in the opposition and nothing else. He is the third of the three named adversaries.

Significance

The charge of rebellion he and the others raised was the most dangerous weapon available against a project carried out under royal commission, and Nehemiah answered it directly.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 6:6.

Scripture

Nehemiah 2:19; Nehemiah 6:1-6
410

Shemaiah (son of Delaiah)

A hired prophet who urged Nehemiah to shut himself in the temple for safety, in order to make him sin.

Family

Son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabeel (Nehemiah 6:10).

Chronology

During the rebuilding of the wall.

Life Synopsis

Nehemiah came to his house, and he was shut up. He said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple, and let us shut the doors of the temple: for they will come to slay thee; yea, in the night will they come to slay thee."

"And I said, Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in. And, lo, I perceived that God had not sent him; but that he pronounced this prophecy against me: for Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. Therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin, and that they might have matter for an evil report, that they might reproach me" (Nehemiah 6:10-13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to give a false prophecy: Nehemiah 6:12-13.
  • Urged Nehemiah to take refuge in the temple, where a layman had no right to go, so that he would sin and be reproached: Nehemiah 6:11-13.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. His advice was plausible, urgent, framed as concern for a man's life, and calculated to produce a specific sin. Nehemiah's detection of it rested on knowing what he was and was not permitted to do.

Significance

The episode is Scripture's clearest example of prophecy used as a weapon, and of a leader tested by advice that appeals to self-preservation. Nehemiah's answer - should such a man as I flee? - is among the best-known lines in the book.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 6:14.

Scripture

Nehemiah 6:10-14
411

Noadiah

A prophetess who, with other prophets, sought to put Nehemiah in fear.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During the rebuilding of the wall.

Life Synopsis

Nehemiah's prayer names her: "My God, think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear" (Nehemiah 6:14). Nothing else is recorded of her.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Sought to put Nehemiah in fear, and is named with Tobiah and Sanballat in his prayer for judgment: Nehemiah 6:14.

Character Assessment

One verse. She is one of only five women called prophetess in Scripture, and the only one of the five against whom anything is recorded. Scripture gives no detail of what she said or did beyond the charge of seeking to intimidate.

Significance

Her inclusion shows that the opposition to the wall included religious voices within the community, not only foreign adversaries.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is named once.

Scripture

Nehemiah 6:14
412

Eliashib

High priest at the rebuilding of the wall; built the sheep gate, but was allied to Tobiah and gave him a chamber in the house of God.

Family

High priest; son of Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:10). His grandson married Sanballat's daughter (Nehemiah 13:28).

Chronology

During Nehemiah's governorship.

Life Synopsis

"Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it" (Nehemiah 3:1).

Later: "And before this, Eliashib the priest, having the oversight of the chamber of the house of our God, was allied unto Tobiah: and he had prepared for him a great chamber, where aforetime they laid the meat offerings, the frankincense, and the vessels, and the tithes of the corn, the new wine, and the oil, which was commanded to be given to the Levites" (Nehemiah 13:4-5). Nehemiah, returning from the king, cast out Tobiah's household stuff and had the chambers cleansed.

What They Did Right

  • Rose up with the priests to build and sanctify the sheep gate, first in the list of the builders: Nehemiah 3:1.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was allied to Tobiah, the chief opponent of the work: Nehemiah 13:4.
  • Gave Tobiah a great chamber in the courts of the house of God, displacing the offerings and the Levites' tithes: Nehemiah 13:5.
  • His grandson married the daughter of Sanballat and was driven out by Nehemiah for it: Nehemiah 13:28.

Character Assessment

A genuinely mixed record and a cautionary one. He led the priests in building the wall's first gate and then handed a storeroom in God's house to the man who had tried to stop it. Scripture records both without reconciling them, and the second is what the book ends with.

Significance

His compromise is the concrete example of the problem Nehemiah's final chapter addresses: the reform did not hold in his absence, and the failure ran through the high priest's own household.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Nehemiah 13:28.

Scripture

Nehemiah 3:1, 3:20-21; Nehemiah 12:10, 12:22-23; Nehemiah 13:4-9, 13:28

Writing Prophets

413

Jonah

Son of Amittai, of Gathhepher; prophet to Israel under Jeroboam II; fled from God's commission to Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, and was angry when the city repented.

Also called Jonas

Family

Son of Amittai, of Gathhepher in Zebulun (2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1).

Chronology

He prophesied in the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel (2 Kings 14:25), placing him in the eighth century before Christ.

Life Synopsis

He had foretold Jeroboam's restoration of Israel's borders (2 Kings 14:25). Then the word came: "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it." He rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord (Jonah 1:1-3).

A great tempest came, and the mariners cast lots and the lot fell on him. He was asleep below. Asked who he was, he answered, "I am an Hebrew; and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land." He told them to throw him overboard, and they rowed hard to bring the ship to land rather than do it, and only threw him in when they could not. The sea ceased, and the men feared the Lord exceedingly and offered a sacrifice (Jonah 1:4-16).

A great fish swallowed him, and he prayed from its belly: "I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the Lord, and he heard me... Salvation is of the Lord" (Jonah 2:1-9). He was vomited on dry land.

The word came a second time and he went. "And he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." The people believed God, proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least, and the king came down from his throne and sat in ashes. "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not" (Jonah 3:4-10).

"But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." He prayed, and his prayer explains the flight: "was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil. Therefore now, O Lord, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live." He sat outside the city to see what would become of it. God prepared a gourd for shade, then a worm to destroy it, then a vehement east wind, and asked, "Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?" and he said, "I do well to be angry, even unto death." The book ends with God's question: "should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" (Jonah 4:1-11). Jonah's answer is not recorded.

What They Did Right

  • Confessed the Lord, the God of heaven who made the sea and the dry land, to the mariners: Jonah 1:9.
  • Told the mariners to cast him into the sea rather than let them perish: Jonah 1:12.
  • Prayed from the fish's belly and ended, "Salvation is of the Lord": Jonah 2:1-9.
  • Went to Nineveh and preached when the word came the second time: Jonah 3:1-4.
  • Foretold truly the restoration of Israel's coast under Jeroboam II: 2 Kings 14:25.

What They Did Wrong

  • Fled from the presence of the Lord toward Tarshish rather than go to Nineveh: Jonah 1:3.
  • Was exceedingly displeased and very angry that God spared a repentant city: Jonah 4:1.
  • Admitted he had fled precisely because he knew God was gracious and merciful and would relent: Jonah 4:2.
  • Twice asked God to take his life: Jonah 4:3, 4:8-9.
  • Cared more for a gourd he had not made than for a hundred and twenty thousand people: Jonah 4:10-11.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him without any attempt to make him sympathetic. He is a true prophet whose predictions came to pass, and the book that bears his name is largely an account of his failures. The most remarkable feature is his own explanation in Jonah 4:2: he did not flee because he doubted God but because he knew what God was like. The book ends with a question put to him that he never answers, which leaves the reader holding it.

Significance

Christ made him the only sign given to his generation: "as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth," and added that the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment against that generation because they repented at Jonah's preaching, "and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here" (Matthew 12:39-41; Luke 11:29-32). The book is Scripture's most direct statement that God's mercy extends beyond Israel, delivered through a prophet who resented it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1-4:11; Matthew 12:39-41; Matthew 16:4; Luke 11:29-32
414

Hosea

Son of Beeri; prophet to the northern kingdom; commanded to marry a wife of whoredoms as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness.

Also called Osee

Family

Son of Beeri (Hosea 1:1). Husband of Gomer; father of Jezreel, Loruhamah, and Loammi (Hosea 1:3-9).

Chronology

He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam II of Israel (Hosea 1:1) - a ministry spanning decades to the eve of Samaria's fall.

Life Synopsis

"The beginning of the word of the Lord by Hosea. And the Lord said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord" (Hosea 1:2). He took Gomer, and she bore three children whose names were the message: Jezreel, for the blood God would avenge; Loruhamah, "for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel"; and Loammi, "for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God" (Hosea 1:3-9).

He was afterward told, "Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods." He bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and an homer and a half of barley, and told her she would abide for him many days (Hosea 3:1-3).

His oracles alternate between the sharpest indictments in the prophets - "there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land"; "my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge" - and some of its tenderest passages: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt... I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms... How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?... mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together" (Hosea 4:1, 4:6; Hosea 11:1-8).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed a command that cost him his marriage and made his household a public sermon: Hosea 1:2-3.
  • Went again and bought back an adulterous wife at God's word: Hosea 3:1-2.
  • Named his children as God directed, carrying the message in his own family: Hosea 1:4-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. What it records instead is obedience of an unusually costly kind: he was told to marry a woman who would be unfaithful, and then told to go back and buy her out of the situation her unfaithfulness had brought her to. The book uses his marriage as the figure for God's dealings with Israel throughout.

Significance

Hosea 11:1 - "out of Egypt have I called my son" - is applied by Matthew to Christ (Matthew 1:15 context; Matthew 2:15). Paul cites Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 concerning the calling of a people who were not a people (Romans 9:25-26), and Christ twice quotes Hosea 6:6, "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7). His ministry ran to the fall of the northern kingdom he warned.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Hosea 1:1-14:9; Matthew 2:15; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10
415

Gomer

Daughter of Diblaim; wife of Hosea; a wife of whoredoms whose unfaithfulness pictured Israel's.

Family

Daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:3); wife of Hosea; mother of Jezreel, Loruhamah, and Loammi.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; which conceived, and bare him a son" (Hosea 1:3). She bore three children in all, each named by God's direction as a sign to Israel. Of the second and third the text does not say "bare him" as it does of the first (Hosea 1:6, 1:8-9), a difference in wording that has been much noticed and that Scripture does not explain.

Hosea 2 describes a wife pursuing her lovers and being hedged in until she says, "I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now" (Hosea 2:5-7). In Hosea 3 the prophet is told to go and love an adulteress again, and buys her for fifteen pieces of silver and a measure of barley, saying, "Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man; so will I also be for thee" (Hosea 3:1-3). The woman of Hosea 3 is not named, and whether she is Gomer is not stated; most read her so, and this reference notes that the identification is inference.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • She is described from the outset as a wife of whoredoms: Hosea 1:2. Scripture gives no narrative of particular acts and records no words of hers.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her no speech and almost no narrative, using her situation rather than her character. She is the figure through which the book states its case, and the case is not finally against her: the whole point of the marriage is that the husband goes and buys her back.

Significance

Her redemption in Hosea 3 - purchased at a price and told she would abide many days - is the book's picture of what God would do with Israel, who would "abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice," and afterward return and seek the Lord (Hosea 3:4-5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Hosea 3:3, if the unnamed woman there is she.

Scripture

Hosea 1:2-9; Hosea 2:1-23; Hosea 3:1-5
416

Amos

A herdman of Tekoa and gatherer of sycomore fruit; sent to prophesy against the northern kingdom in its prosperity, and expelled by the priest of Bethel.

Family

Not recorded. "Among the herdmen of Tekoa" (Amos 1:1).

Chronology

"In the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1).

Life Synopsis

He came from Tekoa in Judah to prophesy in Israel at the height of Jeroboam II's prosperity. His oracles begin with the surrounding nations and close the circle on Israel itself: "For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes" (Amos 2:6).

His charges are social and specific: they trample on the poor, take burdens of wheat from them, afflict the just, take a bribe, and turn aside the poor in the gate (Amos 5:11-12). He denounced the religion that ran alongside it: "I hate, I despise your feast days... But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amos 5:21-24). He described the comfortable: "them that are at ease in Zion... that lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock... but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" (Amos 6:1-6).

Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam accusing him of conspiracy, and told him to flee to Judah and prophesy there, "for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court." Amos answered, "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel" (Amos 7:10-15). He then pronounced a specific judgment on Amaziah's household.

What They Did Right

  • Went from Judah into a hostile kingdom to deliver God's word: Amos 7:14-15.
  • Named injustice against the poor as the specific charge, in a time of national prosperity: Amos 2:6-7; Amos 5:11-12; Amos 8:4-6.
  • Refused to be silenced or relocated by the priest of Bethel, and answered with his own calling: Amos 7:14-15.
  • Interceded twice for Israel at the visions of the locusts and the fire, and the Lord repented: Amos 7:1-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is the clearest instance in the prophets of a man with no professional standing - a herdman and a fruit-gatherer - claiming no credentials but the call itself. His book is the sharpest sustained attack on social injustice in Scripture, and it is addressed to a prosperous and religiously active society.

Significance

Amos 5:24 - let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream - and Amos 8:11, the famine of hearing the words of the Lord, are among the most quoted lines in the prophets. James quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the council of Jerusalem in support of receiving Gentiles (Acts 15:15-17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Amos 1:1-9:15; Acts 15:15-17
417

Amaziah (priest of Bethel)

Priest at the royal sanctuary of Bethel; reported Amos to the king and ordered him out of Israel.

Family

His wife, sons, and daughters are named in the judgment pronounced on him (Amos 7:17).

Chronology

In the reign of Jeroboam II (Amos 7:10).

Life Synopsis

"Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words." He quoted Amos selectively, reporting the word about Jeroboam's death by the sword and omitting the rest (Amos 7:10-11).

To Amos he said, "O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: but prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court" (Amos 7:12-13).

Amos answered with his calling and then with a sentence: "Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line; and thou shalt die in a polluted land: and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land" (Amos 7:16-17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Reported the prophet to the king as a conspirator: Amos 7:10.
  • Told Amos to go and earn his bread prophesying elsewhere, assuming that was his motive: Amos 7:12.
  • Forbade prophecy at Bethel on the ground that it was the king's chapel and the king's court - which states plainly whose sanctuary it had become: Amos 7:13.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. His own words condemn him: he calls the sanctuary the king's chapel, not God's house, and his objection to Amos is jurisdictional rather than theological. Scripture records the specific judgment pronounced on his household without recording its fulfilment.

Significance

The exchange between him and Amos is the clearest confrontation in the prophets between institutional religion and prophetic calling, and it produced Amos's statement of his own commission - the best-known verses in the book.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Amos foretold he would die in a polluted land (Amos 7:17).

Scripture

Amos 7:10-17
418

Isaiah

Son of Amoz; prophet in Judah through four reigns; counsellor to Ahaz and Hezekiah, and the most quoted prophet in the New Testament.

Also called Esaias

Family

Son of Amoz (Isaiah 1:1). His wife is called the prophetess (Isaiah 8:3). Father of Shearjashub and Mahershalalhashbaz (Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 8:3).

Chronology

He prophesied "in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah" (Isaiah 1:1), and his call came in the year king Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1).

Life Synopsis

"In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple." The seraphim cried "Holy, holy, holy," and he said, "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips." A live coal from the altar touched his mouth, and when the Lord asked, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" he answered, "Here am I; send me." The commission that followed was to preach to a people who would not hear (Isaiah 6:1-13).

He went to Ahaz with his son Shearjashub, urging him not to fear Syria and Israel, and offering him a sign. Ahaz refused it, and Isaiah gave the sign of Immanuel: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:1-16). He named his second son Mahershalalhashbaz as a sign of Damascus and Samaria's imminent fall (Isaiah 8:1-4). He walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 20:2-4).

Under Hezekiah he answered Sennacherib's threat with the longest prophetic address to a foreign king in Scripture (2 Kings 19:20-34; Isaiah 37:21-35). He told Hezekiah to set his house in order, and then, before he had gone out into the middle court, was sent back to say fifteen years would be added (2 Kings 20:1-6). After the Babylonian ambassadors he foretold the carrying away to Babylon (2 Kings 20:16-18).

His book contains the fullest Old Testament portraits of the coming king and the suffering servant: the child born and the son given whose name is Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God (Isaiah 9:6); the rod out of the stem of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1-5); and the servant who was despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:1-12).

What They Did Right

  • Confessed his own uncleanness before he was sent: Isaiah 6:5.
  • Volunteered without conditions: "Here am I; send me": Isaiah 6:8.
  • Accepted a commission to a people who would not hear: Isaiah 6:9-13.
  • Confronted Ahaz with God's word and offered him a sign, and gave the Immanuel sign when it was refused: Isaiah 7:3-14.
  • Walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign: Isaiah 20:2-3.
  • Stood with Hezekiah against Sennacherib and prayed with him: 2 Chronicles 32:20; Isaiah 37:1-7.
  • Returned at once with the word of mercy for Hezekiah before leaving the court: 2 Kings 20:4-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His call is the fullest account in the Old Testament of a man seeing God and knowing at once what he himself was. His willingness in Isaiah 6:8 is followed immediately by a commission to fail, and he asks only "Lord, how long?"

Significance

The most quoted prophet in the New Testament. Isaiah 7:14, 9:6, 11:1, 40:3, 53:1-12, and 61:1-2 are all applied to Christ, and Christ read Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16-21). The Ethiopian eunuch was reading Isaiah 53 when Philip found him (Acts 8:28-35). John says Isaiah spoke of Christ "when he saw his glory" (John 12:41).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded in Scripture. Jewish tradition holds that he was sawn asunder under Manasseh, and Hebrews 11:37 mentions those who "were sawn asunder" without naming anyone; the connection is traditional and is not made by Scripture.

Scripture

2 Kings 19:1-20:19; 2 Chronicles 26:22; 2 Chronicles 32:20-32; Isaiah 1:1-66:24; Matthew 3:3; Matthew 8:17; Luke 4:16-21; John 12:38-41; Acts 8:28-35; Romans 10:16-21
419

Shearjashub

A son of Isaiah, whose name means "a remnant shall return"; taken with his father to meet Ahaz.

Also called Shear-jashub

Family

Son of Isaiah (Isaiah 7:3).

Chronology

In the reign of Ahaz (Isaiah 7:1-3).

Life Synopsis

"Then said the Lord unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field" (Isaiah 7:3). Nothing he said or did is recorded; his presence is the point, since his name carried the message that a remnant would return.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his father, and his presence at one meeting. He is included because the name and the occasion are both significant: he was brought along precisely so that the king would hear the name.

Significance

His name states the double message that runs through Isaiah - judgment, in that only a remnant would survive, and mercy, in that a remnant would return. Isaiah later says, "Behold, I and the children whom the Lord hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18), which Hebrews applies to Christ and his people (Hebrews 2:13).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named once.

Scripture

Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 8:18; Isaiah 10:21-22
420

Mahershalalhashbaz

A son of Isaiah, whose name means "haste to the spoil, hasten to the prey"; a sign of the imminent fall of Damascus and Samaria.

Also called Maher-shalal-hash-baz

Family

Son of Isaiah and the prophetess (Isaiah 8:3).

Chronology

In the reign of Ahaz (Isaiah 8:1-4).

Life Synopsis

The Lord told Isaiah to write the name on a great roll before witnesses. "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the Lord to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz. For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 8:1-4).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Nothing he said or did is recorded. His name, written publicly before witnesses before his conception and given at his birth, was a dated prophecy: the time it would take a child to learn to speak.

Significance

With his brother he is named among the signs and wonders in Israel (Isaiah 8:18). His name is the longest in the Bible.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named once.

Scripture

Isaiah 8:1-4, 8:18
421

Micah (the prophet)

The Morasthite; prophet to Samaria and Jerusalem; foretold Bethlehem as the birthplace of the ruler in Israel. Not to be confused with Micah of mount Ephraim, or with Micaiah son of Imlah.

Also called Micah the Morasthite

Family

Not recorded. Of Moresheth in Judah (Micah 1:1).

Chronology

"In the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah" (Micah 1:1) - contemporary with Isaiah.

Life Synopsis

He prophesied against both capitals, naming the sins of the leadership: princes who hate the good and love the evil, who eat the flesh of God's people; heads that judge for reward, priests that teach for hire, prophets that divine for money, "yet will they lean upon the Lord, and say, Is not the Lord among us? none evil can come upon us" (Micah 3:1-11). He then said plainly, "Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps" (Micah 3:12).

That prophecy is quoted a century later in Jeremiah's trial: the elders recalled that Micah the Morasthite had said this in Hezekiah's days, and that Hezekiah had not put him to death but feared the Lord, and Jeremiah's life was spared on the precedent (Jeremiah 26:18-19).

He also foretold the ruler from Bethlehem: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" (Micah 5:2). And his summary of what God requires: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" (Micah 6:8).

What They Did Right

  • Named the specific corruptions of princes, priests, and prophets, including his own profession: Micah 3:5, 3:11.
  • Declared that Jerusalem itself would be ploughed as a field - and was heard rather than killed: Micah 3:12; Jeremiah 26:18-19.
  • Distinguished himself from the prophets who divined for money: "But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the Lord, and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression": Micah 3:8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His book moves between the harshest judgment and some of the tenderest promises in the prophets, and closes with a question about God rather than about Israel: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?" (Micah 7:18).

Significance

Micah 5:2 is the prophecy the chief priests and scribes quoted to Herod when asked where Christ should be born (Matthew 2:5-6). Micah 6:8 is among the most quoted verses in the Old Testament. His preaching, and Hezekiah's response to it, saved Jeremiah's life a century later.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Micah 1:1-7:20; Jeremiah 26:18-19; Matthew 2:5-6
422

Nahum

The Elkoshite; prophet of the burden of Nineveh, foretelling the destruction of the city Jonah had seen spared.

Family

Not recorded. The Elkoshite (Nahum 1:1).

Chronology

Date not established precisely by Scripture. He refers to the fall of No-amon in Egypt as past (Nahum 3:8-10) and Nineveh's destruction as future, which places him between those events.

Life Synopsis

"The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite" (Nahum 1:1). His opening holds two things together: "God is jealous, and the Lord revengeth; the Lord revengeth, and is furious... The Lord is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked... The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him" (Nahum 1:2-7).

The rest is a sustained description of Nineveh's fall - the chariots raging in the streets, the gates of the rivers opened, the palace dissolved, the spoil of silver and gold. He names the charge: "Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not" (Nahum 3:1). The book ends with a question addressed to the king of Assyria: "all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?" (Nahum 3:19).

What They Did Right

  • Declared both God's slowness to anger and his refusal to acquit the wicked in the same breath: Nahum 1:3.
  • Named the Lord as a strong hold in the day of trouble who knows them that trust in him, in the middle of an oracle of destruction: Nahum 1:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing about him personally beyond his name and town. His book is entirely about Nineveh, and it stands deliberately alongside Jonah: the city that repented under Jonah is here destroyed, roughly a century and a half later. Neither book cancels the other, and the pairing is Scripture's clearest statement that mercy shown is not mercy owed indefinitely.

Significance

Nahum 1:15 - "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings" - parallels Isaiah 52:7, which Paul applies to the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:15). His book records the end of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Nahum 1:1-3:19; Romans 10:15
423

Zephaniah

Son of Cushi, of the royal line through Hezekiah; prophesied in Josiah's days of the day of the Lord against Judah and the nations.

Family

"The son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hizkiah" (Zephaniah 1:1) - an unusually long pedigree for a prophet, apparently tracing him to king Hezekiah.

Chronology

"In the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah" (Zephaniah 1:1), which places him around the time of Josiah's reform.

Life Synopsis

His opening is total: "I will utterly consume all things from off the land, saith the Lord" (Zephaniah 1:2). He named those who had turned back from the Lord and "those that have not sought the Lord, nor enquired for him," and "the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The Lord will not do good, neither will he do evil" (Zephaniah 1:6, 1:12).

He described the day of the Lord as "a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness" (Zephaniah 1:15). He called for gathering "before the decree bring forth" and urged the meek of the earth to seek righteousness and meekness, "it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the Lord's anger" (Zephaniah 2:1-3).

The book closes in a register entirely different from its opening: "The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17).

What They Did Right

  • Preached in the reign of a reforming king and named the indifference underneath the reform - men settled on their lees who thought God would do neither good nor evil: Zephaniah 1:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing about him personally beyond his ancestry. His book contains one of the bleakest descriptions of judgment in the prophets and one of the warmest descriptions of God's delight in his people, five chapters apart in a three-chapter book.

Significance

His phrase "the great day of the Lord" (Zephaniah 1:14) shapes later usage, and Zephaniah 3:17 is among the most quoted verses about God's disposition toward his people. His ministry under Josiah runs alongside the finding of the book of the law.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Zephaniah 1:1-3:20
424

Habakkuk

A prophet who complained to God about injustice in Judah, was answered that the Chaldeans were coming, and complained again; ended in one of Scripture's strongest statements of trust.

Family

Not recorded. "Habakkuk the prophet" (Habakkuk 1:1).

Chronology

Date not established precisely by Scripture. The Chaldeans are described as being raised up in his own days (Habakkuk 1:5-6), placing him shortly before the Babylonian invasions.

Life Synopsis

His book opens as a complaint, not an oracle: "O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save! Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause me to behold grievance?... the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth" (Habakkuk 1:2-4).

God answered that he was raising up the Chaldeans, "that bitter and hasty nation," which produced a harder question: "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil... wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?" (Habakkuk 1:6-13).

He then said, "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved" (Habakkuk 2:1). The answer came: write the vision and make it plain; the vision is for an appointed time; "the just shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:2-4), followed by five woes against the oppressor.

The book ends with a prayer and one of the great affirmations of Scripture: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

What They Did Right

  • Took his complaint directly to God rather than abandoning faith or concealing the difficulty: Habakkuk 1:2-4, 1:12-17.
  • Set himself on the tower to watch for God's answer, and to hear what he would say when reproved: Habakkuk 2:1.
  • Ended in settled trust while expecting total loss: Habakkuk 3:17-19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His questions are pressing and near to accusation, and Scripture records God answering them rather than rebuking him for asking.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His book is unusual in the prophets for being addressed mostly to God rather than to the people: it is a record of a man arguing with God and being answered. The movement from "how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear" to "yet I will rejoice in the Lord" happens without his circumstances improving.

Significance

Habakkuk 2:4 - "the just shall live by his faith" - is quoted three times in the New Testament and is foundational to Paul's argument in Romans and Galatians (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38). Paul also quotes Habakkuk 1:5 at Antioch (Acts 13:41).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Habakkuk 1:1-3:19; Acts 13:41; Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38
425

Joel

Son of Pethuel; prophet of the locust plague and the day of the Lord, and of the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh.

Family

Son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The book gives no king's name and no synchronism, and proposed dates range across several centuries.

Life Synopsis

He described a devastating locust plague - palmerworm, locust, cankerworm, and caterpiller - and called the nation to mourning: "Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the Lord your God, and cry unto the Lord" (Joel 1:4-14).

He called for repentance that reached past the outward form: "Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: and rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil" (Joel 2:12-13).

The promise follows: "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten" (Joel 2:25). And then: "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions: and also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit" (Joel 2:28-29). He closed with the valley of decision and the judgment of the nations (Joel 3:1-21).

What They Did Right

  • Called the nation to a fast and to rend their hearts rather than their garments: Joel 2:12-13.
  • Preached God's character as the ground of repentance - gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness: Joel 2:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing about him personally beyond his father's name. His book has no historical anchor at all, which is unusual among the prophets, and its effect is to make the message about the day of the Lord rather than about a particular crisis.

Significance

Peter quoted Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost as the explanation of what was happening - "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16-21) - which makes his book the Old Testament text the church used to interpret its own beginning. Paul also cites Joel 2:32 (Romans 10:13).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Joel 1:1-3:21; Acts 2:16-21; Romans 10:13
426

Obadiah (the prophet)

A prophet whose one-chapter book pronounces judgment on Edom for standing by while Jerusalem was plundered. Not to be confused with Obadiah the governor of Ahab's house.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He refers to a day when strangers carried away Jacob's forces and cast lots on Jerusalem (Obadiah 1:11), which most take as a Babylonian invasion, but the book names no king.

Life Synopsis

"The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord God concerning Edom" (Obadiah 1:1). He charged Edom with pride: "The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?" (Obadiah 1:3).

The specific accusation is not violence but standing by: "In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces... even thou wast as one of them. But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction... neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape" (Obadiah 1:11-14). The judgment: "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obadiah 1:15).

What They Did Right

  • Named the sin of standing by and looking on while a brother was destroyed: Obadiah 1:11-14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing about him beyond his name. The shortest book in the Old Testament, and its charge is unusually precise: Edom did not sack Jerusalem, but watched, rejoiced, and blocked the escape routes.

Significance

Edom descended from Esau, so the book treats the offence as a family matter - "thy brother Jacob" (Obadiah 1:10) - carrying the Jacob and Esau narrative to its end. Its statement that the day of the Lord is near upon all the heathen, and that as thou hast done it shall be done unto thee, is the principle stated at its plainest.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Obadiah 1:1-21
427

Jeremiah

Son of Hilkiah of Anathoth; prophet in Judah's last forty years; called before birth, imprisoned, thrown into a dungeon, and carried to Egypt against his will.

Also called Jeremias, Jeremy

Family

Son of Hilkiah, of the priests in Anathoth in Benjamin (Jeremiah 1:1). He was commanded not to marry or have children (Jeremiah 16:1-2).

Chronology

His call came in the thirteenth year of Josiah, and he prophesied through the reigns of Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1:2-3) - about forty years.

Life Synopsis

"Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations." He answered, "Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child." He was told not to say so, and God touched his mouth (Jeremiah 1:5-9).

His message was almost entirely unwelcome: surrender to Babylon and live. Pashur the priest smote him and put him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:1-2). He was tried for his life for prophesying against the temple, and was saved when the elders cited Micah's precedent and Ahikam the son of Shaphan stood with him (Jeremiah 26:1-24). Hananiah broke the yoke from his neck and prophesied peace; Jeremiah answered that he would die that year, and he did (Jeremiah 28:1-17).

He dictated a scroll to Baruch; Jehoiakim cut it with a penknife and burned it, and Jeremiah dictated it again "and there were added besides unto them many like words" (Jeremiah 36:1-32). Under Zedekiah he was accused of deserting, beaten, and imprisoned, then let down with cords into a miry dungeon where he sank in the mire, and drawn out by Ebedmelech with old cast clouts under his armholes (Jeremiah 37:11-38:13).

In the middle of the siege he bought a field at Anathoth from his cousin, weighed the money, sealed the evidence, and had it put in an earthen vessel - because "houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land" (Jeremiah 32:6-15).

His complaints are as frank as any in Scripture: "O Lord, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived... I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me." And in the same passage: "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay" (Jeremiah 20:7-9). He cursed the day of his birth (Jeremiah 20:14-18).

After the fall he was released by Nebuzaradan and stayed with Gedaliah. When Gedaliah was murdered, the remnant asked his counsel, swore to obey it, and then rejected it and carried him with them to Egypt (Jeremiah 42:1-43:7).

What They Did Right

  • Accepted a commission given before his birth, despite his own objection: Jeremiah 1:5-9.
  • Preached an unwelcome message for forty years to five kings without changing it: Jeremiah 1:2-3.
  • Refused to soften the word at his own trial for his life: Jeremiah 26:12-15.
  • Bought a field in a besieged country as a public act of faith in the restoration: Jeremiah 32:6-15.
  • Rewrote the whole scroll after the king burned it, with more added: Jeremiah 36:27-32.
  • Told Zedekiah the truth repeatedly when a softer answer would have eased his own imprisonment: Jeremiah 38:14-20.
  • Wept for the people he was sent to condemn: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people": Jeremiah 9:1.

What They Did Wrong

  • Complained bitterly that God had deceived him, and cursed the day of his birth: Jeremiah 20:7, 20:14-18. Scripture records these without rebuke and preserves them in the book.
  • Charged God with being to him "as a liar, and as waters that fail": Jeremiah 15:18 - and God's answer was a call to return and a promise to make him a brasen wall, not a condemnation: Jeremiah 15:19-20.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his failures of spirit at length and treats them as part of the record rather than as disqualifications. He is the most emotionally exposed figure in the Old Testament: he complains, accuses God of deceiving him, wishes he had never been born, and keeps preaching for forty years. He was forbidden to marry, put in stocks, tried for his life, imprisoned, sunk in a dungeon, and finally taken to Egypt against his own counsel by people who had sworn to obey it. He is not recorded as having made a single convert.

Significance

Through him came the promise of the new covenant: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts... for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more" (Jeremiah 31:31-34), which Hebrews quotes at length as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12). He also foretold the seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11-12), which Daniel later read and acted on (Daniel 9:2). Some who saw Christ thought he was Jeremiah returned (Matthew 16:14).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was last seen in Egypt, still prophesying (Jeremiah 44:1-30).

Scripture

2 Chronicles 36:12, 36:21-22; Jeremiah 1:1-52:34; Lamentations 1:1-5:22; Daniel 9:2; Matthew 2:17; Matthew 16:14; Matthew 27:9; Hebrews 8:8-12
428

Baruch

Son of Neriah; scribe to Jeremiah; wrote the scroll from the prophet's mouth, read it publicly, and rewrote it after the king burned it.

Family

Son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah (Jeremiah 32:12); his brother Seraiah was a chief officer under Zedekiah (Jeremiah 51:59).

Chronology

He wrote the first scroll in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 36:1-4).

Life Synopsis

"Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the Lord, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book" (Jeremiah 36:4). Jeremiah was shut up and could not go to the house of the Lord, so Baruch read the roll there on a fast day, then before the princes, who told him and Jeremiah to hide (Jeremiah 36:5-19). After Jehoiakim burned it, Baruch wrote it all again at Jeremiah's dictation, with many like words added (Jeremiah 36:32).

He witnessed and kept the deed for the field Jeremiah bought at Anathoth, placing it in an earthen vessel to last many days (Jeremiah 32:12-16).

A short chapter is addressed to him alone. He had said, "Woe is me now! for the Lord hath added grief to my sorrow; I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest." God's answer through Jeremiah was direct: "And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not: for, behold, I will bring evil upon all flesh, saith the Lord: but thy life will I give unto thee for a prey in all places whither thou goest" (Jeremiah 45:1-5). He was carried into Egypt with Jeremiah when the remnant fled (Jeremiah 43:6).

What They Did Right

  • Wrote and publicly read a message certain to anger the king: Jeremiah 36:4-10.
  • Rewrote the entire scroll after it was destroyed: Jeremiah 36:32.
  • Kept the deed of Jeremiah's field as a testimony for many days: Jeremiah 32:12-16.
  • Stayed with Jeremiah through imprisonment, the fall of the city, and the flight to Egypt: Jeremiah 43:6.

What They Did Wrong

  • Sought great things for himself, and was told plainly not to: Jeremiah 45:5. His complaint - that God had added grief to his sorrow and he found no rest - is recorded without rebuke, but the ambition behind it is answered.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one fault and answers it in five verses, and otherwise records sustained faithfulness in a role that carried real danger and no recognition. The word to him in Jeremiah 45 is one of the most quoted in Scripture on ambition in hard times, and it ends with a promise rather than a reproach: his life would be given him for a prey wherever he went.

Significance

The book of Jeremiah exists in written form because of him. The account in Jeremiah 36 - dictated, read, burned, and written again with more added - is Scripture's fullest description of how a prophetic book came to be written.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 43:6.

Scripture

Jeremiah 32:12-16; Jeremiah 36:1-32; Jeremiah 43:1-7; Jeremiah 45:1-5
429

Hanameel

Jeremiah's cousin, who sold him the field at Anathoth during the siege of Jerusalem.

Family

Son of Shallum, Jeremiah's uncle (Jeremiah 32:7).

Chronology

In the tenth year of Zedekiah, while Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the prison (Jeremiah 32:1-2).

Life Synopsis

"And Jeremiah said, The word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it."

"So Hanameel mine uncle's son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the Lord, and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that is in Anathoth... Then I knew that this was the word of the Lord" (Jeremiah 32:6-8).

Jeremiah bought it for seventeen shekels of silver, subscribed the evidence, sealed it, took witnesses, and weighed the money. He gave the evidence to Baruch before witnesses and charged him to put both the sealed and the open copies in an earthen vessel, that they might continue many days - "For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land" (Jeremiah 32:9-15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He came and offered the field as God had told Jeremiah he would, which confirmed the word to the prophet: Jeremiah 32:8. Scripture records nothing of his motive.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his arrival as the confirmation Jeremiah needed - "then I knew that this was the word of the Lord" - and nothing else about him. Selling land in a country under siege and about to be depopulated was a reasonable thing for a man to do; the remarkable party to the transaction is the buyer.

Significance

The purchase he made possible is one of the great enacted prophecies of Scripture: a man in prison, in a city about to fall, buying a field in enemy-held territory and preserving the deed in a jar, because houses and fields and vineyards would be possessed again in the land.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 32:12.

Scripture

Jeremiah 32:6-15
430

Gemariah (son of Shaphan)

A scribe in whose chamber in the house of the Lord Baruch read Jeremiah's roll; one of three who pleaded with the king not to burn it.

Family

Son of Shaphan the scribe (Jeremiah 36:10); brother of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah. His son Michaiah reported the reading to the princes.

Chronology

In the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month (Jeremiah 36:9).

Life Synopsis

"Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the Lord, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the Lord's house, in the ears of all the people" (Jeremiah 36:10).

His son Michaiah heard it and told the princes, who sent for Baruch and had it read again. They were afraid and said they would tell the king, and advised Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (Jeremiah 36:11-19).

When the king began cutting the roll with a penknife and casting it into the fire, "nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them" (Jeremiah 36:25).

What They Did Right

  • Gave the use of his chamber in the house of the Lord for the public reading of Jeremiah's words: Jeremiah 36:10.
  • Made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: Jeremiah 36:25.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records two acts and both are on the right side. His family runs through the book of Jeremiah as a line of protectors - his father Shaphan read the found law to Josiah, his brother Ahikam saved Jeremiah's life, his nephew Gedaliah was made governor, and he lent his room and then pleaded for the scroll.

Significance

His chamber is where Jeremiah's words were first read publicly, and his intercession is one of only three named attempts to stop the burning.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 36:25.

Scripture

Jeremiah 36:10-12, 36:25
431

Ebedmelech

An Ethiopian eunuch in Zedekiah's house who drew Jeremiah out of the dungeon and was promised his life for trusting God.

Also called Ebed-melech

Family

An Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs in the king's house (Jeremiah 38:7).

Chronology

During the final siege of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 38:1-13).

Life Synopsis

The princes had let Jeremiah down with cords into the dungeon of Malchiah, where there was no water but mire, and he sank in the mire.

"Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin; Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying, My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is" (Jeremiah 38:7-9).

The king gave him thirty men. He took old cast clouts and rotten rags from under the treasury and let them down by cords, and said, "Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords." They drew him up (Jeremiah 38:11-13).

God sent him a word by Jeremiah: "I will deliver thee in that day... and thou shalt not be given into the hand of the men of whom thou art afraid. For I will surely deliver thee... because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the Lord" (Jeremiah 39:16-18).

What They Did Right

  • Went to the king on behalf of a prisoner when no one else in the city would: Jeremiah 38:8-9.
  • Told the king plainly that the princes had done evil: Jeremiah 38:9.
  • Took trouble over the manner of the rescue, providing rags to spare the prophet's arms: Jeremiah 38:11-12.
  • God's own word to him: he would be delivered because he had put his trust in the Lord: Jeremiah 39:18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is a foreigner and a eunuch in a court where the Judean princes were trying to kill the prophet, and he is the one who acted. The detail about the rags is recorded for no reason except that it happened, and it is the kind of care the account preserves.

Significance

He saved Jeremiah's life, and received one of only a handful of personal promises of deliverance given to an individual in the prophets. That the promise names his trust as the reason, in a book about a nation that would not trust, is the point of its inclusion.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 39:18.

Scripture

Jeremiah 38:7-13; Jeremiah 39:15-18
432

Pashur

Son of Immer, priest and chief governor in the house of the Lord; struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks, and was renamed Magormissabib.

Also called Pashhur

Family

Son of Immer the priest (Jeremiah 20:1).

Chronology

Date not established precisely; before the fall of Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

"Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things. Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin" (Jeremiah 20:1-2).

The next day he brought him out, and Jeremiah said, "The Lord hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib" - terror on every side. He foretold that Pashur would be a terror to himself and his friends, that Judah would be carried to Babylon, and that Pashur and all his house would go into captivity and die there, "thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies" (Jeremiah 20:3-6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Struck a prophet and put him in the stocks: Jeremiah 20:2.
  • Prophesied lies, in Jeremiah's charge against him: Jeremiah 20:6.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. He held the office charged with order in the temple and used it to silence the man speaking God's word there. The renaming - terror on every side - is the sentence.

Significance

The night in the stocks produced Jeremiah 20:7-18, the most anguished passage in the prophets, containing both "thou hast deceived me" and "his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones."

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Jeremiah foretold he would die in Babylon and be buried there (Jeremiah 20:6).

Scripture

Jeremiah 20:1-6
433

Hananiah (the false prophet)

Son of Azur of Gibeon; prophesied that Babylon's yoke would be broken in two years, broke the yoke from Jeremiah's neck, and died that year.

Family

Son of Azur the prophet, of Gibeon (Jeremiah 28:1).

Chronology

In the fourth year of Zedekiah, the fifth month (Jeremiah 28:1).

Life Synopsis

In the house of the Lord, before the priests and all the people, he said, "Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two full years will I bring again into this place all the vessels of the Lord's house" (Jeremiah 28:2-3).

Jeremiah answered, "Amen: the Lord do so," then set out the test: prophets before them had prophesied war and evil; "when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the Lord hath truly sent him" (Jeremiah 28:6-9).

"Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah's neck, and brake it" (Jeremiah 28:10). Jeremiah went his way, and afterward returned with a word: the wooden yokes would be replaced by yokes of iron. "Then said the prophet Jeremiah unto Hananiah the prophet, Hear now, Hananiah; The Lord hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie... this year thou shalt die, because thou hast taught rebellion against the Lord. So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month" (Jeremiah 28:15-17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Prophesied in the Lord's name what the Lord had not spoken: Jeremiah 28:2, 28:15.
  • Made the people trust in a lie: Jeremiah 28:15.
  • Broke the yoke from the true prophet's neck as a public act: Jeremiah 28:10.
  • Taught rebellion against the Lord: Jeremiah 28:16.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and by name. His message was patriotic, hopeful, dated, and false, and it was delivered in the house of the Lord before the priests and all the people. Jeremiah's initial response - Amen, the Lord do so - shows he had no wish for his own message to be the true one.

Significance

The confrontation is Scripture's clearest case study in distinguishing true prophecy from false, and the test Jeremiah states in Jeremiah 28:9 is the plainest one given: the word that comes to pass. It cost two months to settle.

Death / Outcome

Died in the seventh month of the same year, as Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 28:17).

Scripture

Jeremiah 28:1-17
434

Urijah (the prophet)

Son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim; prophesied like Jeremiah, fled to Egypt, was extradited by Jehoiakim and killed.

Also called Urijah son of Shemaiah

Family

Son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim (Jeremiah 26:20).

Chronology

In the reign of Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20-23).

Life Synopsis

His account appears inside the record of Jeremiah's trial, as evidence of the danger. "And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the Lord, Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim, who prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death: but when Urijah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt; and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt... and they fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people" (Jeremiah 26:20-23).

What They Did Right

  • Prophesied in the name of the Lord against the city and the land, according to all the words of Jeremiah: Jeremiah 26:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • He was afraid and fled to Egypt: Jeremiah 26:21. Scripture records the fear plainly and does not condemn it; the passage is set out as a contrast with Jeremiah, who stayed.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the same message from two men and two different outcomes. Urijah preached the truth, was afraid, ran, was hunted down, and was killed and thrown into a common grave. Jeremiah preached the same truth, stayed, was tried, and was spared because Ahikam stood with him. The text supplies no verdict on the difference, and it is included in the narrative precisely to show that Jeremiah's survival was not owing to anything safer in his message.

Significance

His death shows what Jeremiah's ministry actually risked, and it is the immediate background to the note that Ahikam's hand was with Jeremiah so that he was not given to the people to be killed (Jeremiah 26:24).

Death / Outcome

Extradited from Egypt and killed with the sword by Jehoiakim; his body cast into the graves of the common people (Jeremiah 26:23).

Scripture

Jeremiah 26:20-24
435

Ezekiel

Son of Buzi, a priest; carried captive to Babylon and called there; prophesied by sign and vision, and lost his wife as a sign to the people.

Family

Son of Buzi the priest (Ezekiel 1:3). Married; his wife died as a sign (Ezekiel 24:16-18).

Chronology

"In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month... in the fifth year of king Jehoiachin's captivity" (Ezekiel 1:1-2), by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldeans. His dated oracles run over about twenty years.

Life Synopsis

The heavens were opened and he saw visions of God - the living creatures, the wheels, and above them the likeness of a throne and the appearance of a man. "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face" (Ezekiel 1:1-28). He was made to eat a roll written within and without with lamentations, mourning, and woe, and it was in his mouth as honey for sweetness (Ezekiel 2:9-3:3). He was appointed a watchman to the house of Israel, answerable for warning (Ezekiel 3:17-21; Ezekiel 33:1-9).

His ministry was largely enacted. He lay on his left side three hundred and ninety days and on his right forty; he ate bread by weight and drank water by measure; he shaved his head and beard and divided the hair by weight; he dug through a wall and carried his stuff out at evening as one going into captivity (Ezekiel 4:1-5:4; Ezekiel 12:1-7).

The hardest sign was his wife: "Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down... So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded" (Ezekiel 24:16-18).

He saw the glory of the Lord depart from the temple by stages (Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23), and after the city fell his message changed to restoration: the valley of dry bones that came together and lived (Ezekiel 37:1-14), the promise of a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and the vision of a restored temple with waters issuing from under the threshold (Ezekiel 40:1-47:12).

God told him what the people thought of him: "thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not" (Ezekiel 33:32).

What They Did Right

  • Fell on his face at the vision of the glory of God: Ezekiel 1:28.
  • Ate the roll of lamentations and went, though in bitterness and heat of spirit: Ezekiel 3:1-3, 3:14.
  • Sat where the captives sat, astonished among them seven days, before he spoke: Ezekiel 3:15.
  • Accepted the office of watchman with its accountability: Ezekiel 3:17-21; Ezekiel 33:7-9.
  • Carried out every sign he was given, including lying bound on his side for over a year: Ezekiel 4:1-8.
  • Did in the morning as he was commanded on the day after his wife died: Ezekiel 24:18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His protest at being told to bake with dung is recorded - "Ah Lord God! behold, my soul hath not been polluted" - and God granted the change he asked: Ezekiel 4:14-15.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His obedience is the most physically costly of any prophet: years of enacted signs performed in public, and finally the death of his wife with a prohibition on mourning her. The one time he objected, over ceremonial defilement, God accommodated him.

Significance

His visions of the departing glory and its return frame the book, and the valley of dry bones is the Old Testament's fullest picture of national resurrection. Ezekiel 36:26-27, the promise of a new heart and God's Spirit put within, stands with Jeremiah 31 as the clearest anticipation of the new covenant. God names him "son of man" more than ninety times, the title Christ used most often of himself.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Ezekiel 1:1-48:35
436

The wife of Ezekiel

Unnamed. The wife of the prophet Ezekiel, called the desire of his eyes, whose death was made a sign to the exiles.

Family

Wife of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 24:18).

Chronology

She died on the day the king of Babylon began the siege of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 24:1-2, 24:18).

Life Synopsis

"Also the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down. Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips, and eat not the bread of men."

"So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded" (Ezekiel 24:15-18). The people asked what it meant, and were told that God would profane his sanctuary, the desire of their eyes, and their sons and daughters would fall by the sword, and they would not mourn or weep but pine away for their iniquities (Ezekiel 24:19-24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing she said or did, only what she was to her husband - the desire of his eyes - and that she died. She is included because that description and her death are the substance of one of the most costly signs in the prophets, and because the record should not pass over the person at its centre.

Significance

Her death, and the prohibition on mourning it, was the sign that the temple would fall and the people would be unable to mourn it. The parallel God draws is exact: as she was to Ezekiel, so the sanctuary was to them.

Death / Outcome

Died in the evening of the day Ezekiel was warned, the day the siege of Jerusalem began (Ezekiel 24:18).

Scripture

Ezekiel 24:15-27
437

Pelatiah (son of Benaiah)

A prince of the people seen in Ezekiel's vision devising mischief, who died as the prophet was speaking.

Family

Son of Benaiah (Ezekiel 11:1).

Chronology

During Ezekiel's vision of Jerusalem, in the exile.

Life Synopsis

"Moreover the spirit lifted me up, and brought me unto the east gate of the Lord's house... and I saw among them Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people."

"Then said he unto me, Son of man, these are the men that devise mischief, and give wicked counsel in this city: which say, It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh" (Ezekiel 11:1-3).

Ezekiel was told to prophesy against them, and did. "And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then fell I down upon my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said, Ah Lord God! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?" (Ezekiel 11:13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Named among the men who devise mischief and give wicked counsel in the city: Ezekiel 11:2.
  • Among those saying the danger was not near and telling the people to build houses: Ezekiel 11:3.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the charge, the prophecy, and the death in the same breath, and then records the prophet's reaction - not satisfaction but alarm. Ezekiel fell on his face and asked whether God would make a full end of the remnant. That response is what the passage preserves him for.

Significance

His death during the prophecy is the sign that produced the promise immediately following it: that God would be a little sanctuary to the scattered, gather them, and give them one heart and a new spirit, taking the stony heart out of their flesh (Ezekiel 11:16-20).

Death / Outcome

"And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died" (Ezekiel 11:13).

Scripture

Ezekiel 11:1-13
438

Gog

The chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, of the land of Magog, against whom Ezekiel was told to prophesy.

Family

Of the land of Magog (Ezekiel 38:2).

Chronology

Not established. Ezekiel places the events "in the latter years" and "in the latter days" (Ezekiel 38:8, 38:16).

Life Synopsis

"And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, set thy face against Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him, and say, Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I am against thee, O Gog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" (Ezekiel 38:1-3).

He is described as coming from the north parts with a great company, all of them handling swords, with Persia, Ethiopia, Libya, Gomer, and Togarmah; and as thinking an evil thought - to go up to a land of unwalled villages, to take a spoil (Ezekiel 38:4-13).

The outcome is entirely God's: "And I will turn thee back, and put hooks into thy jaws, and I will bring thee forth" (Ezekiel 38:4); and, "Thus will I magnify myself, and sanctify myself; and I will be known in the eyes of many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord" (Ezekiel 38:23).

The name recurs in Revelation, where after the thousand years Satan is loosed "and shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them together to battle" (Revelation 20:7-8).

Interpretations of these chapters differ widely - as to whether Gog is an individual, a nation, or a figure, and as to when the events belong. This reference sets out what the text says and adopts no scheme.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Thought an evil thought, to go up against a land of unwalled villages to take a spoil: Ezekiel 38:10-12.
  • Came against the mountains of Israel with a great company: Ezekiel 38:14-16; Ezekiel 39:1-2.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative, and Scripture's emphasis throughout is not on him but on who is acting. He is brought forth with hooks in his jaws, turned back, and given to the birds; the repeated purpose clause is that the nations shall know that God is the Lord. Even his invasion is described as something God brings about.

Significance

These two chapters are among the most debated in Scripture, and the recurrence of the name in Revelation 20:8 has shaped a great deal of interpretation. The passage's own stated purpose is the vindication of God's holiness among the nations (Ezekiel 38:23; Ezekiel 39:7).

Death / Outcome

Ezekiel 39:11 records a place of burial appointed for him in Israel, the valley of Hamongog.

Scripture

Ezekiel 38:1-39:16; Revelation 20:7-9
439

Daniel

A youth of the seed royal carried to Babylon; interpreter of dreams to Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar; served under three empires and was thrown to the lions for praying.

Family

Of the children of Judah, of the king's seed or of the princes (Daniel 1:3-6). Renamed Belteshazzar (Daniel 1:7).

Chronology

Carried away in the third year of Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1), and still active in the third year of Cyrus (Daniel 10:1) - a span of about seventy years.

Life Synopsis

Chosen with others for his learning and appearance to stand in the king's palace, "Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank." He proposed a ten-day test of pulse and water, and at the end their countenances appeared fairer (Daniel 1:8-16).

When Nebuchadnezzar demanded that his wise men tell him both his dream and its meaning on pain of death, Daniel asked for time, went to his companions and desired mercies of God, and the secret was revealed in a night vision. He blessed God before going to the king, and disclaimed any wisdom of his own: "But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living" (Daniel 2:14-30).

He read the writing on the wall for Belshazzar, first refusing his gifts and then telling him to his face that he had not humbled himself though he knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 5:17-28).

Under Darius he was set over the presidents, "because an excellent spirit was in him." His rivals could find no fault "forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him," and concluded they must find occasion "concerning the law of his God." They obtained a decree against praying to any god or man but the king for thirty days. "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime" (Daniel 6:1-10). He was cast into the den, and the king found him alive in the morning.

Reading Jeremiah's seventy years, he set his face to seek God by prayer and supplications with fasting, and prayed one of the great confessions of Scripture, using "we" throughout (Daniel 9:1-19). He received the visions of the four beasts, the ram and the goat, the seventy weeks, and the great vision of the last chapters, and was three times called "greatly beloved" (Daniel 9:23; Daniel 10:11, 10:19).

What They Did Right

  • Purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's meat, and proposed a test rather than a confrontation: Daniel 1:8-14.
  • Sought mercies of God with his companions when their lives were at stake, and blessed God before going to the king: Daniel 2:17-23.
  • Disclaimed any wisdom of his own and gave God the credit before Nebuchadnezzar: Daniel 2:27-30.
  • Refused Belshazzar's gifts and told him the truth to his face: Daniel 5:17-23.
