  • Was so faithful in office that his enemies could find no error or fault, and had to legislate against his religion: Daniel 6:4-5.
  • Prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem as he did aforetime, with the windows open, after the decree was signed: Daniel 6:10.
  • Confessed the nation's sin as his own in prayer, saying "we have sinned" though nothing is charged against him: Daniel 9:4-19.
  • Called "greatly beloved" three times by the messenger sent to him: Daniel 9:23; Daniel 10:11, 10:19.
  • Named by God through Ezekiel with Noah and Job as a byword for righteousness: Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records no fault of Daniel's, and his enemies' inability to find one is stated as a matter of record (Daniel 6:4). This is an absence of recorded fault, not a claim of sinlessness - his own prayer in Daniel 9 confesses sin.

Character Assessment

One of a very small number of substantial biblical figures against whom nothing is recorded. What distinguishes the record is that the absence is stated by his enemies: they examined his public life for a charge and found none. He served four kings across two empires and seventy years without a recorded compromise, and his response to a decree against prayer was to change nothing.

Significance

His visions supply the framework of biblical prophecy about the succession of empires and the kingdom that shall never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44; Daniel 7:13-14). The vision of one like the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven is applied by Christ to himself (Matthew 24:30; Matthew 26:64). Christ refers to "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet" (Matthew 24:15). Ezekiel, his contemporary, names him with Noah and Job.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He continued to the first year of Cyrus and received a vision in the third (Daniel 1:21; Daniel 10:1), and was told, "go thou thy way till the end be: for thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days" (Daniel 12:13).

Scripture

Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20; Ezekiel 28:3; Daniel 1:1-12:13; Matthew 24:15
440

Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego

Three youths of Judah taken with Daniel, given Babylonian names, and thrown into the burning fiery furnace for refusing to worship the golden image. Three distinct individuals, recorded together throughout.

Also called Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah

Family

Of the children of Judah; their Hebrew names were Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (Daniel 1:6-7).

Chronology

Carried away with Daniel in the third year of Jehoiakim; the furnace episode followed Nebuchadnezzar's setting up of the image (Daniel 3:1).

Life Synopsis

With Daniel they refused the king's meat and were found fairer and fatter than all the others, and ten times better in wisdom than all the magicians of the realm (Daniel 1:11-20). Daniel requested their promotion over the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49).

When Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image sixty cubits high and commanded all to fall down and worship at the sound of the music, they would not. Accused by the Chaldeans and brought before a furious king, who asked, "who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands?", they answered:

"O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter. If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up" (Daniel 3:16-18).

The furnace was heated seven times more than usual, and the flame killed the men who cast them in. The king rose in haste: "Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?... Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God." They came out with not a hair singed, their coats unchanged, and no smell of fire on them. Nebuchadnezzar blessed their God and decreed that none should speak against him (Daniel 3:19-30).

What They Did Right

  • Refused the king's meat with Daniel: Daniel 1:11-16.
  • Would not bow to the image, in the presence of every official of the empire: Daniel 3:12.
  • Told the king they had no need to answer him in the matter: Daniel 3:16.
  • Stated their obedience without conditioning it on deliverance - "but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods": Daniel 3:17-18.
  • Their conduct brought a pagan king to bless the most high God: Daniel 3:28-29.
  • Hebrews 11:34 refers to those who through faith "quenched the violence of fire".

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them. Their answer in Daniel 3:17-18 is the clearest statement of unconditional obedience in the Old Testament: they affirmed God's power to deliver, refused to presume on it, and settled their course either way. The account is careful to note that the fourth figure appeared only after they were in the fire.

Significance

Their stand is the standing biblical example of refusing state-mandated worship, and their words "but if not" have become the shorthand for obedience that does not depend on outcome. The episode also produced Nebuchadnezzar's first public acknowledgment of God.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. The king promoted them in the province of Babylon (Daniel 3:30).

Scripture

Daniel 1:6-20; Daniel 2:17-18, 2:49; Daniel 3:1-30; Hebrews 11:34
441

Belshazzar

King in Babylon at its fall; drank from the vessels of the temple at a feast and saw the writing on the wall.

Family

Called the son of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 5:2, 5:11, 5:18), a term used in Scripture for descent as well as immediate parentage.

Chronology

He was killed on the night of the feast, when the kingdom passed to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:30-31).

Life Synopsis

"Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand." While he tasted the wine he commanded that the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem be brought, "that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein. They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone" (Daniel 5:1-4).

In the same hour came forth the fingers of a man's hand and wrote on the plaster of the wall. "Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another" (Daniel 5:5-6). His wise men could not read it. The queen recalled Daniel.

Daniel refused his gifts and gave him the history first: Nebuchadnezzar had been humbled until he knew that the most High ruled in the kingdom of men. "And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this; but hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven... and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified" (Daniel 5:17-23). The writing was MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN - numbered, weighed, and divided.

"In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom" (Daniel 5:30-31).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He kept his word and clothed Daniel with scarlet and a chain of gold and made him third ruler, after Daniel had told him he was finished: Daniel 5:29.

What They Did Wrong

  • Drank wine from the vessels of the house of God with his lords, wives, and concubines: Daniel 5:2-3.
  • Praised the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone: Daniel 5:4.
  • Did not humble his heart though he knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar: Daniel 5:22.
  • Did not glorify the God in whose hand his breath was and whose were all his ways: Daniel 5:23.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and the charge is specific: not ignorance but knowledge unacted on. Daniel's indictment turns on the words "though thou knewest all this." He had the example of Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in his own family history and did the opposite.

Significance

His feast is Scripture's image of a kingdom falling while it congratulates itself, and "weighed in the balances, and found wanting" has passed into common speech. The night of his death is the transfer of empire from Babylon to Medo-Persia, which Daniel's earlier visions had foretold.

Death / Outcome

Slain that same night (Daniel 5:30).

Scripture

Daniel 5:1-31; Daniel 7:1; Daniel 8:1
442

Darius the Median

Received the kingdom at Babylon's fall; set Daniel over his presidents, was trapped into signing the decree against prayer, and spent the night fasting while Daniel was in the lions' den.

Family

"The son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes" (Daniel 9:1).

Chronology

"And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old" (Daniel 5:31).

Life Synopsis

He set a hundred and twenty princes over the kingdom with three presidents over them, of whom Daniel was first, and thought to set him over the whole realm (Daniel 6:1-3).

The presidents and princes came to him in a body and proposed a royal statute that whoever asked a petition of any god or man for thirty days, save of the king, should be cast into the den of lions. He signed it (Daniel 6:6-9).

When they reported that Daniel prayed three times a day, "the king, when he heard these words, was sore displeased with himself, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him: and he laboured till the going down of the sun to deliver him" (Daniel 6:14). Forced by the law of the Medes and Persians, he had him cast in, and said, "Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee."

"Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting: neither were instruments of musick brought before him: and his sleep went from him." He rose very early and cried with a lamentable voice, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?" (Daniel 6:18-20). He had the accusers cast in, and wrote to all peoples that men should tremble before the God of Daniel, "for he is the living God, and stedfast for ever" (Daniel 6:24-27).

What They Did Right

  • Recognised the excellent spirit in Daniel and promoted him: Daniel 6:3.
  • Laboured until sundown to find a way to deliver him: Daniel 6:14.
  • Passed the night fasting, without music, and could not sleep: Daniel 6:18.
  • Decreed that men should fear the God of Daniel, the living God, stedfast for ever: Daniel 6:25-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Signed a decree making himself the sole object of petition for thirty days, without asking why it was proposed: Daniel 6:7-9.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as a man flattered into a trap and then unable to escape his own law. His distress is recorded at unusual length - displeased with himself, labouring till sundown, fasting, sleepless, and running to the den at dawn - and his decree afterward is one of the fullest confessions of God by a pagan ruler in Scripture.

Significance

His reign supplies the setting of Daniel 6 and of Daniel's prayer over Jeremiah's seventy years in Daniel 9:1-2. His identity is a well-known historical question outside Scripture; the biblical text simply names him and does not address it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Daniel prospered in his reign and in the reign of Cyrus (Daniel 6:28).

Scripture

Daniel 5:31; Daniel 6:1-28; Daniel 9:1; Daniel 11:1
443

Haggai

A prophet of the return who roused Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the people to finish the temple after sixteen years of delay.

Also called Aggeus

Family

Not recorded. "Haggai the prophet" (Haggai 1:1).

Chronology

"In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month" (Haggai 1:1). His four dated messages span less than four months.

Life Synopsis

The people were saying, "The time is not come, the time that the Lord's house should be built." He answered, "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" and told them to consider their ways: they had sown much and brought in little, eaten without being filled, and earned wages to put into a bag with holes (Haggai 1:2-6).

"Then Zerubbabel... and Joshua... with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the Lord their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him, and the people did fear before the Lord." Haggai then gave a single sentence of encouragement - "I am with you, saith the Lord" - and God stirred up their spirits, and they came and worked (Haggai 1:12-15).

A month later he addressed those who had seen the first house and thought this one as nothing: "Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel... and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the Lord, and work: for I am with you... The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former" (Haggai 2:3-9). He closed with the word to Zerubbabel as a signet (Haggai 2:20-23). Ezra records that the building prospered through his prophesying (Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14).

What They Did Right

  • Confronted the people's excuse for delay and made them consider their ways: Haggai 1:4-7.
  • Was obeyed - the leaders and all the remnant of the people obeyed the voice of the Lord and the words of Haggai: Haggai 1:12.
  • Encouraged the discouraged builders who remembered the former house: Haggai 2:3-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and records something recorded of few prophets: he was heard, and the work resumed within twenty-three days. His book is the shortest ministry with the clearest result in the prophets.

Significance

With Zechariah he is credited by Ezra with the resumption and completion of the temple (Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14). His promise that the glory of the latter house would exceed the former (Haggai 2:9) is applied to the coming of Christ into that temple, and Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes his word about shaking heaven and earth.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14; Haggai 1:1-2:23; Hebrews 12:26-27
444

Zechariah (the prophet)

Son of Berechiah, son of Iddo; prophesied with Haggai to encourage the rebuilding, and received a series of night visions and oracles concerning the coming king.

Family

Son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet (Zechariah 1:1); called the son of Iddo in Ezra 5:1.

Chronology

"In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius" (Zechariah 1:1), two months after Haggai began.

Life Synopsis

His opening is a call to repentance framed by history: "Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried... Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?" (Zechariah 1:4-5).

He received eight night visions - the horses among the myrtle trees, the four horns and four carpenters, the man with the measuring line, Joshua the high priest cleansed and clothed, the candlestick and two olive trees, the flying roll, the ephah, and the four chariots (Zechariah 1:7-6:8). The word to Zerubbabel came within them: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6).

Asked whether the fasts of the exile should continue, he answered with what God had required all along: "Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother: and oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor" (Zechariah 7:9-10).

His later chapters contain some of the most specific messianic material in the prophets: the king coming lowly and riding upon an ass (Zechariah 9:9); the thirty pieces of silver cast to the potter in the house of the Lord (Zechariah 11:12-13); "they shall look upon me whom they have pierced" (Zechariah 12:10); "smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered" (Zechariah 13:7); and the wounds in his hands (Zechariah 13:6).

What They Did Right

  • Called the returned community to repentance rather than assuming the exile had settled the matter: Zechariah 1:2-6.
  • Encouraged the rebuilding, and Ezra credits the work's progress to his prophesying with Haggai: Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14.
  • Answered a question about fasting by pointing to justice and mercy toward the widow, fatherless, stranger, and poor: Zechariah 7:9-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His book combines immediate practical encouragement to a discouraged building project with the most detailed messianic prophecy outside Isaiah.

Significance

Matthew applies Zechariah 9:9 to the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:4-5) and Zechariah 11:12-13 to the thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 27:9-10). Christ quotes Zechariah 13:7 on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:31), and John cites Zechariah 12:10 at the crucifixion (John 19:37). His words to Zerubbabel in Zechariah 4:6 are among the most quoted in the Old Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Christ refers to a Zacharias slain between the temple and the altar (Matthew 23:35), whose identification is disputed; see the entry for Zechariah son of Jehoiada.

Scripture

Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14; Zechariah 1:1-14:21; Matthew 21:4-5; Matthew 26:31; Matthew 27:9-10; John 19:37
445

Malachi

The prophet of the last book of the Old Testament; addressed a returned community grown careless in worship and marriage.

Family

Not recorded. "By Malachi" (Malachi 1:1).

Chronology

Date not established precisely by Scripture. The temple is standing and sacrifices are being offered (Malachi 1:7-10), and the conditions match those Nehemiah found, which places him in the Persian period.

Life Synopsis

His book proceeds by charge and denial: God states a charge, the people answer "Wherein?", and the answer follows. "I have loved you, saith the Lord. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us?" (Malachi 1:2).

The priests offered blind, lame, and sick animals. "Offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person?" (Malachi 1:8). He charged them with dealing treacherously in putting away their wives, and stated God's position plainly: "For the Lord, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away" (Malachi 2:16). He charged the nation with robbing God in tithes and offerings, and issued the one invitation in Scripture to test God: "Prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it" (Malachi 3:8-10).

He recorded a remnant: "Then they that feared the Lord spake often one to another: and the Lord hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the Lord, and that thought upon his name" (Malachi 3:16).

The Old Testament closes with his promise: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord: and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers" (Malachi 4:5-6).

What They Did Right

  • Confronted a priesthood that had made the Lord's table contemptible, using the test of what a governor would accept: Malachi 1:6-8.
  • Stated God's hatred of putting away wives, in a community where it had become common: Malachi 2:14-16.
  • Recorded those who feared the Lord and spoke often one to another, and the book of remembrance written for them: Malachi 3:16.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing about him personally, not even his father's name. His method - the charge, the shrugged question, the answer - is the sharpest portrait in Scripture of religion continuing after conviction has drained out of it.

Significance

The last book of the Old Testament. Its closing promise of Elijah is applied by Christ to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10-13), and the angel quotes Malachi 4:6 to Zacharias about the son to be born to him (Luke 1:17). Malachi 3:1, the messenger sent before the Lord's face, is quoted in all three synoptic Gospels of John the Baptist.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Malachi 1:1-4:6; Matthew 11:10-14; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 1:2; Luke 1:17; Luke 7:27; Romans 9:13

Jesus Christ

Scripture presents Jesus Christ as the central person of its whole narrative, and he is given his own section here rather than being listed among the others. The entry follows the same structure as every other, with one difference: the two headings that elsewhere read what a person did right and what they did wrong are here the testimony of Scripture and his sinlessness, and the entry sets out where and by whom that testimony is given.

446

Jesus Christ

The Son of God, born of the virgin Mary in Bethlehem; the Christ promised in the Old Testament; crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day, and ascended. Scripture presents him as fully man and as God manifest in the flesh.

Also called Jesus of Nazareth, Immanuel, the Son of man, the Son of God, the Word, Messias, the Lamb of God

Family

Son of Mary (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38). Joseph was his legal father, and Scripture is careful that he was not his natural father: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25), and Luke says he was "as was supposed" the son of Joseph (Luke 3:23). Of the house and lineage of David through both recorded genealogies (Matthew 1:1-17; Luke 3:23-38). His brethren are named as James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, and his sisters are mentioned but not named (Matthew 13:55-56; Mark 6:3). John the Baptist was his kinsman through Elisabeth and Mary (Luke 1:36).

Chronology

Born in Bethlehem in the days of Herod the king (Matthew 2:1). John's ministry began in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea (Luke 3:1). "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age" when he began (Luke 3:23). Scripture gives no date of his birth in the year and no day; the traditional dates are later and are not biblical.

Life Synopsis

Birth and early life. Gabriel was sent to Mary at Nazareth with the announcement, and to Joseph in a dream to explain it: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins" - fulfilling Isaiah's word about Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:20-23; Luke 1:26-38). He was born in Bethlehem, laid in a manger, and announced by angels to shepherds (Luke 2:1-20). He was circumcised the eighth day and presented in the temple, where Simeon and Anna recognised him (Luke 2:21-38). Wise men from the east came and worshipped him and were warned not to return to Herod, who then killed the children of Bethlehem; the family fled to Egypt and afterward settled in Nazareth (Matthew 2:1-23). At twelve he was found in the temple among the doctors, and said, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Then he went down with them and was subject to them, and "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man" (Luke 2:41-52).

Baptism and temptation. He came to John at Jordan and was baptized, though John forbade him; the Spirit descended like a dove and a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:13-17). He was then led up of the Spirit into the wilderness and tempted forty days by the devil, answering each temptation from Deuteronomy, and the devil left him (Matthew 4:1-11).

Ministry. He called disciples - fishermen, a tax collector, and others - and appointed twelve apostles (Matthew 4:18-22; Matthew 10:1-4). He taught in synagogues, on a mountain, from a ship, and in the temple, and the people were astonished, "for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:28-29). The Sermon on the Mount sets out the character of the kingdom (Matthew 5-7), and he taught largely in parables (Matthew 13:1-52).

Miracles. He healed lepers, the blind, the deaf, the lame, the palsied, and the possessed; stilled a storm with a word; walked on the sea; fed five thousand and then four thousand; turned water into wine; and raised the dead - the widow's son at Nain, Jairus's daughter, and Lazarus four days in the grave (Matthew 8:1-9:35; Matthew 14:13-33; Luke 7:11-16; John 2:1-11; John 11:1-45). John says that if all were written, the world could not contain the books (John 21:25).

Compassion and relationships. "But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd" (Matthew 9:36). He touched a leper (Matthew 8:3), ate with publicans and sinners (Matthew 9:10-13), received little children when the disciples rebuked those who brought them (Matthew 19:13-15), spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well (John 4:7-26), refused to condemn a woman taken in adultery (John 8:3-11), and wept at the grave of a friend (John 11:35). He befriended Martha, Mary, and Lazarus (John 11:5), and provided for his mother from the cross (John 19:26-27).

Obedience. "I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me" (John 6:38). "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work" (John 4:34). In Gethsemane: "O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done" (Matthew 26:42). Hebrews says he learned obedience by the things which he suffered (Hebrews 5:8), and Philippians that he "became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:8).

Suffering and crucifixion. He was betrayed by Judas for thirty pieces of silver, forsaken by all the disciples, denied by Peter, tried before Caiaphas and the council, sent to Pilate, mocked with a crown of thorns, scourged, and crucified between two thieves at Golgotha. Over him was written the accusation, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS. There was darkness over all the land from the sixth to the ninth hour, and he cried, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" and yielded up the ghost. The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom (Matthew 26:47-27:54). He was buried in the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathaea, and a watch was set and the stone sealed (Matthew 27:57-66).

Resurrection and appearances. On the first day of the week the stone was rolled back and the tomb was empty, and an angel said, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said" (Matthew 28:1-6). He appeared to Mary Magdalene, to the women, to Peter, to two on the road to Emmaus, to the eleven with Thomas absent and again with Thomas present, to seven by the sea of Tiberias, to above five hundred brethren at once, to James, and last of all to Paul (Matthew 28:9-10; Luke 24:13-43; John 20:11-21:14; 1 Corinthians 15:5-8).

Ascension. He gave the commission to teach all nations, and "while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven"; a cloud received him out of their sight, and two men in white said he would so come in like manner (Matthew 28:18-20; Luke 24:50-51; Acts 1:9-11).

The Testimony of Scripture

  • Scripture presents him as sinless, and states it in several distinct ways: he "did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22); he "knew no sin" (2 Corinthians 5:21); he "was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15); "in him is no sin" (1 John 3:5); and he himself asked, "Which of you convinceth me of sin?" (John 8:46).
  • The Father twice declared from heaven, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased": Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5.
  • He always did those things that pleased the Father: John 8:29.
  • Pilate said three times that he found no fault in him, and Pilate's wife called him "that just man": Luke 23:4, 23:14, 23:22; Matthew 27:19.
  • The centurion at the cross said, "Certainly this was a righteous man" and "Truly this was the Son of God": Luke 23:47; Matthew 27:54.
  • The dying thief said, "this man hath done nothing amiss": Luke 23:41.
  • Judas, who betrayed him, said, "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood": Matthew 27:4.
  • He went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil: Acts 10:38.
  • He prayed for those who crucified him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do": Luke 23:34.

Sinlessness

  • Scripture records no sin, fault, or moral failure of Jesus Christ, and this reference records none. This is not an absence of evidence, as it is with several Old Testament figures, but a positive and repeated claim of Scripture, stated by his enemies, his judge, his betrayer, an eyewitness at the cross, and by four New Testament writers. The charges brought against him at his trial are recorded as false witness (Matthew 26:59-60), and Pilate's verdict was that he found in him no fault at all (John 18:38).
  • The accusations his opponents made - that he broke the sabbath, blasphemed, cast out devils by Beelzebub, and was a gluttonous man and a winebibber and a friend of publicans and sinners - are recorded by the Gospels as accusations, and each is answered in the text (Matthew 12:1-13, 12:24-30; Matthew 11:19; John 10:33-38).

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as unique in kind rather than as the best of a series. He is the only person in the Bible of whom sinlessness is affirmed, and it is affirmed by men who had every reason to find fault: the governor who condemned him, the disciple who sold him, the soldier who executed him, and the criminal beside him. At the same time the Gospels present a real human life - he hungered, thirsted, was weary, slept, wept, marvelled, was moved with compassion, was angry, and in Gethsemane was sorrowful even unto death. Hebrews holds both together: a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities is exactly what he is not, because he was tempted in all points as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

Significance

Messianic identity. He is the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the seed of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed (Genesis 22:18; Galatians 3:16), the sceptre from Judah (Genesis 49:10), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22), the son of David whose throne is established for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16), the child born and son given (Isaiah 9:6-7), the virgin's son Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:22-23), the ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:5-6), the king coming lowly on an ass (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:4-5), sold for thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12-13; Matthew 27:9-10), pierced (Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37), and above all the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 - despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and numbered with the transgressors. He said himself that Moses and all the prophets wrote of him (Luke 24:27, 24:44). Statements concerning his deity. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:1-14). "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30). "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58). Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God" (Philippians 2:6). "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Colossians 2:9). "God was manifest in the flesh" (1 Timothy 3:16). "But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever" (Hebrews 1:8). He forgave sins, which the scribes said God alone could do (Mark 2:5-11), received worship (Matthew 14:33; Matthew 28:9, 28:17), and claimed to be Lord of the sabbath (Matthew 12:8). Character as Scripture describes it. Meek and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29); moved with compassion (Matthew 9:36); harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners (Hebrews 7:26); one who when he was reviled, reviled not again (1 Peter 2:23); who pleased not himself (Romans 15:3); and who, having loved his own which were in the world, loved them unto the end (John 13:1). Work. "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28). "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28). "Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Death / Outcome

Crucified at Golgotha under Pontius Pilate, between two thieves, and died about the ninth hour; a soldier pierced his side and there came out blood and water. He was buried in the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathaea. On the third day he rose, appeared over forty days, and ascended from the mount of Olives. Scripture presents his death as voluntary: "No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:18). He "ever liveth to make intercession" (Hebrews 7:25), and will come again (Acts 1:11; Revelation 22:20).

Scripture

Matthew 1:1-28:20; Mark 1:1-16:20; Luke 1:26-24:53; John 1:1-21:25; Acts 1:1-11; Acts 2:22-36; Acts 10:38-43; Romans 1:3-4; Romans 5:6-21; 1 Corinthians 15:1-28; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 4:4-5; Philippians 2:5-11; Colossians 1:13-22; Colossians 2:9; 1 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 1:1-14; Hebrews 2:9-18; Hebrews 4:14-16; Hebrews 7:22-28; Hebrews 9:11-28; 1 Peter 2:21-24; 1 John 3:5; Revelation 1:5-18; Revelation 5:6-14; Revelation 19:11-16

Gospel Period

447

Zacharias

A priest of the course of Abia; father of John the Baptist; struck dumb for unbelief and restored at the naming of his son.

Also called Zachariah the priest

Family

Of the course of Abia; his wife Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron (Luke 1:5). Father of John the Baptist.

Chronology

"In the days of Herod, the king of Judaea" (Luke 1:5).

Life Synopsis

"And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. And they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years" (Luke 1:6-7).

His lot was to burn incense in the temple, and the angel Gabriel appeared to him at the right side of the altar and announced a son to be called John. "And Zacharias said unto the angel, Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years." Gabriel answered, "I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God... And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words" (Luke 1:8-20). He came out unable to speak, and the people perceived he had seen a vision.

When the child was born the neighbours would have named him Zacharias. Elisabeth said, "Not so; but he shall be called John." They appealed to the father, who asked for a writing table and wrote, "His name is John. And they marvelled all. And his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God" (Luke 1:59-64).

He was filled with the Holy Ghost and prophesied the Benedictus: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people... And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways" (Luke 1:67-79).

What They Did Right

  • Righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless: Luke 1:6.
  • Named the child John as he had been told, against the expectation of all the relatives: Luke 1:63.
  • Praised God the moment his speech returned: Luke 1:64.
  • Prophesied the redemption of Israel and his son's office as forerunner: Luke 1:67-79.

What They Did Wrong

  • Asked how he could know it, and Gabriel named the fault: "because thou believest not my words": Luke 1:18-20. Scripture records the unbelief in a man it has just called blameless, and records the discipline as temporary.

Character Assessment

Scripture calls him and his wife righteous and blameless, and then records his unbelief at the very announcement he had presumably prayed for. The nine months of silence are treated as discipline rather than rejection: he received the son, named him rightly, and was filled with the Holy Ghost. The contrast with Mary is often drawn - she asked how it could be and was answered, he asked how he could know and was silenced - and the difference is between a question about means and a demand for proof.

Significance

Father of John the Baptist. His prophecy in Luke 1:68-79 is one of the four songs of the nativity narratives and the first prophecy recorded in the New Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 1:67-79.

Scripture

Luke 1:5-25, 1:57-80; Luke 3:2
448

Elisabeth

Of the daughters of Aaron; wife of Zacharias and mother of John the Baptist; kinswoman of Mary.

Family

Of the daughters of Aaron; wife of Zacharias (Luke 1:5); kinswoman of Mary (Luke 1:36).

Chronology

In the days of Herod the king (Luke 1:5).

Life Synopsis

She was barren and well stricken in years, and both she and her husband were righteous before God and blameless (Luke 1:6-7). When she conceived she hid herself five months, saying, "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men" (Luke 1:24-25).

Mary came to her house and saluted her. "And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost: and she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?... And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord" (Luke 1:41-45).

At the naming she insisted against the whole company, "Not so; but he shall be called John" - though her husband could not speak to tell her what the angel had said (Luke 1:60).

What They Did Right

  • Righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless: Luke 1:6.
  • Acknowledged the Lord's dealing when her reproach was taken away: Luke 1:25.
  • Filled with the Holy Ghost, she recognised Mary's child as her Lord: Luke 1:41-43.
  • Named the ground of Mary's blessedness as her belief: Luke 1:45.
  • Insisted on the name John against the whole family: Luke 1:60.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Two details stand out: she called Mary the mother of her Lord before either child was born, and she knew the name to give her son although her husband had been unable to speak since before the conception. The text does not explain how she knew.

Significance

Mother of John the Baptist, and the first person recorded as calling Mary's unborn child Lord. Her words to Mary supply the phrase "blessed art thou among women" and locate the blessing in Mary's belief.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 1:60.

Scripture

Luke 1:5-45, 1:57-60
449

Simeon (in the temple)

A just and devout man of Jerusalem, waiting for the consolation of Israel, to whom it was revealed that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's Christ. Not to be confused with Simeon the son of Jacob.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the presentation of the infant Christ in the temple, about forty days after the birth (Luke 2:22).

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him. And it was revealed unto him by the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death, before he had seen the Lord's Christ" (Luke 2:25-26).

He came by the Spirit into the temple as the parents brought in the child, took him up in his arms, and blessed God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel" (Luke 2:27-32).

Joseph and his mother marvelled. He blessed them and said to Mary, "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against; (yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:33-35).

What They Did Right

  • Just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Ghost upon him: Luke 2:25.
  • Came into the temple by the Spirit at the right moment: Luke 2:27.
  • Blessed God and declared himself ready to depart, having seen the salvation: Luke 2:28-32.
  • Named the child a light to lighten the Gentiles before any Gentile had heard of him: Luke 2:32.
  • Told Mary the truth about what lay ahead, including the sword: Luke 2:34-35.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He had waited on a promise with no date attached, recognised the child among all the children brought to the temple that day, and asked for nothing except to be dismissed. His word to Mary is the first indication in Luke that this child would bring division and grief as well as salvation.

Significance

His song is one of the four canticles of Luke's nativity narrative and the first statement in the Gospels that the salvation is for the Gentiles as well as for Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He had been told he would not see death before seeing the Lord's Christ (Luke 2:26).

Scripture

Luke 2:25-35
450

Anna

A prophetess of the tribe of Aser, of great age, who departed not from the temple and spoke of Christ to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem.

Family

Daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser. She had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity, and was a widow of about fourscore and four years (Luke 2:36-37).

Chronology

At the presentation of the infant Christ (Luke 2:36-38).

Life Synopsis

"And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; and she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day."

"And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem" (Luke 2:36-38).

What They Did Right

  • Served God with fastings and prayers night and day, and departed not from the temple: Luke 2:37.
  • Gave thanks and spoke of the child to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem: Luke 2:38.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Three verses give her tribe, her father, her marriage, her long widowhood, her practice, and what she did on the day - which is a great deal for a woman named nowhere else in the Bible. She was widowed young and spent the rest of a very long life in the temple, and was there at the one moment that mattered.

Significance

One of a small number of women Scripture calls a prophetess, with Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, and Noadiah. She is the first person recorded as telling others about Christ.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is named once.

Scripture

Luke 2:36-38
451

Mary (the mother of Jesus)

A virgin of Nazareth espoused to Joseph; mother of Jesus Christ by the Holy Ghost.

Also called the virgin Mary

Family

Espoused and afterward married to Joseph (Matthew 1:18-25). Kinswoman of Elisabeth (Luke 1:36). Mother of Jesus, and afterward of James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, and of daughters (Matthew 13:55-56; Mark 6:3). Her sister stood by the cross (John 19:25).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She was espoused to Joseph when Gabriel came, and was present at Pentecost some thirty-three years later (Luke 1:27; Acts 1:14).

Life Synopsis

Gabriel was sent to her at Nazareth: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." She was troubled and cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be. Told she would conceive and bear a son, she asked one question - "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" - and was answered that the Holy Ghost would come upon her. Her reply is the whole of her recorded response: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:26-38).

She went to Elisabeth in the hill country, and there spoke the Magnificat, which is largely about God rather than herself: "My soul doth magnify the Lord... For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden... He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Luke 1:46-55).

She bore him in Bethlehem and laid him in a manger. When the shepherds reported what they had been told, "Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart" (Luke 2:19). At the presentation Simeon told her, "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also" (Luke 2:35). When they found the boy in the temple she said, "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?" and did not understand his answer, but "his mother kept all these sayings in her heart" (Luke 2:48-51).

At Cana she told him, "They have no wine," and after his reply said to the servants, "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:3-5). At one point his friends said he was beside himself, and his mother and brethren stood without desiring to speak with him, and he said, "Whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Mark 3:21, 3:31-35; Matthew 12:46-50).

She stood by the cross, and he committed her to John: "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the disciple, "Behold thy mother!" And from that hour that disciple took her to his own home (John 19:25-27). She is last named among those in the upper room continuing with one accord in prayer (Acts 1:14).

What They Did Right

  • Received the announcement with submission: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word": Luke 1:38.
  • Magnified God rather than herself, and Elisabeth called her blessed "for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord": Luke 1:45-55.
  • Kept and pondered the things said about her son rather than publishing them: Luke 2:19, 2:51.
  • Directed the servants at Cana to do whatever he said: John 2:5.
  • Stood by the cross when most of the disciples had fled: John 19:25.
  • Continued in prayer with the disciples after the ascension: Acts 1:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • She did not understand his answer in the temple, and reproached him for staying behind: Luke 2:48-50. Scripture records this without calling it fault.
  • She was among those who came to lay hold on him when it was said he was beside himself: Mark 3:21, 3:31. The text records her presence and his answer, and passes no judgment on her.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats her with high honour and no exaggeration. Gabriel calls her highly favoured and Elisabeth calls her blessed among women, and the ground Elisabeth gives is her belief. She herself says God has regarded her low estate. The Gospels also record her not understanding him, and record him twice redirecting attention from family relation to obedience - once to her face and once when a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bore him and he answered, "Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it" (Luke 11:27-28). Scripture never records anyone praying to her or worshipping her, and records her among the disciples praying with the rest.

Significance

She is the means by which the Son of God took flesh, fulfilling the sign given to Ahaz that a virgin would conceive (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:22-23). Her song has been sung in the church longer than almost any other text. Simeon's word about the sword was fulfilled at the cross, where she stood.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:14.

Scripture

Matthew 1:16-25; Matthew 2:11-21; Matthew 12:46-50; Matthew 13:55; Mark 3:31-35; Mark 6:3; Luke 1:26-56; Luke 2:1-51; Luke 8:19-21; John 2:1-5; John 19:25-27; Acts 1:14
452

Joseph (husband of Mary)

A carpenter of Nazareth, of the house of David; espoused to Mary and the legal father of Jesus.

Also called Joseph the carpenter

Family

Son of Jacob in Matthew's genealogy and of Heli in Luke's (Matthew 1:16; Luke 3:23), a difference variously explained and not resolved by Scripture. Of the house and lineage of David (Luke 2:4). Husband of Mary; a carpenter (Matthew 13:55).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He appears in the nativity narratives and last in the incident at the temple when Jesus was twelve (Luke 2:41-51); he is not mentioned during the ministry.

Life Synopsis

Finding Mary with child before they came together, and "being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." While he thought on these things the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and explained. "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife: and knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:18-25).

He went up to Bethlehem to be taxed with Mary, and was there at the birth (Luke 2:4-7). Warned in a dream, he rose by night and took the young child and his mother into Egypt, and stayed till Herod died; warned again, he returned, and being afraid of Archelaus and warned a third time, turned aside into Galilee to Nazareth (Matthew 2:13-23). Four times Scripture records him told something in a dream and doing it without a word recorded.

He brought the child to the temple and offered the sacrifice of the poor - a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons (Luke 2:22-24). He went yearly to Jerusalem at the passover, and with Mary sought the boy sorrowing for three days (Luke 2:41-48).

Not one word of his is recorded anywhere in Scripture.

What They Did Right

  • Being a just man, and unwilling to make Mary a public example, he was minded to put her away privily: Matthew 1:19.
  • Obeyed the angel and took Mary as his wife, at obvious cost to his own reputation: Matthew 1:24.
  • Kept her a virgin until the birth: Matthew 1:25.
  • Rose by night and fled to Egypt at the warning, then returned, then turned aside to Galilee - three separate obediences, each immediate: Matthew 2:14, 2:21-23.
  • Fulfilled the law's requirements for the child, offering the sacrifice the poor were permitted: Luke 2:22-24, 2:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and never records him speaking. Everything known of him is action: he decided to protect Mary before he understood anything, and thereafter did what he was told without recorded question or delay, four times. Matthew calls him a just man, which is the only description of his character in the Bible.

Significance

He gave Jesus his legal descent from David, which is why Matthew's genealogy runs through him, and he named the child as the angel directed. His absence from the ministry narratives is generally taken to mean he had died, though Scripture does not say so.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 2:41-51.

Scripture

Matthew 1:16-25; Matthew 2:13-23; Matthew 13:55; Luke 1:27; Luke 2:4-51; Luke 3:23; Luke 4:22; John 1:45; John 6:42
453

John the Baptist

Son of Zacharias and Elisabeth; the forerunner of Christ; preached repentance in the wilderness, baptized Jesus, and was beheaded by Herod.

Also called John the Baptizer

Family

Son of Zacharias the priest and Elisabeth, both of the daughters of Aaron (Luke 1:5-13). Kinsman of Jesus through Elisabeth and Mary (Luke 1:36).

Chronology

His ministry began in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1-2). He was six months older than Jesus (Luke 1:26, 1:36).

Life Synopsis

His birth was announced by Gabriel to his father at the altar of incense, with the word that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children (Luke 1:11-17). He was filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother's womb, and grew and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing (Luke 1:15, 1:80).

"In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, and saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." He had raiment of camel's hair and a leathern girdle, and his meat was locusts and wild honey. Jerusalem and all Judaea went out to him and were baptized, confessing their sins. To the Pharisees and Sadducees he said, "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" and told them not to say they had Abraham to their father (Matthew 3:1-10).

Of Christ he said, "He that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear" (Matthew 3:11), and "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). He forbade Jesus at the baptism - "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?" - and yielded when told to suffer it (Matthew 3:13-15).

When his own disciples complained that the crowds were going to Jesus, he answered, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:26-30).

He rebuked Herod the tetrarch for taking his brother Philip's wife, and was imprisoned for it (Matthew 14:3-4). From prison he sent to ask, "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?" Jesus answered by pointing to what was being done, and then said to the crowds, "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he" (Matthew 11:2-11).

Herodias's daughter danced at Herod's birthday feast and asked, at her mother's prompting, for his head in a charger. The king was sorry, but for his oath's sake commanded it. His disciples came, took the body, buried it, and went and told Jesus (Matthew 14:6-12).

What They Did Right

  • Preached repentance plainly to crowds and to the religious leaders alike: Matthew 3:1-10.
  • Pointed away from himself: "whose shoes I am not worthy to bear": Matthew 3:11.
  • Identified Christ as the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world: John 1:29.
  • Answered his disciples' jealousy with "He must increase, but I must decrease": John 3:30.
  • Rebuked a ruler to his face over his marriage, and was imprisoned and killed for it: Matthew 14:3-4.
  • Christ's own testimony: among them born of women there had not risen a greater: Matthew 11:11.
  • "He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light": John 5:35.
  • "John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true": John 10:41.

What They Did Wrong

  • From prison he sent to ask whether Jesus was indeed the one, or whether they should look for another: Matthew 11:2-3. Scripture records the question without rebuke, and Christ's answer is evidence rather than reproach - and he immediately told the crowd there was no greater man born of women.

Character Assessment

Christ's assessment is the highest given to any man in the Gospels, and it is paired with a qualification about the kingdom rather than about John. His one recorded moment of doubt came from a prison cell and was met with evidence and with public praise. Everything recorded of him points away from himself, which is what the office required and what he did.

Significance

He is the messenger of Malachi 3:1 and the voice in the wilderness of Isaiah 40:3, applied to him in all four Gospels. Christ identified him as the Elijah who was to come, for those willing to receive it (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12-13). He is the last of the prophets before Christ and the only man whose birth and death are both recorded in detail in the Gospels.

Death / Outcome

Beheaded in prison at the request of Herodias's daughter; his head was brought in a charger, and his disciples buried the body and told Jesus (Matthew 14:6-12).

Scripture

Matthew 3:1-17; Matthew 11:2-19; Matthew 14:1-12; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 1:1-11; Mark 6:14-29; Luke 1:5-80; Luke 3:1-22; Luke 7:18-35; John 1:6-36; John 3:22-36; John 5:33-36; John 10:41; Acts 13:24-25; Acts 19:3-4
454

Herod the Great

King of Judaea at the birth of Christ; ordered the killing of the children of Bethlehem. Not to be confused with Herod the tetrarch, Herod Agrippa, or Archelaus.

Also called Herod the king

Family

Father of Archelaus, who reigned in Judaea in his stead (Matthew 2:22), and of Herod the tetrarch and Philip (Matthew 14:1-3).

Chronology

Jesus was born "in the days of Herod the king" (Matthew 2:1), and Herod died while the family was in Egypt (Matthew 2:15, 2:19).

Life Synopsis

Wise men came to Jerusalem asking, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him. When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him" (Matthew 2:1-3). He gathered the chief priests and scribes and demanded where Christ should be born, and was told Bethlehem, out of Micah.

He then called the wise men privily and enquired diligently what time the star appeared, sent them to Bethlehem, and said, "Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also" (Matthew 2:7-8).

When they returned another way, "Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men" (Matthew 2:16). Matthew applies to it Jeremiah's word about Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted (Matthew 2:17-18).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was troubled at the news of a king born, and set out to find him under the pretence of worship: Matthew 2:3-8.
  • Lied to the wise men about his intention: Matthew 2:8.
  • Slew all the children in Bethlehem and its coasts from two years old and under: Matthew 2:16.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned by the record. The account gives his method in full: he consulted the Scriptures accurately, learned exactly where the child would be, established the timing precisely, and used the language of worship to conceal murder. He is the first person in the New Testament to hear where Christ was born and the first to try to kill him.

Significance

The flight into Egypt and the return, occasioned by him, fulfilled Hosea 11:1 - "Out of Egypt have I called my son" (Matthew 2:15). The killing at Bethlehem is the first blood shed on account of Christ.

Death / Outcome

"But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeareth in a dream to Joseph in Egypt" (Matthew 2:19).

Scripture

Matthew 2:1-22; Luke 1:5
455

The wise men

Unnamed. Men from the east who followed a star to Jerusalem seeking the one born King of the Jews, and worshipped him at Bethlehem. Scripture does not say how many there were, does not call them kings, and does not name them.

Also called the magi

Family

Not recorded. "Wise men from the east" (Matthew 2:1).

Chronology

They came "when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of Herod the king" (Matthew 2:1). Herod's enquiry and his order concerning children two years old and under indicate some time had passed since the star appeared (Matthew 2:7, 2:16).

Life Synopsis

"Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him" (Matthew 2:1-2).

Herod sent them to Bethlehem. "When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh. And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way" (Matthew 2:9-12).

Note what the text does and does not say. It says they came into a house, not a stable, and saw the young child rather than a babe. It names three gifts but not three men. It never calls them kings.

What They Did Right

  • Travelled a long way on the strength of a sign, to worship a king not their own: Matthew 2:1-2.
  • Fell down and worshipped him, and presented gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh: Matthew 2:11.
  • Obeyed the warning and did not return to Herod: Matthew 2:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them. They are Gentiles who came looking for the King of the Jews while Jerusalem was troubled and the chief priests, who could quote the prophecy from memory, did not travel the six miles to see. The contrast is made by the narrative without a word of comment.

Significance

They are the first Gentiles recorded as worshipping Christ, and their arrival provoked Herod's massacre and the flight into Egypt. A great deal of tradition has attached to them - names, royal rank, and a fixed number of three - and none of it is in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. They departed into their own country another way (Matthew 2:12).

Scripture

Matthew 2:1-12
456

Archelaus

Son of Herod the Great, who reigned in Judaea in his father's stead; feared by Joseph on the return from Egypt.

Family

Son of Herod the Great (Matthew 2:22).

Chronology

He was reigning when Joseph returned from Egypt (Matthew 2:22).

Life Synopsis

"But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding, being warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee: and he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth" (Matthew 2:22-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records only that he reigned and that Joseph was afraid to go into Judaea because of it. No conduct of his is described.

Character Assessment

One verse, and it records another man's fear of him rather than anything he did. He is included because that fear, with the dream that followed, is the stated reason the family settled in Nazareth.

Significance

His reign is the reason Jesus was brought up in Nazareth rather than in Judaea, which Matthew presents as fulfilling what was spoken by the prophets, "He shall be called a Nazarene" (Matthew 2:23).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Matthew 2:22-23
457

Herod the tetrarch

Son of Herod the Great; tetrarch of Galilee; imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist, and later examined Jesus and mocked him.

Also called Herod Antipas

Family

Son of Herod the Great; brother of Philip, whose wife Herodias he took (Matthew 14:3; Luke 3:19).

Chronology

He was tetrarch of Galilee during the ministry of John and of Christ (Luke 3:1).

Life Synopsis

He had taken Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and John said to him, "It is not lawful for thee to have her." He laid hold on John and bound him in prison for her sake, and "when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet" (Matthew 14:3-5). Mark adds that he feared John, knowing that he was a just and holy man, observed him, and "heard him gladly" (Mark 6:20).

At his birthday feast the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John the Baptist's head in a charger. "And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath's sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her" (Matthew 14:6-11).

Hearing of the fame of Jesus, he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead" (Matthew 14:1-2). Luke records that he desired to see him (Luke 9:9), and that when Pilate sent Jesus to him he "was exceeding glad... and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him. Then he questioned with him in many words; but he answered him nothing." Herod and his men of war set him at nought, mocked him, arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him back; and Pilate and Herod were made friends together that day (Luke 23:8-12).

What They Did Right

  • Feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, observed him, and heard him gladly: Mark 6:20.
  • Was sorry when asked for John's head: Matthew 14:9. Scripture records the regret and then records that he gave the order anyway.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took his brother Philip's wife: Matthew 14:3; Luke 3:19.
  • Imprisoned John for saying it was not lawful: Matthew 14:3-4.
  • Kept a rash oath rather than a man's life, for the sake of those sitting at meat with him: Matthew 14:9.
  • Beheaded John the Baptist: Matthew 14:10.
  • Set Christ at nought and mocked him: Luke 23:11.
  • Christ called him "that fox": Luke 13:32.

Character Assessment

A man who knew better throughout. Mark records that he feared John, knew he was just and holy, and heard him gladly - and he killed him to save face at a dinner. He wanted to see Jesus for the entertainment of a miracle and got silence: Christ answered him nothing, which is the only recorded instance of Christ refusing to speak to anyone who questioned him.

Significance

His killing of John ended the ministry of the forerunner. His examination of Jesus is one of the six stages of the trial, and it is the one at which no charge was brought and no answer given.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded in Scripture. Last mention: Acts 4:27, where he is named with Pilate and the Gentiles as gathered together against Christ.

Scripture

Matthew 14:1-12; Mark 6:14-29; Mark 8:15; Luke 3:1, 3:19-20; Luke 9:7-9; Luke 13:31-32; Luke 23:6-12; Acts 4:27
458

Herodias

Wife of Philip, taken by Herod the tetrarch; sought John the Baptist's death and obtained it through her daughter.

Family

Wife of Philip, Herod's brother, and afterward of Herod the tetrarch (Matthew 14:3). Mother of the daughter who danced (Matthew 14:6).

Chronology

During the ministry of John the Baptist.

Life Synopsis

John had said to Herod, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Mark records her response: "Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not: for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him" (Mark 6:18-20).

Her opportunity came at Herod's birthday. Her daughter danced and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked to the half of his kingdom. "And she went forth, and said unto her mother, What shall I ask? And she said, The head of John the Baptist" (Mark 6:24). The girl came in straightway with haste and asked for it in a charger, and it was given her, and she brought it to her mother.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Held a quarrel against John and would have killed him for telling the truth about her marriage: Mark 6:19.
  • Used her daughter and her husband's rash oath to obtain his execution: Mark 6:24-25.
  • Received the head of a just and holy man as a gift: Mark 6:28.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. Scripture records that Herod protected John from her, which makes her the effective cause of his death. Her single recorded sentence is the instruction to ask for his head.

Significance

Her marriage is the specific sin John was killed for naming, and her persistence is what turned an imprisonment into an execution.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Mark 6:28.

Scripture

Matthew 14:3-11; Mark 6:17-28; Luke 3:19
459

The daughter of Herodias

Unnamed. The girl who danced at Herod's birthday feast and, at her mother's direction, asked for the head of John the Baptist.

Family

Daughter of Herodias (Matthew 14:6); stepdaughter and niece of Herod the tetrarch.

Chronology

At Herod's birthday, during John's imprisonment.

Life Synopsis

"But when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod. Whereupon he promised with an oath to give her whatsoever she would ask" (Matthew 14:6-7). Mark records the oath in full: whatever she asked, to the half of his kingdom.

She went out to her mother and asked what she should request, and was told, "The head of John the Baptist." "And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist" (Mark 6:24-25). It was brought and she gave it to her mother.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Asked for a man's head, and asked for it with haste and with an added demand that it be given immediately: Mark 6:25. Scripture records that the request originated with her mother, and records that she pressed it herself.

Character Assessment

Scripture records that she asked her mother what to request, which shows she had not thought of it, and then records that she came in straightway with haste and added the words "by and by" - at once. The text supplies both facts and no verdict.

Significance

Her dance and her request are the immediate cause of John the Baptist's death.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Mark 6:28.

Scripture

Matthew 14:6-11; Mark 6:22-28
460

Simon Peter

A fisherman of Bethsaida; first-named of the twelve apostles; confessed Christ, denied him three times, was restored, and became the leading voice of the early church.

Also called Peter, Simon, Cephas, Simon Barjona

Family

Son of Jona (Matthew 16:17); brother of Andrew (Matthew 4:18); of Bethsaida, dwelling at Capernaum (John 1:44; Mark 1:29). Married - his wife's mother was healed (Matthew 8:14), and Paul refers to his wife travelling with him (1 Corinthians 9:5).

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; active through Acts, and the writer of two epistles.

Life Synopsis

Andrew brought him to Jesus, who looked on him and said, "Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone" (John 1:40-42). At the lake he was called from his nets - "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men" - and forsook all and followed (Matthew 4:18-20; Luke 5:1-11). After the draught of fishes he fell down saying, "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord."

He walked on the water toward Jesus and began to sink when he saw the wind boisterous, crying, "Lord, save me"; and was answered, "O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" (Matthew 14:28-31). At Caesarea Philippi he answered the question no one else did: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God," and was told that flesh and blood had not revealed it to him but the Father (Matthew 16:15-17). Within six verses he took Christ aside and rebuked him for speaking of the cross, and was answered, "Get thee behind me, Satan: thou art an offence unto me" (Matthew 16:22-23). When many went back, he said, "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life" (John 6:68).

He was told that Satan had desired to have him, and that Christ had prayed for him. He protested that he would go to prison and to death, and was told that before the cock crew he would deny him thrice (Luke 22:31-34). In the garden he slept, then drew a sword and cut off Malchus's ear (John 18:10). He followed afar off into the high priest's palace, and denied Christ three times, the third with cursing and swearing; the cock crew, the Lord turned and looked upon him, and he went out and wept bitterly (Matthew 26:69-75; Luke 22:61-62).

He ran to the sepulchre and went in (Luke 24:12; John 20:6). By the sea of Tiberias he was asked three times, "Lovest thou me?" and grieved at the third, and was three times commissioned to feed the sheep, and told by what death he would glorify God (John 21:15-19).

At Pentecost he stood up with the eleven and preached, and about three thousand souls were added (Acts 2:14-41). He healed the lame man at the gate, was arrested and told the council, "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 4:19; Acts 5:29). He was sent to Cornelius after the vision of the sheet and said, "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons" (Acts 10:34). He was delivered from prison by an angel while the church prayed (Acts 12:1-17), and spoke at the council of Jerusalem for receiving the Gentiles (Acts 15:7-11).

Paul records that at Antioch he withdrew from eating with Gentiles when certain came from James, fearing them of the circumcision, and "I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed" (Galatians 2:11-14).

What They Did Right

  • Left all and followed at the call: Matthew 4:20; Luke 5:11.
  • Confessed Christ as the Son of the living God when asked: Matthew 16:16.
  • Stayed when many went back: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life": John 6:68.
  • Wept bitterly after his denial: Matthew 26:75.
  • Preached at Pentecost and three thousand were added: Acts 2:14-41.
  • Answered the council, "We ought to obey God rather than men": Acts 5:29.
  • Went to Cornelius and declared that God is no respecter of persons: Acts 10:34-35.
  • Spoke at Jerusalem for receiving the Gentiles without the yoke of the law: Acts 15:7-11.
  • Wrote two epistles, including the charge to feed the flock of God, taking the oversight not by constraint but willingly: 1 Peter 5:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • Doubted and began to sink on the water: Matthew 14:30-31.
  • Rebuked Christ for speaking of his death, and was called Satan and an offence: Matthew 16:22-23.
  • Protested that he would never be offended and would die rather than deny him: Matthew 26:33-35.
  • Slept in Gethsemane when asked to watch one hour: Matthew 26:40-43.
  • Struck the high priest's servant with a sword: John 18:10-11.
  • Denied Christ three times, the last time with cursing and swearing: Matthew 26:69-74.
  • At Antioch withdrew from the Gentiles for fear of them of the circumcision, and Paul withstood him to the face because he was to be blamed: Galatians 2:11-14.

Character Assessment

No disciple is recorded in more detail and none is recorded failing more often. He confessed Christ more clearly than anyone and was rebuked more sharply than anyone, within the same chapter. His denial is the most fully told failure in the New Testament, and his restoration is equally full: three questions for three denials, and a commission at the end of each. Paul's public correction of him at Antioch is recorded by Paul without softening, and Peter's own second epistle refers to Paul as "our beloved brother Paul" (2 Peter 3:15). The record is of a man remade rather than a man who did not fail.

Significance

He preached the sermon at Pentecost at which the church began, opened the door to the Gentiles at the house of Cornelius, and stood at the council of Jerusalem for salvation by grace without the law. He wrote two epistles. Christ's word to him about the rock and the keys (Matthew 16:18-19) has been interpreted in sharply different ways for centuries; the passage itself is recorded here without adopting a reading.

Death / Outcome

Not narrated in Scripture. Christ told him by what death he should glorify God, "signifying by what death he should glorify God" (John 21:18-19), and Peter refers to knowing that he must shortly put off his tabernacle (2 Peter 1:14).

Scripture

Matthew 4:18-20; Matthew 8:14; Matthew 14:28-31; Matthew 16:13-23; Matthew 17:1-8, 17:24-27; Matthew 26:33-75; Mark 1:16-36; Luke 5:1-11; Luke 22:31-62; John 1:40-42; John 6:68-69; John 13:6-9, 13:36-38; John 18:10-27; John 20:2-6; John 21:1-22; Acts 1:15-22; Acts 2:14-41; Acts 3:1-4:22; Acts 5:1-42; Acts 8:14-25; Acts 9:32-43; Acts 10:1-11:18; Acts 12:1-19; Acts 15:7-11; Galatians 1:18; Galatians 2:7-14; 1 Peter 1:1; 2 Peter 1:1, 1:14; 2 Peter 3:15
461

Andrew

Brother of Simon Peter; a fisherman of Bethsaida; one of the twelve, who first found his own brother and brought him to Christ.

Family

Son of Jona; brother of Simon Peter (Matthew 4:18; John 1:40-42); of Bethsaida (John 1:44).

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; named among those in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

He was a disciple of John the Baptist, and heard him say, "Behold the Lamb of God," and followed Jesus. "He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. And he brought him to Jesus" (John 1:35-42).

He was called with Peter from the nets (Matthew 4:18-20) and named among the twelve (Matthew 10:2).

Twice more he appears bringing someone to Christ. At the feeding of the five thousand: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" (John 6:8-9). And when certain Greeks came to Philip desiring to see Jesus, Philip told Andrew, "and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus" (John 12:20-22). He was one of the four who asked privately about the destruction of the temple (Mark 13:3-4).

What They Did Right

  • Followed at John's word and then found his own brother and brought him to Christ: John 1:40-42.
  • Left the nets at the call: Matthew 4:20.
  • Brought the boy with the loaves and fishes to Christ's notice, though he could not see what use it was: John 6:8-9.
  • Brought the enquiring Greeks to Christ with Philip: John 12:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. Every one of his four recorded appearances involves bringing someone else to Christ - his brother, a boy with a lunch, and a group of Greeks. He is identified throughout by his relation to Peter rather than the reverse, and the Gospels never record him complaining of it.

Significance

He brought Peter to Christ, which makes him the first recorded person to bring another to Christ in the Gospels. His question about the loaves precedes the feeding of the five thousand.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 4:18-20; Matthew 10:2; Mark 1:16-29; Mark 3:18; Mark 13:3; Luke 6:14; John 1:35-44; John 6:8-9; John 12:20-22; Acts 1:13
462

Zebedee

A fisherman of Galilee; father of James and John, left in the ship with the hired servants when his sons followed Christ.

Family

Father of James and John (Matthew 4:21); husband of the woman who came to Christ about her sons (Matthew 20:20).

Chronology

At the call of the disciples, early in the ministry.

Life Synopsis
