"And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him" (Matthew 4:21-22). Mark adds that they left him "in the ship with the hired servants" (Mark 1:20), which indicates a business of some size.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records no objection from him and no words at all.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his trade, his sons, his boat, his nets, and his hired servants, and nothing that he said or did. He is included because his presence in the account is what gives the call its cost: two sons walked away from their father and the family business in the same moment.

Significance

His sons became two of the inner three, and John outlived all the apostles and wrote five books of the New Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Matthew 27:56, by reference to his children.

Scripture

Matthew 4:21-22; Matthew 20:20; Matthew 26:37; Matthew 27:56; Mark 1:19-20; Luke 5:10
463

James (son of Zebedee)

Son of Zebedee, brother of John; one of the twelve and of the inner three; the first apostle to be martyred.

Also called James the Greater

Family

Son of Zebedee, brother of John (Matthew 4:21). Their mother asked for the chief seats for them (Matthew 20:20). Christ surnamed the two Boanerges, the sons of thunder (Mark 3:17).

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; killed with the sword by Herod, about the time of Peter's imprisonment (Acts 12:1-2).

Life Synopsis

He was in the ship with Zebedee his father, mending nets, when Jesus called him and John; "and they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him" (Matthew 4:21-22).

He was one of the three taken apart at the raising of Jairus's daughter, at the transfiguration, and in Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; Matthew 17:1; Matthew 26:37). Christ surnamed him and his brother Boanerges (Mark 3:17), and the surname suits two recorded incidents: when a Samaritan village would not receive Christ, they said, "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them?" and were rebuked (Luke 9:54-55); and their mother came asking that they might sit on his right hand and on his left in his kingdom. Asked whether they could drink of his cup, they said, "We are able," and were told they would indeed drink of it (Matthew 20:20-23).

"Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword" (Acts 12:1-2).

What They Did Right

  • Left the ship and his father immediately at the call: Matthew 4:22.
  • Was one of the three admitted to the raising of Jairus's daughter, the transfiguration, and Gethsemane: Mark 5:37; Matthew 17:1; Matthew 26:37.
  • Drank of the cup, as Christ had said he would: Matthew 20:23; Acts 12:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • With John, proposed calling down fire on a Samaritan village, and was rebuked: Luke 9:54-55.
  • Sought, through his mother, the chief seats in the kingdom, and claimed to be able to drink Christ's cup: Matthew 20:20-22.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his ambition and his temper plainly, and records that Christ kept him in the inner three anyway. His answer to the question about the cup - we are able - was presumptuous when he said it and true in the end. His death is recorded in a single verse, with no detail and no lament.

Significance

The first of the twelve to be martyred, and the only apostle whose death is recorded in Scripture. The brevity of Acts 12:2, set beside the long account of Peter's deliverance in the same chapter, is one of the New Testament's plainest statements that God's dealings with his servants are not uniform.

Death / Outcome

Killed with the sword by Herod (Acts 12:2).

Scripture

Matthew 4:21-22; Matthew 10:2; Matthew 17:1-8; Matthew 20:20-24; Matthew 26:37; Mark 1:19-20; Mark 3:17; Mark 5:37; Mark 10:35-41; Mark 13:3; Luke 5:10; Luke 8:51; Luke 9:28, 9:54; Acts 1:13; Acts 12:1-2
464

John (son of Zebedee)

Son of Zebedee, brother of James; one of the twelve and of the inner three; called the disciple whom Jesus loved; writer of a Gospel, three epistles, and Revelation. Not to be confused with John the Baptist or John Mark.

Also called the beloved disciple, the evangelist

Family

Son of Zebedee, brother of James (Matthew 4:21). Their mother is generally identified with Salome (Matthew 27:56; Mark 15:40); Scripture does not make the identification explicitly.

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; still living and in exile on Patmos when Revelation was written (Revelation 1:9).

Life Synopsis

He was mending nets with his brother and father when called, and left the ship and his father to follow (Matthew 4:21-22). He was one of the three at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the transfiguration, and Gethsemane.

He told Christ they had forbidden a man casting out devils in his name because he did not follow with them, and was told, "Forbid him not" (Luke 9:49-50). With his brother he proposed fire on the Samaritan village and was rebuked (Luke 9:54-55), and sought the chief seats (Mark 10:35-37).

In his own Gospel he never names himself, referring to "the disciple whom Jesus loved." He leaned on Christ's breast at the supper (John 13:23-25), followed into the high priest's palace (John 18:15-16), stood by the cross and received Christ's mother into his own home (John 19:26-27), outran Peter to the sepulchre and went in and believed (John 20:2-8), and recognised Christ on the shore: "It is the Lord" (John 21:7).

In Acts he is with Peter at the healing of the lame man, before the council, and sent to Samaria (Acts 3:1-4:22; Acts 8:14). Paul names him with James and Cephas as pillars of the church at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9).

He wrote the Gospel that bears his name, stating its purpose - "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name" (John 20:31); three epistles whose theme is love, light, and truth; and the Revelation, received in Patmos "for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ" (Revelation 1:9).

What They Did Right

  • Left the ship and his father at the call: Matthew 4:22.
  • Stood by the cross when the others had fled, and took Christ's mother into his own home: John 19:26-27.
  • Believed at the empty tomb: John 20:8.
  • Recognised the Lord on the shore before the others: John 21:7.
  • Stood with Peter before the council and would not be silenced: Acts 4:19-20.
  • Named a pillar of the church at Jerusalem: Galatians 2:9.
  • Wrote a Gospel, three epistles, and the Revelation.

What They Did Wrong

  • Forbade a man casting out devils because he did not follow with them, and was corrected: Luke 9:49-50.
  • With James, wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and was rebuked: Luke 9:54-55.
  • Sought the chief seats in the kingdom: Mark 10:35-37.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the same ambition and intolerance in him as in his brother, and the same nearness to Christ. The description he chose for himself is the striking thing: not the disciple who loved Jesus but the disciple whom Jesus loved. His writings are the New Testament's fullest treatment of love, and they come from a man Christ nicknamed a son of thunder.

Significance

His Gospel is the fullest statement of Christ's deity - the Word who was God, made flesh - and his first epistle the fullest treatment of assurance. Revelation closes the canon. He was the disciple Christ entrusted with the care of his mother.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Christ's saying about him - "If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?" - was misunderstood as meaning he would not die, and John himself corrects the misunderstanding (John 21:22-23).

Scripture

Matthew 4:21-22; Matthew 10:2; Matthew 17:1-8; Matthew 26:37; Mark 3:17; Mark 5:37; Mark 9:38; Mark 10:35-41; Luke 9:49-56; Luke 22:8; John 13:23-25; John 18:15-16; John 19:26-27; John 20:2-8; John 21:1-24; Acts 1:13; Acts 3:1-11; Acts 4:1-22; Acts 8:14-25; Galatians 2:9; Revelation 1:1-9
465

The mother of Zebedee's children

Wife of Zebedee and mother of James and John; asked for the chief seats for her sons, and was among the women at the cross and at the tomb.

Also called Salome (probable)

Family

Wife of Zebedee; mother of James and John (Matthew 20:20; Matthew 27:56). Comparing Matthew 27:56 with Mark 15:40 she is generally identified with Salome; Scripture does not make the identification explicitly, and this reference notes it as probable rather than certain.

Chronology

During the ministry and at the crucifixion and resurrection.

Life Synopsis

"Then came to him the mother of Zebedee's children with her sons, worshipping him, and desiring a certain thing of him. And he said unto her, What wilt thou? She saith unto him, Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom." He answered the sons rather than her: "Ye know not what ye ask." The other ten were moved with indignation, and he taught them that whoever would be chief must be servant (Matthew 20:20-28).

She was among the women beholding afar off at the crucifixion, "which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him" (Matthew 27:55-56). Mark names Salome among the women who brought spices to the tomb (Mark 16:1).

What They Did Right

  • Followed Jesus from Galilee and ministered to him: Matthew 27:55-56.
  • Was present at the cross when most had fled, and came to the tomb with spices: Matthew 27:56; Mark 16:1.
  • Came worshipping when she made her request: Matthew 20:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • Asked for the two chief places in the kingdom for her own sons, and the request moved the other ten to indignation: Matthew 20:21-24.

Character Assessment

Her one request is recorded plainly as a mistake, and it produced the teaching on greatness that follows it. The rest of her record is service: she followed from Galilee, ministered to him, stood at the cross, and came early to the tomb.

Significance

Her request is the occasion of one of Christ's clearest statements about authority - that whoever will be great must be a servant, and that the Son of man came to minister and to give his life a ransom for many (Matthew 20:26-28).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Mark 16:1.

Scripture

Matthew 20:20-24; Matthew 27:55-56; Mark 15:40-41; Mark 16:1
466

Philip (the apostle)

Of Bethsaida; one of the twelve; found Nathanael and answered him, "Come and see." Not to be confused with Philip the evangelist of Acts.

Family

Of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; named in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

"The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me." He then found Nathanael and said, "We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph." When Nathanael answered, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" Philip did not argue: "Come and see" (John 1:43-46).

Before the feeding of the five thousand Christ asked him where bread could be bought, "and this he said to prove him: for he himself knew what he would do." Philip answered, "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little" (John 6:5-7).

When certain Greeks came saying, "Sir, we would see Jesus," they came to Philip, and he told Andrew (John 12:20-22).

At the last supper he said, "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us," and was answered, "Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:8-9).

What They Did Right

  • Followed at the call, and immediately found Nathanael and brought him: John 1:43-45.
  • Answered scepticism with an invitation rather than an argument: "Come and see": John 1:46.
  • Brought the enquiring Greeks to Christ with Andrew: John 12:21-22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Calculated the cost of feeding the multitude and concluded it was impossible, when he was being proved: John 6:5-7.
  • Asked to be shown the Father after long acquaintance, and was gently reproved for it: John 14:8-9.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a practical man whose instinct was to reckon what was available, and it records Christ correcting that twice. It also records that his first act after being called was to go and find someone else, and that when he could not answer an objection he simply invited the man to look.

Significance

His question at the supper produced one of the clearest statements of Christ's relation to the Father in Scripture: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; John 1:43-48; John 6:5-7; John 12:20-22; John 14:8-9; Acts 1:13
467

Bartholomew

One of the twelve; generally identified with Nathanael of Cana, whom Christ called an Israelite in whom is no guile.

Also called Nathanael

Family

Of Cana in Galilee, if he is Nathanael (John 21:2). The three synoptic lists name Bartholomew immediately after Philip, and John's Gospel pairs Philip with Nathanael and never mentions Bartholomew; the identification is widely held and is inference rather than a statement of Scripture.

Chronology

Called at the beginning of the ministry; named in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

Philip found him and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote of, Jesus of Nazareth. He answered, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" Philip said, "Come and see."

"Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile! Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee. Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel" (John 1:45-49). He was told he would see greater things than these.

He was among the seven by the sea of Tiberias after the resurrection (John 21:2).

What They Did Right

  • Came and looked when invited, despite his objection: John 1:46-47.
  • Christ's own testimony: an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile: John 1:47.
  • Confessed him as the Son of God and the King of Israel at once: John 1:49.

What They Did Wrong

  • Dismissed Nazareth before he had seen anything: John 1:46. Scripture records the prejudice and immediately records that he acted against it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one prejudice and one of the fullest early confessions in the Gospels, minutes apart. Christ's description of him is unique in the New Testament: no one else is called a man without guile.

Significance

His confession - Son of God and King of Israel - comes in the first chapter of John, before any miracle he had witnessed, on the strength of Christ having seen him under a fig tree.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; John 1:45-51; John 21:2; Acts 1:13
468

Thomas

Called Didymus; one of the twelve; refused to believe the resurrection without evidence, and then made the fullest confession in the Gospels.

Also called Didymus

Family

Not recorded. Called Didymus, meaning the twin (John 11:16).

Chronology

Called during the ministry; named in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

When Christ resolved to go to Judaea where they had lately sought to stone him, "then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him" (John 11:16).

At the last supper Christ said they knew where he was going and the way; Thomas answered, "Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?" - which drew the answer, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:5-6).

He was absent when Christ first appeared to the eleven. The others told him they had seen the Lord, and he said, "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe."

Eight days later Christ came and stood in the midst and said to him, "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing. And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God. Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed" (John 20:24-29).

What They Did Right

  • Proposed going with Christ into danger: "Let us also go, that we may die with him": John 11:16.
  • Admitted honestly that he did not understand, which drew out the answer "I am the way, the truth, and the life": John 14:5-6.
  • Made the fullest confession recorded in the Gospels: "My Lord and my God": John 20:28.

What They Did Wrong

  • Refused to believe the testimony of the other ten without physical proof: John 20:25. Christ's words to him name the fault - "be not faithless, but believing" - and the blessing that follows is on those who believe without seeing.

Character Assessment

His reputation rests on one sentence, and Scripture records three others that complicate it. He was the one willing to go and die, the one honest enough to say he did not know the way, and the one who called Christ God outright. The rebuke he received was real, and so was the invitation that came with it: Christ met the exact terms Thomas had set.

Significance

His confession, "My Lord and my God," is the strongest statement of Christ's deity by any disciple in the Gospels, and it comes immediately before John's statement of why he wrote the book (John 20:30-31). The blessing pronounced on those who have not seen and yet believed is spoken over every reader since.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; John 11:16; John 14:5-6; John 20:24-29; John 21:2; Acts 1:13
469

Matthew (the apostle)

A publican sitting at the receipt of custom, called by Christ; one of the twelve; writer of the first Gospel.

Also called Levi, Levi the son of Alphaeus

Family

Called Levi the son of Alphaeus in Mark, and Levi in Luke (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27).

Chronology

Called during the Galilean ministry; named among those in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

"And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him" (Matthew 9:9). Luke adds that he "left all, rose up, and followed him" (Luke 5:28).

He made a great feast in his own house, and many publicans and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples. The Pharisees asked the disciples why their master ate with publicans and sinners, and Jesus answered, "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick... for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Matthew 9:10-13; Luke 5:29-32).

In the list of the twelve in his own Gospel he alone adds the description: "Matthew the publican" (Matthew 10:3). The other lists do not.

What They Did Right

  • Rose and followed at once, leaving his post and his livelihood: Matthew 9:9; Luke 5:28.
  • Made a great feast and gathered his former associates to meet Christ: Luke 5:29.
  • Wrote the Gospel that bears his name.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He had been a publican, a tax collector for Rome, an occupation Scripture repeatedly couples with sinners in the mouths of his contemporaries (Matthew 9:11; Matthew 11:19). The Gospels record the reputation of the trade without charging Matthew personally with any act.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him after his call and one striking detail about how he described himself. Three lists of the twelve name him; only the one in his own Gospel adds "the publican." His first recorded act as a disciple was to fill his house with the people he had worked among so that they could meet Christ.

Significance

He wrote the Gospel most concerned with showing Christ as the fulfilment of the Old Testament, quoting it more than any other Gospel and repeatedly noting that a thing was done "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet." That the Gospel written to the Jews came from a tax collector for Rome is not commented on by Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 9:9-13; Matthew 10:3; Mark 2:14-17; Mark 3:18; Luke 5:27-32; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13
470

James (son of Alphaeus)

One of the twelve, named in all four lists; distinguished from James the son of Zebedee. Nothing he said or did is recorded.

Also called James the less

Family

Son of Alphaeus (Matthew 10:3). A James the less, son of Mary, is named at the cross (Mark 15:40); whether he is the same man is not stated by Scripture.

Chronology

Named among the twelve and in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

He appears only in the four lists of the apostles: Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, and Acts 1:13. In each he is identified as the son of Alphaeus, which distinguishes him from James the son of Zebedee. No word or act of his is recorded anywhere.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He was chosen as one of the twelve and remained with them to the upper room after the ascension: Acts 1:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his father, and his membership among the twelve, and nothing else. He is included because being named one of the twelve, and being present after the ascension, is substantive. That two of the apostles - he and Simon the Canaanite - have no recorded word or deed is itself worth noting: the twelve were not twelve public figures.

Significance

He is one of the twelve who were with Christ from the beginning and were witnesses of the resurrection, which was the stated qualification for the office (Acts 1:21-22).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13
471

Lebbaeus

One of the twelve, called Lebbaeus whose surname was Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark, and Judas the brother of James in Luke and Acts.

Also called Thaddaeus, Judas the brother of James, Judas not Iscariot

Family

Called "Judas the brother of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13).

Chronology

Named among the twelve and in the upper room after the ascension.

Life Synopsis

He appears in the four lists under two names: "Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus" (Matthew 10:3), "Thaddaeus" (Mark 3:18), and "Judas the brother of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). The variation is generally taken to refer to one man with more than one name.

One saying of his is recorded. At the last supper, when Christ said he would manifest himself to those who kept his commandments, "Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?" (John 14:22). The answer follows in John 14:23-24.

What They Did Right

  • Asked the question that drew out Christ's answer about manifesting himself to those who love and keep his word: John 14:22-23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one question, and John is careful to add "not Iscariot" so the reader does not mistake him. His question is a good one: it assumes the manifestation and asks why it would not be universal.

Significance

His single recorded sentence produced Christ's promise that the Father and the Son would come and make their abode with the one who keeps his word (John 14:23).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:16; John 14:22; Acts 1:13
472

Simon the Canaanite

One of the twelve, called the Canaanite in Matthew and Mark and Zelotes in Luke and Acts. Nothing he said or did is recorded.

Also called Simon Zelotes, Simon the zealot

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Named among the twelve and in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13).

Life Synopsis

He appears only in the four lists: "Simon the Canaanite" (Matthew 10:4; Mark 3:18) and "Simon called Zelotes" (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). No word or act of his is recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He was chosen as one of the twelve and was with them after the ascension: Acts 1:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his epithet, and his membership among the twelve. The title Zelotes is generally understood to indicate a background among the zealots, the party of armed resistance to Rome; Scripture does not explain it. If so, he served alongside Matthew, who had collected taxes for Rome, and the Gospels record no friction between them.

Significance

One of the twelve who were with Christ from the beginning and witnesses of the resurrection.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:13.

Scripture

Matthew 10:4; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13
473

Judas Iscariot

One of the twelve; kept the bag; betrayed Christ for thirty pieces of silver and hanged himself.

Family

Son of Simon (John 6:71; John 13:26).

Chronology

Chosen among the twelve; died before the choosing of Matthias (Acts 1:16-26).

Life Synopsis

He was named among the twelve with the description already attached: "and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him" (Matthew 10:4). He was sent out with the rest to preach and to heal (Matthew 10:1-8).

He kept the bag, and John states plainly what that meant: at the anointing in Bethany he objected that the ointment might have been sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor, "This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein" (John 12:4-6).

He went to the chief priests and said, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver. And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him" (Matthew 26:14-16).

At the supper Christ said one of them would betray him, and each asked, "Lord, is it I?" Judas asked, "Master, is it I?" and was answered, "Thou hast said" (Matthew 26:21-25). After the sop, Satan entered into him, and Christ said, "That thou doest, do quickly," and he went immediately out: "and it was night" (John 13:26-30).

He came to the garden with a multitude and gave them a sign: "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he." He said, "Hail, master; and kissed him." Christ answered, "Friend, wherefore art thou come?" and in Luke, "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" (Matthew 26:47-50; Luke 22:48).

"Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself" (Matthew 27:3-5). The priests bought the potter's field with the money, which Matthew records as fulfilling prophecy (Matthew 27:6-10).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He returned the money and said, "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood" (Matthew 27:3-4). Scripture uses a word of remorse rather than of the repentance that leads to life, and records what he did next.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was a thief who carried the bag and took from it: John 12:6.
  • Objected to the anointing out of covetousness disguised as concern for the poor: John 12:5-6.
  • Covenanted with the chief priests to deliver Christ for thirty pieces of silver, and sought opportunity: Matthew 26:14-16.
  • Betrayed him with a kiss: Matthew 26:48-49; Luke 22:48.
  • Christ's own words: "woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born": Matthew 26:24.
  • Called by Christ "a devil" and "the son of perdition": John 6:70; John 17:12.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and the condemnation is Christ's own. What makes the record so grave is proximity: he was one of the twelve, sent out to preach and heal with the others, present at every discourse, and at the supper the other eleven had no idea which of them was meant. Scripture holds together two things without reconciling them - Satan entered into him, and he went and bargained of his own initiative and sought opportunity. His remorse was real and it did not save him.

Significance

His betrayal fulfilled Scripture, which Christ and Peter both state (John 13:18, quoting Psalms 41:9; Acts 1:16, 1:20). The thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field are recorded by Matthew as fulfilling prophecy. Matthias was chosen to take his place among the twelve (Acts 1:15-26).

Death / Outcome

"And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself" (Matthew 27:5). Acts 1:18 adds that falling headlong he burst asunder in the midst and all his bowels gushed out, and that the field was called Aceldama, the field of blood. The relation between the two accounts is a long-standing question; both are recorded here without an attempted harmonization.

Scripture

Matthew 10:4; Matthew 26:14-16, 26:20-25, 26:47-50; Matthew 27:3-10; Mark 14:10-11, 14:43-45; Luke 22:3-6, 22:47-48; John 6:70-71; John 12:4-6; John 13:2, 13:21-30; John 17:12; John 18:2-5; Acts 1:16-26
474

Peter's wife's mother

Unnamed. The mother of Simon Peter's wife, healed of a fever and immediately serving.

Family

Mother of Peter's wife (Matthew 8:14).

Chronology

Early in the Galilean ministry, at Capernaum.

Life Synopsis

"And when Jesus was come into Peter's house, he saw his wife's mother laid, and sick of a fever. And he touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them" (Matthew 8:14-15). Mark records that they told him of her at once, and that he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up (Mark 1:30-31). Luke, a physician, calls it "a great fever," and says he rebuked the fever (Luke 4:38-39).

What They Did Right

  • Arose and ministered to them immediately upon being healed: Matthew 8:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the illness, the healing, and what she did next, in one sentence. The detail all three Gospels preserve is the same: she got up and served. Nothing she said is recorded.

Significance

Her healing establishes incidentally that Peter was married, which Paul confirms (1 Corinthians 9:5). The healing was followed the same evening by the whole city gathering at the door (Mark 1:32-33).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Matthew 8:14-15; Mark 1:29-31; Luke 4:38-39; compare 1 Corinthians 9:5
475

The centurion of Capernaum

Unnamed. A Roman centurion whose servant Christ healed, and of whom Christ said he had not found so great faith in Israel.

Family

Not recorded. He had a servant who was dear to him (Luke 7:2).

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

He came to Jesus beseeching him: "Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented." Jesus said, "I will come and heal him."

"The centurion answered and said, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed. For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it."

"When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel." He added that many would come from the east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom, while the children of the kingdom would be cast out. "And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour" (Matthew 8:5-13). Luke adds that the elders of the Jews said of him, "he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue" (Luke 7:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • Interceded for a servant rather than for himself or his family: Matthew 8:6; Luke 7:2.
  • Judged himself unworthy to have Christ come under his roof: Matthew 8:8.
  • Reasoned from his own experience of authority that a word would be enough: Matthew 8:9.
  • Christ's own verdict: "I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel": Matthew 8:10.
  • Loved the Jewish nation and built them a synagogue, on the testimony of their own elders: Luke 7:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and one of only two occasions in the Gospels where Christ is said to have marvelled - the other being at unbelief in Nazareth (Mark 6:6). He is a Gentile officer of the occupying power, and his faith is set above anything Christ had found in Israel.

Significance

His healing is one of two in the Gospels performed at a distance, and it produced Christ's statement that many would come from east and west to sit down with the patriarchs while the children of the kingdom were cast out - an early and explicit statement that the kingdom would not be confined to Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 7:10.

Scripture

Matthew 8:5-13; Luke 7:1-10
476

The woman of Canaan

Unnamed. A Gentile woman of the coasts of Tyre and Sidon whose daughter was grievously vexed with a devil, and whose persistence Christ commended.

Also called the Syrophenician woman

Family

She had a young daughter (Matthew 15:22). Mark calls her a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation (Mark 7:26).

Chronology

During the ministry, in the coasts of Tyre and Sidon.

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil. But he answered her not a word."

The disciples asked him to send her away because she cried after them. He said, "I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel." She came and worshipped him, saying, "Lord, help me." He answered, "It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it to dogs."

"And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table. Then Jesus answered and said unto her, O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour" (Matthew 15:22-28).

What They Did Right

  • Persisted through silence, the disciples' impatience, and two discouraging answers: Matthew 15:23-27.
  • Worshipped him and asked simply, "Lord, help me": Matthew 15:25.
  • Accepted the terms of his answer and reasoned within them rather than disputing them: Matthew 15:27.
  • Christ's own verdict: "O woman, great is thy faith": Matthew 15:28.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her, and Christ's commendation of her faith is one of only two he gives in those terms - the other to the centurion, also a Gentile. Her answer is the sharpest reply anyone gives Christ in the Gospels, and it is a reply of agreement: she did not deny the order he stated, she found her place within it.

Significance

With the centurion of Capernaum, she is one of two Gentiles in the Gospels whose faith Christ praises above what he found in Israel. Her daughter was healed at a distance and in the same hour.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Mark 7:30.

Scripture

Matthew 15:21-28; Mark 7:24-30
477

The rich young ruler

Unnamed. A young man of great possessions who asked what good thing he should do to have eternal life, and went away sorrowful.

Family

Not recorded. Matthew calls him a young man, Luke a ruler, and all three note his great possessions (Matthew 19:20, 19:22; Mark 10:22; Luke 18:18).

Chronology

Late in the ministry, on the way to Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, one came and said unto him, Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?" Christ answered, "Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God: but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments." Asked which, he named several of the second table and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

"The young man saith unto him, All these things have I kept from my youth up: what lack I yet?" Mark adds, "Then Jesus beholding him loved him."

"Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me. But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions" (Matthew 19:16-22; Mark 10:21).

Christ then said it was easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, and when the disciples asked who then could be saved, answered, "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible" (Matthew 19:23-26).

What They Did Right

  • Came to Christ with a serious question about eternal life, and came running and kneeling: Matthew 19:16; Mark 10:17.
  • Had kept the commandments he named from his youth up, which Christ did not dispute: Matthew 19:20.
  • Mark records that Jesus, beholding him, loved him: Mark 10:21.

What They Did Wrong

  • Went away sorrowful rather than part with his possessions: Matthew 19:22.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a man who was sincere, morally upright, respectful, and unable to do the one thing asked. Christ did not dispute his claim to have kept the commandments and did not accuse him of anything; Mark records love rather than rebuke. He is the only person in the Gospels recorded as being called by Christ and refusing.

Significance

His refusal produced Christ's teaching on riches and the kingdom, and the disciples' question, "Who then can be saved?" - answered with the statement that what is impossible with men is possible with God (Matthew 19:23-26).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He went away sorrowful (Matthew 19:22).

Scripture

Matthew 19:16-26; Mark 10:17-27; Luke 18:18-27
478

Simon the leper

A man of Bethany in whose house Christ was anointed shortly before the passion.

Family

Not recorded. Of Bethany (Matthew 26:6).

Chronology

Two days before the passover (Matthew 26:2, 26:6).

Life Synopsis

"Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, there came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat" (Matthew 26:6-7). The disciples had indignation, saying it might have been sold for much and given to the poor. Christ answered, "Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me... For in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her" (Matthew 26:8-13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He received Christ into his house. Scripture records nothing that he said or did.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his town, his condition, and that Christ was at meat in his house, and nothing else. The name he carries is worth noting: he is called the leper while sitting at table with guests, which indicates he had been one and was not one still, though the text does not say how.

Significance

His house is the setting of the anointing that Christ said would be told for a memorial wherever the gospel was preached - and it is being told here.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named twice.

Scripture

Matthew 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9
479

The woman with the alabaster box

Unnamed in Matthew and Mark. A woman who poured very precious ointment on Christ's head at Bethany, and of whom he said her act would be told wherever the gospel was preached.

Family

Not recorded. John's Gospel records an anointing at Bethany by Mary the sister of Lazarus (John 12:1-8); whether the accounts describe the same event is debated, and Matthew and Mark do not name the woman.

Chronology

Two days before the passover (Matthew 26:2).

Life Synopsis

"There came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat. But when his disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste? For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor."

"When Jesus understood it, he said unto them, Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me. For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always. For in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her" (Matthew 26:7-13). Mark adds Christ's words, "She hath done what she could" (Mark 14:8).

What They Did Right

  • Poured very precious ointment on Christ, at real cost, and was defended by him against the disciples: Matthew 26:7-10.
  • Christ's own verdict: "she hath wrought a good work upon me," and "She hath done what she could": Matthew 26:10; Mark 14:8.
  • Anointed his body beforehand for the burial: Matthew 26:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and one of the strongest commendations Christ gives to anyone. The disciples' objection was reasonable on its face, and he overruled it. Mark's phrase - she has done what she could - is the whole assessment, and it measures the act against her capacity rather than against its usefulness.

Significance

She is the only person in the Gospels of whom Christ said that what she had done would be told wherever the gospel was preached in the whole world, as a memorial of her. It is the one act in Scripture given that promise.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Matthew 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9; compare John 12:1-8
480

Caiaphas

High priest in the year of the crucifixion; presided at Christ's trial before the council and adjured him to say whether he was the Christ.

Family

Son in law of Annas, who was also called high priest (John 18:13).

Chronology

"Being the high priest that same year" (John 11:49, 11:51; John 18:13).

Life Synopsis

After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council. Caiaphas said, "Ye know nothing at all, nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not." John adds: "And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad. Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death" (John 11:47-53).

At the trial the chief priests and all the council sought false witness, and found none that agreed. At last two came. Christ held his peace. "And the high priest answered and said unto him, I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven."

"Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy. What think ye? They answered and said, He is guilty of death" (Matthew 26:57-66).

He is named again in Acts among those before whom Peter and John stood (Acts 4:6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Presided over a council that sought false witness against Christ: Matthew 26:59-60.
  • Proposed the death of one man as expedient for the nation: John 11:49-50.
  • Rent his clothes and pronounced blasphemy, and led the council to declare him guilty of death: Matthew 26:65-66.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative. The most remarkable thing in his record is John's comment on his own words: he spoke not of himself, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation. The office carried the words further than the man intended, and he stated the doctrine of substitution while arranging a judicial murder.

Significance

He presided over the trial that condemned Christ. His unwitting prophecy in John 11:50-52 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of Christ dying for the people, spoken by the man who arranged it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 4:6.

Scripture

Matthew 26:3-4, 26:57-68; Luke 3:2; John 11:47-53; John 18:13-14, 18:24, 18:28; Acts 4:6
481

Pontius Pilate

Governor of Judaea; found no fault in Christ, washed his hands, and delivered him to be crucified.

Family

Married; his wife sent to him during the trial (Matthew 27:19).

Chronology

Governor of Judaea when John began to preach and through the crucifixion (Luke 3:1).

Life Synopsis

Christ was delivered to him bound. He asked, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" and received, "Thou sayest." When accused by the chief priests he answered nothing, "insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly" (Matthew 27:11-14).

He knew why they had brought him: "For he knew that for envy they had delivered him" (Matthew 27:18). He offered them Barabbas or Jesus, expecting them to choose Jesus. While he sat on the judgment seat his wife sent to him: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him" (Matthew 27:19).

The chief priests persuaded the multitude to ask for Barabbas. Pilate asked, "What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ?" and, "Why, what evil hath he done?" They cried the more. "When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it." He released Barabbas, scourged Jesus, and delivered him to be crucified (Matthew 27:20-26).

John records that he said three times he found no fault in him, that he sought to release him, and that he gave way when they said, "If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend" (John 18:38; John 19:4-16). He wrote the title over the cross and refused to change it: "What I have written I have written" (John 19:19-22). He gave the body to Joseph of Arimathaea (Matthew 27:57-58).

What They Did Right

  • Recognised that Christ was delivered for envy: Matthew 27:18.
  • Declared repeatedly that he found no fault in him and sought to release him: Luke 23:4, 23:14-16, 23:22; John 19:12.
  • Refused to alter the title he had written over the cross: John 19:21-22.
  • Granted the body to Joseph of Arimathaea: Matthew 27:58.

What They Did Wrong

  • Condemned a man he had three times declared innocent: Matthew 27:24-26; Luke 23:22-24.
  • Scourged him and delivered him to be crucified to satisfy the crowd: Matthew 27:26.
  • Attempted to transfer his own responsibility by washing his hands: Matthew 27:24. The gesture did not remove the decision, which was his alone to make.
  • Yielded to the threat about Caesar rather than to the evidence: John 19:12-16.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents a man who knew exactly what was happening and did it anyway. He identified the motive, was warned by his wife, stated the verdict three times, and passed sentence to avoid a tumult and a report to Rome. The handwashing is recorded without comment and answers itself: the crowd could shout, but only Pilate could sentence. Christ's own words to him make the responsibility clear while placing it in a wider frame: "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin" (John 19:11).

Significance

His name is in the creeds because Luke and Paul both date the crucifixion by him (Luke 3:1; 1 Timothy 6:13), which fixes the event in secular history. The title he wrote and would not change - Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews, in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin - was the public charge under which Christ died.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 13:28.

Scripture

Matthew 27:1-2, 27:11-26, 27:57-66; Mark 15:1-15; Luke 3:1; Luke 13:1; Luke 23:1-25; John 18:28-19:22; Acts 3:13; Acts 4:27; Acts 13:28; 1 Timothy 6:13
482

Pilate's wife

Unnamed. The wife of the governor, who sent word to him on the judgment seat warning him to have nothing to do with Jesus.

Family

Wife of Pontius Pilate (Matthew 27:19).

Chronology

During the trial of Christ.

Life Synopsis

"When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him" (Matthew 27:19). Nothing further is recorded of her, and Matthew alone records the incident.

What They Did Right

  • Sent a warning to her husband while he sat on the judgment seat, calling Christ "that just man": Matthew 27:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one message and no more. She is one of several people in the passion narrative who declared Christ innocent, and the only one who did so unasked and at no advantage to herself. Her verdict - that just man - agrees with the centurion's, the dying thief's, and Judas's.

Significance

Her warning came at the exact moment of decision, while Pilate sat on the judgment seat, and it was not heeded.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is mentioned once.

Scripture

Matthew 27:19
483

Barabbas

A notable prisoner, a robber who had committed murder in an insurrection; released by Pilate in place of Christ.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the trial of Christ.

Life Synopsis

"And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas" (Matthew 27:16). Mark says he lay bound with those who had made insurrection with him, "who had committed murder in the insurrection" (Mark 15:7). Luke says he was cast into prison "for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder" (Luke 23:19). John calls him a robber (John 18:40).

Pilate offered the crowd a choice at the feast: "Whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?" The chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude to ask Barabbas and destroy Jesus. "Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified" (Matthew 27:17-26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • A robber, guilty of sedition and of murder committed in an insurrection: Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19; John 18:40.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his crimes and his release and nothing about the man himself - no words, no response, no later mention. He exists in the narrative as the alternative that was chosen.

Significance

He is the one person in Scripture of whom it can be said literally that Christ died in his place: he was condemned, and was released, and the man who took his place was crucified. Peter's charge to Jerusalem states it plainly: "ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you" (Acts 3:14).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was released (Matthew 27:26).

Scripture

Matthew 27:16-26; Mark 15:6-15; Luke 23:18-25; John 18:39-40; Acts 3:14
484

Simon of Cyrene

A man of Cyrene, coming out of the country, compelled to bear the cross of Christ.

Family

Mark names him "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21), which indicates his sons were known to the readers. A Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13; the identification is not made by Scripture.

Chronology

On the way to the crucifixion.

Life Synopsis

"And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross" (Matthew 27:32). Mark adds that he was "passing by, coming out of the country," and names his two sons (Mark 15:21). Luke says they "laid on him the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus" (Luke 23:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He bore the cross, but Scripture states plainly that he was compelled to do it, and records nothing that he chose.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records that he was passing by, that he was compelled, and that he carried the cross behind Jesus. Nothing he said is recorded and no motive is given. Mark's naming of his sons suggests the family was afterward known in the church, which is the only hint the text offers about what became of him.

Significance

He is the only person recorded as physically carrying the cross of Christ, and Luke's phrasing - that he might bear it after Jesus - has been read alongside Christ's own words about taking up the cross and following (Luke 9:23). Scripture makes no such connection explicitly.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 23:26.

Scripture

Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26
485

The centurion at the cross

Unnamed. The centurion in charge of the crucifixion, who declared at Christ's death that he was the Son of God.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the crucifixion.

Life Synopsis

"Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God" (Matthew 27:54). Mark records it at the moment of death: "And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39). Luke records, "Certainly this was a righteous man" (Luke 23:47).

He was afterward summoned by Pilate to confirm that Jesus was already dead before the body was released (Mark 15:44-45).

What They Did Right

  • Declared Christ the Son of God at the moment of his death, having watched the whole execution: Matthew 27:54; Mark 15:39.
  • Called him a righteous man: Luke 23:47.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the confession of the officer responsible for the execution, made in the presence of his own men. He had every reason to think otherwise and had watched the entire thing.

Significance

His words are the first confession of Christ as the Son of God after the crucifixion, and they come from a Gentile soldier. Mark's Gospel opens by calling Jesus the Son of God (Mark 1:1) and this is the only human being in that Gospel to say so.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Mark 15:45.

Scripture

Matthew 27:54; Mark 15:39, 15:44-45; Luke 23:47
486

Joseph of Arimathaea

A rich man of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor and a disciple secretly for fear of the Jews; asked Pilate for the body of Christ and laid it in his own new tomb.

Family

Not recorded. Of Arimathaea, a city of the Jews (Luke 23:51).

Chronology

At the burial of Christ.

Life Synopsis

"When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathaea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus' disciple: he went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered. And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed" (Matthew 27:57-60).

Mark calls him "an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God," and says he "went in boldly unto Pilate" (Mark 15:43). Luke adds that he was "a good man, and a just," and "had not consented to the counsel and deed of them" (Luke 23:50-51). John says he was a disciple, "but secretly for fear of the Jews," and that Nicodemus came with him bringing myrrh and aloes (John 19:38-39).

What They Did Right

  • Had not consented to the counsel and deed of the council of which he was a member: Luke 23:51.
  • Went in boldly to Pilate to beg the body, at the moment when the disciples had scattered: Mark 15:43.
  • Gave his own new tomb, and wrapped the body in clean linen: Matthew 27:59-60.
  • Described as an honourable counsellor, a good man, and a just, who waited for the kingdom of God: Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50-51.

What They Did Wrong

  • He had been a disciple secretly, for fear of the Jews: John 19:38. Scripture states the fear plainly, and states equally plainly that he acted openly when it mattered most.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the fear and then records the act that ended it. He was a member of the council that condemned Christ and had not consented to it; he asked a Roman governor for the body of a man executed for sedition; and he gave up a tomb he had cut for himself. Every Gospel records him, which is true of very few minor figures.

Significance

His tomb is the tomb of the resurrection, and his action fulfilled Isaiah's word that the servant would be "with the rich in his death" (Isaiah 53:9). The burial in a known tomb, sealed and guarded, is part of the evidence the Gospels set out for the resurrection.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 19:42.

Scripture

Matthew 27:57-60; Mark 15:42-46; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42; compare Isaiah 53:9
487

Mary Magdalene

A woman of Magdala out of whom went seven devils; followed and ministered to Christ, stood by the cross, and was the first to see him risen.

Family

Not recorded. Of Magdala. Scripture nowhere identifies her with the sinful woman of Luke 7:37-38 or with Mary of Bethany; that identification is a later tradition and is not made by the text.

Chronology

During the ministry, at the crucifixion, and on the resurrection morning.

Life Synopsis

Luke names her among the women who ministered to Christ of their substance: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils" (Luke 8:2-3).

She was at the cross, beholding afar off, and sitting over against the sepulchre when he was buried (Matthew 27:56, 27:61). She came early to the tomb while it was yet dark, found the stone taken away, and ran to Peter and John (John 20:1-2).

She stood outside the sepulchre weeping. Two angels asked why she wept, and she said, "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him." Turning, she saw Jesus and did not know him, supposing him to be the gardener, and said, "Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away."

"Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." He sent her to the brethren, and "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her" (John 20:11-18). Mark states it directly: "he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils" (Mark 16:9).

What They Did Right

  • Ministered to Christ of her substance: Luke 8:2-3.
  • Stood by the cross and watched the burial: Matthew 27:56, 27:61; John 19:25.
  • Came to the tomb while it was yet dark: John 20:1.
  • Stayed at the sepulchre weeping after the disciples had gone home: John 20:10-11.
  • Was the first person to whom the risen Christ appeared, and carried the message to the disciples: Mark 16:9; John 20:16-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records that seven devils went out of her (Luke 8:2; Mark 16:9), which describes a condition from which she was delivered rather than a charge against her. It records no sin of hers.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and a great deal in her favour. The detail that shapes her record is where she was at each point: at the cross, at the burial, at the tomb before dawn, and still there weeping when everyone else had left. She is the first witness of the resurrection, and the first person commissioned to announce it.

Significance

All four Gospels place her at the crucifixion and the tomb. That the risen Christ appeared first to her, and sent her to tell the apostles, is recorded by Mark and John without comment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 20:18.

Scripture

Matthew 27:56, 27:61; Matthew 28:1-10; Mark 15:40, 15:47; Mark 16:1-11; Luke 8:2-3; Luke 24:10; John 19:25; John 20:1-18
488

Jairus

A ruler of the synagogue whose twelve-year-old daughter died while Christ was on the way to her, and was raised.

Family

A ruler of the synagogue; father of one daughter, about twelve years of age (Mark 5:22, 5:42; Luke 8:42).

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet, and besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: I pray thee, come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live" (Mark 5:22-23).

On the way the woman with the issue of blood touched his garment, and Christ stopped to find her. While he yet spake, there came from the ruler's house saying, "Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further? As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe" (Mark 5:35-36).

He took Peter, James, and John, put out the mourners who laughed him to scorn, and took the damsel by the hand: "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. And straightway the damsel arose, and walked... And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat" (Mark 5:37-43).

What They Did Right

  • Fell at Christ's feet and besought him greatly for his daughter, though he was a ruler of the synagogue: Mark 5:22-23.
  • Did not turn back when told she was dead, having been told, "Be not afraid, only believe": Mark 5:35-36.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His position makes his approach costly - the rulers of the synagogues were generally in opposition - and the account puts his faith under a specific strain: Christ stopped on the way to attend to somebody else, and the delay cost the girl her life before he arrived.

Significance

His daughter is one of three people recorded as raised by Christ, with the widow of Nain's son and Lazarus. The interruption of his errand by the woman with the issue of blood is one of the clearest instances in the Gospels of a delay that looked fatal and was not.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 8:56.

Scripture

Matthew 9:18-26; Mark 5:22-43; Luke 8:41-56
489

The woman with the issue of blood

Unnamed. A woman who had suffered twelve years and was healed by touching the hem of Christ's garment in a crowd.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry, on the way to Jairus's house.

Life Synopsis

"And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, and had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse, when she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole" (Mark 5:25-28). Luke, a physician, says she "had spent all her living upon physicians, neither could be healed of any" (Luke 8:43).

"And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague. And Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my clothes?" The disciples pointed out that the multitude thronged him.

"But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague" (Mark 5:29-34).

What They Did Right

  • Came to Christ after twelve years of failed treatment and the loss of everything she had: Mark 5:26-27.
  • Came and told him all the truth when she could have slipped away: Mark 5:33.
  • Christ's own verdict: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole": Mark 5:34.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. She came secretly in the press behind him. Scripture records the manner without condemning it, and Christ's stopping to find her is presented as securing her a word rather than as a rebuke.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Her condition made her ceremonially unclean, which explains the secrecy, and Christ would not let the healing stay anonymous. He is recorded as calling only one person Daughter, and it is her.

Significance

Her healing interrupts the account of Jairus's daughter, and the two are told together: a woman ill for twelve years and a girl of twelve. The delay caused by her healing is what made Jairus's case impossible and the raising necessary.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 8:48.

Scripture

Matthew 9:20-22; Mark 5:25-34; Luke 8:43-48
490

The man of the Gadarenes

Unnamed. A man possessed by many devils who dwelt among the tombs, was delivered, and was sent home to tell what the Lord had done.

Family

Not recorded. He had a home and friends (Mark 5:19).

Chronology

During the ministry, in the country of the Gadarenes.

Life Synopsis

He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no man could bind him, no, not with chains, for the chains had been plucked asunder and the fetters broken in pieces. "And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones" (Mark 5:2-5).

He ran and worshipped Christ, and the devils within him spoke and were sent into the swine (Mark 5:6-13). Those who fed the swine fled and told it, "and they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid" (Mark 5:15).

As Christ was leaving, "he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel" (Mark 5:18-20).

What They Did Right

  • Ran and worshipped Christ before the deliverance: Mark 5:6.
  • Asked to be with him afterward: Mark 5:18.
  • Obeyed when refused, and published throughout Decapolis what had been done for him: Mark 5:19-20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His condition is described at length and is presented as possession rather than as sin. Scripture records no fault of the man.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives the fullest account of a deliverance in the Gospels. The picture of him afterward - sitting, clothed, and in his right mind - is set directly against the man who could not be bound with chains. He is the one person recorded as asking to go with Christ and being told no, and the reason given is a commission.

Significance

He became the first preacher in Decapolis, sent to his own home and friends rather than to travel with Christ. The people of the country, seeing him restored, asked Jesus to depart out of their coasts (Mark 5:17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 8:39.

Scripture

Matthew 8:28-34; Mark 5:1-20; Luke 8:26-39
491

Bartimaeus

Son of Timaeus; a blind beggar of Jericho who would not be silenced, and received his sight.

Family

Son of Timaeus (Mark 10:46).

Chronology

On the last journey to Jerusalem, at Jericho.

Life Synopsis

"And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sat by the highway side begging. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, and say, Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me. And many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me."

"And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called... And he, casting away his garment, rose, and came to Jesus. And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight. And Jesus said unto him, Go thy way; thy faith hath made thee whole. And immediately he received his sight, and followed Jesus in the way" (Mark 10:46-52).

What They Did Right

  • Called Christ the son of David - a messianic title - and would not be silenced when many charged him to hold his peace: Mark 10:47-48.
  • Cast away his garment and came when called: Mark 10:50.
  • Asked plainly for the one thing he wanted: Mark 10:51.
  • Followed Jesus in the way after receiving his sight: Mark 10:52.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is one of the few people healed in the Gospels who is named, and one of the few recorded as following afterward. The crowd tried to silence him and he shouted louder, which the narrative records without comment.

Significance

His cry, "Thou son of David, have mercy on me," is a messianic confession from a blind beggar on the road to the passion week, and Christ did not correct it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He followed Jesus in the way (Mark 10:52).

Scripture

Matthew 20:29-34; Mark 10:46-52; Luke 18:35-43
492

The widow of Nain

Unnamed. A widow of Nain whose only son had died, and whom Christ raised on the way to burial.

Family

A widow; the dead man was the only son of his mother (Luke 7:12).

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

"Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow: and much people of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not."

"And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother. And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people" (Luke 7:11-16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records nothing that she said or did. She did not ask, and is not said to have had faith; the account turns entirely on Christ seeing her.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the whole event as unasked. She made no request and is not recorded speaking. The reason given for the miracle is stated plainly: when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her. It is one of the few miracles in the Gospels performed without anyone asking.

Significance

Her son is one of three people recorded as raised by Christ. The phrase "he delivered him to his mother" echoes Elijah at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:23), and the crowd's response - that God had visited his people - picks up Zacharias's prophecy in Luke 1:68.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 7:15.

Scripture

Luke 7:11-17
493

Zacchaeus

Chief among the publicans at Jericho, and rich; climbed a sycomore tree to see Christ and received him joyfully.

Family

Called a son of Abraham by Christ (Luke 19:9).

Chronology

On the last journey to Jerusalem, at Jericho.

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich. And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way."

"And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house. And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner."

"And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold. And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:1-10).

What They Did Right

  • Sought to see Christ and overcame both the crowd and his own dignity to do it: Luke 19:3-4.
  • Received him joyfully when called down: Luke 19:6.
  • Gave half his goods to the poor and offered fourfold restitution, which is more than the law required: Luke 19:8; compare Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:5.
  • Christ's own verdict: "This day is salvation come to this house": Luke 19:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • He was chief among the publicans and rich, and his own offer of fourfold restitution implies he had taken by false accusation: Luke 19:8. Scripture records the admission in his own words and records the restitution in the same breath.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the crowd's assessment - that he was a sinner - and does not dispute it, and records Christ's assessment, which overrides it. What he offered went beyond the law: restitution of a fifth was required, and he offered four times over, and half his goods besides. The account ends with the sentence that states the purpose of the whole ministry.

Significance

His account produced the statement, "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10), which is Luke's summary of the Gospel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 19:10.

Scripture

Luke 19:1-10
494

Simon the Pharisee

A Pharisee who invited Christ to eat with him, and thought within himself when a sinful woman anointed his feet.

Family

Not recorded. Distinct from Simon the leper of Bethany, though both hosted an anointing.

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

He invited Christ to eat with him. A woman in the city, a sinner, brought an alabaster box of ointment, stood at his feet behind him weeping, washed his feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them.

"Now when the Pharisee which had bidden him saw it, he spake within himself, saying, This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner."

Christ answered the thought with the parable of two debtors, one owing five hundred pence and one fifty, both frankly forgiven, and asked which would love him most. Simon answered rightly. Christ then set out what Simon had not done: "Thou gavest me no water for my feet... Thou gavest me no kiss... My head with oil thou didst not anoint: but this woman hath anointed my feet with ointment. Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little" (Luke 7:36-47).

What They Did Right

  • Invited Christ into his house and to his table: Luke 7:36.
  • Answered the question about the two debtors correctly: Luke 7:43.

What They Did Wrong

  • Judged both the woman and Christ silently, concluding he could not be a prophet: Luke 7:39.
  • Omitted the ordinary courtesies of hospitality - water for the feet, a kiss, oil for the head - which Christ named one by one: Luke 7:44-46.

Character Assessment

Scripture records that he thought rather than spoke, and that Christ answered the thought. The parable he was given ends by defining his own position: to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. He is not condemned outright, and the comparison is left standing.

Significance

The account contains the parable of the two debtors and the statement that love follows forgiveness rather than earning it. It is a different occasion from the anointing at Bethany, though the two are often confused.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 7:44.

Scripture

Luke 7:36-50
495

The woman which was a sinner

Unnamed. A woman of the city, a sinner, who washed Christ's feet with her tears in the house of Simon the Pharisee and was told her sins were forgiven.

Family

Not recorded. Scripture nowhere identifies her with Mary Magdalene or with Mary of Bethany; those identifications are later tradition and are not made by the text.

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

"And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment, and stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment" (Luke 7:37-38).

The Pharisee thought Christ could not be a prophet or he would have known what she was. Christ told the parable of the two debtors, then contrasted her conduct with his host's, and said, "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much."

"And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven. And they that sat at meat with him began to say within themselves, Who is this that forgiveth sins also? And he said to the woman, Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace" (Luke 7:47-50).

What They Did Right

  • Came into a Pharisee's house uninvited to reach Christ: Luke 7:37.
  • Wept, washed his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them: Luke 7:38.
  • Christ's own verdict: she loved much, and "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace": Luke 7:47-50.

What They Did Wrong

  • Scripture calls her "a sinner" and records Christ saying her sins were many: Luke 7:37, 7:47. No particular act is described.

Character Assessment

Scripture states her reputation plainly and then records Christ receiving her, defending her against her host, forgiving her, and dismissing her in peace. The whole account turns on the contrast between what she did and what the respectable host omitted.

Significance

The episode produced the parable of the two debtors and the principle that great forgiveness produces great love. It also produced the question asked at the table - Who is this that forgiveth sins also? - which is the point of the passage.

Death / Outcome
