Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 7:50.

Scripture

Luke 7:36-50
496

Joanna

Wife of Chuza, Herod's steward; one of the women who ministered to Christ of their substance and who brought spices to the tomb.

Family

Wife of Chuza, Herod's steward (Luke 8:3).

Chronology

During the ministry and on the resurrection morning.

Life Synopsis

Luke names the women who went with Christ and the twelve: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, and Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance" (Luke 8:2-3).

She was among the women who came to the sepulchre early with spices, found the stone rolled away, were told by the two men in shining garments that he was risen, and "returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things unto the eleven, and to all the rest. It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and other women that were with them, which told these things unto the apostles. And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not" (Luke 24:1-11).

What They Did Right

  • Ministered to Christ of her own substance: Luke 8:3.
  • Came early to the sepulchre with spices and carried the report to the apostles: Luke 24:1-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Her position is worth noting: the wife of a senior official in the household of the Herod who had beheaded John the Baptist, supporting Christ's work with her own money.

Significance

She is among the first witnesses of the empty tomb, and among those whose report the apostles dismissed as idle tales.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 24:10.

Scripture

Luke 8:2-3; Luke 24:1-10
497

Susanna

One of the women who followed Christ and ministered to him of their substance.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During the Galilean ministry.

Life Synopsis

Named once, among the women who went with Christ and the twelve through every city and village: "and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance" (Luke 8:3).

What They Did Right

  • Ministered to Christ of her own substance: Luke 8:3.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture names her once and records one thing about her, which is that she paid for the ministry out of her own means. Nothing else is recorded.

Significance

Luke's note that the work of Christ and the twelve was supported by these women is the only statement in the Gospels about how it was funded.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Luke 8:1-3
498

Nicodemus

A Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews; came to Christ by night, defended him before the council, and helped bury him.

Family

Not recorded. "A ruler of the Jews" and "a master of Israel" (John 3:1, 3:10).

Chronology

Early in the ministry, then at the feast of tabernacles, and at the burial.

Life Synopsis

"There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews: the same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him."

Christ answered, "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Nicodemus asked how a man could be born when he is old, and was answered with the birth of water and of the Spirit, and with the wind that bloweth where it listeth. "Nicodemus answered and said unto him, How can these things be? Jesus answered and said unto him, Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things?" The conversation continues into the words "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son" (John 3:1-16).

When the officers returned without Christ and the Pharisees said none of the rulers had believed on him, "Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,) Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth? They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee?" (John 7:50-52).

"And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight" - and with Joseph of Arimathaea took the body and wound it in linen clothes with the spices (John 19:39-40).

What They Did Right

  • Came to Christ and acknowledged him a teacher come from God: John 3:2.
  • Spoke for due process before the council, at the cost of being mocked: John 7:50-52.
  • Brought about a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes and helped bury him openly, when the disciples had scattered: John 19:39-40.

What They Did Wrong

  • He came by night, which John mentions three times: John 3:2; John 7:50; John 19:39. Scripture records the fact each time without ever calling it sin.
  • As a master of Israel he did not understand the new birth, and was asked why not: John 3:10.

Character Assessment

Scripture records three appearances and a clear direction across them: by night, then a cautious word in council, then a hundred pounds of spices in daylight. John's repeated note that he came by night is not stated as a charge; it functions as a marker of where he started. His last recorded act is the most public thing anyone did for Christ that day besides Joseph.

Significance

His night conversation produced John 3:16 and the teaching on the new birth, the fullest statement of it in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 19:39.

Scripture

John 3:1-21; John 7:45-52; John 19:38-42
499

The woman of Samaria

Unnamed. A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well to whom Christ revealed himself as the Messiah, and who brought her city to him.

Family

She had had five husbands, and the man she then had was not her husband (John 4:18).

Chronology

Early in the ministry, on the way from Judaea to Galilee.

Life Synopsis

Jesus, wearied with his journey, sat on the well at Sychar, and a woman of Samaria came to draw water. "Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink." She answered, "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans" (John 4:6-9).

He spoke of living water; she asked for it, thinking of the well. He said, "Go, call thy husband, and come hither." She answered, "I have no husband." He replied, "Thou hast well said, I have no husband: for thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly" (John 4:16-18).

She raised the dispute about the right place of worship, and was told that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and in truth. She said, "I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things. Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am he" (John 4:19-26).

"The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men, Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Many of the Samaritans believed on him for the saying of the woman, and after two days many more believed "because of his own word" (John 4:28-42).

What They Did Right

  • Engaged the conversation seriously rather than dismissing it: John 4:9-15.
  • Answered truthfully when asked about her husband, which Christ acknowledged: John 4:17-18.
  • Left her waterpot and went and told the men of the city: John 4:28-29.
  • Many of the Samaritans believed on him for her word: John 4:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • She had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband: John 4:18. Christ stated it plainly and did not moralise, and the account does not return to it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records her circumstances without softening and Christ's dealing with her without condemnation. She is a Samaritan, a woman, and living in an irregular situation, and she receives the first plain declaration of his messiahship recorded in the Gospels - earlier than Peter's confession and given to her directly.

Significance

She is the first person to whom Christ said outright that he was the Christ, and the first evangelist to a non-Jewish town. The conversation produced the teaching that God is a Spirit and must be worshipped in spirit and in truth (John 4:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 4:39.

Scripture

John 4:5-42
500

The impotent man at Bethesda

Unnamed. A man who had an infirmity thirty-eight years, healed at the pool of Bethesda on the sabbath.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During a feast of the Jews at Jerusalem (John 5:1).

Life Synopsis

He lay among a great multitude of impotent folk at the pool called Bethesda, and "had an infirmity thirty and eight years."

"When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me. Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath" (John 5:1-9).

The Jews told him it was not lawful to carry his bed. He answered that the man who made him whole had told him to. He did not know who it was, for Jesus had conveyed himself away.

"Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee. The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole" (John 5:10-15). The Jews then sought to slay Jesus because he had done these things on the sabbath.

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed and rose and walked: John 5:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Christ's words to him afterward - "sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (John 5:14) - imply something in his case that the text does not specify, and this reference does not supply one. That he told the Jews who had healed him is recorded without comment; whether it was gratitude or self-protection the text does not say.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his answer to the question, which does not answer it: asked whether he wanted to be made whole, he explained why he had not been. It records that he did not know who had healed him, that he was found later in the temple, and that he then identified Jesus to the authorities who were looking for him. The narrative supplies no motive and no verdict.

Significance

The healing on the sabbath and Christ's answer - "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" - is the occasion of the first recorded attempt to kill him, and of the discourse in John 5 on his relation to the Father (John 5:16-47).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 5:15.

Scripture

John 5:1-16
501

The man born blind

Unnamed. A man blind from birth whose sight Christ restored, and who was cast out of the synagogue for saying so.

Family

His parents are mentioned and questioned but not named (John 9:18-23).

Chronology

During the Jerusalem ministry.

Life Synopsis

The disciples asked, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." He made clay of spittle, anointed his eyes, and sent him to wash in Siloam; "he went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing" (John 9:1-7).

The Pharisees questioned him repeatedly. His answers grew bolder: first, "A man that is called Jesus made clay"; then, "He is a prophet"; then, when pressed a second time, "Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." When they said they did not know where Christ was from, he answered, "Why herein is a marvellous thing, that ye know not from whence he is, and yet he hath opened mine eyes... Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind. If this man were not of God, he could do nothing." They said, "Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out" (John 9:8-34).

His parents, fearing the Jews, refused to answer for him: "he is of age; ask him" (John 9:20-23).

"Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said unto him, Dost thou believe on the Son of God?... And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him" (John 9:35-38).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed an odd instruction without question and washed: John 9:7.
  • Held to what he knew under repeated hostile questioning: "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see": John 9:25.
  • Reasoned from the fact to the conclusion and said so to the Pharisees' faces: John 9:30-33.
  • Believed and worshipped when Christ found him: John 9:38.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His development across the chapter is the point of the account: from "a man that is called Jesus" to "a prophet" to "if this man were not of God, he could do nothing" to "Lord, I believe." He was excommunicated for the last position but one, and Christ sought him out afterward.

Significance

Christ's answer to the disciples' question - that neither he nor his parents had sinned, but that the works of God should be made manifest - is Scripture's plainest rejection of the assumption that affliction always signals particular guilt. The chapter closes with Christ's saying about seeing and blindness (John 9:39-41).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 9:38.

Scripture

John 9:1-41
502

The woman taken in adultery

Unnamed. A woman brought to Christ in the temple by the scribes and Pharisees, who was not condemned by him.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During the Jerusalem ministry.

Life Synopsis

"And the scribes and Pharisees brought unto him a woman taken in adultery; and when they had set her in the midst, they say unto him, Master, this woman was taken in adultery, in the very act. Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou? This they said, tempting him, that they might have to accuse him."

"But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not. So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground."

"And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more" (John 8:3-11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records only her answer, "No man, Lord." Nothing else that she said or did is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • She was taken in adultery, which the passage states as fact and which Christ's words assume: "go, and sin no more" (John 8:11). He did not dispute the charge; he refused to execute the sentence in the circumstances in which it was brought.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the charge without disputing it and records that Christ did not condemn her. The account is careful about the motive of those who brought her: they did it tempting him, that they might have to accuse him. She was the instrument of a trap, and the man taken with her - the law required both - is not mentioned. Christ's final words hold both together: neither do I condemn thee, and go and sin no more.

Significance

The passage is Scripture's clearest instance of Christ refusing to be used, and of mercy that does not deny the fault. A textual note is owed here: this passage is absent from some early manuscripts, and its place in John has long been discussed. It stands in the King James Version, the translation of record for this work, and it is treated accordingly.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 8:11.

Scripture

John 8:1-11
503

Martha

Sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany; received Christ into her house, was reproved for being cumbered about much serving, and confessed him as the Christ at her brother's grave.

Family

Sister of Mary and of Lazarus, of Bethany (Luke 10:38-39; John 11:1-2).

Chronology

During the ministry, and at the raising of Lazarus.

Life Synopsis

"A certain woman named Martha received him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, which also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word. But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me."

"And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:38-42).

When Lazarus was sick the sisters sent word, and Christ stayed two days. Martha went out to meet him: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee." He said her brother would rise again; she answered that she knew he would at the last day. "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live... Believest thou this? She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world" (John 11:20-27).

At the grave she objected, "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days" (John 11:39). At the supper six days before the passover, "Martha served" (John 12:2). John records that "Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus" (John 11:5).

What They Did Right

  • Received Christ into her house: Luke 10:38.
  • Went out to meet him while her sister sat still in the house: John 11:20.
  • Confessed him as the Christ, the Son of God, before her brother was raised: John 11:27.
  • Served at the supper without complaint on that occasion: John 12:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was cumbered about much serving, and complained that her sister was not helping and that Christ did not care: Luke 10:40. His answer names the fault gently - careful and troubled about many things - and does not condemn the serving itself.
  • Objected at the grave that the body would smell: John 11:39.

Character Assessment

Scripture records her impatience, her practical objections, and one of the fullest confessions in the Gospels. The reproof in Luke 10 is often read as being against work, which the text does not say: he named her being troubled about many things when one was needed, and he did not tell her to stop serving. John records simply that he loved her.

Significance

Her confession in John 11:27 matches Peter's at Caesarea Philippi in substance, and it drew out the statement "I am the resurrection, and the life."

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 12:2.

Scripture

Luke 10:38-42; John 11:1-44; John 12:1-2
504

Mary of Bethany

Sister of Martha and Lazarus; sat at Christ's feet and heard his word, and anointed him for his burial.

Family

Sister of Martha and Lazarus, of Bethany (John 11:1-2).

Chronology

During the ministry, and six days before the passover.

Life Synopsis

She "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word," while her sister served, and when Martha complained she was defended: "Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:39-42).

When Lazarus died she sat still in the house until Martha called her secretly, then rose hastily and came and fell at his feet, saying, "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping, "he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled... Jesus wept" (John 11:20, 11:28-35).

Six days before the passover, at the supper in Bethany, "then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Judas objected that it might have been sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor. "Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this" (John 12:1-8).

What They Did Right

  • Sat at his feet and heard his word, which he called the good part that would not be taken from her: Luke 10:39-42.
  • Fell at his feet in her grief and was met with his tears: John 11:32-35.
  • Anointed him with very costly ointment and was defended against the objection: John 12:3-7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her, and records Christ defending her twice - once against her sister and once against Judas. In all three of her appearances she is at his feet: hearing, weeping, and anointing.

Significance

Her anointing was for his burial, as he said, and it took place days before the crucifixion. Christ's defence of her in Luke 10:42 is one of Scripture's clearest statements of the priority of hearing his word.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: John 12:3.

Scripture

Luke 10:38-42; John 11:1-45; John 12:1-8
505

Lazarus of Bethany

Brother of Martha and Mary; died and was raised after four days in the grave; the chief priests then sought to kill him also.

Family

Brother of Martha and Mary, of Bethany (John 11:1-2). Not to be confused with the beggar Lazarus of Luke 16:20.

Chronology

Shortly before the last passover.

Life Synopsis

"Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha." The sisters sent word: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Christ stayed two days where he was, and then said plainly, "Lazarus is dead. And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe" (John 11:1-15).

When he came, Lazarus had been in the grave four days already. He asked where they had laid him, and wept. At the grave he said, "Take ye away the stone," and Martha objected. He prayed aloud for the sake of those standing by, "and when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go" (John 11:38-44).

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary believed. Others went to the Pharisees, and the council resolved on Christ's death from that day (John 11:45-53). At the supper Lazarus "was one of them that sat at the table with him," and much people came not for Jesus only but to see him also. "But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death; because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus" (John 12:1-11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Nothing he said is recorded, before or after. Scripture records that Christ loved him (John 11:3, 11:5, 11:36) and that his presence at the table caused many to believe (John 12:11).

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records not one word of his, and he is at the centre of the longest miracle narrative in the Gospels. The account is careful about the four days and the objection about the smell, which establishes that this was not a recovery. Of the three people Christ raised, he is the only one afterward marked for death by the authorities.

Significance

His raising is the last and greatest of the recorded miracles before the passion, and it is the immediate cause of the council's decision to kill Christ (John 11:47-53). John's statement that Jesus wept at his grave (John 11:35) is the shortest verse in the Bible.

Death / Outcome

He died once and was raised (John 11:14, 11:43-44). His second death is not recorded.

Scripture

John 11:1-45; John 12:1-11, 12:17
506

Annas

Father in law of Caiaphas; called high priest; Christ was brought to him first after the arrest.

Family

Father in law of Caiaphas, who was the high priest that year (John 18:13).

Chronology

"Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests" when the word of God came to John (Luke 3:2).

Life Synopsis

"And led him away to Annas first; for he was father in law to Caiaphas, which was the high priest that same year" (John 18:13).

"The high priest then asked Jesus of his disciples, and of his doctrine. Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing. Why askest thou me? ask them which heard me, what I have said unto them: behold, they know what I said." An officer struck him with the palm of his hand, and Christ answered, "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me? Now Annas had sent him bound unto Caiaphas the high priest" (John 18:19-24).

He is named again among the rulers before whom Peter and John stood (Acts 4:6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Examined a prisoner privately about his disciples and his doctrine, before any charge or witnesses, and allowed him to be struck: John 18:19-23.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one examination and no verdict on the man. What the passage records is Christ's answer, which objects to the procedure rather than to the question: he had taught openly, and the proper course was to ask those who heard him.

Significance

His hearing was the first of the six stages of the trial. That both he and Caiaphas are called high priest is a well-known feature of the Gospel record and reflects the standing he retained after the office had passed on.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 4:6.

Scripture

Luke 3:2; John 18:13-24; Acts 4:6
507

Malchus

The servant of the high priest whose right ear Peter cut off in the garden, and whom Christ healed.

Family

Servant of the high priest (John 18:10). A kinsman of his was among those who accused Peter in the palace (John 18:26).

Chronology

At the arrest in Gethsemane.

Life Synopsis

"Then Simon Peter having a sword drew it, and smote the high priest's servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant's name was Malchus" (John 18:10). John alone names him; Luke, a physician, alone records that it was the right ear and that Christ "touched his ear, and healed him" (Luke 22:50-51). Christ said, "Suffer ye thus far," and to Peter, "Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" (Matthew 26:52; John 18:11).

In the high priest's palace, "one of the servants of the high priest, being his kinsman whose ear Peter cut off, saith, Did not I see thee in the garden with him?" - which drew Peter's third denial (John 18:26-27).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He came with the band that arrested Christ, in the service of the high priest. Scripture records no act of his and no words.

Character Assessment

Scripture names him and records what was done to him and for him, and nothing that he did. He is the last person Christ healed before the crucifixion, and he was a member of the party that had come to arrest him.

Significance

His healing is the only recorded instance of Christ repairing an injury inflicted by one of his own disciples, and it took place while he was being arrested. His kinsman's question in the palace produced Peter's final denial.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Matthew 26:51-52; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50-51; John 18:10-11, 18:26
508

The young man who fled naked

Unnamed. A young man who followed Christ after the arrest with a linen cloth cast about his naked body, and fled when they laid hold on him.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the arrest in Gethsemane.

Life Synopsis

"And they all forsook him, and fled. And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body; and the young men laid hold on him: and he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked" (Mark 14:50-52). Mark alone records the incident, and gives no name.

What They Did Right

  • He followed after all the disciples had forsaken Christ and fled: Mark 14:50-51. Scripture records the fact without commendation.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • He too fled when they laid hold on him: Mark 14:52. Scripture records it without condemnation, in a passage where every follower did the same.

Character Assessment

Two verses, recorded only by Mark, with no name and no explanation of who he was or why he was there in a linen cloth. Many have suggested he was Mark himself; Scripture does not say so, and this reference does not assert it. What the incident records is that at the arrest even the one man still following ran.

Significance

The detail is one of several in Mark that read like eyewitness recollection, and its inclusion serves the chapter's point that they all forsook him and fled.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Mark 14:50-52
509

The penitent thief

Unnamed. One of two malefactors crucified with Christ, who rebuked the other, asked to be remembered, and was promised paradise that day.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the crucifixion.

Life Synopsis

Both malefactors at first reviled him (Matthew 27:44; Mark 15:32). Luke records what followed: "And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us."

"But the other answering rebuked him, saying, Dost not thou fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss. And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:39-43).

What They Did Right

  • Feared God and rebuked his fellow: Luke 23:40.
  • Admitted his own guilt and the justice of his sentence: Luke 23:41.
  • Declared Christ innocent - "this man hath done nothing amiss" - at the moment when almost everyone else was mocking: Luke 23:41.
  • Asked to be remembered when he came into his kingdom, addressing a dying man as a king: Luke 23:42.

What They Did Wrong

  • He was a malefactor, justly condemned, and by his own admission receiving the due reward of his deeds: Luke 23:41.
  • He had earlier joined in reviling Christ: Matthew 27:44; Mark 15:32.

Character Assessment

Scripture records both his railing and his repentance, hours apart, and records Christ's answer without qualification. He had no time to do anything afterward, which is what makes the account so often cited: the promise rested on nothing he could offer.

Significance

He is the only person to whom Christ personally promised paradise, and the promise was given the same day. His confession that Christ had done nothing amiss is one of several declarations of innocence in the passion narrative, and it comes from a man dying beside him.

Death / Outcome

Crucified with Christ (Luke 23:32-33, 23:39-43).

Scripture

Matthew 27:38, 27:44; Mark 15:27, 15:32; Luke 23:32-43
510

Alexander and Rufus

Sons of Simon of Cyrene, named by Mark as though known to his readers. Two individuals, recorded only together and only by relation.

Family

Sons of Simon of Cyrene, who bore the cross (Mark 15:21).

Chronology

At the crucifixion, by reference to their father.

Life Synopsis

"And they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to bear his cross" (Mark 15:21). Neither is mentioned again in the Gospels. A Rufus is greeted in Romans: "Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine" (Romans 16:13); whether he is the same man is not stated by Scripture.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records their names, their father, and nothing else. They are included because Mark names them for identification, which indicates they were known to the readers of his Gospel - the only reason to identify a man by his sons rather than his father.

Significance

Their being named is the strongest hint in the Gospels that Simon of Cyrene's family afterward belonged to the church.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Mark 15:21; compare Romans 16:13
511

Cleopas

One of two disciples walking to Emmaus on the resurrection day, to whom Christ expounded the Scriptures and who knew him in the breaking of bread.

Family

Not recorded. His companion is unnamed (Luke 24:18).

Chronology

The day of the resurrection.

Life Synopsis

Two of them went that same day to Emmaus, about threescore furlongs from Jerusalem, talking of all that had happened. "And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him."

Asked what they were discussing, "the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days?" They recounted the death of Jesus of Nazareth, "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel," and the women's report of the empty tomb.

"Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself."

They constrained him to stay, "And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight. And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" They rose the same hour and returned to Jerusalem (Luke 24:13-35).

What They Did Right

  • Constrained the stranger to stay with them at evening: Luke 24:29.
  • Returned to Jerusalem the same hour, seven miles at night, to tell the eleven: Luke 24:33.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was slow of heart to believe all that the prophets had spoken, and was told so: Luke 24:25.
  • Said, "We trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel" - in the past tense, on the day of the resurrection: Luke 24:21.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the rebuke and the remedy in the same passage. He is one of two named recipients of a private exposition by the risen Christ of everything in Moses and the prophets concerning himself - and Luke does not record its content, which readers have regretted ever since.

Significance

The Emmaus road is the fullest account of a resurrection appearance in the Gospels, and it establishes the pattern of understanding Christ from the whole of the Old Testament. Their words - did not our heart burn within us while he opened to us the scriptures - are among the most quoted in Luke.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 24:35.

Scripture

Luke 24:13-35

Acts of the Apostles

512

Matthias

Chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the twelve apostles.

Family

Not recorded. He had companied with the apostles all the time the Lord went in and out among them, from the baptism of John to the ascension (Acts 1:21-22).

Chronology

Between the ascension and Pentecost.

Life Synopsis

Peter stood up among about a hundred and twenty and set out the qualification: "Wherefore of these men which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection."

"And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And they prayed, and said, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen... And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles" (Acts 1:15-26).

What They Did Right

  • Had companied with the apostles from the baptism of John to the ascension: Acts 1:21-22.
  • Was numbered with the eleven apostles: Acts 1:26.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his qualification, his selection, and nothing further. He is never mentioned again. Nothing he said or did is recorded, which he shares with James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Canaanite.

Significance

His appointment restored the twelve before Pentecost. This is the last recorded use of casting lots in Scripture, and it occurs before the giving of the Holy Ghost.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 1:26.

Scripture

Acts 1:15-26
513

Ananias and Sapphira

A married couple who sold a possession, kept back part of the price, and lied about it; both fell down dead. Two individuals, judged separately and recorded together.

Family

Husband and wife (Acts 5:1).

Chronology

In the early days of the church at Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

"But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, and kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet."

"But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land? Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost" (Acts 5:1-5).

About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing. Peter asked whether they had sold the land for so much, and she said, "Yea, for so much." He answered, "How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out." She fell down straightway and died (Acts 5:7-10).

"And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things" (Acts 5:11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. They did sell a possession and did bring part of the price. Peter's words make clear the property and the money were theirs to do with as they chose; the offence was not the amount.

What They Did Wrong

  • Kept back part of the price while presenting it as the whole: Acts 5:2.
  • Lied to the Holy Ghost, and to God rather than to men: Acts 5:3-4.
  • Agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord: Acts 5:9.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Peter's questions establish precisely what the sin was not: they were under no obligation to sell, and under no obligation to give all of it. The sin was the pretence. Scripture records that great fear came on the whole church, and it is the first recorded judgment within the church.

Significance

The episode follows immediately after Barnabas selling his land and laying the money at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:36-37), and the contrast is the point. It establishes at the outset that the church was not to be a place where appearances could be traded on.

Death / Outcome

Both fell down and died, about three hours apart, and were carried out and buried (Acts 5:5-10).

Scripture

Acts 5:1-11
514

Gamaliel

A Pharisee and doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people; counselled the council to let the apostles alone; Paul's teacher.

Family

Not recorded. Paul was brought up at his feet (Acts 22:3).

Chronology

During the early church at Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

When the council was cut to the heart and took counsel to slay the apostles, "then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles forth a little space."

He cited two failed movements, Theudas and Judas of Galilee, both of which came to nothing when their leaders were slain. "And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God. And to him they agreed" (Acts 5:34-40).

Paul later cited him before the multitude: "I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers" (Acts 22:3).

What They Did Right

  • Restrained a council intent on killing the apostles, and was heeded: Acts 5:34-40.
  • Reasoned that a work of God could not be overthrown, and that opposing it risked fighting against God: Acts 5:38-39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His counsel was prudential rather than a confession of faith, and Scripture records no belief on his part. The apostles were beaten before being released (Acts 5:40).

Character Assessment

Scripture records one speech and its effect, and passes no verdict on the man. His argument is often quoted as wisdom and is sometimes read as evasion - it decides nothing about the truth of the claim and simply waits. What it did was save the apostles' lives.

Significance

He was Paul's teacher, which means the man who trained the persecutor also argued for restraint toward the persecuted. His principle - that what is of God cannot be overthrown - has been quoted ever since.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 22:3.

Scripture

Acts 5:33-40; Acts 22:3
515

Stephen

One of the seven chosen to serve tables; full of faith and power; the first martyr of the church.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Shortly after Pentecost, during the early church at Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

When the Grecians murmured that their widows were neglected, the twelve had seven men chosen "of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom." Stephen is named first: "a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 6:1-5).

"And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people." Certain of the synagogue disputed with him, "and they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake." They suborned men to accuse him of blasphemy against Moses and against God, and brought him before the council. "And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel" (Acts 6:8-15).

His defence is the longest speech in Acts: a survey of Israel's history from Abraham through Joseph, Moses, the tabernacle, and the temple, showing at each stage that God was not confined to a place and that Israel had resisted those he sent. He closed, "Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye. Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?" (Acts 7:2-53).

They were cut to the heart and gnashed on him with their teeth. "But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God." They stopped their ears, ran upon him with one accord, cast him out of the city, and stoned him, the witnesses laying their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul.

"And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep" (Acts 7:54-60).

What They Did Right

  • Chosen as a man of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom: Acts 6:3-5.
  • Full of faith and power, doing great wonders and miracles: Acts 6:8.
  • His opponents could not resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spoke: Acts 6:10.
  • Delivered the longest defence in Acts without retracting a word of it: Acts 7:2-53.
  • Prayed for those killing him: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge": Acts 7:60.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He was appointed to a practical task - serving tables - and is remembered for a sermon and a death. His last two sentences are deliberate echoes of Christ's from the cross: the commending of his spirit and the prayer for his killers.

Significance

The first martyr of the church. His death scattered the disciples and so spread the gospel beyond Jerusalem (Acts 8:1-4; Acts 11:19). Saul of Tarsus was present and consenting, and afterward referred to it twice (Acts 22:20; Acts 26:10). His speech is the fullest statement in the New Testament of the argument that God's dealings were never bound to the temple.

Death / Outcome

Stoned outside Jerusalem, praying for his killers (Acts 7:58-60). Devout men carried him to his burial and made great lamentation over him (Acts 8:2).

Scripture

Acts 6:1-8:2; Acts 11:19; Acts 22:20
516

Philip the evangelist

One of the seven; preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch; afterward called the evangelist, with four daughters who prophesied. Not to be confused with Philip the apostle.

Family

One of the seven (Acts 6:5; Acts 21:8). He had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy (Acts 21:9).

Chronology

From the choosing of the seven through Paul's last journey to Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

He was chosen as one of the seven, men of honest report full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom (Acts 6:5). When the church was scattered after Stephen's death, "Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them... and there was great joy in that city" (Acts 8:5-8).

The angel of the Lord then sent him south to the desert road to Gaza, and he found the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah in his chariot. The Spirit said, "Go near, and join thyself to this chariot." Philip ran, heard him reading, and asked, "Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me?" "Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus" (Acts 8:26-35). The eunuch was baptized, and the Spirit caught Philip away to Azotus, and he preached through all the cities till he came to Caesarea (Acts 8:38-40).

Years later Paul's company "entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven; and abode with him" (Acts 21:8).

What They Did Right

  • Chosen as a man of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom: Acts 6:3-5.
  • Preached Christ in Samaria, to a people the Jews would have nothing to do with: Acts 8:5.
  • Left a city-wide revival at the word of an angel to go to a desert road for one man: Acts 8:26-27.
  • Ran to the chariot when told, and began at the scripture the man was reading: Acts 8:30-35.
  • Preached through every city from Azotus to Caesarea: Acts 8:40.
  • Housed Paul and his company, and had four daughters who prophesied: Acts 21:8-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. Two of his recorded acts are notable for what they cost: he preached in Samaria, and he left a successful work to walk into a desert for one traveller. Both are recorded as obedience to a specific direction.

Significance

He took the gospel to Samaria, fulfilling the second stage of Christ's commission (Acts 1:8), and to the Ethiopian, who carried it further south than any recorded preaching of the period. His exposition of Isaiah 53 to the eunuch is the New Testament's clearest example of preaching Christ from the Old Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 21:8-9.

Scripture

Acts 6:5; Acts 8:5-40; Acts 21:8-9
517

Simon Magus

A sorcerer of Samaria who bewitched the people, professed belief, and offered money for the power to give the Holy Ghost.

Also called Simon the sorcerer

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During Philip's mission in Samaria.

Life Synopsis

"But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one: to whom they all gave heed, from the least to the greatest, saying, This man is the great power of God" (Acts 8:9-10).

"Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done" (Acts 8:13).

When Peter and John came and laid hands on the believers and they received the Holy Ghost, "and when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles' hands the Holy Ghost was given, he offered them money, saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost."

"But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money. Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God. Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee. For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity."

"Then answered Simon, and said, Pray ye to the Lord for me, that none of these things which ye have spoken come upon me" (Acts 8:18-24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records that he believed and was baptized and continued with Philip (Acts 8:13), and then records Peter's verdict that his heart was not right in the sight of God. The two statements stand together and the text does not reconcile them.

What They Did Wrong

  • Used sorcery and gave out that himself was some great one: Acts 8:9.
  • Offered money for the power to confer the Holy Ghost: Acts 8:18-19.
  • Peter's charge: his heart was not right in the sight of God, and he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity: Acts 8:21-23.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his profession of faith and his baptism, and then Peter's assessment of his heart, without harmonizing them. His final words are ambiguous: he asked Peter to pray that none of these things would come upon him, which is a request about consequences rather than about the sin. The text stops there and records nothing further of him.

Significance

His offer gave the English language the word simony. The episode establishes early that the gifts of God are not for sale and that baptism and profession are not by themselves proof of a right heart.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 8:24.

Scripture

Acts 8:9-24
518

The Ethiopian eunuch

Unnamed. A eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had charge of all her treasure; converted and baptized on the desert road to Gaza.

Family

Not recorded. A servant of Candace queen of the Ethiopians (Acts 8:27).

Chronology

Shortly after the scattering of the church from Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

He had come to Jerusalem to worship and was returning, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Esaias. Philip was sent to join the chariot and asked whether he understood what he read. "And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him."

The place he was reading was Isaiah 53: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth." He asked, "I pray thee, of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man? Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus."

As they went on their way they came to a certain water, and he said, "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they went down both into the water, and Philip baptized him. "And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing" (Acts 8:27-39).

What They Did Right

  • Travelled a great distance to Jerusalem to worship: Acts 8:27.
  • Was reading the prophet Isaiah on the journey home: Acts 8:28.
  • Admitted he could not understand without help, and invited a stranger up into his chariot: Acts 8:31.
  • Asked directly what hindered him from being baptized, and acted at once: Acts 8:36-38.
  • Went on his way rejoicing: Acts 8:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His question about Isaiah 53 is the one the whole passage exists to answer, and his readiness to be taught by a stranger who ran up beside his chariot is recorded without comment. The account ends with him going on rejoicing and Philip gone.

Significance

He is the first recorded convert from Africa, and one of the earliest Gentile converts in Acts. The passage he was reading, Isaiah 53, is the fullest Old Testament account of the suffering servant, and the episode is the New Testament's plainest example of Christ being preached from it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:39).

Scripture

Acts 8:26-39
519

Paul

A Pharisee of Tarsus who persecuted the church, was arrested by Christ on the road to Damascus, and became the apostle to the Gentiles; writer of thirteen epistles.

Also called Saul of Tarsus, Saul

Family

"Of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5). Born at Tarsus in Cilicia, brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). A Roman citizen by birth (Acts 22:28). His sister's son appears in Acts 23:16. He was unmarried at the time of writing 1 Corinthians 7:8.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was a young man at Stephen's death (Acts 7:58) and was still a prisoner at Rome at the close of Acts, dwelling two whole years in his own hired house (Acts 28:30).

Life Synopsis

He first appears consenting to Stephen's death: the witnesses laid their clothes at his feet, "and Saul was consenting unto his death." He then "made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison" (Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1-3). Breathing out threatenings and slaughter, he obtained letters to Damascus.

On the road a light shone from heaven and he fell to the earth and heard, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?... I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." He was led blind into the city and neither ate nor drank three days, until Ananias came and laid hands on him (Acts 9:1-19). "And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God" (Acts 9:20).

Barnabas brought him to the apostles when the disciples were afraid of him (Acts 9:26-27). From Antioch he was separated by the Holy Ghost with Barnabas, and made three missionary journeys: through Cyprus and Asia Minor, then Macedonia and Greece, then Ephesus and back. He preached at Antioch in Pisidia, was stoned and left for dead at Lystra, cast out a spirit at Philippi and was beaten and imprisoned and sang at midnight, reasoned at Athens on Mars' hill, spent eighteen months at Corinth and three years at Ephesus, and raised Eutychus at Troas (Acts 13:1-20:12).

At the council of Jerusalem he and Barnabas contended that the Gentiles need not be circumcised (Acts 15:1-29). He withstood Peter to the face at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14) and parted from Barnabas over John Mark (Acts 15:36-40).

Warned repeatedly, he went to Jerusalem: "I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 21:13). He was seized in the temple, defended himself before the multitude, the council, Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, appealed to Caesar, was shipwrecked on Malta, and reached Rome, where he dwelt two years in his own hired house, "preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him" (Acts 21:27-28:31).

His own summary of what it cost: five times forty stripes save one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three shipwrecks, a night and a day in the deep, perils of waters, robbers, his own countrymen, the heathen, the city, the wilderness, the sea, and false brethren; weariness, painfulness, watchings, hunger, thirst, fastings, cold and nakedness, "beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches" (2 Corinthians 11:23-28).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed the heavenly vision from the first hour: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?": Acts 9:6; Acts 26:19.
  • Preached Christ in the synagogues immediately after his conversion: Acts 9:20.
  • Endured beatings, stoning, imprisonment, and shipwreck without turning back: 2 Corinthians 11:23-28.
  • Sang praises at midnight in the stocks at Philippi, and stayed to save the jailer's life: Acts 16:25-28.
  • Worked with his own hands so as not to be chargeable to anyone: Acts 20:33-35; 1 Thessalonians 2:9.
  • Contended at Jerusalem that Gentiles should not be burdened with the law: Acts 15:1-12; Galatians 2:3-5.
  • Withstood Peter to the face when the truth of the gospel was at stake: Galatians 2:11-14.
  • Went up to Jerusalem knowing what awaited him: "neither count I my life dear unto myself": Acts 20:24; Acts 21:13.
  • Wrote thirteen epistles, and stated at the end, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith": 2 Timothy 4:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • Persecuted the church of God and wasted it, haling men and women to prison: Acts 8:3; Galatians 1:13.
  • Consented to Stephen's death and kept the witnesses' clothes: Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1; Acts 22:20.
  • Gave his voice against the saints when they were put to death, and compelled them to blaspheme: Acts 26:10-11.
  • Contended so sharply with Barnabas over John Mark that they parted asunder: Acts 15:39. Scripture records the contention without assigning fault to either, and Paul later asked for Mark as profitable to him for the ministry (2 Timothy 4:11).
  • Reviled the high priest at his trial, and withdrew the words when told who it was: Acts 23:3-5.
  • His own assessment: "I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God" (1 Corinthians 15:9), and "sinners; of whom I am chief" (1 Timothy 1:15).

Character Assessment

Scripture records his persecution of the church in full and never lets him forget it, chiefly because he never let himself forget it: he mentions it in Acts three times and in four epistles. Against that stands a body of work unmatched in the New Testament. He is the one figure who describes his own record from both sides - blameless as touching the law, and chief of sinners - and resolves it not by balance but by grace: "But by the grace of God I am what I am" (1 Corinthians 15:10). His failures after conversion are recorded too, and are not softened: a quarrel sharp enough to break a partnership, and an outburst in court he had to retract.

Significance

He carried the gospel from Jerusalem across Asia Minor and Greece to Rome, and his epistles set out the doctrine of justification by faith, the nature of the church, and the practical shape of Christian life. Thirteen New Testament books bear his name. His conversion is recorded three times in Acts, which is true of no other event in the book.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded in Scripture. His last written words anticipate it: "I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand" (2 Timothy 4:6).

Scripture

Acts 7:58-8:3; Acts 9:1-30; Acts 11:25-30; Acts 13:1-28:31; Romans 1:1-16:27; 1 Corinthians 15:8-10; 2 Corinthians 11:22-33; 2 Corinthians 12:1-10; Galatians 1:11-2:21; Philippians 3:4-14; 1 Timothy 1:12-16; 2 Timothy 4:6-8
520

Ananias of Damascus

A disciple at Damascus, devout according to the law and of good report; sent to restore Saul's sight and to baptize him. Not to be confused with Ananias the husband of Sapphira or Ananias the high priest.

Family

Not recorded. "A devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there" (Acts 22:12).

Chronology

Three days after Saul's conversion on the Damascus road.

Life Synopsis

The Lord said to him in a vision, "Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth."

"Then Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem: and here he hath authority from the chief priests to bind all that call on thy name. But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: for I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake."

"And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost. And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized" (Acts 9:10-18).

What They Did Right

  • Answered "Behold, I am here, Lord" when called: Acts 9:10.
  • Went to the man he had every reason to fear, and called him Brother Saul at the first word: Acts 9:17.
  • Described by Paul as a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews at Damascus: Acts 22:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • He objected before obeying, citing what he had heard of Saul: Acts 9:13-14. Scripture records the objection and God's answer, and no rebuke.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his fear plainly and his obedience immediately after. The detail that carries the account is his greeting: the first word spoken to the church's chief persecutor by a Christian after his conversion was Brother.

Significance

He restored Paul's sight, baptized him, and delivered the commission - that he was a chosen vessel to bear the name before Gentiles, kings, and Israel, and would be shown how much he must suffer. Paul recounted his part before the multitude at Jerusalem years later.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 22:12-16.

Scripture

Acts 9:10-19; Acts 22:12-16
521

Barnabas

A Levite of Cyprus named Joses, surnamed Barnabas by the apostles - the son of consolation; sold his land for the church, vouched for Paul, and parted from him over John Mark.

Also called Joses

Family

A Levite of the country of Cyprus (Acts 4:36); cousin of Marcus, that is John Mark (Colossians 4:10).

Chronology

From the early days at Jerusalem through the first missionary journey and after.

Life Synopsis

"And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus, having land, sold it, and brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet" (Acts 4:36-37).

When Saul came to Jerusalem after his conversion and the disciples were all afraid of him, "But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared unto them how he had seen the Lord in the way" (Acts 9:26-27).

Sent to Antioch to look into the preaching to the Greeks, "who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord: for he was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith: and much people was added unto the Lord. Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul" (Acts 11:22-26).

The Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them," and they went out on the first journey (Acts 13:2-3). At Lystra the people called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius, and they rent their clothes and ran in among them (Acts 14:12-14). At Jerusalem they declared what God had wrought among the Gentiles (Acts 15:12).

"And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work. And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus" (Acts 15:37-39).

Paul records that at Antioch even Barnabas was carried away with the dissimulation over eating with Gentiles (Galatians 2:13).

What They Did Right

  • Sold his land and laid the money at the apostles' feet: Acts 4:37.
  • Vouched for Saul when the whole church was afraid of him: Acts 9:27.
  • Was glad at the grace of God among the Greeks and exhorted them to cleave to the Lord: Acts 11:23.
  • Described by Scripture as "a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith": Acts 11:24.
  • Went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him into the work: Acts 11:25-26.
  • Hazarded his life for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, with Paul: Acts 15:26.
  • Took Mark when Paul would not, and Mark was afterward profitable for the ministry: Acts 15:39; 2 Timothy 4:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was carried away with the dissimulation at Antioch, withdrawing from the Gentiles: Galatians 2:13.
  • Contended so sharply with Paul over Mark that they parted asunder: Acts 15:39. Scripture assigns fault to neither man.

Character Assessment

Scripture calls him a good man, full of the Holy Ghost and of faith - a description given to almost no one else. Twice he took a risk on a man nobody else would have: Saul, whom the church feared, and Mark, who had already deserted. Both were vindicated, and Paul himself later asked for Mark. His one recorded failure is being carried away by Peter's example at Antioch, which the text records without excusing.

Significance

He brought Paul into the church and then into the work, which makes him indirectly responsible for a great part of the New Testament. He was the senior partner at first - "Barnabas and Saul" - and the order reverses to "Paul and Barnabas" as the journey proceeds, which Acts records without comment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Corinthians 9:6.

Scripture

Acts 4:36-37; Acts 9:26-27; Acts 11:19-30; Acts 12:25; Acts 13:1-15:39; 1 Corinthians 9:6; Galatians 2:1-13; Colossians 4:10
522

Dorcas

A disciple at Joppa, full of good works and almsdeeds, who died and was raised by Peter.

Also called Tabitha

Family

Not recorded. The widows stood about her weeping (Acts 9:39).

Chronology

During Peter's ministry in the coastal cities.

Life Synopsis

"Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. And it came to pass in those days, that she was sick, and died: whom when they had washed, they laid her in an upper chamber."

The disciples sent to Peter at Lydda. "Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber: and all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them."

"But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed; and turning him to the body said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up. And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive. And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord" (Acts 9:36-42).

What They Did Right

  • Full of good works and almsdeeds which she did: Acts 9:36.
  • Made coats and garments for the widows, who brought them out to show Peter: Acts 9:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her, and describes her work in a way that is unusually concrete: not a reputation but garments, held up by the women who were wearing them. Nothing she said is recorded.

Significance

Her raising is one of two recorded resurrections in Acts, and it was known throughout all Joppa so that many believed. Peter's words - Tabitha, arise - closely echo Christ's to Jairus's daughter, at which Peter had been present.

Death / Outcome

She died and was raised (Acts 9:37, 9:40). Her second death is not recorded.

Scripture

Acts 9:36-42
523

Cornelius

A centurion of the Italian band at Caesarea; a devout man who feared God, to whom Peter was sent; the first Gentile household received into the church.

Family

"A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway" (Acts 10:2). He had kinsmen and near friends (Acts 10:24).

Chronology

During Peter's ministry at Joppa and Caesarea.

Life Synopsis

"There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band, a devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway."

He saw in a vision about the ninth hour an angel of God saying, "Cornelius... Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God. And now send men to Joppa, and call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter" (Acts 10:1-6). He called two household servants and a devout soldier and sent them.

While they came, Peter saw the vision of the sheet let down with all manner of beasts, and the voice, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" (Acts 10:9-16). He went with the men.

"And Cornelius waited for them, and had called together his kinsmen and near friends." He fell down at Peter's feet and worshipped him, and Peter took him up saying, "Stand up; I myself also am a man." He explained the vision, and said, "Now therefore are we all here present before God, to hear all things that are commanded thee of God" (Acts 10:24-33).

Peter began, "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him." While he yet spake, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word, and they of the circumcision were astonished, and they were baptized (Acts 10:34-48).

What They Did Right

  • A devout man who feared God with all his house, gave much alms, and prayed always: Acts 10:2.
  • Obeyed the vision at once and sent for a man he had never met: Acts 10:7-8.
  • Gathered his kinsmen and near friends to hear, rather than keeping it to himself: Acts 10:24.
  • Said, "Now therefore are we all here present before God, to hear all things that are commanded thee of God": Acts 10:33.

What They Did Wrong

  • Fell down at Peter's feet and worshipped him, and was corrected: Acts 10:25-26.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes him in terms it uses of few people, and he was a Roman officer outside the covenant. His one recorded fault was excessive reverence toward the man God sent him, corrected in a sentence. His sentence in Acts 10:33 is one of the best descriptions in Scripture of how to hear preaching.

Significance

His household was the first Gentile company received into the church without becoming Jews, and the episode settled the question at Jerusalem (Acts 11:1-18) and was cited again at the council (Acts 15:7-9). Peter's conclusion - that God is no respecter of persons - is the doctrinal turning point of Acts.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 10:48.

Scripture

Acts 10:1-48; Acts 11:1-18; Acts 15:7-9
524

Herod Agrippa I

King who vexed the church, killed James the brother of John, imprisoned Peter, and was struck by an angel for accepting the honour due to God.

Also called Herod the king

Family

Of the Herod family. Father of Agrippa II, Bernice, and Drusilla, who appear later in Acts.

Chronology

About the time of the famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28; Acts 12:1).

Life Synopsis

"Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword. And because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also" (Acts 12:1-3). He put him in prison with four quaternions of soldiers, intending to bring him out after Easter, and Peter was delivered by an angel while prayer was made without ceasing by the church (Acts 12:4-17). He examined the keepers and commanded that they be put to death (Acts 12:19).

"And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them. And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost. But the word of God grew and multiplied" (Acts 12:21-24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Vexed the church and killed James the brother of John with the sword: Acts 12:1-2.
  • Proceeded to take Peter because it pleased the Jews: Acts 12:3.
  • Had the guards put to death: Acts 12:19.
  • Received the acclamation that his was the voice of a god and gave not God the glory: Acts 12:22-23.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture states his motive for the second arrest plainly - because it pleased the Jews - and states the cause of his death in one clause: because he gave not God the glory. The chapter sets his end against the church's growth in a single sentence: he was eaten of worms and gave up the ghost, but the word of God grew and multiplied.

Significance

He killed the first apostle to die and imprisoned the leading one, and Acts 12 is the chapter in which the church's prayer and God's judgment are set side by side. His son Agrippa II and daughters Bernice and Drusilla appear in Paul's later trials.

Death / Outcome

Smitten by the angel of the Lord and eaten of worms (Acts 12:23).

Scripture

Acts 12:1-24
525

Rhoda

A damsel in the house of Mary the mother of John Mark who recognised Peter's voice at the gate and was not believed.

Family

Not recorded. A servant in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12-13).

Chronology

The night of Peter's deliverance from prison.

Life Synopsis

Many were gathered together praying at the house of Mary. "And as Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda. And when she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate."

"And they said unto her, Thou art mad. But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Then said they, It is his angel. But Peter continued knocking: and when they had opened the door, and saw him, they were astonished" (Acts 12:12-16).

What They Did Right

  • Recognised Peter's voice and reported it truthfully: Acts 12:14.
  • Constantly affirmed it when told she was mad: Acts 12:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • In her gladness she left Peter standing outside the gate: Acts 12:14. Scripture records it as a detail rather than a fault.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a servant girl who was right when a whole prayer meeting was wrong, and who held her ground when they told her she was mad. The gathering had been praying without ceasing for exactly what she was reporting.

Significance

The scene is Acts' quiet comment on the prayer it has just described: the church prayed earnestly for Peter's release and did not believe the girl who told them it had happened.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Acts 12:12-16
526

John Mark

Son of Mary of Jerusalem; went out with Barnabas and Saul and turned back; the occasion of their parting, and afterward called profitable by Paul.

Also called Marcus, Mark

Family

Son of Mary, in whose house the church prayed (Acts 12:12); cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10). Peter calls him "Marcus my son" (1 Peter 5:13).

Chronology

From the early Jerusalem church through Paul's imprisonments.

Life Synopsis

The church was gathered praying in his mother's house on the night of Peter's release (Acts 12:12). Barnabas and Saul took him with them from Jerusalem (Acts 12:25), and he was their minister on the first journey (Acts 13:5).

"And John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). Scripture gives no reason.

When Paul proposed revisiting the churches, "Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work. And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus" (Acts 15:37-39).

Years later Paul writes from prison, "Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas, (touching whom ye received commandments: if he come unto you, receive him)" (Colossians 4:10), and names him among his fellowlabourers (Philemon 1:24). His last recorded mention of him is a request: "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter writes of "Marcus my son" (1 Peter 5:13).

What They Did Right

  • Served as minister to Barnabas and Saul on the first journey: Acts 13:5.
  • Was afterward reckoned by Paul among his fellowlabourers and as profitable for the ministry: Philemon 1:24; 2 Timothy 4:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Departed from Paul and Barnabas at Pamphylia and returned to Jerusalem: Acts 13:13. Scripture gives no reason and no condemnation, but Paul's later refusal to take him is stated in exactly those terms: he "went not with them to the work" (Acts 15:38).

Character Assessment

Scripture records one failure and a full recovery, with the recovery attested by the man who had refused him. Paul's final surviving letter asks for him by name as profitable for the ministry - the same man he would not take on a journey years earlier. Barnabas's judgment was vindicated, and the text never says who was right about the original quarrel.

Significance

He is traditionally the writer of the Gospel of Mark; Scripture does not state this. His restoration is the New Testament's clearest case of a man who failed early in the work and was afterward useful in it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Peter 5:13.

Scripture

Acts 12:12, 12:25; Acts 13:5, 13:13; Acts 15:37-39; Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 1:24; 1 Peter 5:13
527

Elymas

A Jewish sorcerer and false prophet at Paphos who withstood Paul and Barnabas before the deputy, and was struck blind.

Also called Barjesus

Family

Called Barjesus (Acts 13:6); Elymas is given as the interpretation of his name (Acts 13:8).

Chronology

On the first missionary journey, at Paphos in Cyprus.

Life Synopsis
