"And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus: which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith."

"Then Saul, (who also is called Paul,) filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him, and said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand" (Acts 13:6-11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Practised sorcery and was a false prophet: Acts 13:6.
  • Withstood Paul and Barnabas, seeking to turn the deputy from the faith: Acts 13:8.
  • Paul's charge: full of all subtilty and all mischief, a child of the devil, an enemy of all righteousness, perverting the right ways of the Lord: Acts 13:10.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, in the sharpest language Paul uses against any individual in Acts. The judgment was temporary - blind for a season - and its form matched Paul's own conversion, which he had experienced on a road not many years before.

Significance

The episode is where Acts first calls him Paul rather than Saul, and where he takes the lead from Barnabas. The deputy believed, "being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord" (Acts 13:12).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 13:11.

Scripture

Acts 13:6-12
528

Sergius Paulus

Deputy of Cyprus, a prudent man, who sent for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God and believed.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

On the first missionary journey, at Paphos.

Life Synopsis

"The deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God" (Acts 13:7). Elymas withstood them and sought to turn him from the faith, and was struck blind.

"Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord" (Acts 13:12).

What They Did Right

  • Called for Barnabas and Saul and desired to hear the word of God: Acts 13:7.
  • Believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord: Acts 13:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture calls him a prudent man and records that he sought out the preaching himself. The text is careful about what astonished him: not the blinding of the sorcerer but the doctrine of the Lord.

Significance

He is the first recorded convert of the first missionary journey and the first Roman official recorded as believing.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 13:12.

Scripture

Acts 13:7-12
529

Silas

A chief man among the brethren at Jerusalem and a prophet; Paul's companion on the second journey; imprisoned with him at Philippi.

Also called Silvanus

Family

Not recorded. A Roman citizen, by implication of Acts 16:37.

Chronology

From the council of Jerusalem through the second missionary journey.

Life Synopsis

He was chosen with Judas Barsabas to carry the letter from the council to Antioch, "chief men among the brethren." "And Judas and Silas, being prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them" (Acts 15:22-32).

When Paul and Barnabas parted, "Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God" (Acts 15:40).

At Philippi they were seized, their clothes rent off, beaten with many stripes, and thrust into the inner prison. "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them" (Acts 16:22-25). In the morning, when the magistrates sent to let them go quietly, Paul objected that they had been beaten openly uncondemned, being Romans, and required the magistrates to come themselves (Acts 16:35-39).

He was left at Berea with Timothy and rejoined Paul at Corinth (Acts 17:14; Acts 18:5). Paul names him in the salutations of both Thessalonian letters (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1), and Peter writes, "By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly" (1 Peter 5:12).

What They Did Right

  • Chosen as a chief man among the brethren and sent with the council's letter: Acts 15:22.
  • Exhorted and confirmed the brethren as a prophet: Acts 15:32.
  • Sang praises with Paul at midnight after being beaten and put in the stocks: Acts 16:25.
  • Called by Peter "a faithful brother": 1 Peter 5:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He served both Paul and Peter, carried the council's decision to the churches, and is named in the greeting of two epistles. His most memorable moment is a duet in a prison at midnight.

Significance

He replaced Barnabas as Paul's companion at the start of the second journey, on which the gospel first entered Europe. His name appears in the openings of 1 and 2 Thessalonians and in the close of 1 Peter.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Peter 5:12.

Scripture

Acts 15:22-40; Acts 16:19-40; Acts 17:1-15; Acts 18:5; 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12
530

Timothy

A disciple of Lystra, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father; Paul's most constant companion, called his own son in the faith.

Also called Timotheus

Family

Son of a Jewish woman who believed and of a Greek father (Acts 16:1). His mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois, both of unfeigned faith (2 Timothy 1:5). From a child he had known the holy scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15).

Chronology

Joined Paul on the second journey and was with him to the end.

Life Synopsis

"Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus... which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium. Him would Paul have to go forth with him" (Acts 16:1-3).

He accompanied Paul through Macedonia and Greece, was sent back to Thessalonica to establish and comfort the church (1 Thessalonians 3:2), was sent to Corinth (1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Corinthians 16:10), and to Philippi. Paul's commendation of him is the warmest he gives anyone: "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state. For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's. But ye know the proof of him, that, as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel" (Philippians 2:19-22).

He is named with Paul in the opening of six epistles. Two letters are addressed to him, in which Paul charges him: "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity" (1 Timothy 4:12), and "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season" (2 Timothy 4:2).

Paul's last surviving letter is to him, asking him to come before winter and to bring the cloak and the books (2 Timothy 4:9-13, 4:21).

What They Did Right

  • Was well reported of by the brethren at Lystra and Iconium before Paul took him: Acts 16:2.
  • Served with Paul as a son with the father in the gospel: Philippians 2:22.
  • Paul's testimony: no man likeminded, who would naturally care for the churches' state: Philippians 2:20.
  • Knew the holy scriptures from a child, and held the unfeigned faith of his mother and grandmother: 2 Timothy 1:5; 2 Timothy 3:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Paul's charges to him suggest a man who needed encouragement - "Let no man despise thy youth" (1 Timothy 4:12), "stir up the gift of God which is in thee" (2 Timothy 1:6), and "God hath not given us the spirit of fear" (2 Timothy 1:7) - but Scripture records no fault of his.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives him the highest personal commendation Paul offers anyone. The letters to him are pastoral in tone throughout, urging courage rather than correcting error, and Paul's last recorded request is that he come.

Significance

Two New Testament epistles are addressed to him, and he is named in the opening of six others. He is the clearest New Testament example of a younger man trained in the work by an older one, and of faith passed down through a household.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Hebrews 13:23 mentions that "our brother Timothy is set at liberty."

Scripture

Acts 16:1-3; Acts 17:14-15; Acts 18:5; Acts 19:22; Acts 20:4; Romans 16:21; 1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Corinthians 16:10-11; 2 Corinthians 1:1, 1:19; Philippians 1:1; Philippians 2:19-23; Colossians 1:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Thessalonians 3:2-6; 2 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Timothy 1:1-2, 4:12; 2 Timothy 1:1-8, 3:14-15, 4:1-21; Philemon 1:1; Hebrews 13:23
531

Lydia

A seller of purple of the city of Thyatira, worshipping God at Philippi; the first recorded convert in Europe.

Family

Not recorded. She had a household, which was baptized with her (Acts 16:15).

Chronology

On the second missionary journey, at Philippi.

Life Synopsis

On the sabbath they went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made, and spoke to the women who resorted there.

"And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us" (Acts 16:13-15).

After Paul and Silas were released from prison, "they went out of the prison, and entered into the house of Lydia: and when they had seen the brethren, they comforted them, and departed" (Acts 16:40).

What They Did Right

  • Worshipped God and resorted to the place of prayer: Acts 16:13-14.
  • Attended to the things spoken, her heart having been opened by the Lord: Acts 16:14.
  • Was baptized with her household and constrained the preachers to lodge with her: Acts 16:15.
  • Kept her house open to them after their imprisonment, when association was dangerous: Acts 16:40.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. The account is careful about the order: she heard, and the Lord opened her heart, and she attended. Her hospitality is recorded twice, and the second time is after Paul and Silas had been publicly beaten and jailed.

Significance

She is the first recorded convert on European soil, and her house became the meeting place of the church at Philippi - the congregation to which Paul later wrote the warmest of his letters.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 16:40.

Scripture

Acts 16:13-15, 16:40
532

The Philippian jailer

Unnamed. The keeper of the prison at Philippi, who was about to kill himself when the doors opened, and was converted with all his house that night.

Family

He had a household, all of whom believed and were baptized (Acts 16:33-34).

Chronology

On the second missionary journey, at Philippi.

Life Synopsis

Having received the charge to keep them safely, "he thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks. And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them."

"And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed. And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled. But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here."

"Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas, and brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house."

"And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway. And when he had brought them into his house, he set meat before them, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house" (Acts 16:24-34).

What They Did Right

  • Asked the right question, and asked it at once: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?": Acts 16:30.
  • Washed their stripes the same hour of the night - the stripes he had been responsible for: Acts 16:33.
  • Was baptized with all his house straightway, and set meat before them, and rejoiced: Acts 16:33-34.

What They Did Wrong

  • He thrust them into the inner prison and made their feet fast in the stocks, having received the charge: Acts 16:24. Scripture records the severity without a separate condemnation; he was carrying out an order.
  • He drew his sword to kill himself: Acts 16:27. The text records the despair and Paul's intervention without comment.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a man doing his job harshly at ten in the evening and washing his prisoners' wounds by midnight. His question is the plainest in the New Testament and receives the plainest answer. The account gives no gradual process: the same hour of the night.

Significance

His conversion, with Lydia's and the slave girl's deliverance, makes the church at Philippi a company drawn from three entirely different levels of society. His question and the answer to it are among the most quoted verses in Acts.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 16:34.

Scripture

Acts 16:23-36
533

Aquila and Priscilla

A married couple, tentmakers, expelled from Rome by Claudius; Paul's fellowlabourers, who took Apollos aside and expounded the way of God more perfectly. Two individuals, recorded together throughout.

Also called Prisca

Family

Aquila was a Jew born in Pontus; Priscilla was his wife (Acts 18:2). She is called Prisca in 2 Timothy 4:19.

Chronology

From Paul's stay at Corinth on the second journey onward.

Life Synopsis

"And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them. And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers" (Acts 18:2-3).

They sailed with Paul to Ephesus and remained there (Acts 18:18-19). "And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus... knowing only the baptism of John. And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly" (Acts 18:24-26).

Paul salutes them in three epistles: "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus: who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles. Likewise greet the church that is in their house" (Romans 16:3-5). Also 1 Corinthians 16:19 and 2 Timothy 4:19.

What They Did Right

  • Took Paul in and worked alongside him at their common trade: Acts 18:2-3.
  • Took Apollos aside privately and expounded the way of God more perfectly, rather than correcting him publicly: Acts 18:26.
  • Laid down their own necks for Paul's life, so that all the churches of the Gentiles gave thanks: Romans 16:4.
  • Hosted a church in their house: Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them and names them together every time. Their handling of Apollos is the detail most often drawn: an eloquent and learned preacher was corrected by two tentmakers, in private, and became more useful for it. Priscilla is named first in four of the six mentions, which the text does not explain.

Significance

They corrected the teaching of Apollos, hosted churches in two cities, and risked their lives for Paul. They are the New Testament's fullest picture of a married couple working together in the ministry.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:19.

Scripture

Acts 18:1-3, 18:18-26; Romans 16:3-5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19
534

Apollos

A Jew of Alexandria, eloquent and mighty in the scriptures, who knew only the baptism of John until Aquila and Priscilla instructed him; afterward a powerful preacher at Corinth.

Family

Born at Alexandria (Acts 18:24).

Chronology

During Paul's third journey, at Ephesus and Corinth.

Life Synopsis

"And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus. This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John. And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly."

"And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace: for he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ" (Acts 18:24-28).

At Corinth his name became a party slogan: "every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos." Paul answered, "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed?... I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Corinthians 1:12; 1 Corinthians 3:4-6). Paul later says he greatly desired him to come to Corinth, and that his will was not at all to come at this time (1 Corinthians 16:12).

What They Did Right

  • Eloquent, mighty in the scriptures, fervent in the spirit, teaching diligently: Acts 18:24-25.
  • Received correction from two tentmakers although he was a learned man: Acts 18:26.
  • Helped much those who had believed, and mightily convinced the Jews publicly from the scriptures: Acts 18:27-28.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He knew only the baptism of John, which Scripture presents as incomplete knowledge rather than fault, and he accepted instruction at once: Acts 18:25-26. The party spirit at Corinth is charged to the Corinthians and never to him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. What it records is a gifted man being taught by people with far less standing, and being better for it. When his name was used to divide a church, Paul defended him rather than distancing himself, and Paul afterward urged him to go back to the church that had made a faction of his name.

Significance

With Paul he is the New Testament's illustration of the relation between workers: one plants, another waters, God gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6-8). His instruction by Aquila and Priscilla is Scripture's clearest example of correcting a teacher privately and constructively.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Titus 3:13.

Scripture

Acts 18:24-28; Acts 19:1; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 1 Corinthians 3:4-8, 3:22; 1 Corinthians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 16:12; Titus 3:13
535

Demetrius the silversmith

A silversmith of Ephesus who made silver shrines for Diana and raised the riot against Paul.

Family

Not recorded. He had craftsmen and workmen of like occupation (Acts 19:24-25).

Chronology

At the end of Paul's three years at Ephesus.

Life Synopsis

"For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen; whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth. Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands: so that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised."

"And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians. And the whole city was filled with confusion... Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together" (Acts 19:24-32). The townclerk quieted them and dismissed the assembly.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Raised a riot against Paul to protect his trade: Acts 19:24-29. His own speech names the motive first - by this craft we have our wealth - and the honour of the goddess second.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative, and Scripture lets his own speech convict him: he put the money before the religion in the order of his argument, and the crowd took up the religion. Acts adds the observation that most of the rioters did not know why they had come together.

Significance

The riot is the fullest account in Acts of opposition arising from economic interest rather than theology, and it demonstrates the effect of Paul's three years at Ephesus: the trade in idols had measurably declined.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 19:38.

Scripture

Acts 19:23-41
536

Eutychus

A young man of Troas who fell asleep during Paul's long preaching, fell from the third loft, was taken up dead, and was restored.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

On Paul's last journey to Jerusalem, at Troas.

Life Synopsis

"And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight. And there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together."

"And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead."

"And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him. When he therefore was come up again, and had broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even till break of day, so he departed. And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted" (Acts 20:7-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He fell asleep during a sermon that ran past midnight, sitting in a window. Scripture records the circumstances - many lights in the room, a long address, a deep sleep - without a word of blame.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the accident with unusual detail and no reproach for anyone, including the preacher who continued afterward until daybreak. It is the second recorded resurrection in Acts.

Significance

The account preserves the earliest description of a Christian gathering on the first day of the week for the breaking of bread and preaching (Acts 20:7).

Death / Outcome

He was taken up dead and restored (Acts 20:9-12).

Scripture

Acts 20:7-12
537

Agabus

A prophet from Judaea who foretold the famine under Claudius and bound his own hands and feet with Paul's girdle to foretell his arrest.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At Antioch before the famine, and at Caesarea before Paul's last visit to Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

"And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch. And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar." The disciples at Antioch determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea (Acts 11:27-30).

Years later, at the house of Philip the evangelist in Caesarea, "there came down from Judaea a certain prophet, named Agabus. And when he was come unto us, he took Paul's girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."

The company besought Paul not to go up. "Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done" (Acts 21:10-14).

What They Did Right

  • Foretold the famine, which came to pass, and so occasioned the relief sent from Antioch to Judaea: Acts 11:28-30.
  • Delivered the warning about Paul's arrest by a sign as the prophets had done, and it was fulfilled: Acts 21:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records two prophecies and both fulfilments, and nothing against him. His second message is notable for what it did not say: he foretold what would happen and did not tell Paul not to go. The company drew that conclusion themselves, and Paul refused it.

Significance

His famine prophecy produced the first recorded relief collection between churches. His sign at Caesarea is the last Old Testament-style enacted prophecy in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 21:11.

Scripture

Acts 11:27-30; Acts 21:10-14
538

Claudius Lysias

The chief captain of the band at Jerusalem who rescued Paul from the mob, learned he was a Roman, and sent him to Felix under guard.

Family

Not recorded. He obtained his Roman freedom with a great sum (Acts 22:28).

Chronology

At Paul's arrest in Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

When all the city was in an uproar and they went about to kill Paul, "the chief captain of the band" took soldiers and centurions and ran down, and the beating stopped. He commanded him to be bound with two chains, and, unable to learn the truth for the tumult, had him carried into the castle. Paul asked leave to speak to the people (Acts 21:31-40).

When the crowd erupted again he commanded that Paul be examined by scourging. "And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?" The chief captain came and asked, "Tell me, art thou a Roman? He said, Yea. And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born." Those who should have examined him departed, "and the chief captain also was afraid, after he knew that he was a Roman, and because he had bound him" (Acts 22:24-29).

When Paul's sister's son reported the ambush of more than forty men, he took the young man aside privately, heard him, charged him to tell no one, and sent Paul to Caesarea by night with two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen, with a letter to Felix (Acts 23:16-30).

What They Did Right

  • Rescued Paul from a mob that was beating him to death: Acts 21:31-32.
  • Ceased from the examination when he learned Paul was a Roman: Acts 22:29.
  • Took the young man's report seriously, questioned him privately, and protected his source: Acts 23:18-22.
  • Provided a heavy escort to get Paul out of Jerusalem alive: Acts 23:23-24.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ordered a man scourged for examination before any charge was established: Acts 22:24.
  • His letter to Felix gave a flattering account of his own conduct, claiming he had rescued Paul "having understood that he was a Roman" - which was not the order of events: Acts 23:27 compared with Acts 22:25-29.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a capable officer who saved Paul's life more than once and shaded his own report. The discrepancy between his letter and the narrative is left for the reader to notice; Acts does not point it out.

Significance

His interventions kept Paul alive through the most dangerous period of his imprisonment and moved the case to Caesarea, where the hearings before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa took place.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 24:22.

Scripture

Acts 21:31-40; Acts 22:24-30; Acts 23:10-35; Acts 24:7, 24:22
539

Paul's sister's son

Unnamed. A young man, nephew of Paul, who overheard the plot to ambush him and reported it to the chief captain.

Family

Son of Paul's sister (Acts 23:16).

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonment at Jerusalem.

Life Synopsis

More than forty men had bound themselves under a curse that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul, and had arranged for the council to request that he be brought down to them.

"And when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul. Then Paul called one of the centurions unto him, and said, Bring this young man unto the chief captain: for he hath a certain thing to tell him."

The chief captain "took him by the hand, and went with him aside privately, and asked him, What is that thou hast to tell me?" He reported the plot in full and was charged to tell no man that he had shown these things (Acts 23:12-22).

What They Did Right

  • Reported the ambush at real risk to himself: Acts 23:16-21.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one action and no name. He is the only relative of Paul's who appears in the narrative, and his intervention is what kept Paul alive to reach Rome.

Significance

His warning produced the night transfer to Caesarea and everything that followed - the hearings, the appeal to Caesar, and the voyage to Rome.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 23:22.

Scripture

Acts 23:12-22
540

Felix

Governor of Judaea before whom Paul was tried; heard him about the faith in Christ, trembled, and left him bound two years hoping for a bribe.

Family

Married to Drusilla, a Jewess (Acts 24:24).

Chronology

Paul was left bound before him two years, until Festus succeeded him (Acts 24:27).

Life Synopsis

Paul was sent to him at Caesarea. Tertullus accused him, and Paul answered. "And when Felix heard these things, having more perfect knowledge of that way, he deferred them, and said, When Lysias the chief captain shall come down, I will know the uttermost of your matter" (Acts 24:22). He commanded a centurion to keep Paul and to let him have liberty, and to forbid none of his acquaintance to minister to him.

"And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ. And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee."

"He hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him: wherefore he sent for him the oftener, and communed with him. But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix' room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound" (Acts 24:24-27).

What They Did Right

  • Gave Paul liberty and allowed his acquaintance to minister to him: Acts 24:23.
  • Sent for him and heard him concerning the faith in Christ: Acts 24:24.

What They Did Wrong

  • Deferred a decision he was competent to make: Acts 24:22, 24:25.
  • Hoped for a bribe, and sent for Paul the oftener on that account: Acts 24:26.
  • Left Paul bound for two years to please the Jews: Acts 24:27.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a man who trembled at the preaching and did nothing about it. The three subjects Paul reasoned of - righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come - were pointed at a governor who took bribes and had taken another man's wife, and the text records that he trembled and postponed. His convenient season is not recorded as ever coming.

Significance

His two-year delay kept Paul in Caesarea and produced the hearings before Festus and Agrippa. His trembling and postponement is the New Testament's clearest picture of conviction without decision.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 25:14.

Scripture

Acts 23:24-26; Acts 24:1-27; Acts 25:14
541

Drusilla

A Jewess, wife of Felix; present when Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come.

Family

A Jewess; wife of Felix (Acts 24:24). Daughter of Herod Agrippa I; sister of Agrippa II and Bernice.

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonment at Caesarea.

Life Synopsis

"And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ. And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled" (Acts 24:24-25). Nothing further is recorded of her.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records only that she was a Jewess, that she was the wife of Felix, and that she was present at the hearing. It records no words or acts of hers.

Character Assessment

Scripture names her twice in one verse and records nothing she said or did. She is included because her presence is specified and because the subject Paul chose - righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come - was addressed to a room that contained her as well as her husband.

Significance

She is one of three of Herod Agrippa I's children who appear in Paul's trials, with Agrippa II and Bernice.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Acts 24:24-25
542

Festus

Successor to Felix as governor; heard Paul, received his appeal to Caesar, and told him he was mad.

Also called Porcius Festus

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

He came into Felix's room after Paul had been bound two years (Acts 24:27).

Life Synopsis

Within three days of arriving he went up to Jerusalem, where the chief priests asked that Paul be sent there, laying wait to kill him in the way. He answered that Paul should be kept at Caesarea and that they should come down and accuse him (Acts 25:1-6).

At the hearing the Jews laid many grievous complaints which they could not prove. Festus, "willing to do the Jews a pleasure," asked Paul whether he would go up to Jerusalem to be judged. Paul answered, "I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged... I appeal unto Caesar." Festus conferred with the council and answered, "Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go" (Acts 25:7-12).

He explained the case to Agrippa, admitting the accusers had brought no charge such as he supposed, "but had certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive" (Acts 25:19). He also admitted he had nothing certain to write to his lord (Acts 25:26-27).

As Paul spoke before Agrippa, "Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad. But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness" (Acts 26:24-25). Afterward he agreed with Agrippa that Paul might have been set at liberty had he not appealed (Acts 26:31-32).

What They Did Right

  • Refused to send Paul to Jerusalem where an ambush was laid, insisting on a proper hearing at Caesarea: Acts 25:3-6, 25:16.
  • Acknowledged that the charges could not be proved and that he had nothing certain to write: Acts 25:18-19, 25:26-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was willing to do the Jews a pleasure and asked Paul to go to Jerusalem, which forced the appeal to Caesar: Acts 25:9.
  • Interrupted Paul's defence by declaring him mad: Acts 26:24.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a competent official who understood the legal position and could not understand the case. His summary of the whole dispute - certain questions of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive - is unintentionally the most accurate statement of the matter anyone makes in Acts.

Significance

His question to Paul produced the appeal to Caesar, which took the gospel to Rome, and his hearing before Agrippa produced Paul's fullest recorded defence.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 26:32.

Scripture

Acts 24:27; Acts 25:1-27; Acts 26:24-32
543

Herod Agrippa II

King before whom Paul made his defence at Caesarea; said he was almost persuaded to be a Christian.

Also called King Agrippa

Family

Son of Herod Agrippa I; brother of Bernice and Drusilla.

Chronology

Shortly after Festus became governor.

Life Synopsis

He came with Bernice to salute Festus, who laid Paul's case before him. "Then Agrippa said unto Festus, I would also hear the man myself. To morrow, said he, thou shalt hear him" (Acts 25:22).

They entered with great pomp, and Paul made his defence, recounting his upbringing, his persecution of the church, his conversion, and his commission, and ending, "Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come" (Acts 26:1-23).

When Festus interrupted, Paul turned to the king: "For the king knoweth of these things, before whom also I speak freely: for I am persuaded that none of these things are hidden from him; for this thing was not done in a corner. King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest."

"Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds" (Acts 26:26-29).

Rising up, he said to Festus, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds. Then said Agrippa unto Festus, This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar" (Acts 26:31-32).

What They Did Right

  • Asked to hear Paul himself and gave him leave to speak: Acts 25:22; Acts 26:1.
  • Declared that Paul had done nothing worthy of death or of bonds: Acts 26:31.

What They Did Wrong

  • Answered Paul's appeal with "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian," and went no further: Acts 26:28. Scripture records the reply and records nothing after it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records that he knew the prophets, that Paul said so to his face, and that he did not deny it. His reply is one of the most quoted sentences in Acts, and the account ends with him rising up and leaving the room. He is another of Acts' portraits of a man who understood the case and did not act.

Significance

His hearing produced Paul's most complete recorded defence and the fullest of the three accounts of his conversion. His verdict, with Festus's, establishes that the Roman authorities found no crime in Paul.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 26:32.

Scripture

Acts 25:13-26:32
544

Bernice

Sister of Herod Agrippa II; present with him at Paul's defence at Caesarea.

Family

Daughter of Herod Agrippa I; sister of Agrippa II and Drusilla (Acts 25:13).

Chronology

At Paul's hearing before Agrippa.

Life Synopsis

"And after certain days king Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus" (Acts 25:13). The next day "Agrippa was come, and Bernice, with great pomp, and was entered into the place of hearing, with the chief captains, and principal men of the city" (Acts 25:23). After Paul finished, "the king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and they that sat with them" (Acts 26:30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records her presence three times and no words or acts of hers.

Character Assessment

Scripture names her only as present. She is included because her attendance at the hearing is specified three times, which is more than the text does for most of the company.

Significance

She is the third of Herod Agrippa I's children to appear in Paul's trials, with Agrippa II and Drusilla.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 26:30.

Scripture

Acts 25:13, 25:23; Acts 26:30
545

Julius the centurion

A centurion of Augustus' band who had charge of Paul on the voyage to Rome, and treated him courteously.

Family

Not recorded. Of Augustus' band (Acts 27:1).

Chronology

On the voyage from Caesarea to Rome.

Life Synopsis

"And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band" (Acts 27:1).

"And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself" at Sidon (Acts 27:3).

He did not take Paul's advice about wintering, believing the master and owner of the ship rather (Acts 27:11). But when the soldiers counselled killing the prisoners lest any swim out and escape, "the centurion, willing to save Paul, kept them from their purpose; and commanded that they which could swim should cast themselves first into the sea, and get to land" (Acts 27:42-43).

What They Did Right

  • Courteously entreated Paul and gave him liberty at Sidon: Acts 27:3.
  • Kept the soldiers from killing the prisoners, in order to save Paul: Acts 27:43.

What They Did Wrong

  • Believed the master and owner of the ship rather than Paul about sailing on, and the ship was lost: Acts 27:11. Scripture records the decision and its outcome without further comment.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a fair-minded officer who made one poor judgment and one decision that saved every life aboard. His refusal to let the prisoners be killed is recorded with its motive stated: willing to save Paul.

Significance

His decision preserved all two hundred and seventy-six persons on the ship, as Paul had said would happen (Acts 27:22-24, 27:44).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 27:43.

Scripture

Acts 27:1-3, 27:11, 27:31-43
546

Publius

The chief man of the island of Melita, who lodged Paul's company three days; his father was healed of a fever and a bloody flux.

Family

His father lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux (Acts 28:8).

Chronology

After the shipwreck, on Melita.

Life Synopsis

"In the same quarters were possessions of the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius; who received us, and lodged us three days courteously."

"And it came to pass, that the father of Publius lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux: to whom Paul entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him. So when this was done, others also, which had diseases in the island, came, and were healed: who also honoured us with many honours; and when we departed, they laded us with such things as were necessary" (Acts 28:7-10).

What They Did Right

  • Received and lodged a company of shipwrecked strangers, including prisoners, three days courteously: Acts 28:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his hospitality and the healing of his father, and nothing he said. The account notes that the islanders showed no common kindness (Acts 28:2), and Publius is the named instance of it.

Significance

The healing of his father opened the way for the healing of others throughout the island during the three months Paul's company wintered there.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 28:8.

Scripture

Acts 28:7-10

Epistles and Revelation

547

James (the Lord's brother)

Brother of the Lord; did not believe during the ministry; saw the risen Christ, became a pillar of the church at Jerusalem, and wrote the epistle of James.

Also called James the Just

Family

Son of Mary; named first among the brethren of Christ - James, Joses, Simon, and Judas (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). Brother of Jude (Jude 1:1).

Chronology

From the resurrection through the council of Jerusalem and Paul's last visit (Acts 15:13; Acts 21:18).

Life Synopsis

During the ministry, "neither did his brethren believe in him" (John 7:5). After the resurrection Paul records, "After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles" (1 Corinthians 15:7). The brethren of the Lord are named among those continuing in prayer in the upper room (Acts 1:14).

When Peter was delivered from prison he said, "Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren" (Acts 12:17). Paul, going up to Jerusalem three years after his conversion, saw no other apostle "save James the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19), and later names "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars" (Galatians 2:9).

At the council of Jerusalem, after Peter and Barnabas and Paul had spoken, "James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me," cited Amos, and gave the judgment: "Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God" (Acts 15:13-21). The letter went out on those terms.

When Paul returned to Jerusalem for the last time, "Paul went in with us unto James; and all the elders were present" (Acts 21:18).

His epistle opens, "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" - without mentioning the relationship - and is the most practical book in the New Testament: faith without works is dead, the tongue is a fire, be doers of the word and not hearers only, and pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction and to keep oneself unspotted from the world (James 1:22, 1:27; James 2:17-26; James 3:5-6).

What They Did Right

  • Received an appearance of the risen Christ: 1 Corinthians 15:7.
  • Gave the judgment at the council that the Gentiles should not be troubled: Acts 15:19.
  • Reckoned with Cephas and John as a pillar of the church, and gave Paul the right hand of fellowship: Galatians 2:9.
  • Called himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ rather than his brother: James 1:1.
  • Wrote the epistle of James.

What They Did Wrong

  • He did not believe in Christ during the ministry: John 7:5. Scripture records this of the brethren generally, and records the change without narrating it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his unbelief plainly and his later standing plainly, and never explains the turn beyond one clause: he was seen of James. The most striking thing in his own writing is the opening: a man who had grown up in the same house calls himself a servant. His judgment at the council settled the question that could have split the church.

Significance

He presided over the church at Jerusalem, gave the decisive ruling at the council of Acts 15, and wrote the epistle bearing his name. His teaching that faith without works is dead has been set against Paul's justification by faith for centuries; both writers use Abraham as their example, and this reference records the tension without adjudicating it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Acts 21:18.

Scripture

Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3; John 7:5; Acts 1:14; Acts 12:17; Acts 15:13-29; Acts 21:18; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 1:19; Galatians 2:9, 2:12; James 1:1
548

Jude

Brother of James and of the Lord; writer of the epistle of Jude. Not to be confused with Judas Iscariot or with Lebbaeus.

Also called Judas the Lord's brother, Juda

Family

Named among the brethren of Christ (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3); brother of James (Jude 1:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He is named among the Lord's brethren, who did not believe during the ministry (Matthew 13:55; John 7:5), and is presumably among the brethren present in the upper room (Acts 1:14).

His epistle opens, "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" - naming his human relation to James rather than to Christ (Jude 1:1). He says he had intended to write of the common salvation, and instead found it needful to exhort them "that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 1:3).

The letter warns of men crept in unawares, and cites the angels that kept not their first estate, Sodom and Gomorrha, Cain, Balaam, and Core. He records the dispute of Michael the archangel with the devil about the body of Moses, and the prophecy of Enoch the seventh from Adam (Jude 1:9, 1:14-15).

It closes with one of the great benedictions: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen" (Jude 1:24-25).

What They Did Right

  • Called himself the servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, claiming no relation to Christ himself: Jude 1:1.
  • Wrote to urge that believers earnestly contend for the faith once delivered: Jude 1:3.
  • Wrote the epistle of Jude.

What They Did Wrong

  • He is named among the brethren who did not believe during the ministry: John 7:5. Scripture records it of them collectively.

Character Assessment

Scripture records almost nothing of him outside his own letter, and the letter itself is notable for what he does not claim. Like his brother James, he could have introduced himself as the Lord's brother and did not.

Significance

His epistle preserves two things found nowhere else in Scripture: Michael's dispute with the devil over the body of Moses, and the prophecy of Enoch. Its closing doxology is among the most quoted in the New Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3; John 7:5; Acts 1:14; Jude 1:1-25
549

Luke

The beloved physician; Paul's companion; writer of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.

Also called Lucas, the beloved physician

Family

Not recorded. Paul distinguishes him from those "of the circumcision" (Colossians 4:11-14), which indicates he was a Gentile.

Chronology

He joined Paul's company at Troas on the second journey and was with him at the last.

Life Synopsis

He never names himself, but the narrative of Acts shifts into the first person plural at Troas - "immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia" (Acts 16:10) - and again on the last journey to Jerusalem and the voyage to Rome (Acts 20:5-21:18; Acts 27:1-28:16). These passages are traditionally taken to mark his presence.

Paul names him three times: "Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you" (Colossians 4:14); among his fellowlabourers (Philemon 1:24); and in his last letter, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11).

His Gospel opens with a statement of method: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us... it seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, that thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed" (Luke 1:1-4). Acts opens by referring back to it (Acts 1:1).

What They Did Right

  • Accompanied Paul through the imprisonments and the voyage to Rome: Acts 27:1-28:16.
  • Was the only one with Paul at the last: "Only Luke is with me": 2 Timothy 4:11.
  • Called by Paul the beloved physician and named among his fellowlabourers: Colossians 4:14; Philemon 1:24.
  • Wrote two books of the New Testament, setting out his method of investigation at the start: Luke 1:1-4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and he records nothing about himself. He wrote more of the New Testament by volume than any other writer and never once names himself in either book. Paul's three references are all warm, and the last is the loneliest sentence in his letters.

Significance

His Gospel and Acts together trace the story from the announcement to Zacharias to Paul preaching in Rome. His medical background shows in details other writers omit - the great fever, the man full of leprosy, the woman who had spent all her living on physicians. He is the only Gentile writer in the Bible.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:11.

Scripture

Luke 1:1-4; Acts 1:1; Acts 16:10-17; Acts 20:5-21:18; Acts 27:1-28:16; Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 1:24
550

Theophilus

The man to whom Luke addressed both his Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

Family

Not recorded. Luke calls him "most excellent Theophilus" (Luke 1:3), a form of address used elsewhere in Acts for governors (Acts 23:26; Acts 24:3; Acts 26:25).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, that thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed" (Luke 1:3-4).

"The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach" (Acts 1:1). Nothing else is recorded of him.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Luke states that he had been instructed in these things: Luke 1:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, a form of address, and that he had received instruction. Nothing else. He is included because two books of the New Testament are addressed to him by name, and Luke's stated purpose in writing was that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught.

Significance

The two longest books of the New Testament were written to him, and Luke's stated reason for writing to him - certainty - is the clearest statement of purpose by any Gospel writer.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named twice.

Scripture

Luke 1:3-4; Acts 1:1
551

Titus

A Greek, Paul's own son after the common faith; carried the severe letter to Corinth and was left in Crete to set things in order.

Family

A Greek (Galatians 2:3).

Chronology

From before the council of Jerusalem through Paul's later ministry.

Life Synopsis

Paul took him to Jerusalem with Barnabas, "But neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised" - which Paul cites as the point on which he would not yield for an hour (Galatians 2:1-5).

He was sent to Corinth in a difficult season, and Paul records his own relief at his return: "Nevertheless God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus; and not by his coming only, but by the consolation wherewith he was comforted in you" (2 Corinthians 7:6-7). Paul says he had no rest in his spirit because he did not find him at Troas (2 Corinthians 2:13), and calls him "my partner and fellowhelper concerning you" (2 Corinthians 8:23). Of the collection: "But thanks be to God, which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus for you. For indeed he accepted the exhortation; but being more forward, of his own accord he went unto you" (2 Corinthians 8:16-17). Paul asks, "Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit?" (2 Corinthians 12:18).

The epistle to him states his charge: "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee" (Titus 1:5).

What They Did Right

  • Stood as the test case that Gentiles need not be circumcised, and was not compelled: Galatians 2:3-5.
  • Brought Paul comfort when he was cast down: 2 Corinthians 7:6-7.
  • Went to Corinth of his own accord, being forward in the matter: 2 Corinthians 8:16-17.
  • Made no gain of the Corinthians, and walked in the same spirit and steps as Paul: 2 Corinthians 12:18.
  • Was left in Crete to set in order what was wanting and ordain elders: Titus 1:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is entrusted with the two hardest assignments in Paul's correspondence - the Corinthian crisis and the churches of Crete - and Paul's language about him is unusually personal: he had no rest in his spirit when Titus was not where he expected.

Significance

His uncircumcision at Jerusalem was the practical test of the gospel Paul preached. One New Testament epistle is addressed to him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:10, where he had gone to Dalmatia.

Scripture

2 Corinthians 2:13; 2 Corinthians 7:6-15; 2 Corinthians 8:6-23; 2 Corinthians 12:18; Galatians 2:1-5; 2 Timothy 4:10; Titus 1:4-5
552

Philemon

A believer of Colosse in whose house a church met; Paul wrote to him on behalf of his runaway servant Onesimus.

Family

Paul greets "Apphia our beloved, and Archippus our fellowsoldier" with him, generally taken as his household (Philemon 1:2).

Chronology

During one of Paul's imprisonments.

Life Synopsis

Paul addresses him as "our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer," and thanks God on hearing of his love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all saints, "for we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother" (Philemon 1:1-7).

He then makes the request: "Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient, yet for love's sake I rather beseech thee... I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds: which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me."

"Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved... If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account; I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides" (Philemon 1:8-19).

"Having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee, knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say" (Philemon 1:21). Paul's answer is not recorded.

What They Did Right

  • His love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and toward all saints were reported to Paul: Philemon 1:5.
  • The bowels of the saints were refreshed by him: Philemon 1:7.
  • Hosted a church in his house: Philemon 1:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records only good of him, and records a request being made of him that we never learn the answer to. Paul deliberately refused to command - "for love's sake I rather beseech thee" - and left the decision with him. That the letter was preserved and circulated is generally taken as evidence he did what was asked; Scripture does not say so.

Significance

The letter to him is the shortest of Paul's and the New Testament's most direct treatment of how the gospel bears on the relation between master and servant. Paul's offer to pay the debt himself is one of Scripture's plainest pictures of substitution.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Philemon 1:1.

Scripture

Philemon 1:1-25; compare Colossians 4:9
553

Onesimus

A servant of Philemon who ran away, was converted through Paul in prison, and was sent back with a letter asking that he be received as a brother.

Family

Not recorded. Paul calls him "my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Philemon 1:10).

Chronology

During one of Paul's imprisonments.

Life Synopsis

Paul writes to Philemon: "I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds: which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me: whom I have sent again: thou therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels."

"For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord" (Philemon 1:10-16).

Paul offers to stand for whatever he owes: "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account" (Philemon 1:18).

He is named again in the letter to the same city: "With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Colossians 4:9).

What They Did Right

  • Became profitable, where he had been unprofitable: Philemon 1:11.
  • Returned to the master he had wronged, carrying the letter that asked for his reception: Philemon 1:12.
  • Called by Paul a faithful and beloved brother: Colossians 4:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • He departed from his master, and Paul's words allow that he may have wronged him or owed him: Philemon 1:15, 1:18. Scripture states it conditionally and does not detail the offence.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a runaway who became a brother, and records the change in a play on his own name: Onesimus means profitable, and Paul says he had been unprofitable and now was profitable. He went back, which is the hardest thing in the account, and he carried the letter asking for his own reception.

Significance

The letter concerning him is the New Testament's clearest working out of what the gospel does to the relation between a master and his servant - not by abolishing the relation in a sentence but by making them brothers within it. Paul's assumption of his debt is the epistle's central image.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Colossians 4:9.

Scripture

Colossians 4:9; Philemon 1:10-19
554

Archippus

Called Paul's fellowsoldier; charged to take heed to the ministry he had received.

Family

Greeted with Philemon and Apphia, and generally taken to be of their household (Philemon 1:2).

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonment.

Life Synopsis

"And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house" (Philemon 1:2).

"And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfil it" (Colossians 4:17).

What They Did Right

  • Called Paul's fellowsoldier: Philemon 1:2.
  • Had received a ministry in the Lord: Colossians 4:17.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The charge sent to him through the church - take heed that thou fulfil it - has often been read as implying he had grown slack. Scripture does not say so, and the same exhortation is given elsewhere to men against whom nothing is charged.

Character Assessment

Scripture records two mentions, one warm and one a charge. The charge is unusual in being sent to him through a letter to the whole church rather than privately, and the text gives no reason.

Significance

The message to him is the New Testament's shortest statement of a minister's duty: take heed to the ministry you received, that you fulfil it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Philemon 1:2.

Scripture

Colossians 4:17; Philemon 1:2
555

Epaphroditus

A messenger of the church at Philippi who brought their gift to Paul in prison, fell sick near to death, and was sent back with a commendation.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonment.

Life Synopsis

"Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants. For he longed after you all, and was full of heaviness, because that ye had heard that he had been sick."

"For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. I sent him therefore the more carefully, that, when ye see him again, ye may rejoice, and that I may be the less sorrowful."

"Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation: because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me" (Philippians 2:25-30). Paul also acknowledges the gift he brought: "having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God" (Philippians 4:18).

What They Did Right

  • Called by Paul brother, companion in labour, fellowsoldier, messenger, and one who ministered to his wants: Philippians 2:25.
  • Was full of heaviness because the Philippians had heard he was sick - distressed at their distress rather than his own: Philippians 2:26.
  • Came nigh unto death for the work of Christ, not regarding his life: Philippians 2:30.
  • Paul directed that such men be held in reputation: Philippians 2:29.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The detail that carries the account is his heaviness: he was near death and what troubled him was that his church had heard about it. Paul's instruction to hold such men in reputation is one of the few times he directs that anyone be publicly honoured.

Significance

He carried the Philippians' gift, which Paul calls a sacrifice acceptable and wellpleasing to God, and he is presumably the bearer of the epistle to the Philippians.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Philippians 4:18.

Scripture

Philippians 2:25-30; Philippians 4:18
556

Epaphras

A faithful minister of Christ from Colosse; brought Paul word of the Colossians' love, and laboured fervently for them in prayer.

Family

Not recorded. "One of you" - of Colosse (Colossians 4:12).

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonment.

Life Synopsis

"As ye also learned of Epaphras our dear fellowservant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ; who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit" (Colossians 1:7-8).

"Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis" (Colossians 4:12-13).

Paul also calls him "my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus" (Philemon 1:23).

What They Did Right

  • A dear fellowservant and faithful minister of Christ: Colossians 1:7.
  • Brought Paul word of the Colossians' love in the Spirit: Colossians 1:8.
  • Always laboured fervently in prayer that they might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God: Colossians 4:12.
  • Paul bore him record of great zeal for three churches: Colossians 4:13.
  • Shared Paul's imprisonment: Philemon 1:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. What it records chiefly is prayer: the fullest description in the New Testament of one man praying for a church, including what he asked for. Paul says he laboured at it and testifies to his zeal by name for three separate congregations.

Significance

He appears to have brought the gospel to Colosse, and his report to Paul occasioned the epistle. His prayer - that they might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God - is a model the letter itself works out.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Philemon 1:23.

Scripture

Colossians 1:7-8; Colossians 4:12-13; Philemon 1:23
557

Tychicus

A beloved brother and faithful minister; carried Paul's letters and was repeatedly sent to comfort the churches.

Family

Of Asia (Acts 20:4).

Chronology

From the third missionary journey through Paul's last imprisonment.

Life Synopsis

He accompanied Paul into Asia (Acts 20:4). Paul describes him three times in nearly the same words: "But that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things: whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that ye might know our affairs, and that he might comfort your hearts" (Ephesians 6:21-22); and "All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord" (Colossians 4:7-8).

He is named again as a possible replacement for Titus in Crete (Titus 3:12), and, in Paul's last letter, "And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus" (2 Timothy 4:12).

What They Did Right

  • Called a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellowservant in the Lord: Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7.
  • Was sent repeatedly to make known Paul's affairs and to comfort the hearts of the churches: Ephesians 6:22; Colossians 4:8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His whole recorded ministry is carrying letters and news, and Paul twice states the purpose in the same terms: that the churches might know how he was, and that their hearts might be comforted.

Significance

He is the likely bearer of the epistles to the Ephesians and the Colossians, and travelled with Onesimus when the letter to Philemon was carried (Colossians 4:7-9).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:12.

Scripture

Acts 20:4; Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-9; 2 Timothy 4:12; Titus 3:12
558

Trophimus

An Ephesian whose presence in Jerusalem with Paul was the pretext for the riot that led to his arrest; later left sick at Miletum.

Family

An Ephesian (Acts 21:29); of Asia (Acts 20:4).

Chronology

On Paul's last journey to Jerusalem, and afterward.

Life Synopsis

He travelled with Paul into Asia (Acts 20:4). At Jerusalem, the Jews of Asia stirred up the people, "crying out, Men of Israel, help: This is the man, that teacheth all men every where against the people, and the law, and this place: and further brought Greeks also into the temple, and hath polluted this holy place. (For they had seen before with him in the city Trophimus an Ephesian, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple.)" (Acts 21:27-29).

The accusation was an inference and Acts says so plainly - they supposed. The riot that followed led to Paul's arrest, his imprisonment, and ultimately his voyage to Rome.

Paul's last letter records, "Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick" (2 Timothy 4:20).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He accompanied Paul into Asia and to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). Scripture records nothing that he said or did.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The charge that Paul had brought him into the temple was an assumption on the part of the crowd, and Acts states it as such: "whom they supposed" (Acts 21:29).

Character Assessment

Scripture records that his being seen in the city with Paul was enough to start a riot, and is careful to say the charge rested on a supposition. Nothing he said is recorded. Paul's note that he left him sick at Miletum is one of several places showing that healing was not always given, even through an apostle.

Significance

The mistaken assumption about him set in motion Paul's arrest, the hearings before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, the appeal to Caesar, and the voyage to Rome.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:20.

Scripture

Acts 20:4; Acts 21:27-29; 2 Timothy 4:20
559

Aristarchus

A Macedonian of Thessalonica; seized in the riot at Ephesus, a companion on the voyage to Rome, and Paul's fellowprisoner.

Family

A Macedonian of Thessalonica (Acts 19:29; Acts 27:2).

Chronology

From the riot at Ephesus through Paul's imprisonment at Rome.

Life Synopsis

In the Ephesian riot the crowd "caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel," and rushed with one accord into the theatre (Acts 19:29). He accompanied Paul into Asia (Acts 20:4).

On the voyage to Rome: "one Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us" (Acts 27:2).

Paul names him from prison: "Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you" (Colossians 4:10), and among his fellowlabourers (Philemon 1:24).

What They Did Right

  • Was seized by a mob as one of Paul's companions in travel: Acts 19:29.
  • Sailed with Paul to Rome and shared his imprisonment: Acts 27:2; Colossians 4:10.
  • Named among Paul's fellowlabourers: Philemon 1:24.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and nothing that he said. What it records is presence: in the theatre at Ephesus, on the ship, and in prison at Rome. He stayed through the three most dangerous episodes of Paul's later life.

Significance

He is one of the few of Paul's companions Scripture calls a fellowprisoner, and one of the two named in the Ephesian riot.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Philemon 1:24.

Scripture

Acts 19:29; Acts 20:4; Acts 27:2; Colossians 4:10; Philemon 1:24
560

Onesiphorus

A man of Ephesus who often refreshed Paul, was not ashamed of his chain, and sought him out diligently in Rome until he found him.

Family

Paul salutes "the household of Onesiphorus" and prays mercy on his house (2 Timothy 1:16; 2 Timothy 4:19).

Chronology

During Paul's final imprisonment at Rome.

Life Synopsis

"The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain: but, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me. The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well" (2 Timothy 1:16-18).

"Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus" (2 Timothy 4:19).

What They Did Right

  • Often refreshed Paul: 2 Timothy 1:16.
  • Was not ashamed of his chain, at a time when others had turned away: 2 Timothy 1:15-16.
  • Sought him out very diligently in Rome until he found him: 2 Timothy 1:17.
  • Ministered to him in many things at Ephesus: 2 Timothy 1:18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The sentence before his mention is that all they in Asia had turned away from Paul, which is what gives his conduct its weight: he came to Rome and searched a city for a prisoner nobody wanted to be associated with. Paul greets his household rather than him in the closing salutation, which some take to mean he had died; the text does not say.

Significance

He is the counter-example to Demas in the same letter, and Paul's prayer for him - that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day - is the only such petition Paul makes for a named individual.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:19.

Scripture

2 Timothy 1:15-18; 2 Timothy 4:19
561

Demas

A fellowlabourer of Paul who afterward forsook him, having loved this present world.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During Paul's imprisonments; he departed before the writing of 2 Timothy.

Life Synopsis

He is named twice without comment among Paul's companions: "Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you" (Colossians 4:14), and among "Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers" (Philemon 1:24).

The third mention is the last: "For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:10-11).

What They Did Right

  • He was reckoned among Paul's fellowlabourers and named in the greetings of two epistles: Colossians 4:14; Philemon 1:24.

What They Did Wrong

  • Forsook Paul, having loved this present world, and departed to Thessalonica: 2 Timothy 4:10. Scripture states the cause in four words and gives no further detail.

Character Assessment

Scripture records three mentions and a decline across them: named with Luke, named among the fellowlabourers, and then gone. The reason given is not persecution, doctrine, or a quarrel, but that he loved this present world. The text says nothing more - not what he did afterward, and not whether he returned.

Significance

His departure is set in the same sentence as Crescens and Titus going elsewhere on legitimate errands, and immediately before "Only Luke is with me." It is the New Testament's plainest example of a man who was in the work and left it for no reason but preference.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:10.

Scripture

Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:10; Philemon 1:24
562

Phebe

A servant of the church at Cenchrea, commended by Paul to the church at Rome; a succourer of many and of himself.

Family

Not recorded. "Our sister" and "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea" (Romans 16:1).

Chronology

At the writing of the epistle to the Romans.

Life Synopsis

"I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: that ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Romans 16:1-2).

What They Did Right

  • A servant of the church at Cenchrea: Romans 16:1.
  • A succourer of many, and of Paul himself: Romans 16:2.
  • Commended by Paul to a church that did not know her, with a request that they assist her: Romans 16:1-2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records two verses and nothing that she said. The commendation is formal - the standard form of a letter of introduction - and its substance is that she had helped many people including Paul, which he states as the reason they should help her.

Significance

She is generally taken to have carried the epistle to the Romans, since Paul commends her to them at its close; Scripture does not state this. Her commendation opens the longest list of greetings in the New Testament.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Romans 16:1-2
563

Andronicus and Junia

Kinsmen and fellowprisoners of Paul, of note among the apostles, and in Christ before him. Two individuals, greeted together.

Family

Called Paul's kinsmen (Romans 16:7).

Chronology

They were in Christ before Paul, so before his conversion.

Life Synopsis

"Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me" (Romans 16:7). Nothing else is recorded of either.

What They Did Right

  • Of note among the apostles: Romans 16:7.
  • Were in Christ before Paul: Romans 16:7.
  • Shared imprisonment with him: Romans 16:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, entirely favourable, and it packs in four facts: kinship, imprisonment, standing, and priority. The phrase "of note among the apostles" has been read both as meaning well known to the apostles and as meaning notable apostles themselves; the Greek admits both and this reference does not decide it.

Significance

They are among the earliest believers named in Scripture, having been in Christ before Paul's conversion.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Romans 16:7
564

Erastus

The chamberlain of the city of Corinth; a believer who sent greeting in the epistle to the Romans.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During Paul's ministry at Corinth and after.

Life Synopsis

"Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother" (Romans 16:23). He was sent with Timothy into Macedonia from Ephesus (Acts 19:22), and Paul's last letter records, "Erastus abode at Corinth" (2 Timothy 4:20).

What They Did Right

  • Ministered to Paul and was sent with Timothy into Macedonia: Acts 19:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment
