Scripture records his office, his service, and where he stayed, and nothing else. He is included because his position is specified: the city treasurer of Corinth was a believer and is named in the New Testament.

Significance

He is the highest-ranking municipal official named as a believer in Paul's letters.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:20.

Scripture

Acts 19:22; Romans 16:23; 2 Timothy 4:20
565

Sosthenes

Chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, beaten before the judgment seat; a Sosthenes is afterward named with Paul in the opening of 1 Corinthians.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

During Paul's eighteen months at Corinth, and at the writing of 1 Corinthians.

Life Synopsis

When the Jews brought Paul before Gallio and the case was dismissed, "then all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things" (Acts 18:17).

Paul's first letter to Corinth opens, "Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother" (1 Corinthians 1:1). Whether the two are the same man is not stated by Scripture, and this reference notes the question without deciding it.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. If the two references are to the same man, he moved from ruling the synagogue that opposed Paul to being named as a brother in the opening of Paul's letter. Scripture does not make the identification.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a beating and, separately, a name in a greeting. It never connects them. The possibility that the man beaten outside the court became the brother named beside Paul is real and is not asserted here.

Significance

Acts 18:17 is one of the clearest pictures in Scripture of official indifference - Gallio cared for none of those things - and the name reappearing in 1 Corinthians 1:1 is one of the New Testament's quiet loose ends.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Corinthians 1:1.

Scripture

Acts 18:17; 1 Corinthians 1:1
566

Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus

Three men of Corinth who came to Paul at Ephesus and refreshed his spirit; the house of Stephanas was the firstfruits of Achaia. Three individuals, named together.

Family

The household of Stephanas was baptized by Paul (1 Corinthians 1:16).

Chronology

During Paul's stay at Ephesus.

Life Synopsis

"I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,) that ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth."

"I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Corinthians 16:15-18).

What They Did Right

  • The house of Stephanas was the firstfruits of Achaia and addicted itself to the ministry of the saints: 1 Corinthians 16:15.
  • All three refreshed Paul's spirit and supplied what was lacking: 1 Corinthians 16:17-18.
  • Paul directed the church to acknowledge and submit to such men: 1 Corinthians 16:16-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them. Paul's phrase about the house of Stephanas is unusually strong - they addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints - and he asks the Corinthians to recognise them, in a letter otherwise largely occupied with correcting that church.

Significance

They came from a divided and troubled congregation and are the men Paul singles out for commendation in it. Stephanas's household was among the very few Paul baptized personally (1 Corinthians 1:16).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once together.

Scripture

1 Corinthians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 16:15-18
567

Euodias and Syntyche

Two women of Philippi who laboured with Paul in the gospel and were entreated by name to be of the same mind. Two individuals, named together.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the writing of the epistle to the Philippians.

Life Synopsis

"I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord. And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life" (Philippians 4:2-3).

What They Did Right

  • Laboured with Paul in the gospel: Philippians 4:3.
  • Their names are in the book of life: Philippians 4:3.

What They Did Wrong

  • They were not of the same mind, and Paul beseeches each of them by name in a letter to be read to the whole church: Philippians 4:2. The nature of the disagreement is not recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a disagreement between two women without recording what it was about or who was right. Paul addresses each separately and identically - beseech, and beseech - assigns no fault, and asks a third party to help them. In the same breath he says they laboured with him in the gospel and that their names are in the book of life.

Significance

Theirs is the only named personal quarrel in the epistles addressed directly to the parties, and it appears in the letter most concerned with having the mind of Christ and esteeming others better than oneself (Philippians 2:2-5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Philippians 4:2-3
568

Lois and Eunice

Timothy's grandmother and mother, in whom unfeigned faith dwelt first. Two individuals, named together in one verse.

Family

Lois was Timothy's grandmother and Eunice his mother (2 Timothy 1:5). Eunice was a Jewess who believed, married to a Greek (Acts 16:1).

Chronology

Before and during Timothy's youth at Lystra.

Life Synopsis

"Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed; but his father was a Greek" (Acts 16:1).

"When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also" (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul adds, "and that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation" (2 Timothy 3:15).

What They Did Right

  • Unfeigned faith dwelt first in them, and was passed to Timothy: 2 Timothy 1:5.
  • Taught him the holy scriptures from a child, in a household where the father was a Greek: 2 Timothy 3:15; Acts 16:1.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them and nothing that either said. Paul names the faith as unfeigned - not merely present but genuine - and traces it through three generations of one household. Timothy's father was a Greek and is never said to have believed, which makes the teaching entirely theirs.

Significance

They are Scripture's clearest example of faith and scriptural instruction passing through a household, and the source of the man to whom two epistles are addressed.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 2 Timothy 3:15
569

Alexander the coppersmith

A man who did Paul much evil and greatly withstood his words.

Family

Not recorded. Scripture names an Alexander at Ephesus (Acts 19:33) and an Alexander delivered to Satan with Hymenaeus (1 Timothy 1:20); whether these are the same man is not stated.

Chronology

Before the writing of 2 Timothy.

Life Synopsis

"Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words" (2 Timothy 4:14-15).

Paul writes in the next verse, "At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me" (2 Timothy 4:16), though he does not connect the two.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did Paul much evil and greatly withstood his words: 2 Timothy 4:14-15.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the charge in two verses and no detail of what he did. Paul's response is to commit the matter - the Lord reward him according to his works - and to warn Timothy to beware of him, which is practical rather than vindictive.

Significance

He is named in Paul's last letter among the losses of that period, alongside Demas's departure and the note that at his first answer no man stood with him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 4:15.

Scripture

2 Timothy 4:14-15; compare Acts 19:33; 1 Timothy 1:20
570

Hymenaeus and Philetus

Two men who erred concerning the truth, saying the resurrection was past already, and overthrew the faith of some. Two individuals, named together in 2 Timothy.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Before the writing of 1 and 2 Timothy.

Life Synopsis

"Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck: of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Timothy 1:19-20).

"But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus; who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some" (2 Timothy 2:16-18).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made shipwreck concerning faith and a good conscience: 1 Timothy 1:19-20.
  • Erred concerning the truth, teaching that the resurrection was past already: 2 Timothy 2:18.
  • Overthrew the faith of some: 2 Timothy 2:18.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture names the specific error - that the resurrection had already happened - and the specific damage: the faith of some was overthrown. Paul's stated purpose in delivering Hymenaeus to Satan was corrective, that he might learn not to blaspheme.

Significance

Theirs is one of the few named doctrinal errors in the New Testament with its content specified, and Paul's response - that the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his (2 Timothy 2:19) - is the answer given to it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Timothy 2:17.

Scripture

1 Timothy 1:19-20; 2 Timothy 2:16-19
571

Gaius (of the third epistle)

The beloved brother to whom John wrote his third epistle, commended for walking in the truth and for receiving strangers faithfully.

Family

Not recorded. Scripture names other men called Gaius - of Macedonia (Acts 19:29), of Derbe (Acts 20:4), and Paul's host at Corinth (Romans 16:23) - and does not identify them with one another.

Chronology

At the writing of the third epistle of John.

Life Synopsis

"The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth. Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth. For I rejoiced greatly, when the brethren came and testified of the truth that is in thee, even as thou walkest in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth."

"Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers; which have borne witness of thy charity before the church: whom if thou bring forward on their journey after a godly sort, thou shalt do well: because that for his name's sake they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth" (3 John 1:1-8).

What They Did Right

  • Walked in the truth, as the brethren testified: 3 John 1:3-4.
  • Did faithfully whatsoever he did to the brethren and to strangers: 3 John 1:5.
  • His charity was borne witness of before the church: 3 John 1:6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is the addressee of a letter written largely because someone else in the church was doing the opposite, and his commendation is specific: he received people he did not know, and it was reported publicly.

Significance

John's wish for him - that he might prosper and be in health, even as his soul prospered - is among the most quoted verses in the shorter epistles.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 3 John 1:1.

Scripture

3 John 1:1-8
572

Demetrius (of good report)

A man commended by John as having good report of all men and of the truth itself. Not to be confused with Demetrius the silversmith of Ephesus.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the writing of the third epistle of John.

Life Synopsis

"Demetrius hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself: yea, and we also bear record; and ye know that our record is true" (3 John 1:12).

What They Did Right

  • Had good report of all men, and of the truth itself, with John's own record added: 3 John 1:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, and it contains three separate testimonials: all men, the truth itself, and John. Nothing he said or did is recorded, only that everyone who knew him spoke well of him.

Significance

He is set against Diotrephes in the same letter, and his commendation is the last thing John writes before the closing greetings.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

3 John 1:12
573

Diotrephes

A man in a church addressed by John, who loved to have the preeminence, refused to receive the brethren, and cast out those who would.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

At the writing of the third epistle of John.

Life Synopsis

"I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church" (3 John 1:9-10).

"Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God" (3 John 1:11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Loved to have the preeminence: 3 John 1:9.
  • Refused to receive John and the brethren: 3 John 1:9-10.
  • Prated against them with malicious words: 3 John 1:10.
  • Forbade those who would receive the brethren, and cast them out of the church: 3 John 1:10.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. No doctrinal error is charged against him at all: the whole indictment is about position and control. He is the New Testament's clearest example of trouble in a church arising from a man's love of preeminence rather than from false teaching.

Significance

He is set in the same short letter against Gaius, who received the brethren, and Demetrius, who had a good report of all men - three named men in fourteen verses, one bad and two good.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Named once.

Scripture

3 John 1:9-11
574

The elect lady

Unnamed. The recipient of the second epistle of John, addressed with her children, and warned about deceivers.

Family

She had children, some of whom John found walking in truth, and a sister whose children send greeting (2 John 1:1, 1:4, 1:13).

Chronology

At the writing of the second epistle of John.

Life Synopsis

"The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth; and not I only, but also all they that have known the truth" (2 John 1:1).

"I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children walking in truth, as we have received a commandment from the Father. And now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another" (2 John 1:4-5).

He warns that many deceivers have entered into the world who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh, and instructs, "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed" (2 John 1:7-10). He closes, "The children of thy elect sister greet thee" (2 John 1:13).

Whether the letter addresses an individual woman or a congregation figuratively has long been discussed; the text reads as an address to a person, and this reference treats it so while noting the question.

What They Did Right

  • Her children were found walking in truth: 2 John 1:4.
  • Loved in the truth by John and by all who had known the truth: 2 John 1:1.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. The letter is written to warn her about who she receives into her house, which indicates hospitality was her practice and the danger was that it would be exploited.

Significance

Her letter contains the New Testament's most specific instruction on receiving teachers, and one of its clearest tests of doctrine: whether they confess that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture

2 John 1:1-13
575

Antipas

Called by Christ his faithful martyr; slain at Pergamos, where Satan's seat is.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Before the writing of Revelation.

Life Synopsis

In the letter to the church at Pergamos: "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth" (Revelation 2:13). Nothing else is recorded of him.

What They Did Right

  • Called by Christ himself "my faithful martyr": Revelation 2:13.
  • Was slain for the faith in a city Christ describes as the place where Satan dwells: Revelation 2:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, and the commendation in it comes directly from Christ. Nothing is recorded of his life, his words, or the manner of his death. He is the only individual believer named in the letters to the seven churches.

Significance

He is the last named martyr in Scripture, and the only person Christ personally calls his faithful martyr.

Death / Outcome

Slain at Pergamos (Revelation 2:13).

Scripture

Revelation 2:13
576

Jezebel of Thyatira

A woman in the church at Thyatira who called herself a prophetess and taught the servants of God to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols. Distinct from Jezebel the wife of Ahab, whose name Christ applies to her.

Family

Not recorded. Christ speaks of her children (Revelation 2:23).

Chronology

At the writing of Revelation.

Life Synopsis

"Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols."

"And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not. Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds. And I will kill her children with death; and all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works" (Revelation 2:20-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Called herself a prophetess: Revelation 2:20.
  • Taught and seduced the servants of God to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols: Revelation 2:20.
  • Was given space to repent and repented not: Revelation 2:21.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. The charge against the church is that it suffered her - tolerated her - rather than that it agreed with her. The detail Scripture emphasises is the space given: she was granted time to repent and did not use it.

Significance

Christ's use of the name Jezebel connects her to the woman who established Baal worship in Israel, and the charge is the same in substance: teaching God's people to combine his worship with idolatry and immorality. Her case is why the church at Thyatira was rebuked despite its works, charity, service, faith, and patience (Revelation 2:19).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Judgment is pronounced in Revelation 2:22-23.

Scripture

Revelation 2:18-23
577

The two witnesses

Two unnamed witnesses of Revelation, given power to prophesy twelve hundred and sixty days, killed by the beast, and raised after three days and a half.

Family

Not recorded. Called "the two olive trees, and the two candlesticks standing before the God of the earth" (Revelation 11:4).

Chronology

Not established. Their period is given as a thousand two hundred and threescore days (Revelation 11:3).

Life Synopsis

"And I will give power unto my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth."

Fire proceeds out of their mouth and devours their enemies. "These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will."

"And when they shall have finished their testimony, the beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them." Their bodies lie in the street of the great city three days and a half, and those who dwell on the earth rejoice over them and send gifts to one another.

"And after three days and an half the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them which saw them. And they heard a great voice from heaven saying unto them, Come up hither. And they ascended up to heaven in a cloud" (Revelation 11:3-12).

What They Did Right

  • Prophesied for the full period appointed them, clothed in sackcloth: Revelation 11:3.
  • Finished their testimony before they were overcome: Revelation 11:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes their powers, their period, their death, and their resurrection, and does not name them. Their signs recall Elijah shutting heaven and Moses turning waters to blood, and many have concluded from this who they are; Revelation does not say, and this reference does not supply an identification.

Significance

Their account contains the phrase that has shaped much thinking about martyrdom: they were not overcome until they had finished their testimony (Revelation 11:7).

Death / Outcome

Killed by the beast, and raised after three days and a half, ascending in a cloud (Revelation 11:7-12).

Scripture

Revelation 11:3-13
578

The beast

The beast of Revelation, rising out of the sea, to whom the dragon gives his power and seat and great authority; makes war with the saints and is cast into the lake of fire.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. His period of authority is given as forty and two months (Revelation 13:5).

Life Synopsis

"And I stood upon the sand of the sea, and saw a beast rise up out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns... And the dragon gave him his power, and his seat, and great authority." One of his heads was as it were wounded to death, and his deadly wound was healed, and all the world wondered after the beast (Revelation 13:1-3).

"And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months. And he opened his mouth in blasphemy against God, to blaspheme his name, and his tabernacle, and them that dwell in heaven. And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations" (Revelation 13:5-7).

He is finally taken with the false prophet and cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone (Revelation 19:20).

A note is owed here. Interpretations of this figure differ sharply and always have - whether a person, an empire, a system, or a succession of them; whether the events are past, present, or future. Scripture describes him in the language of vision, and this reference sets out what the text says without adopting any scheme of interpretation.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Received his power, seat, and authority from the dragon: Revelation 13:2.
  • Spoke great things and blasphemies against God, his name, his tabernacle, and them that dwell in heaven: Revelation 13:5-6.
  • Made war with the saints and overcame them: Revelation 13:7.
  • Received the worship of all whose names are not written in the book of life: Revelation 13:8.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Two things the text is careful about: his authority is given rather than seized - the passive is used repeatedly - and his period is limited to forty-two months. Even at the height of his power, Revelation presents him as permitted and bounded.

Significance

His mark, his number, and his war with the saints have been among the most discussed passages in Scripture. His end is stated without ambiguity: taken, and cast alive into the lake of fire.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. Cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone (Revelation 19:20).

Scripture

Revelation 11:7; Revelation 13:1-18; Revelation 14:9-11; Revelation 17:8-14; Revelation 19:19-20; Revelation 20:10
579

The false prophet

A second beast of Revelation, coming up out of the earth, who causes the earth to worship the first beast and deceives by miracles; cast with him into the lake of fire.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"And I beheld another beast coming up out of the earth; and he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon. And he exerciseth all the power of the first beast before him, and causeth the earth and them which dwell therein to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed."

"And he doeth great wonders, so that he maketh fire come down from heaven on the earth in the sight of men, and deceiveth them that dwell on the earth by the means of those miracles which he had power to do in the sight of the beast" (Revelation 13:11-14). He causes all to receive a mark, and that none might buy or sell without it (Revelation 13:16-17).

He is afterward called the false prophet: "And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him, with which he deceived them that had received the mark of the beast, and them that worshipped his image. These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone" (Revelation 19:20).

As with the beast, interpretations of this figure differ widely, and this reference records what the text says without adopting one.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Had two horns like a lamb and spake as a dragon - the appearance of one thing and the voice of another: Revelation 13:11.
  • Caused the earth to worship the first beast: Revelation 13:12.
  • Deceived men by miracles he had power to do: Revelation 13:13-14.
  • Caused all to receive a mark, without which none might buy or sell: Revelation 13:16-17.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. The detail Scripture emphasises is deception by genuine signs: he did great wonders and by them deceived. His appearance is lamblike and his speech draconic, which is the passage's own summary of what he is.

Significance

He is the clearest statement in Scripture that miraculous power is not by itself evidence of truth - a point Christ made in warning that false christs and false prophets would show great signs and wonders (Matthew 24:24).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. Cast alive into the lake of fire with the beast (Revelation 19:20).

Scripture

Revelation 13:11-18; Revelation 16:13; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 20:10

Figures in the Parables of Christ

These are figures in the parables Christ told, not people whose histories Scripture records. They are kept separate for that reason, and the section is not chronological. None of them has a name except Lazarus the beggar, none has a family or a date, and the entries say so rather than inventing one. They are included because these figures carry some of Christ's plainest teaching and readers look for them. The two headings that elsewhere read what a person did right and wrong are here what the parable commends and condemns.

580

The good Samaritan

The traveller in Christ's parable who cared for a wounded man that a priest and a Levite had passed by.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken by Christ in answer to a lawyer's question, "And who is my neighbour?" (Luke 10:29).

Life Synopsis

A lawyer, willing to justify himself, asked who his neighbour was. Christ answered with a story: a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves, who stripped him, wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead.

A priest came down that way, saw him, and passed by on the other side. A Levite came, looked on him, and passed by on the other side.

"But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, and went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Christ then turned the lawyer's question around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise" (Luke 10:30-37).

What the Parable Commends

  • Had compassion when he saw the man, which the parable states before any of his actions: Luke 10:33.
  • Bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast: Luke 10:34.
  • Brought him to an inn and took care of him himself before leaving: Luke 10:34.
  • Paid the host and guaranteed whatever more it cost, undertaking a liability he could not measure: Luke 10:35.
  • Christ's own verdict, given through the lawyer's mouth: he was the one that shewed mercy: Luke 10:36-37.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The parable records nothing against this figure.

Character Assessment

The parable's force lies in who the man was. A Samaritan was the one person in the story a Jewish audience would not have expected to help, and the two who passed by were the ones whose office should have obliged them. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the word Samaritan in his answer; he said, "He that shewed mercy on him."

Significance

The parable defines neighbour not as a category to be identified but as something to be done, and Christ's closing instruction - go, and do thou likewise - makes it a command rather than a definition. The account of the captives clothed and carried to Jericho in 2 Chronicles 28:15 is set on the same road; Scripture draws no connection.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. He departed on the morrow, promising to return (Luke 10:35).

Scripture

Luke 10:25-37
581

The priest and the Levite

Two figures in the parable of the good Samaritan who saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side. Two figures, described identically and recorded together.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31-32).

The parable gives them no words, no reason, and no consequence. It states only that each saw the man and each went round him. Of the Levite it adds that he came to the place and looked on him, which is a step nearer than the priest and the same result.

What the Parable Commends

  • The parable records nothing to this figure's credit.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Both saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side: Luke 10:31-32. The parable offers no excuse for either and none is implied in the text.

Character Assessment

The parable withholds their reasoning entirely, and the withholding is deliberate: any reason a hearer supplies for them is a reason he has supplied himself. They are the two men in the story whose office in Israel most directly concerned the service of God, and they are the two who did nothing.

Significance

Their inaction is what makes the Samaritan's mercy the answer to the lawyer's question. The parable does not say they were wicked men; it says they passed by.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 10:31-32
582

The prodigal son

The younger of two sons in Christ's parable, who took his portion, wasted it, came to himself, and returned to his father.

Family

Younger son of the father in the parable; brother of the elder son (Luke 15:11-12).

Chronology

Not applicable. The third of three parables spoken in answer to the murmuring that Christ received sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:1-2).

Life Synopsis

"A certain man had two sons: and the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living. And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

A mighty famine arose, he began to be in want, and joined himself to a citizen of that country who sent him into the fields to feed swine. "And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him."

"And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants."

"And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." He began his speech, and got as far as "am no more worthy to be called thy son" - the father did not let him finish the request to be made a servant (Luke 15:11-21).

What the Parable Commends

  • Came to himself, and reckoned honestly with his own condition: Luke 15:17.
  • Resolved to return and to confess, naming the sin as against heaven and against his father: Luke 15:18-19.
  • Arose and came, and made the confession he had prepared: Luke 15:20-21.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Demanded his portion of his father's goods while his father lived: Luke 15:12.
  • Went into a far country and wasted his substance with riotous living: Luke 15:13.
  • His own confession is the parable's charge: "I have sinned against heaven, and before thee": Luke 15:21.

Character Assessment

The parable is careful about the order of events. He came to himself before he came to his father, and the reasoning that turned him was not remorse but hunger and a memory of his father's household. The father ran before any confession was made, and the confession was cut short. What restored him was not the completeness of his repentance but his father's sight of him a great way off.

Significance

The third of the three parables of Luke 15 - the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son - all spoken because the Pharisees and scribes murmured that Christ received sinners and ate with them. Each ends in joy, and the third ends in an argument about it.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. The parable ends with the feast and the elder brother outside (Luke 15:32).

Scripture

Luke 15:11-24
583

The father of the prodigal son

The father in Christ's parable, who divided his living, watched for his son's return, ran to meet him, and went out to entreat the elder brother.

Family

Father of two sons (Luke 15:11).

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

He divided his living at his younger son's demand, without recorded protest (Luke 15:12).

"But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." He interrupted the confession and said to his servants, "Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: and bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry: for this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found" (Luke 15:20-24).

When the elder son was angry and would not go in, "therefore came his father out, and intreated him." To his complaint he answered, "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" (Luke 15:28-32).

What the Parable Commends

  • Saw his son a great way off, which the parable states plainly and which implies he was watching: Luke 15:20.
  • Ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him before a word of confession was spoken: Luke 15:20.
  • Restored him fully - the best robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast - rather than to the servant's place his son had asked for: Luke 15:22-23.
  • Went out to the elder son and entreated him, rather than commanding him in: Luke 15:28.
  • Assured the elder son of everything he had, while insisting on the joy: Luke 15:31-32.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The parable records nothing against this figure.

Character Assessment

He is the only figure in the parable who goes out twice - once running to the younger son, once out to the elder. The parable gives him no reproach for either son: the returning one is interrupted before he can ask for less than sonship, and the resentful one is entreated rather than ordered. Both departures from what a hearer would expect are the point.

Significance

He is the central figure of the parable, which is more properly about him than about either son. His words - this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found - are repeated twice, once to the servants and once to the elder brother, and they answer the murmuring that occasioned all three parables of Luke 15.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 15:11-32
584

The elder brother

The elder of the two sons in Christ's parable, who had served his father many years and would not go in to the feast for his brother's return.

Family

Elder son of the father in the parable; brother of the prodigal (Luke 15:11, 15:25).

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing. And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant." Told that his brother had come and his father had killed the fatted calf because he had received him safe and sound, "he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and intreated him."

"And he answering said to his father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: but as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf."

"And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" (Luke 15:25-32). The parable ends there. Whether he went in is not recorded.

What the Parable Commends

  • He had served his father many years and had not transgressed his commandment, which his father did not dispute: Luke 15:29.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Was angry and would not go in: Luke 15:28.
  • Described his years with his father as service rather than sonship: Luke 15:29.
  • Refused to call his brother his brother, saying "this thy son" - and was answered with "this thy brother": Luke 15:30, 15:32.
  • Supplied a detail about his brother's spending that the parable had not stated: Luke 15:30.

Character Assessment

The parable does not dismiss his grievance and neither does his father, who grants that everything he has is his. What it exposes is the position he had taken up: many years of faultless service reckoned as work done for wages, and a brother he would not name as a brother. The story ends with him still outside, and that ending is deliberate - it was spoken to men who were murmuring at the table.

Significance

He is the figure the parable was aimed at. Luke 15 opens with the Pharisees and scribes murmuring that Christ received sinners and ate with them, and the last thing in the chapter is a man refusing to come in to exactly such a meal. Christ leaves the question of whether he came in unanswered.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 15:25-32
585

The rich fool

The rich man in Christ's parable whose ground brought forth plentifully, who built greater barns, and was required to give up his soul that night.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken after a man asked Christ to make his brother divide the inheritance with him (Luke 12:13-15).

Life Synopsis

"And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully: and he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?"

"And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry."

"But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God" (Luke 12:16-21).

What the Parable Commends

  • The parable records nothing to this figure's credit. The parable charges him with no crime. His land was his own, his harvest was lawful, and building barns was prudent.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Thought within himself and took counsel with no one, in a soliloquy of eleven first-person pronouns: Luke 12:17-19.
  • Laid up treasure for himself and was not rich toward God, which is the parable's stated moral: Luke 12:21.
  • Reckoned on many years, which he did not have: Luke 12:19-20.
  • God's own verdict is the single word: "Thou fool": Luke 12:20.

Character Assessment

The parable is unusual in that the man does nothing illegal, dishonest, or cruel. He is not charged with getting his wealth wrongly or with refusing the poor. What he is charged with is leaving God out of a calculation about his own life, and the charge is delivered by God directly, which happens in no other parable.

Significance

It was spoken to answer a request about an inheritance, and Christ prefaced it: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luke 12:15). The phrase rich toward God is the parable's own summary of what he lacked.

Death / Outcome

"This night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luke 12:20).

Scripture

Luke 12:13-21
586

The unjust steward

The steward in Christ's parable accused of wasting his master's goods, who reduced his master's debtors' bills before he was put out, and was commended for his foresight.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods. And he called him, and said unto him, How is it that I hear this of thee? give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward."

"Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses."

He called his lord's debtors and reduced their bills - a hundred measures of oil written down to fifty, a hundred measures of wheat to fourscore.

"And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light. And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Luke 16:1-9).

What the Parable Commends

  • He is commended, and the parable is explicit about the grounds: not for his honesty but because he had done wisely, in acting decisively about his future while he still could: Luke 16:8.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Was accused of wasting his master's goods, which he did not dispute: Luke 16:1.
  • The parable names him the unjust steward even in the sentence commending him: Luke 16:8.

Character Assessment

The hardest of the parables, and its difficulty is on the surface of the text rather than hidden. The man is dishonest, is called dishonest, and is commended - and the ground of the commendation is stated so as to exclude the obvious misreading: he had done wisely, and the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light. The commendation is of foresight, not of fraud. Whether the lord who commends him is the master in the story or Christ himself has been read both ways, and the text permits both.

Significance

The parable is followed immediately by sayings on faithfulness in that which is least, on serving two masters, and on God and mammon (Luke 16:10-13), which the Pharisees, who were covetous, heard and derided (Luke 16:14).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 16:1-13
587

The rich man and Lazarus

Two figures in Christ's parable: a rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, and a beggar named Lazarus laid at his gate. Lazarus is the only figure in any parable of Christ given a name.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states. The rich man speaks of five brethren and of his father's house (Luke 16:27-28).

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, and desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores."

"And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried; and in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom."

He asked that Lazarus be sent to dip his finger in water and cool his tongue. Abraham answered that he had received his good things in his lifetime and Lazarus evil things, and that between them a great gulf was fixed.

He then asked that Lazarus be sent to his father's house to warn his five brethren. "Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. And he said, Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent. And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead" (Luke 16:19-31).

What the Parable Commends

  • Of Lazarus the parable records nothing that he did at all - no words, no acts, no faith described. What it records is his condition and his outcome: he was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: Luke 16:22.
  • Of the rich man, his concern for his five brethren is the one thing in his favour that the parable records: Luke 16:27-28.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The rich man fared sumptuously every day while a beggar full of sores lay at his gate: Luke 16:19-21. The parable charges him with no act of cruelty; the charge is the gate and what lay outside it.
  • Even in torment he spoke of Lazarus as someone to be sent on errands, twice: Luke 16:24, 16:27.

Character Assessment

The parable states no reason for either outcome beyond the reversal itself - he received his good things, and Lazarus evil things. Nothing is said of the rich man's dishonesty or of Lazarus's faith. That silence is uncomfortable and it is deliberate, and the passage's own conclusion moves the question elsewhere: to whether men will hear Moses and the prophets. Lazarus is the only named figure in any parable; the rich man, whom later tradition calls Dives, is not named in Scripture.

Significance

Its closing sentence - if they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead - stands in Luke's Gospel before another Lazarus is raised from the dead in John's, and before Christ's own resurrection. Scripture makes no explicit connection between the two Lazaruses, and this reference makes none.

Death / Outcome

Both died: Lazarus was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom, and the rich man was buried and lifted up his eyes in hell (Luke 16:22).

Scripture

Luke 16:19-31
588

The importunate widow

The widow in Christ's parable who wearied an unjust judge by her continual coming until he avenged her.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states. She had an adversary, unnamed (Luke 18:3).

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken "to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint" (Luke 18:1).

Life Synopsis

"And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: and there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary."

"And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me."

"And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" (Luke 18:1-8).

What the Parable Commends

  • Came, and kept coming, to the only man who could give her justice, having nothing else to bring: Luke 18:3, 18:5.
  • Her persistence is the whole point of the parable, stated in its opening line: that men ought always to pray, and not to faint: Luke 18:1.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The parable records nothing against this figure.

Character Assessment

A widow with an adversary and no advocate had no standing and no leverage, and the parable gives her nothing but persistence. Christ's argument from her is one of contrast rather than comparison: if a judge who feared neither God nor man would act to be rid of her, how much more will God, who is neither unjust nor unwilling, avenge his own elect who cry to him day and night.

Significance

One of two parables Luke prefaces with its own purpose. Its closing question - when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? - turns the parable from a lesson about persistence into a question about the hearer.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 18:1-8
589

The unjust judge

The judge in Christ's parable who feared not God nor regarded man, and avenged a widow only to be rid of her.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable.

Life Synopsis

"There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man" (Luke 18:2). A widow came repeatedly asking to be avenged of her adversary.

"And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me" (Luke 18:4-5).

"And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith" (Luke 18:6).

What the Parable Commends

  • The parable records nothing to this figure's credit. He did at last avenge her, and the parable states his motive: that she would otherwise weary him.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Feared not God, neither regarded man - the parable's own description, which he then repeats about himself: Luke 18:2, 18:4.
  • Refused a widow justice for a time, and granted it at last only for his own convenience: Luke 18:4-5.

Character Assessment

He is the negative term in an argument from the lesser to the greater, and the parable is careful that he not be mistaken for a picture of God. He acts from self-interest, reluctantly, and late; God is set against him at every point - he avenges his own elect, who cry to him day and night, and he does it speedily.

Significance

Christ's instruction, "Hear what the unjust judge saith," directs the hearer to the man's own words rather than to his character, which is where the argument turns.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 18:1-8
590

The Pharisee and the publican

Two figures in Christ's parable who went up into the temple to pray; the one thanked God that he was not as other men, and the other would not lift up his eyes.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken "unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others" (Luke 18:9).

Life Synopsis

"Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess."

"And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner."

"I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Luke 18:10-14).

What the Parable Commends

  • Of the publican: he stood afar off, would not lift up his eyes, smote upon his breast, and asked for mercy naming himself a sinner: Luke 18:13.
  • Christ's verdict: this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: Luke 18:14.
  • Of the Pharisee, the parable disputes none of his claims - he did fast twice in the week and give tithes of all he possessed: Luke 18:12.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Of the Pharisee: he prayed thus with himself, and the prayer contains no petition at all: Luke 18:11.
  • He thanked God for what he was not, and named a specific man present as the comparison: Luke 18:11.
  • The parable was spoken to those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised others, which names the fault exactly: Luke 18:9.

Character Assessment

The parable turns on a comparison the hearers would have made the other way round. Nothing the Pharisee says about himself is denied; his fasting and his tithing stand. What is denied is the standing he built on them. The publican offers nothing at all except a request for mercy, and it is he who goes home justified.

Significance

The closing sentence - every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted - is repeated elsewhere in the Gospels (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11). The publican's words are among the shortest recorded prayers in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Luke 18:9-14
591

The unmerciful servant

The servant in Christ's parable who was forgiven ten thousand talents and then took his fellowservant by the throat for a hundred pence.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states. He had a wife and children, whom his lord commanded to be sold with him (Matthew 18:25).

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken in answer to Peter's question, "how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" (Matthew 18:21).

Life Synopsis

A certain king took account of his servants, and one was brought who owed him ten thousand talents. Having nothing to pay, he was ordered sold with his wife and children.

"The servant therefore fell down, and worshipped him, saying, Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt."

"But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest. And his fellowservant fell down at his feet, and besought him, saying, Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. And he would not: but went and cast him into prison, till he should pay the debt."

His fellows told their lord, who called him: "O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" He was delivered to the tormentors till he should pay all (Matthew 18:23-34).

What the Parable Commends

  • The parable records nothing to this figure's credit.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Took his fellowservant by the throat for a hundred pence, having just been forgiven ten thousand talents: Matthew 18:28.
  • Refused the very words he had himself used and been heard on - have patience with me, and I will pay thee all: Matthew 18:26, 18:29-30.
  • His lord's verdict: "O thou wicked servant... shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?": Matthew 18:32-33.

Character Assessment

The parable's whole force is in the disproportion between the two debts, and the numbers are chosen to make it absurd rather than merely unfair. His own plea and his fellowservant's are word for word the same, and he had been granted more than he asked - he asked for patience and was given release.

Significance

Spoken in answer to Peter's question about forgiving seven times, and closed with the application: "So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses" (Matthew 18:35).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. He was delivered to the tormentors till he should pay all that was due (Matthew 18:34).

Scripture

Matthew 18:21-35
592

The wicked husbandmen

The tenants in Christ's parable who beat and killed the householder's servants and then killed his son to seize the inheritance.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken in the temple in the last week, to the chief priests and elders (Matthew 21:23, 21:33).

Life Synopsis

A householder planted a vineyard, hedged it, dug a winepress, built a tower, let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country. At the season he sent servants to receive the fruits.

"And the husbandmen took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another. Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they did unto them likewise."

"But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son. But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance. And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him."

Christ asked what the lord of the vineyard would do to them, and they answered themselves: "He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen" (Matthew 21:33-41).

"And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that he spake of them" (Matthew 21:45).

What the Parable Commends

  • The parable records nothing to this figure's credit.

What the Parable Condemns

  • Beat, killed, and stoned the servants sent to them, and did the same to a second company: Matthew 21:35-36.
  • Killed the son, having recognised exactly who he was: Matthew 21:38-39.
  • Their motive is stated in their own words: "This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance": Matthew 21:38.

Character Assessment

The parable is unusual in that its hearers pronounced their own sentence before they understood it, and then understood it. Matthew records the moment plainly: they perceived that he spake of them. The recognition scene inside the parable - they knew he was the heir and killed him for that reason - is the sharpest thing in it.

Significance

Christ closed with Psalms 118:22-23, the stone which the builders rejected become the head of the corner, and said the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits (Matthew 21:42-43). It was spoken days before the crucifixion, to the men who arranged it.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. The hearers themselves said the lord of the vineyard would miserably destroy them (Matthew 21:41).

Scripture

Matthew 21:33-46; Mark 12:1-12; Luke 20:9-19
593

The ten virgins

Ten figures in Christ's parable who took their lamps to meet the bridegroom; five were wise and took oil, and five were foolish and took none.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken on the mount of Olives in the last week, among the sayings on watchfulness (Matthew 24:3; Matthew 25:1).

Life Synopsis

"Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom. And five of them were wise, and five were foolish. They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them: but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps."

"While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him."

The foolish asked the wise for oil and were refused, and sent to buy for themselves. "And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut."

"Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not. Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh" (Matthew 25:1-13).

What the Parable Commends

  • The five wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps, against a delay they could not measure: Matthew 25:4.
  • They were ready when the cry came, and went in: Matthew 25:10.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The five foolish took their lamps and took no oil: Matthew 25:3.
  • They sought to borrow what could not be lent, and went to buy it too late: Matthew 25:8-10.

Character Assessment

The parable is careful about what did not distinguish them. All ten were invited, all ten took lamps, all ten slumbered and slept, and the sleeping is charged against none of them. The single difference is what they brought, and it could not be transferred at the last moment. The wise are not blamed for refusing, and the parable does not present the refusal as unkindness but as impossibility.

Significance

Its closing instruction - watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh - is the stated point, and the parable stands with the talents and the sheep and goats in Christ's last discourse before the passion.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. The door was shut (Matthew 25:10).

Scripture

Matthew 25:1-13
594

The servants entrusted with talents

Three servants in Christ's parable given five talents, two talents, and one; two traded and doubled them, and the third hid his in the earth.

Family

Not applicable. A figure in a parable, given no parentage, tribe, or household beyond what the parable states.

Chronology

Not applicable. Spoken on the mount of Olives, following the parable of the ten virgins (Matthew 25:14).

Life Synopsis

A man travelling into a far country called his servants and delivered his goods to them, "and unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability."

The first two traded and doubled what they had. "But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money."

To each of the first two the lord said, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord" - the same words to the man with two as to the man with five.

The third said, "Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: and I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine."

His lord answered, "Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed: thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury." The talent was taken from him and given to the man with ten (Matthew 25:14-30).

What the Parable Commends

  • The first two traded with what they were given and doubled it: Matthew 25:16-17.
  • Both received the same commendation, though the amounts differed: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant": Matthew 25:21, 25:23.

What the Parable Condemns

  • The third hid his lord's money in the earth and returned exactly what he had been given: Matthew 25:18, 25:25.
  • He gave fear as his reason, and a view of his master that his master took up and used against him: Matthew 25:24-26.
  • His lord's verdict: "Thou wicked and slothful servant": Matthew 25:26.

Character Assessment

The parable measures the servants against what each was given rather than against each other - the man with two received word for word the commendation given to the man with five. The third is not charged with losing anything; he returned the full sum. He is charged with doing nothing with it, and the reason he gives is fear grounded in an opinion of his master that the parable neither confirms nor denies but simply holds him to.

Significance

It stands with the ten virgins in Christ's last discourse, and where that parable turns on being ready, this one turns on what is done in the meantime. A closely related parable of ten pounds is recorded in Luke 19:12-27.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. The unprofitable servant was cast into outer darkness (Matthew 25:30).

Scripture

Matthew 25:14-30; compare Luke 19:12-27

Angels, Spirits, and the Adversary

These are not human beings, and they are kept separate from the human entries for that reason. The section is not chronological: these beings appear across the whole span of Scripture, so no date or period is given for any of them and the left margin shows a dash throughout. Where Scripture describes an order rather than an individual - the cherubim, the seraphim, the four beasts - the entry says so and does not invent persons. This section covers the whole canon, Old Testament and New, since these beings cannot be divided between them.

595

Satan

A created personal being, not human; the adversary of God and of God's people. Scripture names him Satan, the devil, that old serpent, the dragon, the accuser of the brethren, the tempter, the wicked one, the prince of this world, and the god of this world.

Also called the devil, the serpent, Beelzebub, the wicked one, the accuser, the tempter, Lucifer (disputed)

Family

Not applicable. Scripture nowhere describes his origin in narrative form. Two passages - the taunt against the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:12-15 and the lamentation over the king of Tyrus in Ezekiel 28:12-19 - have long been read as describing his fall behind the figure of a human king. Both passages are addressed in their contexts to human rulers, and this reference notes the traditional application without asserting it as the plain sense.

Chronology

Not applicable. He appears from the primeval period through to the close of Revelation. Scripture gives no date of his creation and no account of when he fell.

Life Synopsis

He appears first as the serpent in Eden, questioning God's command, denying the stated penalty, and impugning God's motive (Genesis 3:1-5). Genesis does not name him; the identification is made explicitly in the New Testament, where he is "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world" (Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2).

In Job he presents himself among the sons of God before the Lord, and his question is the book's premise: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" He is permitted to strike Job's possessions, his children, and then his body, but is limited each time (Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-7). In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to resist him, and is rebuked by the Lord (Zechariah 3:1-2). He provoked David to number Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1).

He tempted Christ in the wilderness forty days, using Scripture, and departed from him for a season (Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13). Christ described him: "He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (John 8:44). He entered into Judas (Luke 22:3; John 13:27), and desired to have Peter, that he might sift him as wheat - and Christ said, "but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Luke 22:31-32).

The Epistles describe his methods: he is transformed into an angel of light, and his ministers as ministers of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14-15); he has devices believers should not be ignorant of (2 Corinthians 2:11); he walks about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8); and he is to be resisted, and will flee (James 4:7).

His end is stated: judgment was pronounced in Eden (Genesis 3:14-15), Christ came "that he might destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8), and through death destroyed "him that had the power of death, that is, the devil" (Hebrews 2:14). Revelation records him cast down, bound, loosed, and finally cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:1-3, 20:7-10).

What They Did Right

  • Nothing commendable is recorded of him anywhere in Scripture.

What They Did Wrong

  • Questioned and contradicted God's word, and misrepresented his motive: Genesis 3:1-5.
  • Accused Job of serving God only for reward: Job 1:9-11.
  • Stood to resist the high priest before the Lord: Zechariah 3:1.
  • Provoked David to number Israel: 1 Chronicles 21:1.
  • Tempted Christ, quoting Scripture out of its sense: Matthew 4:1-11.
  • Is a murderer from the beginning, a liar, and the father of lies: John 8:44.
  • Entered into Judas Iscariot: Luke 22:3; John 13:27.
  • Blinds the minds of them that believe not: 2 Corinthians 4:4.
  • Transforms himself into an angel of light: 2 Corinthians 11:14.
  • Deceives the whole world, and accuses the brethren before God day and night: Revelation 12:9-10.

Character Assessment

Uniformly and absolutely negative throughout Scripture; no passage records anything to his credit. Several things the text is careful about deserve stating. He is created and limited, not a rival power: in Job he can do nothing without permission and is given precise bounds twice. He is a liar by nature, which means his statements are not to be weighed on their merits. And he can quote Scripture accurately while using it falsely, which is why the temptation of Christ is answered from Scripture rather than by assertion. Scripture never presents him as an explanation that removes human responsibility - Eve was deceived and was still in the transgression, and David numbered Israel and was still charged with it.

Significance

The promise of Genesis 3:15, that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head, is the first statement of redemption in Scripture and is spoken as a sentence on him. His defeat is presented as accomplished at the cross and completed at the end: Christ destroyed him that had the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and he is finally cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable. Revelation 20:10 records his final judgment: cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, to be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Scripture

Genesis 3:1-15; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Job 1:6-2:7; Zechariah 3:1-2; Matthew 4:1-11; Matthew 12:24-29; Matthew 13:19, 13:39; Luke 10:18; Luke 22:3, 22:31; John 8:44; John 12:31; Acts 5:3; Romans 16:20; 2 Corinthians 2:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Corinthians 11:3, 11:14; Ephesians 2:2; Ephesians 6:11-12; 1 Thessalonians 2:18; 1 Timothy 3:6-7; Hebrews 2:14; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8; 1 John 3:8; Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:9-12; Revelation 20:1-10
596

The angel of the Lord

A distinct designation used throughout the Old Testament for a divine messenger who appears, speaks, and is repeatedly identified with the Lord himself by those he addresses and by the narrator. Whether the phrase denotes a created angel or an appearance of God is disputed, and Scripture does not settle it in so many words.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. He appears from Genesis through Zechariah, and the phrase is used again in the New Testament.

Life Synopsis

He found Hagar by a fountain in the wilderness, told her she would bear Ishmael, and promised to multiply her seed exceedingly - a promise in the first person - and she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, "Thou God seest me" (Genesis 16:7-13).

He called to Abraham out of heaven to stop the knife and said, "now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from me" (Genesis 22:11-12).

He appeared to Moses in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush, "and God called unto him out of the midst of the bush" (Exodus 3:2-4). He went before the camp of Israel (Exodus 14:19), and God said of the angel he sent before them, "beware of him, and obey his voice, provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him" (Exodus 23:20-21).

He withstood Balaam with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:22-35), came to Gideon under the oak and was addressed as "my Lord" (Judges 6:11-24), and appeared to Manoah and his wife, refusing to give his name "seeing it is secret," and ascending in the flame of the altar, so that Manoah said, "We shall surely die, because we have seen God" (Judges 13:3-22).

He smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35), stood between earth and heaven with a drawn sword over Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 21:16), and stood among the myrtle trees in Zechariah's vision, and rebuked Satan on behalf of Joshua the high priest (Zechariah 1:11; Zechariah 3:1-2).

What They Did Right

  • Provided for Hagar in the wilderness and gave her a promise: Genesis 16:7-12.
  • Stayed Abraham's hand at the sacrifice: Genesis 22:11-12.
  • Called Moses from the bush and commissioned him: Exodus 3:2-10.
  • Went before Israel and encamped round about them that fear God: Exodus 14:19; Psalms 34:7.
  • Rebuked Satan on behalf of the high priest: Zechariah 3:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The interpretive question is genuine and long-standing. In several passages the narrator moves without transition between "the angel of the Lord" and "the Lord," those addressed conclude they have seen God, and he speaks in the first person as God, receives worship, and forgives or refuses to pardon. In others he is plainly sent and distinguished from the one who sends. Many hold him to be a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ; others hold that a messenger fully representing God may speak in God's name. This reference sets out what the passages say and does not decide between the readings.

Significance

He is the figure through whom God is repeatedly said to have appeared and spoken in the Old Testament narrative, at the most decisive moments: to Hagar, to Abraham at Moriah, to Moses at the bush, to Israel at the sea, to Gideon, to Manoah, and over Jerusalem.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Genesis 16:7-13; Genesis 22:11-18; Exodus 3:2-6; Exodus 14:19; Exodus 23:20-23; Numbers 22:22-35; Judges 2:1-4; Judges 6:11-24; Judges 13:3-22; 2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Kings 19:5-7; 2 Kings 19:35; 1 Chronicles 21:15-30; Psalms 34:7; Isaiah 63:9; Zechariah 1:11-12; Zechariah 3:1-6
597

Michael

An archangel; called one of the chief princes and the prince who stands for the children of Daniel's people; contended with the devil about the body of Moses and wars against the dragon.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. He appears in Daniel, Jude, and Revelation.

Life Synopsis

The messenger who came to Daniel explained a delay: "But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me" (Daniel 10:13). He is later called "Michael your prince" (Daniel 10:21), and: "And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people" (Daniel 12:1).

Jude records a dispute: "Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee" (Jude 1:9).

Revelation records war in heaven: "And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, and prevailed not" (Revelation 12:7-8).

He is the only being Scripture calls an archangel by name, and 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says the Lord shall descend with the voice of the archangel, without naming him.

What They Did Right

  • Came to help a messenger withstood by the prince of Persia: Daniel 10:13.
  • Stands for the people of God: Daniel 10:21; Daniel 12:1.
  • In dispute with the devil, brought no railing accusation but said, "The Lord rebuke thee": Jude 1:9.
  • Fought against the dragon and prevailed: Revelation 12:7-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him.
