Jude's use of him is the point most often drawn: an archangel in dispute with the devil over the body of Moses would not bring a railing accusation but referred the matter to the Lord, and Jude sets this against men who speak evil of things they do not understand.

Significance

The only being named archangel in Scripture. His standing up in Daniel 12:1 is set at a time of trouble such as never was, and is followed immediately by the clearest Old Testament statement of resurrection (Daniel 12:2).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Daniel 10:13, 10:21; Daniel 12:1; Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:7-9; compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16
598

Gabriel

An angel who stands in the presence of God; sent to Daniel with understanding of visions, and to Zacharias and to Mary with the announcements of John the Baptist and of Christ.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. He appears in Daniel and in Luke.

Life Synopsis

Daniel saw the vision of the ram and the goat and heard a voice say, "Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision." He came near, and Daniel was afraid and fell on his face; Gabriel said, "Understand, O son of man: for at the time of the end shall be the vision" (Daniel 8:15-17). He came again while Daniel was praying: "O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding. At the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth, and I am come to shew thee; for thou art greatly beloved" (Daniel 9:21-23).

He appeared to Zacharias at the altar of incense to announce John's birth. When Zacharias asked how he should know it, he answered, "I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings. And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words" (Luke 1:11-20).

Six months later he was sent to Nazareth to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph, and delivered the announcement of the birth of Christ, ending, "For with God nothing shall be impossible" (Luke 1:26-38).

What They Did Right

  • Came at the beginning of Daniel's supplications to give him skill and understanding, and told him he was greatly beloved: Daniel 9:21-23.
  • Announced the births of John the Baptist and of Christ: Luke 1:13-17, 1:30-33.
  • Stated his own standing and commission plainly when questioned: Luke 1:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He appears four times and each time to explain or announce, which is what distinguishes him in the record: he is the messenger who brings understanding rather than judgment.

Significance

He delivered the announcement of the incarnation, and in Daniel 9 the prophecy of the seventy weeks. His statement to Zacharias - that he stands in the presence of God - is the only description Scripture gives of an angel's position.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Daniel 8:15-27; Daniel 9:20-27; Luke 1:11-20, 1:26-38
599

The cherubim

An order of created beings, not individuals; set at the east of Eden to keep the way of the tree of life, represented in gold over the mercy seat, and described at length in Ezekiel's visions. They are entered here as an order rather than as persons, since Scripture never names one or records one acting alone.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. They appear from Genesis through Revelation.

Life Synopsis

"So he drove out the man: and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life" (Genesis 3:24).

Two cherubim of beaten gold were made for the ends of the mercy seat, their faces toward each other and looking downward, their wings covering it. "And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims" (Exodus 25:18-22). God is repeatedly said to dwell or to sit between the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; Psalms 80:1; Psalms 99:1; Isaiah 37:16). Cherubim were woven into the curtains of the tabernacle and the veil, and carved on the walls and doors of Solomon's temple (Exodus 26:1, 26:31; 1 Kings 6:23-35).

Ezekiel saw four living creatures by the river Chebar, each with four faces and four wings, with wheels beside them, and later identified them: "This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel by the river of Chebar; and I knew that they were the cherubims" (Ezekiel 1:4-28; Ezekiel 10:20). He saw the glory of the Lord depart from the threshold and stand over them as they mounted up (Ezekiel 10:18-19).

David's psalm says the Lord "rode upon a cherub, and did fly" (2 Samuel 22:11; Psalms 18:10).

What They Did Right

  • Keep the way of the tree of life as they were set: Genesis 3:24. Scripture records their office rather than assessing their conduct.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes their appearance, their position, and their office, and never individuates them. Two things are consistent across the passages: they are associated with the immediate presence of God, and they are associated with guarding access to it. No cherub is ever named. Ezekiel 28:14-16 addresses a figure as "the anointed cherub that covereth," in a lamentation over the king of Tyrus; whether that is a description of Satan is disputed, and the point is noted in the entry for Satan rather than assumed here.

Significance

The mercy seat between the two cherubim is the place God named as where he would meet and commune with Israel (Exodus 25:22), and Hebrews describes the cherubim of glory shadowing the mercyseat (Hebrews 9:5). Their first appearance guards the way to the tree of life, and Revelation ends with access to that tree restored (Revelation 22:2, 22:14).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18-22; Exodus 26:1, 26:31; Numbers 7:89; 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; 2 Samuel 22:11; 1 Kings 6:23-35; 2 Kings 19:15; Psalms 18:10; Psalms 80:1; Psalms 99:1; Isaiah 37:16; Ezekiel 1:4-28; Ezekiel 10:1-22; Hebrews 9:5
600

The seraphim

An order of beings seen by Isaiah above the throne, each having six wings, crying one to another, "Holy, holy, holy." They are entered as an order rather than as individuals; Scripture names none and describes them in one passage only.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. They appear in Isaiah 6.

Life Synopsis

"In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke" (Isaiah 6:1-4).

When Isaiah said, "Woe is me! for I am undone," one of them flew to him with a live coal taken with the tongs from off the altar, laid it on his mouth, and said, "Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged" (Isaiah 6:5-7).

What They Did Right

  • Cry the holiness of the Lord of hosts continually: Isaiah 6:3.
  • One brought the live coal from the altar and pronounced Isaiah's iniquity taken away and his sin purged: Isaiah 6:6-7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes them in four verses and nowhere else by that name. Two details are usually drawn from the passage: four of their six wings are used for covering rather than for flight, in the presence of God; and the cleansing they bring is from the altar, not from themselves.

Significance

Their cry is the only place in Scripture where an attribute of God is repeated three times, and it is echoed by the four beasts in Revelation 4:8 who rest not day and night saying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty." The passage is the setting of Isaiah's call, and John says Isaiah spoke of Christ when he saw his glory (John 12:41).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Isaiah 6:1-7; compare Revelation 4:8; John 12:41
601

The four beasts

Four living creatures round about the throne in Revelation, full of eyes, each with six wings, giving glory and honour and thanks continually. An order, not named individuals.

Also called the four living creatures

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. They appear throughout Revelation.

Life Synopsis

"And round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind. And the first beast was like a lion, and the second beast like a calf, and the third beast had a face as a man, and the fourth beast was like a flying eagle. And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come" (Revelation 4:6-8).

With the four and twenty elders they fall down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints, and sing a new song (Revelation 5:8-9). They call "Come and see" at the opening of the first four seals (Revelation 6:1-7), and say Amen at the worship of the Lamb (Revelation 5:14; Revelation 19:4).

What They Did Right

  • Give glory and honour and thanks to him that sits on the throne, resting not day and night: Revelation 4:8-9.
  • Fall down before the Lamb and join the new song of redemption: Revelation 5:8-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes their appearance and their occupation and does not individuate them. Their four faces correspond to those of Ezekiel's living creatures, whom Ezekiel identifies as cherubim (Ezekiel 1:10; Ezekiel 10:20), and many take them to be the same order; Revelation does not say so, and this reference notes the correspondence without asserting the identification.

Significance

They are among the closest beings to the throne in Revelation, and their unceasing cry of God's holiness is the same as the seraphim's in Isaiah 6:3 - the two passages, separated by centuries and languages, record the same words.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Revelation 4:6-11; Revelation 5:6-14; Revelation 6:1-7; Revelation 7:11; Revelation 14:3; Revelation 15:7; Revelation 19:4; compare Ezekiel 1:5-14; Ezekiel 10:20
602

The lying spirit

A spirit that came forth and stood before the Lord in Micaiah's vision, undertaking to be a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

At the end of Ahab's reign, before Ramothgilead (1 Kings 22:1-2).

Life Synopsis

Micaiah described what he had seen: "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. And the Lord said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramothgilead? And one said on this manner, and another said on that manner."

"And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him. And the Lord said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so. Now therefore, behold, the Lord hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the Lord hath spoken evil concerning thee" (1 Kings 22:19-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Undertook to be a lying spirit in the mouths of the prophets: 1 Kings 22:22.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the vision without explaining it, and it raises one of the hardest questions in the Old Testament: God asks who will persuade Ahab, a spirit volunteers to lie, and God says go and do so. The passage supplies no commentary. What can be observed is the setting: Micaiah tells Ahab the whole thing to his face before the battle, so the king was told plainly that he was being deceived and went anyway. This reference records what the text says and does not attempt to resolve the difficulty.

Significance

The passage is cited in nearly every serious treatment of how God deals with those settled on their own course, and it stands alongside 2 Thessalonians 2:11, where God sends strong delusion to those who received not the love of the truth.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

1 Kings 22:19-23; 2 Chronicles 18:18-22; compare 2 Thessalonians 2:11
603

The prince of Persia and the prince of Grecia

Two beings identified only by title, described as withstanding the messenger sent to Daniel. They are entered together because Scripture treats them the same way and records nothing of either beyond their opposition.

Also called the prince of the kingdom of Persia

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia (Daniel 10:1).

Life Synopsis

Daniel had been mourning three full weeks when a messenger came to him and explained the delay: "Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia" (Daniel 10:12-13).

At his departure: "Now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come. But I will shew thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth: and there is none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince" (Daniel 10:20-21).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Withstood a messenger sent from God for twenty-one days: Daniel 10:13.
  • Are set in opposition to the messenger and to Michael: Daniel 10:20-21.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives them titles and an action and nothing else - no names, no origin, and no explanation of what the opposition consisted of. The passage is the clearest statement in the Old Testament that conflict exists behind visible events and that prayer is answered from the first day even when the answer is delayed. It is also brief, and any account of these beings beyond what the two passages say is inference.

Significance

The account is the reason Daniel 10 is cited so often on delayed answers to prayer: Daniel's words were heard from the first day, and the messenger took twenty-one days to arrive.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Daniel 10:12-13, 10:20-21
604

Abaddon

The angel of the bottomless pit, named in Hebrew Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon; king over the locusts of the fifth trumpet.

Also called Apollyon

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

Not applicable. He appears at the fifth trumpet in Revelation.

Life Synopsis

At the sounding of the fifth angel a star fell from heaven to the earth, and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit. Smoke arose as the smoke of a great furnace, and out of it came locusts with power as scorpions, commanded not to hurt the grass or any green thing but only those men without the seal of God in their foreheads, and not to kill them but to torment them five months.

"And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon" (Revelation 9:1-11). Both names carry the sense of destruction.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his office and his name and no conduct beyond it. He is king over the locusts of the fifth trumpet, and the whole judgment is bounded by explicit limits given from outside: what may be hurt, who may be hurt, and for how long (Revelation 9:4-5).

Character Assessment

Scripture names him and describes his position, and nothing more. What the passage emphasises is limitation: the locusts are told what they may not touch, whom they may not kill, and how long they have. Even the destroyer operates under bounds.

Significance

He is the only individual evil being besides Satan given a proper name in Revelation. The Hebrew word abaddon appears elsewhere in the Old Testament for destruction or the place of the dead (Job 26:6; Job 28:22; Proverbs 15:11), and the passage supplies its Greek equivalent.

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Revelation 9:1-11; compare Job 26:6; Job 28:22; Proverbs 15:11
605

Legion

The unclean spirits that possessed the man of the Gadarenes, who answered Christ's question with the name Legion, "for we are many." A collective that answered as one and is entered here on that basis.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

During Christ's ministry, in the country of the Gadarenes (Mark 5:1).

Life Synopsis

The man had his dwelling among the tombs, and no man could bind him, no, not with chains; the fetters were plucked asunder, and night and day he was in the mountains and in the tombs crying and cutting himself with stones (Mark 5:2-5).

Seeing Jesus afar off he ran and worshipped him, and cried, "What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not." Jesus asked, "What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many." They besought him not to send them away out of the country, and not into the deep, but into the herd of swine. He gave them leave, and about two thousand swine ran violently down a steep place into the sea (Mark 5:6-13; Luke 8:30-33).

The man was afterward found sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind, and asked to go with him; he was told to go home and tell his friends how great things the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:15-20).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. They acknowledged Christ as Son of the most high God (Mark 5:7). James notes that the devils also believe, and tremble (James 2:19), so the acknowledgment is recorded as knowledge rather than as anything to their credit.

What They Did Wrong

  • Possessed and tormented a man so that he lived among the tombs and cut himself with stones: Mark 5:3-5.
  • Entered the herd of swine and destroyed it: Mark 5:13.

Character Assessment

Scripture records their recognition of Christ, their fear, their petition, and their destructiveness. Two things stand out. They knew exactly who he was when the people of the country did not. And they could do nothing without leave - they besought him and he gave them leave, which is the same pattern as Job.

Significance

The account is the fullest description in the Gospels of possession and deliverance, and it ends with a man who had been uncontrollable sitting clothed and in his right mind. The people of the country then asked Jesus to depart from their coasts (Mark 5:17).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Matthew 8:28-34; Mark 5:1-20; Luke 8:26-39; compare James 2:19
606

The unclean spirit at Ephesus

An evil spirit that answered the seven sons of Sceva when they attempted to use the name of Jesus over the man it possessed.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

During Paul's ministry at Ephesus (Acts 19:10-13).

Life Synopsis

Certain vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over those with evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, "We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth." Seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew and chief of the priests, did so.

"And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye? And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded" (Acts 19:13-16).

"And this was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus; and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds. Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men" (Acts 19:17-19).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Overcame and wounded seven men: Acts 19:16. Scripture records the act; the passage's weight falls on the exorcists' presumption rather than on the spirit.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one sentence from it, and that sentence is the point of the passage: it knew Jesus, it knew Paul, and it did not know men using a name they had no relation to. The episode is a warning against treating the name of Christ as a technique.

Significance

The outcome was that fear fell on all at Ephesus, the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified, and the people burned their books of curious arts to the value of fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:17-20).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Acts 19:11-20
607

The spirit of divination at Philippi

A spirit in a damsel at Philippi that brought her masters much gain by soothsaying, and followed Paul crying out that he and his companions were the servants of the most high God.

Family

Not applicable.

Chronology

During Paul's second journey, at Philippi (Acts 16:12-16).

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying: the same followed Paul and us, and cried, saying, These men are the servants of the most high God, which shew unto us the way of salvation. And this did she many days."

"But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour" (Acts 16:16-18). Her masters, seeing that the hope of their gains was gone, dragged Paul and Silas to the magistrates, and they were beaten and imprisoned.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. What it said was true - they were the servants of the most high God showing the way of salvation. Paul nonetheless silenced it, which is recorded without explanation and is consistent with Christ's own practice of not accepting such testimony (Mark 1:34; Mark 3:11-12).

What They Did Wrong

  • Possessed a girl and was used for gain by her masters: Acts 16:16.

Character Assessment

Scripture records that it spoke the truth and that Paul, grieved, cast it out anyway. The narrative does not explain why, and the pattern in the Gospels is the same: Christ would not permit devils to speak, though they knew him. The girl's deliverance cost Paul a beating and a night in the stocks, and produced the conversion of the jailer.

Significance

The episode is the clearest New Testament instance of true words from a source Christ's servants would not accept, and it is the occasion of the imprisonment at Philippi and the jailer's conversion (Acts 16:19-34).

Death / Outcome

Not applicable.

Scripture

Acts 16:16-24; compare Mark 1:34; Mark 3:11-12

Dates. The figures on the left margin are years from the creation of Adam, calculated by addition from the ages given in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. They are not stated anywhere in Scripture. They follow the Masoretic Hebrew text, which the King James Version translates; the Septuagint gives materially different ages and a span roughly a thousand years longer. If the genealogies omit generations, as some Hebrew genealogies demonstrably do, these figures are minimums. A dash means no date can be established from Scripture, which is the case for 575 of the 607 people here.
